bio: Jerusalem, also called Zion, Jebus and Salem, was the chief city of ancient Israel in the hill country of Judah. It is the present-day city of Jerusalem, and the location shown here lies in its Old City. Its Canaanite king Adonizedek opposed Joshua (Josh 10:1). David made it his capital, reigning there thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah, and brought the ark there (2 Sam 5:5; 2 Chr 1:4). Solomon built the temple there, and it remained the seat of Judah's kings until the Babylonian army broke down its walls and carried its people captive (2 Kgs 25:10; Jer 52:29). After Cyrus of Persia ordered the temple rebuilt, exiles returned to restore the city (Ezra 1:2; Neh 1:2). Jesus was presented, taught, tried and put to death there, and it was the first center of the church (Luke 2:22; Acts 1:4). Later writers also speak of a heavenly or new Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Rev 3:12).

Egypt was the ancient kingdom of the Nile valley in the northeast corner of Africa. Its usual Hebrew name, Mizraim, is a dual form that Smith's Bible Dictionary links to the country's two parts, Upper Egypt (the valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta). Abram went there during a famine (Gen 12:10). Jacob's family later settled there (Exod 1:1), and Joseph died there (Gen 50:26). The Israelites were later enslaved, and Moses led them out after the plagues (Exod 10:21; Deut 34:11). That deliverance is recalled throughout Scripture (Lev 11:45; Amos 2:10; Mic 6:4; Jude 1:5). Under the kings, Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter and bought horses from Egypt (1 Kgs 3:1; 2 Chr 1:16). The prophets warned against relying on Egypt and announced judgment on it (Ezek 17:15; Jer 46:25). Joseph and Mary fled there with the infant Jesus (Matt 2:13).

Babylon was the great city on the Euphrates that served as capital of the Babylonian (Chaldean) empire. Its ruins lie near Hillah in modern Iraq, about 50 miles south of Baghdad, which is where the location shown here is placed. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of Babel. Its king Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and carried the people of Judah and the temple vessels to Babylon (2 Kgs 24:11; Ezra 6:5; Dan 1:1). The exiled king Jehoiachin lived out his days there on the king's allowance. Zedekiah also died there, unable to see it, as Ezek 12:13 foretold. The exile lasted until Persia's rise, when captives returned to Judah (2 Chr 36:20; Ezra 2:1). The prophets announced Babylon's fall (Isa 13:1; Jer 50:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Babylon of Revelation as a symbolic name for Rome. For 1 Pet 5:13, some readers also see Rome, while Smith's and Easton's take it as the literal city.

Jordan is the main river of the land of Israel. It flows south from the foot of Mount Hermon, through Lake Huleh and the Sea of Galilee, to the Salt (Dead) Sea. It marked the eastern edge of Canaan, so "this side Jordan" and "beyond Jordan" were standard ways of dividing the land (Josh 15:5; 2 Kgs 10:33). Jacob crossed it with only his staff, and Moses was not allowed to cross it. Israel under Joshua passed over near Jericho while priests carrying the ark stood in the riverbed. Its fords were held in war (Judg 3:28; 12:6), and Jeremiah mentions its swelling. Elijah went to the Jordan before he was taken up. John the Baptist preached throughout the region around it and baptized people in the river. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes its sources near Hermon and its winding descent. The point shown here lies in the upper valley north of the Sea of Galilee.

Moab was a country east of the Dead Sea and the Jordan, in present-day Jordan, bordered on the north by the Arnon (Num 22:36). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite Jericho before entering Canaan. There Balak king of Moab summoned Balaam, Moses delivered the law, and Israel mourned his death (Num 22:1; Deut 1:5; Deut 34:8). Eglon king of Moab oppressed Israel in the time of the judges (Judg 3:12). Ruth and Orpah were Moabites, and Naomi's family lived there during a famine (Ruth 1:1). David sheltered his parents with Moab's king, later conquered Moab, and made it tributary (1 Sam 22:4; 2 Sam 8:2). It rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 1:1). Its god was Chemosh (1 Kgs 11:7). Prophets including Isaiah, Jeremiah and Amos spoke oracles against it. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the modern Kerak region.

Zion was originally the fortified stronghold of the Jebusite city of Jerusalem, which David captured and renamed the city of David (2 Sam 5:7; 1 Chr 11:5). Solomon later brought the ark up from there to his new temple (1 Kgs 8:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this first Zion on the southeastern hill of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name later seems to have shifted to the temple hill, and that in Christian times it came to be used for the southwestern hill. In the Psalms and Prophets, Zion often appears alongside Jerusalem as a name for the whole city and its people, frequently called the "daughter of Zion" (Ps 102:21; Amos 1:2; Zeph 3:14). It is described as the LORD's holy hill and dwelling place (Ps 2:6; Joel 3:21), and the New Testament quotes such passages (Matt 21:5; 1 Pet 2:6). The location shown here treats Zion as Jerusalem as a whole.

Assyria was a region on the upper Tigris River, probably in what is now northern Iraq, and the heart of a major Mesopotamian empire. Easton's Bible Dictionary derives the name from its early capital, Asshur on the Tigris. Genesis places the Tigris (Hiddekel) east of Assyria (Gen 2:14). Micah calls it 'the land of Nimrod' (Mic 5:6), which fits Gen 10:11 when read as Nimrod going out into Assyria. Its kings appear often as powerful adversaries of Israel and Judah. Pul and Tiglath-pileser exacted tribute and deported the eastern tribes. Shalmaneser besieged Samaria, and the king of Assyria resettled its cities with foreigners. Sennacherib invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem under Hezekiah, and Assyrian captains took Manasseh to Babylon. Nahum and Zephaniah foretold Assyria's fall and the desolation of Nineveh. The location shown here marks its heartland near Nineveh.

Samaria, meaning "watch-mountain" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel, and its name came to stand for the kingdom and its territory (1 Kgs 13:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that King Omri built the city on a hill bought from Shemer. Later kings of Israel reigned there (1 Kgs 22:51; 2 Kgs 13:1; 2 Kgs 15:13), and Ahab built an altar to Baal in it (1 Kgs 16:32). A Syrian siege caused severe famine (2 Kgs 6:25). In Hoshea's ninth year Assyria took Samaria and deported Israel (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:10), as prophets such as Hosea and Micah had warned (Hos 13:16; Mic 1:6). Foreign settlers were later placed in its cities (Ezra 4:10). In the New Testament, Samaria is the region between Judea and Galilee that Jesus passed through (John 4:4). The location shown here marks the region. The ancient city is the modern Sebastia.

Gilead was a hilly region east of the Jordan River, also called "mount Gilead" and "the land of Gilead." Jacob headed toward it after fleeing Laban (Gen 31:21), and traders carried balm and spices from it to Egypt (Gen 37:25; Jer 8:22). Its grazing land drew the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and Moses gave part of it to Machir of Manasseh (Num 32:1, 40). The Jabbok River divided it, with half once ruled by Sihon king of the Amorites (Josh 12:2). Jephthah led its people against Ammon, and the prophet Elijah came from there (Judg 11:9; 1 Kgs 17:1). Tiglath-pileser of Assyria took it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as about 60 miles long, running from near the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. That is roughly the hill country of northwestern Jordan, where the location shown here is placed.

Edom was the region and nation south and southeast of the Dead Sea, also called the land of Seir, where Esau's descendants, the Edomites, settled (Gen 32:3; 36:43). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "red." Horite clans lived there earlier (Gen 36:21), and Edom had kings before Israel did (1 Chr 1:43). It bordered Judah's southern frontier (Num 34:3; Josh 15:1). Edom's king refused Israel passage during the wilderness journey, so Israel went around it (Num 20:14; Judg 11:18). Saul fought Edom, David garrisoned it, and Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber in Edom on the Red Sea (2 Sam 8:14; 1 Kgs 9:26). Bozrah and Teman were among its places (Isa 63:1; Jer 49:7). Several prophets announced judgment on Edom for its hostility to Judah, and it is also called Idumea (Ezek 25:12; 36:5; Obad 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the rugged hills east of the Arabah. The location shown here is a general point for the wider surrounding area.

Canaan, also called the Promised Land, was the region between the Jordan River and the Dead Sea on the east and the Mediterranean on the west. Terah's family set out from Ur for it (Gen 11:31), and Abraham lived there as a foreigner. Hebron, Shechem and Bethlehem lay within it (Gen 23:2; Gen 33:18; Gen 48:7). Famine drove Jacob's family to Egypt (Gen 47:4), but Jacob was buried in Canaan at Machpelah (Gen 50:13). God promised the land to Israel as a possession (Exod 6:4; Lev 25:38). Moses viewed it from Mount Nebo (Deut 32:49), and under Joshua Israel ate its produce and divided it by lot (Josh 5:12; Acts 13:19). Lands east of the Jordan were treated as outside it (Num 35:14; Josh 22:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name first meant only the coastal plain around Sidon. Zephaniah applies it to the Philistine coast (Zeph 2:5). The location shown here is a central point for the whole region.

Syria is the King James name for the region north and northeast of Israel, called Aram in Hebrew. In the Old Testament it usually means the Aramean kingdom ruled from Damascus (1 Kgs 15:18). Its kings Benhadad, Hazael and Rezin repeatedly fought Israel and Judah, besieging Samaria and marching on Jerusalem (1 Kgs 20:1; 2 Kgs 6:24; 2 Kgs 16:5). Naaman commanded its army (2 Kgs 5:1). Israelites worshipped its gods (Judg 10:6), and it traded with Tyre (Ezek 27:16). Amos foretold its people's exile to Kir (Amos 1:5). In the New Testament Syria is a Roman province, governed at one point by Cyrenius (Luke 2:2). Jesus' fame spread through it (Matt 4:24), and Paul strengthened churches there and sailed to and from it (Acts 15:41; Acts 21:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that in Roman times it also included part of Palestine. The location shown here is a general point near the modern Syria–Turkey border.

Galilee was the northern region of the land of Israel; its Hebrew name means "circuit" or "district" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). In the Old Testament it lay in the hill country of Naphtali, where Kedesh was a city of refuge (Josh 20:7). Solomon gave Hiram of Tyre twenty of its cities, and the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser later captured it and deported its people. Isaiah calls it "Galilee of the nations," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a reference to its mixed population. In the New Testament it was a province ruled by Herod as tetrarch. It held Nazareth, Cana and Capernaum. Jesus grew up there and taught and healed throughout it, his first miracle was at Cana, many of his disciples came from there, and after his resurrection he met the eleven on a mountain there. The location shown here is a central point within the region.

Bethel (of Palestine), meaning "house of God," was a town in the central hill country about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, west of Ai and south of Shiloh. Its earlier name was Luz (Gen 28:19). Abraham built an altar east of it on entering Canaan (Gen 12:8), and Jacob named the place and later returned to build an altar there (Gen 35:3). It lay on the Ephraim–Benjamin border and was taken by the house of Joseph (Judg 1:22). In the time of the judges Israel gathered there before the LORD, and Samuel included it on his circuit (1 Sam 7:16). After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam set up a golden calf and altar there (1 Kgs 12:29). Amos and Hosea denounced its altars, and Josiah later destroyed them (2 Kgs 23:15). Men of Bethel returned after the exile. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Beitin given in Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Jericho was an ancient walled city on the plain west of the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea, called "the city of palm trees" (2 Chr 28:15). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite it before crossing the Jordan. Joshua sent spies there, and Rahab hid them. The city was shut up against Israel, its walls fell after Israel marched around it for seven days, and its king was destroyed. It was assigned to Benjamin. Hiel of Bethel later rebuilt it at the cost of his sons, as Joshua had foretold. Elijah and Elisha stopped there, and a company of prophets lived there. Zedekiah was captured in its plains, and 345 of its people returned from exile. Jesus healed blind Bartimaeus nearby and passed through the town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the Old Testament city near Elisha's Fountain, at Tell es-Sultan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hebron was an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-arba after Arba, a great man among the Anakim (Josh 14:15). It was said to have been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt (Num 13:22). Abram settled by Mamre at Hebron, and he buried Sarah in the cave of Machpelah there. Isaac and Jacob also lived there. Its king Hoham joined the alliance against Joshua, who took the city. It was given to Caleb, who drove out the sons of Anak, and it later became a priestly city and a city of refuge. David reigned from Hebron over Judah for seven and a half years, and six of his sons were born there. Abner was buried there, and all Israel anointed David king there. Absalom later launched his revolt from Hebron, and Rehoboam fortified it. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern city of Hebron (el-Khalil), which matches the location shown here.

Lebanon is the mountainous region north of Israel, named in Deuteronomy and Joshua as the northern limit of the land promised to Israel, reaching toward the Euphrates (Deut 1:7; Josh 1:4). Joshua 13:5 also mentions "Lebanon toward the sunrising," which Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify as the eastern Anti-Lebanon range, beside the western Lebanon range proper. The name probably means "white," perhaps from its snow (Jer 18:14) or pale limestone. Lebanon was famous for its cedars and other timber. Hiram's servants cut and floated logs down the coast for Solomon's building works (1 Kgs 5:9; 2 Chr 2:8), and cedar was brought to Joppa again for the second temple (Ezra 3:7). Solomon also built in Lebanon (1 Kgs 9:19). Poets and prophets used its cedars, wine, fragrance and streams as images of height, pride and abundance (Ps 104:16; Isa 2:13; Hos 14:7). The location shown here is in the modern country of Lebanon.

Damascus was an ancient city of Syria, about 130 miles northeast of Jerusalem, and the capital of the Aramean (Syrian) kingdom (Isa 7:8). It first appears in Abram's pursuit of the eastern kings and as the home of his steward Eliezer. David defeated the Syrians of Damascus and garrisoned the region. Later a rebel band led by Rezon took power there. Its kings, including Benhadad, Hazael and Rezin, alternately fought and allied with Israel and Judah. Then the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser took the city and deported its people to Kir, and Ahaz copied an altar he saw there. Naaman praised its rivers Abana and Pharpar. In Acts, Saul was converted near Damascus, about AD 32 by inference from context, and preached there. He later escaped the governor serving King Aretas. It is the present-day Syrian capital, which the location shown here matches.

Bashan was a fertile region east of the Jordan River, north of Gilead, stretching toward Mount Hermon and east to Salcah. Before Israel arrived it was the kingdom of Og, an Amorite king who lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. Israel defeated him in battle at Edrei. Moses then gave Bashan to the half-tribe of Manasseh, and it was known as "the land of giants." Its towns included Golan, a city of refuge, the towns of Jair, and the region of Argob with sixty walled cities, which was later one of Solomon's administrative districts. Syria later took Bashan from Israel; the surrounding passage names Hazael as the conqueror. Psalms and the prophets use Bashan as a byword for richness: its strong bulls, fattened cattle, oak forests and pastures. It probably corresponds to the modern Golan Heights and the Hauran plain in southern Syria. The location shown here marks a point within that general area.

Tyre was a major Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 miles south of Sidon, at the modern town of Sur in Lebanon. It is first named as a "strong city" on Asher's border (Josh 19:29). Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar and craftsmen to build David's house and later supplied Solomon (2 Sam 5:11; 1 Kgs 5:1; 2 Chr 2:3). Ezekiel describes it as a wealthy merchant city "at the entry of the sea" (Ezek 27:3). Prophets announced judgment on it for its pride and for selling captives, and Ezekiel mentions Nebuchadnezzar's long siege (Isa 23:1; Amos 1:9; Ezek 29:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes a mainland fortress and an island city offshore, famous for its purple dye. In the New Testament people from the region came to Jesus, who also visited it, and Paul stopped there on his way to Jerusalem (Mark 3:8; Matt 15:21; Acts 21:7).

Sodom was a city of the plain near the Dead Sea. It is named with Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19). Lot settled near it after parting from Abram, and its men are described as exceedingly wicked (Gen 13:12–13). Its king fought in the vale of Siddim, where Lot was taken captive. Abram later rescued him and refused the king's offer of goods (Gen 14:8–22). After two angels visited Lot, the city was destroyed by fire and brimstone from heaven (Gen 19:1–28; Luke 17:29). Prophets and New Testament writers repeatedly use Sodom as a byword for sin and for sudden, total overthrow. Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it south of the Dead Sea, near Jebel Usdum ("Mount Sodom"), while Easton's Bible Dictionary favors the northern end. The location shown here follows the southern identification.

Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel in New Testament times, lying west of the Jordan and south of Samaria, with Jerusalem as its chief city. The name derives from Judah, and Ezra 9:9 speaks of the restored community 'in Judah and in Jerusalem' after the exile. Bethlehem, where Jesus was born, lay in Judea (Matt 2:1; Luke 2:4), which was ruled by Herod and later by his son Archelaus (Luke 1:5; Matt 2:22). Crowds from Judea went out to John the Baptist and followed Jesus (Mark 1:5; Matt 4:25), who travelled between Judea and Galilee (John 4:3). Acts names Judea as a stage in the spread of the apostles' witness (Acts 1:8) and as home to early churches (Acts 9:31; Gal 1:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name was sometimes used for Palestine generally (Acts 28:21).

Midian was a desert region and people south and east of Canaan, named, according to Gen 25:2, after a son of Abraham by Keturah. Moses fled there from Pharaoh, served Jethro, the priest of Midian, and kept his flocks until God sent him back to Egypt. His sons Gershom and Eliezer were probably born there. Later the elders of Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam against Israel, and Israel killed five Midianite kings. In the time of the judges Midian oppressed Israel for seven years, about 1258 BC by inference from context, until Gideon's three hundred men routed them. Prophets later recalled "the day of Midian." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the Midianites as Arabian nomads and traders whose pastures reached into Sinai. The location shown here lies east of the Gulf of Aqaba, in modern northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Gibeah, meaning "a hill," was a town of Benjamin (Josh 18:28), also called Gibeah of Benjamin and Gibeah of Saul. In Judges a Levite stopped there for the night rather than lodge in a foreign city. The men of the town surrounded the house where he stayed and abused his concubine until she died. Israel's tribes then demanded the guilty men, Benjamin refused to hand them over, and after two defeats Israel took and destroyed the town by ambush (Judg 19:12–15; 20:4–37). Gibeah later appears as Saul's home and royal residence (1 Sam 10:26; 15:34; 22:6). The Ziphites came there to report on David's movements, and seven of Saul's descendants were hanged there (2 Sam 21:6). Hosea recalls "the days of Gibeah" (Hos 9:9). Name is shared by several places. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Tell el-Ful, about 3 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Shechem was a city in the hill country of central Canaan, later in the territory of Ephraim. Abram stopped there at the plain of Moreh on entering Canaan (Gen 12:6), about 1921 BC by inference from context. Jacob camped before the city on returning from Padan-aram, and his daughter was defiled there by Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite (Gen 33:18; 34:2). Joseph's brothers later pastured flocks there. Under Joshua it became a Levitical city of refuge, the site of a covenant assembly, and the burial place of Joseph's bones (Josh 20:7; 24:1, 25, 32). Abimelech was made king there and later fought its men (Judg 9). Rehoboam went there to be crowned, and Jeroboam rebuilt it as his residence (1 Kgs 12:1, 25). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim at modern Nablus, which the location shown here follows.

Heshbon was the royal city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who had taken the land of the former king of Moab as far as the Arnon (Num 21:26). Israel captured it under Moses and settled in it and its villages (Num 21:25; Deut 2:24–30). The tribe of Reuben rebuilt it (Num 32:37), and it lay on the border between Reuben and Gad (Josh 13:17, 26). It was later assigned to the Levites (Josh 21:39; 1 Chr 6:81). The Song of Solomon mentions its fishpools (Song 7:4). In the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah it appears as a Moabite city facing judgment (Isa 15:4; Jer 48:2, 34), suggesting that Moab had regained it. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at the ruins of Hesban, about 20 miles east of the Jordan near the northern end of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification.

Negeb is the dry region in the far south of Canaan, south of the hill country of Judah. The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be dry." The King James Version usually translates it simply as "the south." Abram journeyed through it, and returned there from Egypt before going on to Bethel (Gen 12:9; 13:1–3). Isaac later lived there (Gen 24:62). The spies Moses sent went up through the Negeb toward Hebron, and they reported that Amalekites lived there (Num 13:22, 29). King Arad also lived in this region (Num 21:1). Joshua conquered it (Josh 10:40), and Simeon's inheritance lay within it (Josh 19:8). The Bible names several parts of it, such as the Negeb of Judah and of the Kenites (1 Sam 27:10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a pastoral land of rolling hills between the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean. Jeremiah lists its cities among those that would be restored (Jer 33:13).

Gibeon was a large Hivite city, described as greater than Ai and one of the royal cities. Its people made peace with Joshua, and it was the only city that did so (Josh 11:19). When five Amorite kings attacked it for this, Joshua defeated them there, and in that battle he called on the sun to stand still over Gibeon. The city was later assigned to Benjamin and given to the priests. At the pool of Gibeon, Joab's men fought Abner's, and Asahel was killed in that battle. Joab later killed Amasa at the great stone in Gibeon. The tabernacle and the altar of burnt offering stood at its high place, where Solomon sacrificed and received a dream from God. Gibeonites helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall after the exile. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with modern el-Jib, northwest of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Gilgal was Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, on the east border of Jericho, where Joshua set up twelve stones taken from the river (Josh 4:19–20). The text links its name to the LORD "rolling away" the reproach of Egypt (Josh 5:9), and Israel kept the Passover there. It served as Joshua's base during the conquest (Josh 9:6; 10:6–15). Later, Samuel judged Israel there on his yearly circuit. Saul was made king there and later offered sacrifice there without waiting for Samuel, and Samuel killed Agag there (1 Sam 7:16; 11:15; 13:8–12; 15:33). Judah met David there on his return across the Jordan (2 Sam 19:15). Hosea and Amos condemn the worship practised at Gilgal. Several places share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this Gilgal near Jericho, and Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Shiloh. The location shown here follows an identification with Jaljulia in the Sharon plain.

Beersheba was a city in the far south of Israel. Genesis explains the name as "well of the oath", recalling the covenant Abraham and Abimelech swore there (Gen 21:31–32). A second account links the name to a well dug by Isaac's servants (Gen 26:33). Abraham planted a grove, worshipped and lived there (Gen 21:33; 22:19). Jacob set out from it for Haran, and later offered sacrifices there before going down to Egypt (Gen 28:10; 46:1). It was allotted to Judah and to Simeon (Josh 15:28; 19:2). It marked the southern limit of the land in the phrase "from Dan even to Beersheba" (Judg 20:1). Samuel's sons judged there, Elijah fled there, and Amos named it alongside the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal (1 Sam 8:2; 1 Kgs 19:3; Amos 5:5). It was resettled after the exile (Neh 11:27). The location shown here follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's identification with Tell es-Seba, east of the modern city.

Bethlehem was a town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Ephrath, on whose road Rachel was buried (Gen 35:19; 48:7). It was the home of the judge Ibzan and of Elimelech's family. Naomi returned there with Ruth, and Boaz lived there. David's family lived there too. Samuel came to the town to anoint David, and his warriors broke through a Philistine garrison to bring him water from its well by the gate. Rehoboam fortified it, and people from Bethlehem were among those who returned from exile. Matthew and Luke call it the city of David, where Jesus was born, where shepherds and wise men came, and where Herod killed the young boys. It is the modern town of Bethlehem (Beit Lahm), about 5 miles south of Jerusalem, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of bread." Another Bethlehem lay in Zebulun, and this entry is the Judean town.

Euphrates is the great river of western Asia, still known by that name, flowing from the mountains of eastern Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Genesis names it as the fourth river of Eden (Gen 2:14). Often called simply "the river" or "the great river," it marks the northeastern limit of the land promised to Abram and Israel (Gen 15:18; Josh 1:4). David fought Hadadezer of Zobah at this border, and Solomon ruled the region west of it from Tiphsah to Gaza. At Carchemish on its banks, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Pharaoh Necho (Jer 46:2). Jeremiah hid a linen belt by the river, and he had a scroll weighted with a stone and thrown into it, both as prophetic signs. Revelation describes angels bound at the river and its waters drying up for the kings of the east. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "sweet water" or "the great stream." The location shown here lies on its middle course in eastern Syria.

Gath was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, and one of the places where some of the Anakim remained after Joshua's conquest (Josh 11:22; 13:3). The Philistines carried the captured ark of God there (1 Sam 5:8). Gath was the home of the giant Goliath and of other men of great stature who fell to David and his servants. While fleeing Saul, David twice took refuge with Achish king of Gath, and six hundred men from Gath later followed him. Shimei went there to bring back runaway servants. David took Gath, and it appears among the cities Rehoboam fortified. Hazael of Syria later captured it, and Uzziah broke down its walls. Its name, meaning "winepress," appears in the saying "Tell it not in Gath" (2 Sam 1:20; Mic 1:10). Several sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the common identification with Tell es-Safi, given in Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Ai was a Canaanite city east of Bethel, "beside Bethaven," whose name is usually taken to mean "the ruin" or "heap." Abraham camped and built an altar between Bethel and Ai (called Hai in the KJV) when he entered Canaan and again on his return from the south. Under Joshua, Israel's first small attack on Ai was driven back with thirty-six dead. A second assault used an ambush on the west side of the city. It drew the defenders out, then took and burned Ai. Twelve thousand inhabitants were killed, and the king was hanged and buried under a heap of stones at the gate. The city was left "an heap for ever" (Josh 8:28). After the exile, men of Bethel and Ai were listed among the returnees. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Ai at Haiyan; the location shown here follows the alternative identification with the mound et-Tell.

Mizpah (also spelled Mizpeh, meaning "watchtower") was a city of Benjamin near Jerusalem, one of several places with this name. The tribes of Israel assembled there before the LORD to act against Benjamin and swore oaths there (Judg 20:1; 21:1). Samuel gathered Israel there to fast and confess, defeated the attacking Philistines, and set up the Ebenezer stone nearby. He judged Israel there on his yearly circuit and later called the people there to choose a king. King Asa fortified it with stones taken from Ramah. After Jerusalem fell to Babylon, it became the seat of the governor Gedaliah, whom Ishmael son of Nethaniah murdered there. Men of Mizpah later helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Neby Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Scopus, and many modern scholars favor Tell en-Nasbeh. The location shown here follows the Neby Samwil identification.

The Nile is the great river of Egypt, flowing north through northeast Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. The King James Version never uses the name, and usually calls it simply "the river." Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat and seven lean cows coming up out of it (Gen 41:1–3, 17–18). He later ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into it (Exod 1:22). Moses struck its waters and turned them to blood, so that the fish died and the Egyptians dug beside it for drinking water (Exod 7:17–24). Frogs later swarmed out of it (Exod 8:3). The prophets use the river as a picture of Egypt's wealth and pride, and foretell that it will dry up (Ezek 29:3, 9; 30:12; Zech 10:11). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Sihor or Shihor as another name for the Nile (Isa 23:3; Jer 2:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Shihor as a separate stream. This entry follows the first view.

Shiloh was a city in the hill country of Ephraim where Israel set up the tabernacle after the conquest (Josh 18:1). There Joshua and Eleazar the priest divided the land among the tribes by lot (Josh 18:10; 19:51). The house of God stayed there through the time of the judges. It drew yearly pilgrims and held a feast at which the daughters of Shiloh danced (Judg 18:31; 21:19–21; 1 Sam 1:3). Eli and his sons served there as priests, Hannah brought the young Samuel there, and the LORD revealed himself to Samuel there (1 Sam 1:24; 3:21). The ark was taken from Shiloh into battle and lost to the Philistines (1 Sam 4:3–4). Jeremiah later pointed to Shiloh's fate as a warning to Jerusalem (Jer 7:12; 26:6). Judg 21:19 places it north of Bethel, east of the Bethel–Shechem road. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Seilun, the site shown here.

Sidon (also spelled Zidon) was an ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Tyre. It is the modern Saida in Lebanon, and the location shown here marks that site. Genesis names it as the northern limit of Canaanite territory. It lay within the area allotted to Asher, but Asher never drove out its people (Judg 1:31). Its sailors and merchants were known across the sea (Isa 23:2; Ezek 27:8), and Israel at times worshipped its gods (Judg 10:6). Isaiah calls it a mother to Tyre, and Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Joel announce judgment against it. Elijah stayed at Zarephath, a town belonging to Sidon. Jesus travelled into the region of Tyre and Sidon, where he healed a Canaanite woman's daughter (Matt 15:21), and people from there came to hear him. Paul's ship called at Sidon on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:3).

Nazareth was a town in Galilee, the home of Joseph and Mary, where the angel Gabriel announced Jesus' birth to Mary (Luke 1:26). Joseph left it for Bethlehem before the birth, and the family returned there afterward (Luke 2:4; Luke 2:39). Jesus was brought up there, and as an adult he read in its synagogue (Luke 4:16) before leaving to live in Capernaum (Matt 4:13). As a result he was widely known as "Jesus of Nazareth," a title used by crowds, by Pilate on the cross, and by the apostles (John 19:19; Acts 2:22). Nathanael's question, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46), suggests the town had little standing, though the reason is debated. Matthew links the name to the prophetic saying "He shall be called a Nazarene" (Matt 2:23). The town is not named in the Old Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern town of Nazareth (en-Nasirah), which matches the location shown here.

The Red Sea is the long arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia. At its northern end it splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba on either side of the Sinai Peninsula. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain its Hebrew name, Yam Suph, as "sea of weeds" or reeds. It is best known as the water the Israelites crossed on dry ground when leaving Egypt, where Pharaoh's chariots and army drowned (Exod 15:4; Heb 11:29), an event recalled often in later books. The name also covers the Gulf of Aqaba. Israel's wilderness routes went "by the way of the Red sea" around Edom, and Solomon built ships at Ezion-geber on its shore (1 Kgs 9:26). It also marked one limit of Israel's promised borders (Exod 23:31). Easton's places the crossing at the Gulf of Suez. The exact point is uncertain, and the location shown here marks the sea as a whole.

Persia was the empire, and originally the homeland, of the Persians, in what is now Iran. In the Bible it appears mainly as the power that followed Babylon. Babylon's captives served there "until the reign of the kingdom of Persia" (2 Chr 36:20), and Cyrus king of Persia proclaimed that the Jews could return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Ezra names the later kings Darius and Artaxerxes, under whom the work was opposed, then finished and carried on. Esther and Daniel pair Persia with Media, as in the two-horned ram of Dan 8:20. Ezekiel lists Persians as soldiers in the army of Tyre and as allies of Gog. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name properly means the province of Fars in southwestern Iran. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes an empire stretching from the Indus to Thrace. The location shown here is a general point in Persis (modern Fars, in southwestern Iran), the Persians' homeland, near Persepolis, representing the wider region.

Seir was a mountainous region, also called Mount Seir, identified with the country of Edom (Gen 32:3; Gen 36:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it along the eastern side of the Arabah, from the southeastern end of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqaba, in what is now southern Jordan. The location shown here lies within that area. Its earliest inhabitants were the Horites (Gen 14:6; Gen 36:30). The descendants of Esau later destroyed them and settled in their place, and Seir was said to be given to Esau as his possession (Deut 2:12; Josh 24:4). Jacob met Esau on his way back to Seir, and Israel passed by its borders on the journey to Canaan (Gen 33:16; Deut 2:4, 8). Mount Halak, which "goes up to Seir," marked the southern limit of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17). Later, King Amaziah of Judah defeated the people of Seir (2 Chr 25:11), and Ezekiel named Seir alongside Moab in an oracle (Ezek 25:8).

Gomorrah was a city of the plain of the Jordan, nearly always named alongside Sodom. Genesis lists it at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19) and describes the region as well watered before its destruction (Gen 13:10). Its king, Birsha, joined the kings of Sodom, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar in a failed battle in the Valley of Siddim, after which the invaders carried off the cities' goods (Gen 14:2, 8–11). Because of the great outcry against their sin, the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, and the land smoked like a furnace (Gen 18:20; 19:24, 28). This is dated to about 1897 BC, by inference from context. Later writers used Gomorrah as a byword for wickedness and total ruin (Isa 1:9; Jer 49:18; Jude 1:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary places the cities near the northern end of the Dead Sea; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors the south. The location shown here follows the southern view.

Hamath was a major city of Syria, the capital of a kingdom of the same name, identified with modern Hama on the Orontes River; the location shown here follows that identification. Amos calls it "Hamath the great" (Amos 6:2). Its king Toi sent greetings to David after David defeated Hadadezer (2 Sam 8:9), and Solomon built store cities in its territory (2 Chr 8:4). Jeroboam II of Israel later recovered it (2 Kgs 14:28). Assyria conquered it, and the Assyrian envoys pointed to its fallen king and gods as a warning to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13). People from Hamath were resettled in Samaria, where they made the god Ashima (2 Kgs 17:24, 30). Riblah "in the land of Hamath" was where Pharaoh Necho imprisoned Jehoahaz and Nebuchadnezzar judged Zedekiah (2 Kgs 23:33; Jer 52:9). Ezekiel names Hamath on Israel's northern border (Ezek 47:16–17).

Carmel was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Ziph and Juttah (Josh 15:55). After his campaign against the Amalekites, Saul came there and set up a monument before moving on to Gilgal (1 Sam 15:12). The wealthy Nabal, who lived in nearby Maon, kept his flocks at Carmel and sheared his sheep there. David sent young men to him there to ask for provisions, and after Nabal's death his widow Abigail, called 'the Carmelitess', became David's wife (1 Sam 25:2–40; 27:3). Hezrai (or Hezro) the Carmelite, one of David's mighty men, probably came from this town. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruins of Kurmul, about 10 miles south-southeast of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several verses using the name, especially in the prophets, refer instead to Mount Carmel near the Mediterranean coast, which is a separate place.

Jezreel was a town on the border of Issachar, named with Chesulloth and Shunem (Josh 19:18). It was part of the territory Abner placed under Ish-bosheth (2 Sam 2:9). King Ahab kept a palace there, and Naboth's vineyard lay next to it (1 Kgs 21:1). Elijah ran ahead of Ahab's chariot to its entrance (1 Kgs 18:46). King Joram went to Jezreel to recover from wounds received fighting the Syrians. There Jehu, seen approaching by the watchman on its tower, killed Joram, had Jezebel thrown down, and wiped out Ahab's house (2 Kgs 9:15–37; 10:11). Hosea later named his son Jezreel, recalling that bloodshed (Hos 1:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the town with the modern village of Zerin, on the northwestern spur of Mount Gilboa above the valley that bears its name. The same name belongs to other places, including a town in Judah.

Lachish was a fortified city in the lowlands (Shephelah) of southwestern Judah. Its Amorite king Japhia joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem's coalition against Gibeon. Joshua later took the city on the second day of the siege and defeated Horam of Gezer, who came to help it (Josh 10:3, 10:31–33). It was assigned to Judah, and Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:9). King Amaziah fled there and was killed (2 Kgs 14:19). Sennacherib of Assyria besieged it and sent his officers from there to Jerusalem (2 Kgs 18:14, 18:17; 2 Chr 32:9). Babylon's army later attacked it as one of Judah's last fortified cities (Jer 34:7), and returning exiles resettled it (Neh 11:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes Assyrian palace reliefs that show its siege. Older works identified it with Tell el-Hesy. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell ed-Duweir (Tel Lachish).

Gad was the territory east of the Jordan given to the tribe of Gad. Moses assigned it to them, along with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, from the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og (Num 32:33; Josh 13:8). Joshua 13:24–28 describes it as including Jazer, the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites as far as Aroer near Rabbah. It also ran from Heshbon to Mahanaim and took in the Jordan valley towns of Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon, up to the Sea of Chinnereth. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it roughly in the center of the land east of the Jordan, north of Reuben and around the Jabbok. The location shown here lies in that part of central Gilead, in present-day Jordan. The Gadites also built Dibon and Aroer farther south (Num 32:34). Jeremiah 49:1 speaks of the Ammonite king taking possession of Gad, and Ezekiel's vision gives Gad a new southern portion (Ezek 48:27–28).

Macedonia was a Roman province north of Greece and the first part of Europe where Paul preached. In a night vision a man of Macedonia begged Paul, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," and he crossed over to Philippi, described as the chief city of that part of the province (Acts 16:9–12). Paul later sent Timothy and Erastus there and passed through again on his way to Jerusalem (Acts 19:21–22; 20:1–3). Its churches, including those at Philippi and Thessalonica, gave to the poor believers in Jerusalem and supplied Paul's own needs (Rom 15:26; 2 Cor 8:1; 11:9; Phil 4:15). Paul wrote 2 Corinthians during this period, probably from Macedonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was governed by a proconsul, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places his residence at Thessalonica. The region corresponds broadly to northern Greece today, and the location shown here is near modern Thessaloniki.

Mount Zion was one of the hills on which Jerusalem stood, and its name is often used for the city itself, especially as the place where the LORD is said to dwell and reign (Ps 74:2; Isa 8:18; Mic 4:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as the southeastern hill, the stronghold David took from the Jebusites and made "the city of David" (2 Sam 5:7). Later tradition gave the name to Jerusalem's southwestern hill. The location shown here follows the eastern-ridge view, placing it near the Temple Mount. Psalms praise it as the city of the great King and as immovable (Ps 48:2; 125:1). The prophets speak of attacks against it, of a remnant escaping from it, and of deliverance there (Isa 29:8; 37:32; Joel 2:32; Obad 1:17), while Lamentations describes it as desolate (Lam 5:18). In the New Testament it stands for the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Rev 14:1).

Asher was the territory given to the tribe of Asher, named for Jacob's son, in the fifth lot of the land division (Josh 19:24). It ran along the Mediterranean coast from Mount Carmel northward toward Tyre and Sidon, with Manasseh to the south, Zebulun and Issachar to the southeast, and Naphtali to the east (Josh 19:26–29, 34; Josh 17:10). It held twenty-two towns with their villages. Manasseh also held certain towns that lay within Asher and Issachar (Josh 17:11). Asher did not drive out the Canaanites of coastal cities such as Accho, Sidon and Achzib and lived among them (Judg 1:31–32). The Song of Deborah pictures Asher staying by the seashore (Judg 5:17). Under Solomon, Asher formed part of an administrative district (1 Kgs 4:16), and Ezekiel's vision assigns it a strip of land and a city gate (Ezek 48:2, 34). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes its soil as among the richest in Palestine. The location shown here is in western Galilee.

Dan was Israel's northernmost town, near the sources of the Jordan below Mount Hermon. Originally called Laish or Leshem, it was captured by members of the tribe of Dan, who renamed it after their ancestor (Josh 19:47; Judg 18:29). Its mention in Abram's pursuit of Lot's captors (Gen 14:14) probably uses the later name for the same area. The phrase "from Dan even to Beersheba" became a standard way of naming the whole land from north to south. Jeroboam set up one of his two golden calves here, and Jehu kept it (1 Kgs 12:29; 2 Kgs 10:29). Ben-hadad of Syria struck the town in Asa's reign, and Jeremiah pictured news of invasion arriving from Dan. "Danjaan" (2 Sam 24:6) is probably the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the site as Tell el-Kady (Tel Dan), which the location shown here matches.

Ekron was the northernmost of the five chief Philistine cities, each ruled by its own lord (Josh 13:3). It lay on Judah's northern border and was assigned first to Judah and then to Dan (Josh 15:11, 45–46; 19:43). Judah is said to have taken it (Judg 1:18), but it was later back in Philistine hands. The captured ark of God was sent there, and its people feared it would kill them (1 Sam 5:10). The Philistines then returned the ark with gold offerings (1 Sam 6:16–17). Israel pursued the Philistines to its gates after David killed Goliath (1 Sam 17:52). King Ahaziah sent to consult Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, and Elijah condemned him for it (2 Kgs 1:2–3, 16). Prophets announced judgment on the city (Amos 1:8; Zeph 2:4). Easton's and Smith's dictionaries placed it at the village of Akir. The location shown here follows the later identification with Tel Miqne.

Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, is the mountain where the LORD came down in fire and smoke, the mountain quaked, and Moses was called to the summit (Exod 19:18–20). The people were kept back by boundaries set around it (Exod 19:23). There Moses received the two stone tablets, and later a second pair, and came down with his face shining (Exod 31:18; Exod 34:4, 29). Leviticus presents its laws as given there, and later passages look back to it (Lev 27:34; Neh 9:13; Acts 7:38). Paul uses it as a figure of the covenant of bondage, placing it in Arabia (Gal 4:24–25). The giving of the Ten Commandments there is dated to about 1491 BC, by inference from context. Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Ras Sufsafeh in the southern Sinai Peninsula, while others look to northwestern Arabia. The location shown here follows the southern Sinai identification.

Ramoth-gilead was a fortified city east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead. Under Solomon it was the base of Ben-geber, an officer whose district included the towns of Jair and the region of Argob in Bashan (1 Kgs 4:13). Later the Syrians held it. Ahab of Israel, joined by Jehoshaphat of Judah, marched to retake it despite the prophet Micaiah's warning, and he was mortally wounded there (1 Kgs 22:3–29; 2 Chr 18). His son Joram fought Hazael of Syria at the city and was wounded, while Israel kept hold of it (2 Kgs 8:28; 9:14). There a young prophet sent by Elisha anointed Jehu king (2 Kgs 9:1–4). Other passages name it a city of refuge in Gad. Its site is debated: Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Reimun or Gerasa (Jerash), and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Jel'ad. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell er-Rumeith in northern Jordan.

Susa, called Shushan in the King James Version, was a royal city in the province of Elam, where the Persian king kept a palace or citadel. Daniel saw a vision there beside the river Ulai (Dan 8:2), and Nehemiah was serving there when he heard news of Jerusalem (Neh 1:1). Most of the events of the Book of Esther take place at Susa: King Ahasuerus held court and feasts there, Esther and Mordecai lived there, Haman's decree went out from it, and the Jews of the city defended themselves and then celebrated with feasting (Esth 1:2; 3:15; 9:15–18). Its people, the Susanchites, appear among the groups opposing Jerusalem's rebuilding (Ezra 4:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Shush in southwestern Iran, where excavated ruins include a great columned palace hall, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Ashdod was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, near the Mediterranean coast between Gaza and Joppa. Some of the Anakim still lived there after Joshua's conquest. It was allotted to Judah, though it was listed among the lands still remaining to be taken (Josh 13:3; 15:47). After capturing the ark of God, the Philistines placed it in the temple of their god Dagon at Ashdod. There Dagon's image fell before it, and the people were struck with tumors. King Uzziah of Judah later broke down its walls. Isaiah records its capture by the commander of Sargon, king of Assyria. Several prophets announced judgment on it. After the exile, Nehemiah found Jews married to women of Ashdod whose children spoke its language. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is called Azotus in Acts 8:40. The location shown here is the ancient mound of Esdud (Tel Ashdod), a few miles inland.

Gaza, called Azzah in some passages (1 Kgs 4:24; Jer 25:20), was a city near the Mediterranean coast in the far southwest of Canaan, on the route toward Egypt. Gen 10:19 names it as a limit of Canaanite territory. Joshua's campaigns reached it, and some Anakim remained there. It was allotted to Judah, which took it (Judg 1:18), but it later appears as one of the five chief Philistine cities (1 Sam 6:17). Samson visited Gaza and was later imprisoned there, blinded and made to grind grain (Judg 16:21). Hezekiah struck the Philistines as far as Gaza, and Amos, Jeremiah, Zephaniah and Zechariah announced judgment on it. In Acts 8:26 Philip was sent to the desert road running from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he met the Ethiopian official, about AD 32 by inference from context. The location shown here is modern Gaza City.

West Manasseh was the territory of the half of the tribe of Manasseh that settled west of the Jordan River, in the central hill country of Canaan. The other half held Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan (Josh 17:1, 17:5–6). The western lot went to the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida, and the daughters of Zelophehad also received land there (Josh 17:2–4). Its border ran from near Shechem to the Kanah brook, which divided it from Ephraim to the south. It reached the Mediterranean on the west and touched Asher and Issachar to the north and east (Josh 17:7–10). Some Ephraimite towns lay inside it (Josh 16:9). Manasseh also claimed cities such as Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor, but could not drive out their Canaanite inhabitants and later made them pay tribute (Josh 17:11–13; Judg 1:27). This area is roughly the northern Samaria hills of today.

Amalek is the name of a nomadic people and of the desert region they roamed south of Canaan. Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim soon after the exodus. Joshua defeated them while Moses held up his hand on a hill, and the LORD declared war with Amalek "from generation to generation." Deuteronomy tells Israel to remember that attack and blot out Amalek's memory. Saul later came to "a city of Amalek" and captured its king Agag, but he was rebuked for not fully carrying out the command. David took spoil from Amalek. Easton's Bible Dictionary places them between the Dead Sea and the Red Sea, "from Havilah until thou comest to Shur." Their origin is debated. Tyndale House's proper-names index traces them to Esau's family, while Easton's notes that they already appear in Abraham's day (Gen 14:7). The location shown here is a general marker in the central Negev.

Asia in the New Testament is the Roman province covering western Asia Minor, in present-day western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Jews from Asia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost and later disputed with Stephen (Acts 2:9; 6:9). On his second journey Paul was forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach there (Acts 16:6). He later stayed over two years at Ephesus, so that people across the province heard his message. This provoked a riot by craftsmen whose trade depended on the worship of Diana (Acts 19:10, 26–27). Jews from Asia later stirred up the crowd that seized Paul in the temple (Acts 21:27). The province held the seven churches addressed in Revelation (Rev 1:4). Easton's takes a few passages to mean wider Asia Minor. This entry follows the provincial sense, and the location shown here marks the general region.

Nineveh was a great city on the east bank of the Tigris and the capital of the Assyrian empire. Gen 10:11 says Asshur built it, or, in the Revised Version's reading, Nimrod. This entry follows the Nimrod reading. Sennacherib king of Assyria returned to live there after his campaign against Judah (2 Kgs 19:36). God sent Jonah to preach against its wickedness. Described as a city of three days' journey with more than 120,000 people, it fasted and put on sackcloth, from the king down (Jonah 3:3–7; 4:11). Jesus later pointed to its repentance (Matt 12:41). Nahum and Zephaniah foretold its desolation, and it fell to the Medes and Babylonians late in the seventh century BC, about 625 BC according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The location shown here is the ruin mound of Kuyunjik, opposite modern Mosul in northern Iraq.

Sinai is the desert region, and the mountain within it, where the Israelites camped after leaving Egypt. They came from Rephidim into the wilderness of Sinai in the third month after the Exodus and camped before the mount (Exod 19:1–2). While they were there, Moses received commands about the offerings, the people were counted, Nadab and Abihu died, and the Passover was kept in the second year (Lev 7:38; Num 1:1; 3:4; 9:5). The people then moved on toward the wilderness of Paran (Num 10:12). Later poetry recalls Sinai as the place the LORD came from, where the mountain shook (Deut 33:2; Judg 5:5; Ps 68:8). Other passages call the same place Horeb. Tradition places the mountain in the southern Sinai Peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors Jebel Musa, and Easton's Bible Dictionary points to the nearby bluff of Ras Sufsafeh. The location shown here marks the region broadly within that peninsula.

Beth-shemesh, meaning "house of the sun" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a city on the northern border of Judah, near the Philistine lowland (Josh 15:10). It was given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:16; 1 Chr 6:59). When the Philistines sent back the ark of the LORD on a cart, the cows took the road straight to Beth-shemesh, where the people were reaping wheat. The cart stopped at a great stone in the field of Joshua, and offerings were made there. Many men of the town were then struck down for looking into the ark (1 Sam 6:12–20). Beth-shemesh lay in one of Solomon's supply districts (1 Kgs 4:9). Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah there (2 Kgs 14:11–13), and the Philistines later took it under Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18). Several places share this name. The location shown here follows the identification with ʿAin Shems given by Easton's Bible Dictionary, about 14 miles west of Jerusalem.

Ephesus was a major city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of Asia Minor. Its ruins lie near modern Selçuk in Turkey. The city was known as the guardian of the goddess Diana's worship (Acts 19:35). Paul first stopped there briefly, reasoning in the synagogue before sailing for Jerusalem with a promise to return (Acts 18:19–21). The Alexandrian teacher Apollos also came there. Paul returned on his next journey, and his preaching across Asia stirred opposition. According to Acts 19:24 the image-makers started a riot, by inference from context about AD 53. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Cor 16:8; 15:32). Later he called its church elders to meet him at Miletus. Paul's letter to the Ephesians is addressed to believers there, Timothy stayed on there, and Tychicus was sent there. Ephesus heads the seven churches addressed in Revelation. Tradition holds that the apostle John spent his last years there.

Ramah was a city in the territory of Benjamin, listed with Gibeon and Beeroth (Josh 18:25). It lay near Gibeah on the road north from Jerusalem, and Deborah judged Israel between Ramah and Bethel (Judg 4:5; 19:13). Baasha king of Israel fortified it to blockade Asa king of Judah. He later abandoned the work, and Asa used its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah (1 Kgs 15:17–22; 2 Chr 16:1–6). Isaiah and Hosea name it among Benjamin's towns facing invasion (Isa 10:29; Hos 5:8). Nebuzaradan released Jeremiah there after he had been taken in chains (Jer 40:1), and Jer 31:15 pictures Rachel weeping in Ramah. Its people returned after the exile (Ezra 2:26; Neh 7:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the village of er-Ram, about 5 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that view. Several places share the name. The "Ramath of the south" in Simeon (Josh 19:8) is a separate town.

Caesarea was a port city on the Mediterranean coast of Judea, about 70 miles northwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Herod the Great built it on the site of an older town called Strato's Tower and named it after Caesar Augustus. It became the seat of the Roman governors. In Acts, Philip preached his way there and later lived there (Acts 8:40; 21:8), and believers sent Saul from it to Tarsus (Acts 9:30). The centurion Cornelius lived there and received Peter (Acts 10:1, 24). Herod Agrippa I stayed there and, as the account continuing in Acts 12 relates, died there. Paul landed there after his second journey. He was later held there as a prisoner before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa until he appealed to Caesar. It is distinct from Caesarea Philippi. The location shown here is the coastal ruins at modern Caesarea in Israel.

Capernaum was a city of Galilee on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in the Gospels. After leaving Nazareth, Jesus settled there, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt 4:13), and it became a main center of his ministry. He taught in its synagogue on the sabbath (Mark 1:21; Luke 4:31), and John 6:59 places the bread of life discourse there. Events connected with the city include the healing of a centurion's servant (Matt 8:5) and of a nobleman's son who lay sick there (John 4:46). Tribute collectors also questioned Peter there (Matt 17:24). Jesus pronounced judgment on the city despite the mighty works done in it (Matt 11:23; Luke 10:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "Nahum's town." The site has been placed either at Tell Hum or at Khan Minyeh, further southwest. The location shown here follows the Tell Hum identification.

Cush was a region south of Egypt, usually rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version. Ezekiel describes Egypt as stretching "from the tower of Syene" (probably modern Aswan) to the border of Cush (Ezek 29:10), and the prophets regularly pair it with Egypt (Isa 20:3–5; Ezek 30:4; Nah 3:9). Its king Tirhakah marched out to fight the Assyrian king, identified as Sennacherib from the surrounding chapter, in Hezekiah's time (2 Kgs 19:9; Isa 37:9). Isaiah and Zephaniah speak of the land "beyond the rivers of Ethiopia" (Isa 18:1; Zeph 3:10), probably the Upper Nile and its tributaries. It is also listed with Seba, the Sabeans, Libya and Persia. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some also placed a Cush in Asia, but it identifies the African Cush with Nubia and Abyssinia. The location shown here follows the African identification, in what is now northern Sudan.

Horeb is the mountain called "the mountain of God," where Moses came while tending Jethro's flock (Exod 3:1) and where the Israelites camped during the Wilderness Wanderings. There God made a covenant with Israel, spoke to the people out of the fire, and gave the law that Moses placed in the ark as two stone tablets (Deut 5:2; Deut 4:15; 1 Kgs 8:9). There the people also made and worshipped a golden calf (Ps 106:19). Near Horeb Moses struck a rock to bring out water (Exod 17:6). It lay eleven days' journey from Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir (Deut 1:2). Later the prophet Elijah traveled forty days to reach it (1 Kgs 19:8). Horeb is generally treated as another name for Sinai. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees it as the whole range of which Sinai was one peak. Several sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the traditional identification with Jebel Musa in southern Sinai.

Naphtali was the territory in northern Israel allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, which received the sixth lot when the land was divided (Josh 19:32–39). Its border ran along the Jordan on the east, with Zebulun to the south and Asher to the west. It contained nineteen fortified cities, including Hazor, Kedesh and Chinnereth. Its hill country was called mount Naphtali, and Kedesh there became a city of refuge (Josh 20:7). Under Solomon it was one of the supply districts, governed by Ahimaaz. Benhadad of Syria struck it, and Tiglathpileser of Assyria later conquered it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Isaiah pairs it with Zebulun as an afflicted land in "Galilee of the nations," and Matthew links that passage to Jesus settling in Capernaum. The region took its name from Jacob's son Naphtali. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "that struggles or fights." The location shown here is in upper Galilee, north of the Sea of Galilee.

River, in the phrase "beyond the river" (also rendered "on this side the river" in the King James Version), was the Persian name for the region west of the river, which is by inference the Euphrates. Seen from the Persian court, this territory, including Samaria and Judah, lay "beyond" it. The region had its own governor, Tatnai, who questioned the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem and then carried out Darius's orders to support it (Ezra 5:3; 6:13). Royal tribute collected there was used to pay for the work (Ezra 6:8). Artaxerxes instructed its treasurers to supply Ezra and gave Ezra authority over its people (Ezra 7:21, 25). Nehemiah carried royal letters to its governors (Neh 2:7–9). The name is shared by several places, and the location shown here marks Jerusalem as a reference point within the wider region.

Zebulun was the territory allotted to the Israelite tribe descended from Jacob's son Zebulun. It lay in what was later called lower Galilee, and the location shown here is in the hills near Nazareth. Jacob's blessing links Zebulun with the sea and with ships, reaching toward Sidon (Gen 49:13). In Joshua it received the third lot. Its border ran from Sarid toward Chisloth-tabor, Daberath and Japhia, north to Hannathon and the valley of Jiphthah-el. It held twelve cities, including Nahalal, Shimron and a Bethlehem, probably the northern town of that name. It bordered Asher and Naphtali. Isaiah pairs the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali as afflicted regions, and Matthew applies that passage to Jesus living at Capernaum. In Ezekiel's vision, Zebulun has a portion between Issachar and Gad and a city gate on the south side. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "dwelling" or "habitation."

Anathoth was a town in the territory of Benjamin that was given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:18; 1 Chr 6:60). Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his fields there (1 Kgs 2:26). Abiezer, one of David's monthly army commanders, came from Anathoth (1 Chr 27:12). Isaiah names it among the towns on the route of an army advancing on Jerusalem (Isa 10:30). It is best known as the home of the prophet Jeremiah, who came from a priestly family there (Jer 1:1). Men of Anathoth threatened his life (Jer 11:21–23). While imprisoned, he bought his cousin Hanameel's field there for seventeen shekels (Jer 32:7–9). After the exile, 128 men of Anathoth returned, and Benjamites resettled it (Ezra 2:23; Neh 11:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Anata, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification.

Arabah is the Hebrew name for the deep rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee down the Jordan valley to the Dead Sea and on south to the Gulf of Aqaba. The King James Version usually translates it "the plain" and keeps "Arabah" only in Josh 18:18, which describes Benjamin's border. It is linked with Chinnereth and with the "sea of the plain," the Salt Sea (Deut 3:17; Josh 12:3). Its southern stretch is linked with Elath and Ezion-geber (Deut 2:8). Joshua lists it among the main regions of the land (Josh 11:16). Abner crossed it to reach the Jordan and Mahanaim (2 Sam 2:29), and Zedekiah fled toward it when Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:4). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its Arabic names as el-Ghor for the Jordan section and Wadi el-Arabah south of the Dead Sea. Because the name covers a long region, the location shown here marks the central Jordan valley.

Ephraim (Territory) was the land allotted to the tribe of Ephraim, descended from Joseph's son Ephraim, in the central hill country west of the Jordan. Joshua 16 traces its borders. The south ran from the Jordan near Jericho up past Bethel, then west by lower Beth-horon and Gezer to the Mediterranean. The north, shared with Manasseh, followed the brook Kanah to the sea, with Ephraim to the south and Manasseh to the north. Ephraim also held towns inside Manasseh's land, including Tappuah. The Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but lived under tribute. The hill region, called "mount Ephraim," held Timnath-serah, the town given to Joshua (Josh 19:50). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the phrase as the section of the central range belonging to Ephraim. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fruitful." The location shown here lies in the central hills north of Bethel, in today's West Bank.

Kadesh, also called Kadesh-Barnea, was an oasis in the wilderness of Zin, on the southern edge of Canaan near the border of Edom. In Abraham's time it was also called En-mishpat, and it served as a landmark for his travels and for the well where Hagar met the angel. Kadesh was Israel's main camp in the wilderness. The spies reported back to Moses there, and the people stayed there 'many days.' Miriam died and was buried there. At the 'water of Meribah in Kadesh' the people quarreled over water. From Kadesh Moses asked the king of Edom for passage, and when he was refused, Israel moved on to Mount Hor. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries identify the site with Ain Kadeis in northeastern Sinai. Many later scholars prefer the nearby, better-watered spring of Ein el-Qudeirat, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Keilah was a walled town in the lowlands of Judah, listed among the cities of Judah's territory with Achzib and Mareshah (Josh 15:44). When Philistines raided its threshing floors, David, after twice asking the LORD, went down with his men, defeated them and rescued the town (1 Sam 23:1–5). The priest Abiathar joined him there with an ephod. Saul saw a chance to trap David inside a town with gates and bars. David asked the LORD and was told that the men of Keilah would hand him over, so he and about six hundred men left, and Saul called off his march (1 Sam 23:6–13). After the exile, two rulers of half the district of Keilah, Hashabiah and Bavai, helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:17–18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet Qila, southwest of Bethlehem. Easton's also mentions an alternative site, Khuweilfeh. The location shown here follows Khirbet Qila.

Kiriath-jearim was a city in the hill country west of Jerusalem. It was one of the four Gibeonite cities that Israel reached in Josh 9:17. It was also called Baalah and Kiriath-baal, and it stood on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin, where it is assigned to Judah. The "Kirjath" listed among Benjamin's towns in Josh 18:28 may be the same place. The Danites camped behind it at a spot they named Mahaneh-dan. After the Philistines returned the ark, the men of the city brought it to the house of Abinadab, where it stayed twenty years until David took it up to Jerusalem. Men of Kiriath-jearim were among those who returned from exile, and the prophet Urijah son of Shemaiah came from there. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kuriet el-'Enab, about 7.5 miles west-northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers its exact position unsettled. The location shown here is approximate.

Libnah was a Canaanite royal city in the Shephelah (lowland) of Judah, near Lachish. Joshua captured it after Makkedah, killed its king and then moved on to Lachish (Josh 10:29–32, 39; 12:15). It was later assigned to Judah and given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 15:42; 21:13). It revolted against King Jehoram of Judah at the same time as Edom (2 Kgs 8:22). Sennacherib of Assyria attacked it after leaving Lachish (2 Kgs 19:8). Hamutal, mother of kings Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, was the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The name means "whiteness." The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Arak el-Menshiyeh, and other proposals include Tell es-Safi and el-Benawy. The location shown here is a rough point in the southern Shephelah, close to Tel Burna, which some modern scholars propose. A wilderness camp also bore this name.

Antioch (Syria) was a major city on the Orontes River, capital of the Roman province of Syria and, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, the third city of the Roman empire after Rome and Alexandria. It is the modern Antakya in southern Turkey. Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death brought the gospel there, and some preached to Greeks. Jerusalem sent Barnabas, who brought Saul, and the two taught there for a year. It was here that the disciples were first called Christians. Nicolas, one of the seven chosen in Jerusalem, was a proselyte from Antioch. Its church sent Barnabas and Saul on their first missionary journey and welcomed them back, and it received the Jerusalem leaders' letter to Gentile believers. Paul returned there after his second journey, and in Gal 2:11 he describes confronting Peter there. This entry treats Galatians as written from Antioch, one of several proposed places.

Benjamin (Territory) was the land allotted by lot to the tribe of Benjamin, lying between Judah to the south and the descendants of Joseph to the north (Josh 18:11). Its northern border ran from the Jordan past Jericho and up through the hill country toward Bethel (Luz). It then descended past Lower Beth-horon and turned to Kirjath-jearim, a city of Judah (Josh 18:12–14). The southern border ran from Kirjath-jearim to the waters of Nephtoah and along the valley of Hinnom just south of Jebus, then went down past En-rogel and En-shemesh to the northern end of the Dead Sea. The Jordan formed the eastern side (Josh 18:15–20). Its cities included Jericho, Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Gibeath and Jebus, which is Jerusalem (Josh 18:21–28). This was a small strip of central hill country north of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "son of the right hand."

East Manasseh (Half-Tribe) was the territory east of the Jordan River settled by half of the tribe of Manasseh. It covered northern Gilead and the former kingdom of Og in Bashan. Moses assigned it after the clans of Machir, Manasseh's son, captured Gilead from the Amorites. Jair took the towns he named Havoth-jair, and Nobah took Kenath (Num 32:39–42; Deut 3:13–15). Josh 13:29–31 describes the territory as running from Mahanaim through all Bashan, including sixty towns of Jair and the cities of Ashtaroth and Edrei. Its people later spread north toward Mount Hermon and fought alongside Reuben and Gad. The Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglath-pileser deported them to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:18, 23, 26). Ezekiel's vision gives Manasseh a single portion beside Naphtali. The region lies in present-day northern Jordan and southern Syria. The location shown here is a central point near the modern Jordan–Syria border.

Elam was an ancient country east of Babylonia. The location shown here is in the lowlands and hills of what is now southwestern Iran, around the modern province of Khuzestan. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as an Assyrian word meaning "high" and links the people to Elam, a son of Shem (Gen 10:22). In Abraham's day Chedorlaomer king of Elam led a coalition of four kings (Gen 14:1, 9). Shushan (Susa), where Daniel saw a vision by the river Ulai, lay in the province of Elam (Dan 8:2). The prophets describe Elam's archers and chariots (Isa 22:6). Isaiah calls on Elam and Media to attack, by context against Babylon (Isa 21:2). Jeremiah, early in Zedekiah's reign, foretold that Elam's bow would be broken and its people scattered, and later restored (Jer 49:34–39). Ezekiel pictures Elam among the nations slain by the sword (Ezek 32:24).

Geba, whose name means "hill," was a town in the territory of Benjamin, also spelled Gaba (Josh 18:24). It was given to the Levites (Josh 21:17; 1 Chr 6:60). In Saul's early reign the Philistines kept a garrison there until Jonathan attacked it (1 Sam 13:3). King Asa fortified Geba with stones and timber taken from Baasha's works at Ramah (1 Kgs 15:22; 2 Chr 16:6). The phrase "from Geba to Beersheba" marked the northern and southern limits of Judah (2 Kgs 23:8). Isaiah names it on the route of an invading army approaching Jerusalem from the north (Isa 10:29). Its people returned after the exile (Ezra 2:26; Neh 7:30; Neh 11:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Jeba, about six miles north of Jerusalem and facing Michmash across a gorge. The location shown here follows that identification. Several other biblical places share the name.

Gezer was an ancient Canaanite royal city in the foothills west of Jerusalem, between lower Beth-horon and the Mediterranean (Josh 16:3). Its king Horam came to help Lachish and was destroyed by Joshua (Josh 10:33). It marked the western edge of Ephraim's territory and was given with its pasturelands to the Levites. Ephraim did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who stayed on and paid tribute (Josh 16:10; Judg 1:29). David pursued the Philistines as far as Gezer, and a later battle with them was fought there (1 Chr 20:4). The parallel in 2 Sam 21:18 calls the place Gob. A pharaoh captured and burned the city and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife, and Solomon then rebuilt it (1 Kgs 9:15–17). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tell el-Jezer (Tell Gezer), and the location shown here follows that identification.

The Holy Place was the outer room of Israel's sanctuary, lying in front of the inner sanctuary, called the "oracle" or Most Holy Place. Heb 9:2 describes the tabernacle's first room as holding the lampstand, the table and the showbread. In Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the ends of the ark's carrying poles could be seen from the Holy Place when the ark was installed, and the cloud filled the house as the priests came out (1 Kgs 8:8–10; 2 Chr 5:9–11). Hezekiah ordered the Levites to clear filth from it after its lamps and incense had been neglected (2 Chr 29:5–7). Ezekiel's temple vision uses the term for the sanctuary and nearby priestly areas (Ezek 42:14; 45:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the tabernacle's Holy Place as 20 cubits long and says it held the golden incense altar. The term applies to more than one sanctuary. The location shown here is the temple site in Jerusalem.

Joppa was an ancient seaport on the Mediterranean coast, listed on the border of Dan's territory (called Japho in Josh 19:46). It served as the landing point for cedar from Lebanon, floated down the coast for Solomon's temple and again for the rebuilding of the temple after the exile, then carried up to Jerusalem (2 Chr 2:16; Ezra 3:7). Jonah went down to Joppa to find a ship bound for Tarshish. In Acts, Peter came from nearby Lydda to Joppa after the death of the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas), and many there believed. He stayed many days with Simon, a tanner whose house was by the sea. While praying in Joppa he saw his vision of a great sheet let down from heaven, and messengers from Cornelius came to fetch him from there. Joppa is the modern Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv, and the location shown here follows that identification.

The Mount of Olives, also called mount Olivet, is the ridge east of Jerusalem, facing the temple across the Kidron Valley. David climbed it weeping and barefoot as he fled from Absalom (2 Sam 15:30). Zechariah foretold that the Lord's feet would stand on it and that it would split from east to west, forming a great valley (Zech 14:4). In the Gospels, Jesus approached Jerusalem by way of Bethphage and Bethany on its slopes, and the crowd of disciples praised God as he came down it (Mark 11:1; Luke 19:29, 37). He sat there with his disciples to speak about the end of the age (Matt 24:3; Mark 13:3). In his last days he spent his nights there (Luke 21:37), and he went there after the Last Supper (Luke 22:39; Mark 14:26). After his ascension the disciples returned from it to Jerusalem, a sabbath day's journey (Acts 1:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern Jebel et-Tur, about 200 feet above the city.

Rabbah, also called Rabbath of the children of Ammon, was the chief city of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan. Deut 3:11 says the giant iron bedstead of Og, king of Bashan, was kept there. It lay beyond the land given to Gad (Josh 13:25). David sent Joab to besiege it, and David stayed in Jerusalem (2 Sam 11:1; 1 Chr 20:1). Joab took the "royal city" and the "city of waters," probably the lower town by its stream, and then called David to capture the rest (2 Sam 12:26–29). Later Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah brought supplies to David at Mahanaim. Amos, Jeremiah and Ezekiel foretold its destruction. It is generally identified with modern Amman, Jordan, which the location shown here follows. A separate Rabbah in Judah, named with Kirjath-jearim (Josh 15:60), has an unknown location.

Issachar was the region allotted to the tribe of Issachar, named after Jacob's son (Gen 30:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'reward.'
