It was the fourth lot drawn when Joshua divided the land. Its border ran by Jezreel, Chesulloth and Shunem, reached Tabor, and ended at the Jordan, and it took in sixteen cities with their villages. This places it mainly in the eastern Jezreel Valley and the hills around it, the area shown here. Manasseh lay to its west and held several towns inside Issachar, including Bethshean, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. Under Solomon it was one of the administrative districts that supplied the royal household, governed by Jehoshaphat son of Paruah. In Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, Issachar receives a strip between Simeon and Zebulun, and one of the city's southern gates bears its name.

Mahanaim was a town east of the Jordan River, near the Jabbok. Its name means "two camps". Jacob gave it the name after meeting God's angels there on his way home (Gen 32:2). It marked a boundary between the lands of Gad and eastern Manasseh (Josh 13:26, 30). It was also given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:38; 1 Chr 6:80). After Saul's death, Abner made Saul's son Ishbosheth king there (2 Sam 2:8, 12). Later David took refuge there during Absalom's revolt, and Barzillai and others brought him food and supplies (2 Sam 17:24, 27; 19:32). Under Solomon it was the seat of a district officer (1 Kgs 4:14). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruin of Mukhumah south of the Jabbok. The rough location shown here places it near the Jabbok a little east of the Jordan Valley.

Ramah was the hometown of Elkanah and Hannah and the home of their son Samuel, the city of Mount Ephraim called Ramathaim-zophim in 1 Sam 1:1. Samuel lived there as judge of Israel and built an altar there. The elders came to him at Ramah to ask for a king, and he returned there after anointing David and after his break with Saul. David fled to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah to escape Saul, and Saul followed and prophesied there. Samuel was buried in his house at Ramah. Several places share this name, and this one's site is disputed. Smith's Bible Dictionary follows the tradition placing it at Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia weighs Beit Rima and Ramallah. The location shown here follows a western identification in the hills northwest of Shiloh, near the modern village of Rantis.

Tirzah was a city in the hill country of central Israel. Its king appears among the Canaanite rulers defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:24). It later served as a royal residence and capital of the northern kingdom. Jeroboam's household lived there (1 Kgs 14:17), and Baasha, Elah, Zimri and Omri reigned from it. Elah was assassinated there by Zimri, who ruled for seven days before Omri besieged the city. According to 1 Kgs 16:18, Zimri then burned the palace over himself. After six years Omri moved the capital to Samaria (1 Kgs 16:23–24). Menahem set out from Tirzah to kill Shallum and seize the throne (2 Kgs 15:14). The Song of Solomon compares the beloved's beauty to Tirzah (Song 6:4). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions Teiasir and Telluza, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds et-Tireh. The location shown here follows the Telluza identification, a village north-east of Nablus.

Ammon was the land of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan River and north of Moab, near the upper Jabbok River. On the way from Egypt, Israel was told not to take it, because it had been given to the descendants of Lot (Deut 2:19, 37). Easton's Bible Dictionary traces the people to Ammon, or Ben-ammi, Lot's son. The Ammonites, ruled by a king (Jer 27:3), later fought Israel. Jephthah subdued them, striking twenty cities from Aroer to Minnith (Judg 11:27, 33). In Jehoshaphat's day they joined Moab and Mount Seir against Judah, but the allies turned on one another (2 Chr 20:10, 22–23). Prophets list Ammon among the nations facing judgment, and Ezekiel foretold that its city Rabbah would become a stable for camels (Ezek 25:5). Nehemiah objected to Jews marrying Ammonite wives (Neh 13:23). The location shown here is Rabbah, the capital, at modern Amman in Jordan.

Arnon was the river, flowing through a deep valley east of the Dead Sea, that formed the border between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north (Num 21:13; Judg 11:18). On their way to Canaan the Israelites went around Moab and camped beyond the Arnon. They then defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites, and took his land from the Arnon north to the Jabbok (Num 21:24; Judg 11:22). Sihon had earlier taken that territory from Moab (Num 21:26). Centuries later the king of Ammon claimed the same land, and Jephthah answered him (Judg 11:13, 26). Balak met Balaam at a Moabite city on the Arnon frontier (Num 22:36). The prophets mention its fords in oracles against Moab (Isa 16:2; Jer 48:20). It is the modern Wadi Mujib in Jordan, which enters the Dead Sea from the east, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean, about 60 miles off the Syrian coast, and still known by that name today. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the Old Testament "Chittim" (Kittim), which the prophets mention as a place linked to Tyre's sea trade and as a source of fine ivory-inlaid goods. In the New Testament it was the home of Barnabas and of Mnason, an early disciple. Believers scattered after Stephen's death preached there, and men from Cyprus were among the first to speak about Jesus to Greeks at Antioch. Barnabas and Saul sailed there from Seleucia at the start of their first missionary journey. After Barnabas and Paul separated, Barnabas returned to the island with Mark. Paul's later voyages passed by it, once sailing in its shelter because of contrary winds.

Great Sea is the biblical name for the Mediterranean Sea, which formed the western border of the land promised to Israel. Numbers sets it as the west boundary, and the northern boundary line also starts from it (Num 34:6–7). Joshua uses it to describe the western limit of the land, toward the sunset, and of Judah's territory, with Philistine towns such as Ashdod and Gaza lying along its coast (Josh 1:4; 15:12, 47). Kings ruling the coastal region facing Lebanon are also mentioned (Josh 9:1). In Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, the Great Sea again marks the west side and the starting or ending point of the northern and southern borders, and its abundant fish are compared to those of a healed Dead Sea (Ezek 47:10, 15, 19–20). The STEPBible Proper Names index notes that it is also called the Sea of the Philistines. The location shown here is a general point in the central Mediterranean.

Jabesh-gilead was a city in Gilead, east of the Jordan River. When it sent no one to the assembly at Mizpah against Benjamin, Israel's forces killed its inhabitants and spared 400 young women, who were given as wives to the surviving Benjamites (Judg 21:8–14). Later Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, and the people were promised help, which by inference from the surrounding chapter came from Saul (1 Sam 11:1, 9). After the Philistines killed Saul, the men of Jabesh-gilead took his and Jonathan's bodies from the wall of Beth-shan and buried them. David praised their kindness and later moved the bones (1 Sam 31:11; 2 Sam 2:4–5; 21:12). The ancient name probably survives in the Wadi Yabis. The exact site is debated. Proposals include ed-Deir and Meriamin near Pella (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The location shown here lies about five miles south of Pella, broadly following Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Jazer (also spelled Jaazer) was an Amorite city east of the Jordan. Moses sent men to spy it out, and Israel took its surrounding villages and drove out the Amorites (Num 21:32). Its land was good for cattle, and the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked for it. Gad rebuilt it (Num 32:1, 35), and it marked part of Gad's border (Josh 13:25). It was later given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:39). Joab's census team passed toward it (2 Sam 24:5), and in David's fortieth year capable men of the Hebronites were found at 'Jazer of Gilead' (1 Chr 26:31). Isaiah and Jeremiah mention it in their laments over Moab's vineyards (Isa 16:8–9; Jer 48:32). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors a ruin about 10 miles west of Amman, while others suggest Yajuz to the north. The location shown here follows a site west of Amman.

Megiddo was a Canaanite royal city on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley, whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:21). It was assigned to Manasseh, but the tribe did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Josh 17:11; Judg 1:27). Deborah's song places the battle against the kings of Canaan 'by the waters of Megiddo' (Judg 5:19). Under Solomon it lay in Baana's district and was among the cities he fortified with forced labor (1 Kgs 4:12; 9:15). King Ahaziah of Judah, wounded by Jehu's men, fled there and died (2 Kgs 9:27). King Josiah was killed at Megiddo confronting Pharaoh Necho, about 609 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 23:29–30; 2 Chr 35:22). Zechariah recalls a great mourning 'in the valley of Megiddon' (Zech 12:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a minority identification with Mujedd'a near Bethshean. The location shown here follows the el-Lejjun identification (modern Tel Megiddo).

The Most Holy Place was the innermost room of the temple, where the ark of the covenant was kept. In Solomon's temple it was an inner chamber, also called the oracle, lined with cedar, twenty cubits square, overlaid with fine gold and closed by gold doors (1 Kgs 6:16; 2 Chr 3:8; 1 Kgs 7:50). Two gold-covered cherubim stood inside, and at the temple's dedication the priests set the ark beneath their wings. 1 Chr 6:49 assigns the work of the place most holy to Aaron and his sons. Ezekiel's visionary temple also has a most holy place measuring twenty cubits square, set within a sacred land allotment. The STEPBible Proper Names index applies the name to the matching room in the tabernacle as well. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, where Solomon's temple stood.

Reuben was the territory given to the tribe of Reuben, descendants of Jacob's eldest son, east of the Jordan River in what is now central Jordan. Moses assigned it to the tribe by families (Josh 13:15). It ran north from Aroer on the Arnon River (probably the modern Wadi Mujib) across the plain around Medeba, with the Jordan as its western edge (Josh 13:16, 23). The land had been the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon and was defeated by Moses along with the Midianite princes (Josh 13:21). Its towns included Heshbon, Dibon, Kirjathaim, Sibmah, Beth-peor and Beth-jeshimoth, and the Reubenites built or rebuilt several of them (Num 32:37). Four of its cities, Bezer, Jahazah, Kedemoth and Mephaath, were given to the Levites (Josh 21:36–37). The location shown here is a central point on the Medeba plateau, near Heshbon.

Ziklag was a town in the Negev, the southern region of Judah. It is listed among Judah's towns (Josh 15:31) and among those given to Simeon (Josh 19:5; 1 Chr 4:30). Later it was held by the Philistines, and Achish, king of Gath, gave it to David, after which it belonged to the kings of Judah (1 Sam 27:6). While David lived there, warriors from several tribes joined him (1 Chr 12:1, 20). Amalekites raided and burned it (1 Sam 30:1, 14). David recovered the captives and sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah (1 Sam 30:26). At Ziklag he heard of Saul's death and had the messenger killed (2 Sam 1:1; 4:10). It was resettled after the exile (Neh 11:28). The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions 'Asluj and Khirbet Zuheilikah. The location shown here follows a site north of Beersheba, near Tel Halif.

Ashkelon was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, a seaport on the Mediterranean coast north of Gaza. Its location is not in doubt: it is the ancient site of Ashkelon in modern Israel, near the present-day city of the same name, and the location shown here matches that site. Judah is said to have taken it early in the period of the judges (Judg 1:18), but it was soon a Philistine city again. It was one of the five cities that sent a golden tumor offering when the Philistines returned the ark (1 Sam 6:17). Samson went down there and killed thirty men to pay off his riddle wager (Judg 14:19). David named it in his lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:20). Jeremiah, Amos, Zephaniah and Zechariah all announced judgment and desolation against it. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is also mentioned in Egyptian records.

Bethany was a village at the Mount of Olives, about fifteen furlongs (roughly 2 miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18). It was the home of Lazarus and his sisters Mary and Martha (John 11:1), and the place where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead. In his last week Jesus lodged at Bethany and went into Jerusalem by day (Matt 21:17; Mark 11:11–12). There, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman poured costly ointment on his head (Mark 14:3; Matt 26:6). John places Jesus at Bethany six days before Passover (John 12:1). It is named with Bethphage on the approach to Jerusalem (Mark 11:1), and Luke says Jesus led his disciples out as far as Bethany when he blessed them (Luke 24:50). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern village of el-Azariyeh, "place of Lazarus," which the location shown here matches. A different Bethany lay beyond the Jordan (John 1:28).

Goshen was a region of Egypt where Jacob and his family settled during the time of Joseph, and where the Israelites lived until the Exodus. Joseph offered it to his family so they could live near him with their flocks and herds (Gen 45:10). Joseph met Jacob there (Gen 46:28–29), and Pharaoh granted it to them as "the best of the land" for their livestock (Gen 47:6). There they prospered and multiplied (Gen 47:27). Exodus says that the plagues of flies and hail spared Goshen (Exod 8:22; 9:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it east of the Nile in the eastern Nile Delta. Easton's links it with Wadi Tumilat, while the encyclopedia connects it with the district around Phakousa. The location shown here, near modern Faqus, follows that second identification. The name is also used for other places, in southern Canaan.

Hazor was a major Canaanite city in northern Israel, described as formerly "the head of all those kingdoms" (Josh 11:10). Its king Jabin gathered a northern coalition against Joshua, who captured Hazor, killed its people and burned it, the only city of that region he burned (Josh 11:1, 11:13). It was later allotted to Naphtali. In the time of the judges another Jabin, reigning in Hazor, oppressed Israel through his commander Sisera (Judg 4:2). Solomon later fortified it with Megiddo and Gezer, and the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured it and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). Several other places share the name. Older works placed it near Kedesh, at Khurbet Harrah (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or Tell Khuraibeh (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The location shown here follows the identification with Tell el-Qedah (Tel Hazor), north of the Sea of Galilee.

Riblah was a city "in the land of Hamath" in Syria that foreign kings used as a military headquarters during campaigns against Judah. Pharaoh Necho held King Jehoahaz in chains there and imposed tribute on Judah (2 Kgs 23:33). Later Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon based himself at Riblah during the siege of Jerusalem. The captured King Zedekiah was brought before him there, and his sons and the nobles of Judah were killed in front of him. Other leading men brought by Nebuzaradan were also executed there (2 Kgs 25:6, 20–21; Jer 39:5–6; 52:9–10, 26–27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Diblath" in Ezek 6:14 should probably be read as Riblah. The same name appears for a point on Israel's boundary in Num 34:11, which Smith's Bible Dictionary treats as a separate place. The location shown here is the village of Ribleh on the east bank of the Orontes River in western Syria, about 35 miles northeast of Baalbek.

River of Arnon is the stream and deep gorge east of the Dead Sea that marked the southern limit of Israel's land beyond the Jordan. Modern versions such as the ESV call it the Valley of the Arnon, because the Hebrew word can mean either a seasonal stream or the ravine it runs through. Israel crossed it to fight Sihon the Amorite king of Heshbon (Deut 2:24). Sihon's land ran from Aroer on its bank to the Jabbok, and the conquered territory east of the Jordan stretched from the Arnon to Mount Hermon. This land was given to Reuben and Gad. A city also stood "in the midst of the river." In 2 Kgs 10:33 it marks the southern edge of the lands that Hazael took from Israel, by inference from the surrounding passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the border with Moab, almost dry in summer, and identifies it with the modern Wadi el-Mujib, which the location shown here follows.

Zobah was an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel in the time of Saul, David and Solomon. Saul fought "the kings of Zobah" (1 Sam 14:47), suggesting it then had several rulers. Under David it was ruled by Hadadezer son of Rehob, whom David defeated as Hadadezer went to secure his border at the Euphrates. David also struck down the Syrians of Damascus who came to help him and took spoil from Zobah. The Ammonites later hired troops from Zobah against David. Rezon, who fled from Hadadezer, became an adversary of Solomon. Igal, one of David's mighty men, was from Zobah. Its exact extent is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it from the eastern slopes of Lebanon toward the Euphrates, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Hamath and Damascus along the Anti-Lebanon. The location shown here follows that area, roughly between modern Homs and Baalbek.

Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece, including the Peloponnesus, with Corinth as its main city. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name once meant a narrow strip on the northern Peloponnesus, but the New Testament always uses it for the larger province. It was governed by a proconsul, rendered "deputy" in the King James Version, and Gallio held that office when Jews in Corinth brought Paul before his judgment seat (Acts 18:12). Apollos later went there and helped the believers (Acts 18:27). Paul addressed 2 Corinthians to the church at Corinth and to all the saints in Achaia, and he called the household of Stephanas its firstfruits (2 Cor 1:1; 1 Cor 16:15). Achaia is often paired with Macedonia, the province to its north, so that the two together cover all of Greece. The churches of both gave money for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Rom 15:26; 2 Cor 9:2).

Haran was a city in Upper Mesopotamia where Terah settled with Abram, Sarai and Lot after leaving Ur of the Chaldees on the way to Canaan, and where Terah died (Gen 11:31–32). Abram left Haran for Canaan at seventy-five, taking his household and the possessions gathered there (Gen 12:4–5). By inference from context this was about 1921 BC. Later Rebekah sent Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran to escape Esau, and on arriving he met shepherds from the town (Gen 27:43; 28:10; 29:4). The Assyrian envoy listed Haran among places conquered by Assyrian kings (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12), and Ezekiel names its merchants among Tyre's trading partners (Ezek 27:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Balikh River, a tributary of the Euphrates, on the east–west caravan route. It is the modern Harran in southeastern Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Kadesh-barnea was a desert oasis on the southern edge of the promised land, an eleven days' journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir (Deut 1:2). After leaving Horeb, Israel crossed the wilderness and arrived here (Deut 1:19). From Kadesh-barnea Moses sent spies, including Caleb, to explore Canaan. When the people refused to go up and take the land, a journey of thirty-eight years followed before they crossed the brook Zered (Num 32:8; Deut 9:23; Deut 2:14; Josh 14:6–7). Later it marked a point on the southern border of the land and of Judah's territory, and the southern limit of Joshua's campaigns (Num 34:4; Josh 15:3; Josh 10:41). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with 'Ain el-Kadeis. The location shown here matches nearby 'Ain el-Qudeirat in northeastern Sinai, the larger spring in the same area.

Lebo-hamath was a place on the far northern edge of the land promised to Israel. The King James Version translates the Hebrew as "the entering in of Hamath," treating it as the approach to the Syrian city of Hamath. Many modern translations read it as a town name, Lebo-hamath. It marks the northern limit of the land the spies explored (Num 13:21), of Israel's assigned border (Num 34:8; Ezek 47:20), and of the territory still unconquered after Joshua (Josh 13:5; Judg 3:3). It became a standard way to describe Israel's full extent, "from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of Egypt" (1 Kgs 8:65; 1 Chr 13:5). Jeroboam II restored the border there (2 Kgs 14:25). The location shown here follows the view that it was the town name, probably modern Lebweh (Labweh) in Lebanon's northern Beqaa Valley.

Mount Hor was a mountain on the border of Edom where the Israelites camped after leaving Kadesh during their wilderness journey. Here God told Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain in full view of the people, and Aaron died there at 123 years old, in the fortieth year after the exodus. From Mount Hor Israel went on by the way of the Red Sea to go around Edom, then camped at Zalmonah. Moses' own death was later compared to Aaron's death on this mountain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Jebel Harun, a prominent two-peaked mountain near Petra in southern Jordan, and notes another view placing it at Jebel Madurah, west of the Arabah. The location shown here follows the Jebel Harun identification. A different Mount Hor on Israel's northern border appears in Num 34:7–8.

Mount Seir was the mountain range given to Esau's descendants, the Edomites, as their homeland (Deut 2:5). It lay on the route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (Deut 1:2), and the Israelites travelled around it for many days during their wilderness journey (Deut 2:1). God forbade Israel to take any of its land. In Hezekiah's time some 500 men of Simeon went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). Under Jehoshaphat, the people of Mount Seir joined Ammon and Moab against Judah and were defeated (2 Chr 20:10, 22). Ezekiel prophesied that Mount Seir and all Idumea (Edom) would be made desolate because it rejoiced at Israel's ruin (Ezek 35:2–15). The location shown here places it in the highlands east of the Arabah, south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. The name is shared with another Mount Seir on Judah's border.

Paddan-aram was the region in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham's relatives lived, in Genesis. It was the home of Bethuel and his son Laban, whose sister Rebekah became Isaac's wife (Gen 25:20). Isaac later sent Jacob there to find a wife among Laban's daughters rather than among the Canaanites (Gen 28:2–7). Jacob's sons were born there, except Benjamin, as was his daughter Dinah (Gen 35:26; Gen 46:15). He became wealthy there before returning to Canaan (Gen 31:18; Gen 33:18). The name probably means "field" or "plain of Aram." Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the district around Haran, and Genesis's other accounts of Jacob's stay call his destination Haran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a site near Damascus. The location shown here follows the Haran identification, near modern Harran in southeastern Turkey.

River, often "the River" in the Hebrew Bible, refers in these passages to the Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia. Deut 11:24 names it outright as the northeastern limit of the land promised to Israel. Balaam's hometown of Pethor lay "by the river" (Num 22:5), probably on the Euphrates. In Joshua's farewell speech the King James Version says "the flood". Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this means the Euphrates, which the Revised Version renders "river". Abraham came from beyond it, and his ancestors served other gods there (Josh 24:3, 14–15). Isaiah pictures Assyria as "them beyond the river" and as its flooding waters (Isa 7:20; 8:7). Later prophets use it as a boundary of future rule (Mic 7:12; Zech 9:10). Because "the river" can mean other rivers elsewhere, the name is shared. The location shown here marks a point on the Euphrates in eastern Syria.

Succoth, meaning "booths", was a city east of the Jordan, in the valley near the Jabbok River. Jacob settled there after parting from Esau. He built a house and made booths for his cattle, which gave the place its name (Gen 33:17). It later fell to the tribe of Gad as part of the former kingdom of Sihon (Josh 13:27). During Gideon's pursuit of the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, the leaders of Succoth refused bread to his weary men. On his return Gideon punished its seventy-seven princes and elders with thorns and briers (Judg 8:5–16). Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kgs 7:46). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Deir Alla, north of the Jabbok. Some have proposed Sakut, west of the Jordan. The location shown here follows Tell Deir Alla. A different Succoth appears in the Exodus account in Egypt.

Aijalon was a town in the low hills northwest of Jerusalem, allotted to the tribe of Dan and given to the Kohathite Levites (Josh 19:42; Josh 21:24; 1 Chr 6:69). The valley of the same name is where Joshua called on the moon to stand still (Josh 10:12). Amorites held on there, though the house of Joseph made them pay tribute. Saul's army drove the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon. Benjamite clan heads living there drove out the people of Gath. Rehoboam fortified it, and the Philistines captured it in the reign of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Yalo, and the location shown here follows that view. The Aijalon in Zebulun where the judge Elon was buried (Judg 12:12) is probably a separate town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Jalun in Galilee.

Aroer was a city on the northern edge of the Arnon gorge, east of the Dead Sea. It marked the southern limit of the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon (Josh 12:2). After Israel took his land, Moses gave the region running north from Aroer to the tribes of Reuben and Gad (Deut 2:36; Deut 3:12; Josh 13:16). Jephthah later cited Israel's long occupation of Aroer and its towns in his dispute with the Ammonites (Judg 11:26). The Syrian king Hazael's conquests reached as far south as Aroer (2 Kgs 10:33). By Jeremiah's time the city belonged to Moab (Jer 48:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify it with the ruins of Ara'ir on the north rim of the Wadi Mujib, and the location shown here matches that site. Other places in the Bible share the name Aroer.

Chaldea was the region of southern Mesopotamia around Babylon, the alluvial plain formed by the Euphrates and Tigris near the Persian Gulf. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Chaldea proper as the southern part of Babylonia, though the name was commonly used for the whole Mesopotamian plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the prophets used the term for all Babylonia. In the Bible it appears mainly in Jeremiah and Ezekiel as the homeland of the Babylonians (Ezek 23:15). It was the land where the exiles from Judah lived, and Ezekiel was brought there in a vision to the captives (Ezek 11:24). Ezekiel also portrays Judah's political dealings with Chaldea as unfaithfulness (Ezek 16:29; 23:16). Jeremiah foretells that Chaldea will be plundered and repaid for the harm its people did in Zion (Jer 50:10; 51:24, 35). The location shown here is in present-day southern Iraq.

Dan was the region allotted to the tribe of Dan, the seventh lot drawn when Joshua divided the land west of the Jordan. It lay between Judah and Ephraim and stretched toward the Mediterranean coast. Its towns included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Jehud and Bene-berak, with its border running toward Joppa (Japho). The Danites could not fully hold this land. The Amorites confined them to the hill country and kept them out of the valley, and by the time of the judges the tribe still had no settled inheritance. Judges 18 goes on to tell how part of the tribe moved north and took Laish, which they renamed Dan. That northern city is a separate place from the region described here. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "judgment" or "he that judges." The location shown here marks the tribe's original southern territory in the Shephelah, west of Jerusalem.

Debir was a Canaanite town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-sepher (Josh 15:15; Judg 1:11) and also Kirjath-sannah (Josh 15:49). Joshua captured it, killed its king and destroyed its inhabitants (Josh 10:38–39), and its king appears in the list of defeated kings (Josh 12:13). It had been home to the Anakim, whom Joshua drove from the area (Josh 11:21). The surrounding passages say Othniel later took the town and won the hand of Caleb's daughter Achsah. Debir became one of Judah's cities and was given with its pasturelands to the priests (Josh 21:15; 1 Chr 6:58). Several places share the name. The site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary points to a valley about three miles west of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors edh-Dhaheriyeh, about 11 miles southwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the edh-Dhaheriyeh identification.

Dibon was a city east of the Jordan, north of the Arnon River, that changed hands between Moab and Israel. An old victory song over Moab mentions it (Num 21:30), which suggests it was originally Moabite. The Gadites and Reubenites named it among the lands they asked Moses for (Num 32:3), and Gad is said to have built or rebuilt it (Num 32:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this is why it was also called Dibon-gad. Joshua, however, lists it among the cities allotted to Reuben (Josh 13:9, 13:17). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it was Moabite again and appears in their oracles against Moab (Isa 15:2; Jer 48:18, 22). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the "Dimon" of Isa 15:9 to be the same city. The name was shared by another place in Judah. The location shown here follows the usual identification with the ruins at modern Dhiban in Jordan, about 3 miles north of the Arnon.

Gerar was an ancient city in the far south of Canaan, near Gaza, named as a point on the Canaanite border (Gen 10:19). Abraham lived there for a time, and its king, Abimelech, took Sarah after Abraham said she was his sister (Gen 20:1–2). During a later famine Isaac also settled in Gerar, where the local herdsmen quarreled with his men over wells. Abimelech, called king of the Philistines, later came from Gerar with his army commander Phichol to make peace with him (Gen 26:1, 6, 20, 26). Centuries afterward King Asa chased a defeated Ethiopian army as far as Gerar and plundered the surrounding towns (2 Chr 14:13–14). The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favored Um Jerrar, southwest of Gaza near the coast. The location shown here matches Tel Haror (Tell Abu Hureira), northwest of Beersheba, which is probably the most widely held identification today.

Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom east of the Jordan, called "Geshur in Syria" (2 Sam 15:8). The Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites, who went on living among them (Josh 13:13). In David's time its king was Talmai son of Ammihud. His daughter Maacah married David and was the mother of Absalom (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). After killing his half-brother Amnon, Absalom fled to his grandfather in Geshur and stayed there three years, until Joab went and brought him back to Jerusalem (2 Sam 13:37–38; 14:23). 1 Chr 2:23 links Geshur and Aram with the capture of the towns of Jair. The name is usually explained as meaning "bridge." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place Geshur in the rugged lava region of el-Lejah in northeast Bashan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Jaulan (Golan) area. The location shown here follows the Lejah identification.

Hormah was a Canaanite town in the far south of Canaan, earlier called Zephath (Judg 1:17). Its name is usually explained as meaning "devoted to destruction" or "banned" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Israelites who tried to enter the land against Moses' warning were driven back as far as Hormah by Amalekites, Canaanites and Amorites (Num 14:45; Deut 1:44). Israel later destroyed the Canaanite cities there and named the place Hormah (Num 21:3). Judges 1:17 credits Judah and Simeon with destroying Zephath. Its king is listed among the kings Joshua defeated, next to the king of Arad (Josh 12:14). The town was assigned to Judah and also to Simeon (Josh 15:30; 19:4; 1 Chr 4:30), and David sent it a share of spoil (1 Sam 30:30). Its site is uncertain, and some place it nearer Arad. The location shown here follows the identification with Zephath at Sebaiteh (modern Shivta), favored by Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Kedar was the land and people of a nomadic Arab tribe in the deserts east of Israel, named after Ishmael's second son (Gen 25:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary places them in northwestern Arabia, and the rough location shown here lies in that region. The biblical writers knew Kedar for its tents, used as an image in Song 1:5 and as a picture of living far from home in Ps 120:5. They also knew it for its flocks and rams, which its princes traded with Tyre (Ezek 27:21; Isa 60:7), and for its archers (Isa 21:17). Isaiah also mentions villages where Kedar lived in the wilderness (Isa 42:11). Jeremiah treats Kedar as a distant eastern land (Jer 2:10) and foretells that Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon would attack it (Jer 49:28). Isaiah announces that its glory would fail within a year (Isa 21:16). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

Kedesh, also called Kedesh in Galilee, was a city in the hill country of Naphtali in northern Israel. It was originally a Canaanite royal city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:22). It was allotted to Naphtali and later set apart as a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person. It was also given, with its surrounding lands, to the Levites (Josh 20:7; 21:32; 1 Chr 6:76). Barak gathered the men of Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh before the battle with Sisera, and Heber the Kenite camped nearby (Judg 4:9–11). Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured it in Pekah's reign and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29). It is usually identified with Tel Kedesh (Kedes), northwest of the Huleh Valley, and the location shown here follows that view. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some place Barak's Kedesh near the Sea of Galilee instead. Several other places share the name.

Kidron was a seasonal torrent valley just outside Jerusalem, on its eastern side between the city and the Mount of Olives, according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. David crossed it weeping as he fled from Absalom toward the wilderness (2 Sam 15:23), and Solomon made crossing it the limit of Shimei's confinement (1 Kgs 2:37). Reforming kings used it as a place to destroy and dump objects of idol worship. Asa burned his mother Maachah's idol there, Hezekiah's Levites carried the temple's uncleanness to it, and Josiah burned cult objects and scattered their dust and ashes there, near graves (1 Kgs 15:13; 2 Chr 29:16; 2 Kgs 23:4–12). Jeremiah foresaw its fields made holy. The location shown here lies near Ekron rather than Jerusalem. It matches a different Kidron from 1 Maccabees, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia possibly identifies with the village of Katrah.

Michmash was a town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, set on the north side of a steep gorge facing Gibeah and Geba to the south. Saul first held it with two thousand men (1 Sam 13:2). The Philistines then camped there in force (1 Sam 13:5, 16), and their garrison guarded the "passage of Michmash," the crossing of the ravine (1 Sam 13:23). Jonathan's attack across this pass, between two crags facing Michmash and Gibeah, led to a Philistine rout that reached Aijalon (1 Sam 14:5, 31). Isaiah pictures an invader from the north leaving his baggage at Michmash on the way to Jerusalem (Isa 10:28). After the exile Benjamites lived there again (Neh 11:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Mukhmas above the Wadi es-Suweinit, about 7 miles north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Rome was the capital of the Roman Empire, in Italy, and is the modern city of the same name. Visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). The emperor Claudius once expelled all Jews from the city, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth (Acts 18:2). Paul long intended to visit Rome. He wrote to the believers there before he came (Rom 1:7, 15), and in Jerusalem he was told he must bear witness there too (Acts 23:11). He finally arrived as a prisoner, about AD 57 by inference from context. He was allowed to live by himself under guard (Acts 28:16), and Acts 28:30 says this lasted two years. Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Philemon and 2 Timothy are traditionally held to have been written there. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the most celebrated city of its day, with about 1,200,000 inhabitants.

Salt Sea is the biblical name for the lake now called the Dead Sea, at the southern end of the Jordan valley. It is also called "the sea of the plain" (Deut 3:17; Josh 3:16; Josh 12:3). Gen 14:3 says the vale of Siddim, where the kings gathered for battle in Abraham's day, "is the salt sea," which suggests the valley was later covered by its waters or lay beside them. The sea marked the southeastern corner and eastern edge of the promised land (Num 34:3, 12). It also formed the eastern border of Judah, and its northern bay, where the Jordan enters, marked the line between Judah and Benjamin (Josh 15:2, 5; Josh 18:19). When Israel crossed the Jordan near Jericho, the water flowing down toward it was cut off (Josh 3:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Arabs call it Bahr Lut, the Sea of Lot.

Zoar was a small city in the plain of the Jordan, earlier called Bela (Gen 14:2, 8). Its king joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim in battle in the vale of Siddim. When Sodom was destroyed, Lot fled to Zoar, and Genesis ties the name, meaning "little," to that episode (Gen 19:22–23). He later left it out of fear and lived in a mountain cave with his daughters (Gen 19:30). Zoar marks the limit of the land Moses viewed before his death (Deut 34:3), and Isaiah and Jeremiah name it as a refuge in their oracles against Moab (Isa 15:5; Jer 48:34). Its site is debated. Josephus, Eusebius and medieval sources place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary and others favor Tell esh-Shaghur north of the sea. The location shown here follows the southern view, probably near modern Safi in Jordan.

Zorah was a town in the low hill country (the Shephelah) west of Jerusalem. It appears among the towns of Judah under the spelling Zoreah (Josh 15:33) and is later listed in the inheritance of Dan, alongside Eshtaol (Josh 19:41). It was the home of Manoah, Samson's father (Judg 13:2). The Spirit of the LORD began to move Samson in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol, and he was buried there in his father's tomb (Judg 13:25; 16:31). Zorah and Eshtaol also sent out the five Danite spies and then the 600 armed men who moved north (Judg 18:2, 8, 11). Rehoboam later fortified it (2 Chr 11:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Sur'ah on a hill above the Valley of Sorek, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Adullam was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed with Jarmuth, Socoh and Azekah. It was once the seat of a Canaanite king defeated by Joshua, and Gen 38:1 already mentions it in the story of Judah. Rehoboam later fortified it, and Jews resettled it after the return from Babylon. Micah names it among towns of Judah facing judgment. It is best known for the nearby cave of Adullam, where David took refuge and his family joined him. Later, three of his chief warriors came to him there while the Philistines camped in the valley of Rephaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the city with the ruin of 'Aid el-Ma, about 13 miles west-southwest of Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near Deir Dubban. The location shown here follows the 'Aid el-Ma identification.

Chebar was a river or waterway in "the land of the Chaldeans" (Babylonia), where some of the Jews taken captive from Judah lived. The priest Ezekiel was among these exiles when he saw his first visions of God beside it (Ezek 1:1–3). Exiles also lived there at Tel-abib (Ezek 3:15). Ezekiel later compared other visions, including the glory of the LORD and the cherubim, to what he had first seen by the Chebar (Ezek 3:23; 10:15, 20, 22; 43:3). Its exact identity is uncertain. Some have linked it with the Habor (Khabur) River of northern Mesopotamia. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Nebuchadnezzar's royal canal joining the Tigris and Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to a navigable canal near Nippur, the modern Shatt en-Nil. The location shown here places it in central Mesopotamia near ancient Nehardea, in line with the royal canal view.

Cilicia was a Roman province on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, between the Taurus Mountains and the Mediterranean, in what is now southern Turkey around Adana. Its chief city, Tarsus, was Paul's birthplace (Acts 21:39; 22:3), and the governor Felix noted that Paul came from this province (Acts 23:34). Jews from Cilicia belonged to a Jerusalem synagogue whose members debated with Stephen (Acts 6:9). Paul went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia soon after his conversion (Gal 1:21). Churches there received the Jerusalem council's letter to Gentile believers (Acts 15:23), and Paul later passed through, strengthening them, at the start of his second journey (Acts 15:41). On his voyage to Rome his ship crossed the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes the region was known for goat's-hair cloth used in tentmaking.

Edrei was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, and one of the two royal cities of Og, king of Bashan, the other being Ashtaroth. Og came out with his whole army to fight the Israelites under Moses at Edrei and was defeated, and his kingdom passed to Israel. Edrei marked a limit of Og's realm, with Salchah at the other end, and it was later assigned to the clan of Machir son of Manasseh. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the ruins of Edr'a at the edge of the rocky Lejah region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers modern Der'a (Daraa) in southern Syria, noted for an ancient underground city, and the location shown here follows that identification. A town of the same name listed among the fortified cities of Naphtali in Josh 19:37 is probably a different place.

Eglon was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, near Lachish. Its king, Debir, joined the alliance of five Amorite kings led by Adonizedek of Jerusalem that attacked Gibeon (Josh 10:3–5). After the coalition's defeat, the five kings were brought out of a cave and put to death (Josh 10:23). Joshua then moved from Lachish to Eglon, besieged and destroyed it, and went on to Hebron (Josh 10:34–37). Eglon appears in the list of defeated kings and was later allotted to Judah (Josh 12:12; 15:39). Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary finds the name preserved at Khirbet Ajlan, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Flinders Petrie's preference for Tell Nejileh, southeast of Tell el-Hesi. The location shown here appears to follow the Tell Nejileh identification. The city is distinct from Eglon, the king of Moab.

The Brook of Egypt (the "river of Egypt" in the King James Version) was a seasonal watercourse at the southwestern edge of Israel's land, between Canaan and Egypt. It marked the end of Israel's promised southern border, which ran from Azmon to the Mediterranean (Num 34:5; Josh 15:4), and it bounded Judah's coastal towns beyond Gaza (Josh 15:47). Israelites came to Solomon's seven-day feast from as far as Hamath in the north to this stream in the south (1 Kgs 8:65; 2 Chr 7:8). The king of Babylon later took all of Egypt's holdings from here to the Euphrates (2 Kgs 24:7). Isaiah and Ezekiel also use it as a southern limit (Isa 27:12; Ezek 47:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word means a wadi, a desert valley that is usually dry but subject to sudden floods. This entry follows the usual identification with Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai. Some have instead linked it with an eastern branch of the Nile.

Jabesh is a shortened form of Jabesh-gilead, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "dryness." When Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, its men offered to submit to him. The elders asked for seven days to seek help from Israel. When the news reached Saul, he promised relief by the next day (1 Sam 11:1–10). After Saul and his sons died, the valiant men of Jabesh marched all night to Beth-shan, recovered the bodies from the wall, burned them, buried the bones under a tree (an oak in 1 Chr 10:12) at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. By inference, they were repaying Saul's earlier rescue. The name probably survives in the Wadi Yabis in northern Jordan. Proposed sites include Tell Abu al-Kharaz and Tell el-Maqlub. The location shown here lies near the lower wadi toward the Jordan Valley.

Jezreel is the name of a city, one of several places in the Bible called Jezreel. Josh 15:56 lists a Jezreel among the towns of the hill country of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it southeast of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unidentified. Ahinoam "the Jezreelitess," one of David's wives, was probably from this Judahite town. She went with David to Gath, was captured and recovered at Ziklag, moved with him to Hebron, and bore his firstborn son Amnon there. The verses grouped here also include the Jezreel near which Israel camped by a spring before fighting the Philistines from Aphek. That Jezreel is usually taken as the northern city and valley of that name. The two may be separate places. The location shown here is a rough one in the north, near the eastern Jezreel Valley, and follows that northern placement.

The Kingdom of Judah was the southern Israelite kingdom that formed when the united monarchy split after Solomon's death. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, kept rule over the Israelites living in Judah's cities, and he gathered the men of Judah and Benjamin in an attempt to win back the northern tribes (1 Kgs 12:17, 21). From his capital at Jerusalem he fortified cities for defence (2 Chr 11:5). Judah later faced threats from its neighbours, including a plot to install the son of Tabeal as king (Isa 7:6). It also faced Sennacherib of Assyria, who captured its fortified cities in Hezekiah's fourteenth year (2 Kgs 18:13). King Josiah removed idolatrous priests and practices from its cities to carry out the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 23:5, 24). The location shown here marks Jerusalem, its capital. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of "Judah" as "the praise of the Lord."

Makkedah was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. After Joshua defeated the five allied Amorite kings at Gibeon, Israel pursued their forces as far as Azekah and Makkedah. The five kings hid in a cave there, and when this was reported, Joshua had them shut inside until the pursuit ended. The Israelite army then returned to Joshua's camp at Makkedah. That same day Joshua captured the city, killed its king and inhabitants, and moved on to Libnah. Makkedah appears in the list of defeated kings and among the lowland towns allotted to Judah. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions Sumeil, near Beit Jibrin, and the Palestine Exploration surveyors proposed el-Mughar, "the caves," near Ekron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no certainty is possible. The location shown here lies in the northern lowland area associated with the el-Mughar view.

Media was an ancient country in what is now western and northwestern Iran, the homeland of the Medes. In the books of Esther and Daniel it is closely joined with Persia. The Persian king's court included the "seven princes of Persia and Media" (Esth 1:14), royal acts were recorded in "the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia" (Esth 10:2), and Daniel's two-horned ram stands for the kings of Media and Persia (Dan 8:20). Isaiah calls on Elam and Media to besiege, which in context is aimed at Babylon (Isa 21:2), and Jeremiah lists the kings of the Medes among nations made to drink the cup of judgment. Ezra records that the decree of Cyrus was found at Achmetha, the Ecbatana of the Greeks, in the province of the Medes. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Persia under Cyrus absorbed Media in the sixth century BC. The location shown here is a central point for the region.

Memphis was the ancient capital of Lower (northern) Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile about 12 miles south of modern Cairo. The location shown here matches the ruins near the village of Mit Rahina. In the King James Bible it appears as Memphis only in Hos 9:6, where the Hebrew is Moph. Elsewhere it is called Noph, a shortened form of its Egyptian name Men-nofer (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The prophets name it among Egypt's leading cities in oracles of judgment. Isaiah says its princes are deceived, and Jeremiah and Ezekiel foretell that it will be laid waste, left without inhabitants and stripped of its idols (Jer 46:19; Ezek 30:13). Jeremiah 44:1 also lists Noph among the places where Jews lived in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the city declined after the Persian king Cambyses attacked it, about 525 BC.

Paran was a desert region south of Canaan, usually called "the wilderness of Paran." Ishmael lived there after leaving Abraham's household, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt (Gen 21:21). After leaving Sinai, the Israelites' guiding cloud stopped there, and they camped there after Hazeroth (Num 10:12; 12:16). Moses sent the spies out from Paran, and they reported back at Kadesh within it (Num 13:3, 26). It is also named as a landmark in Deut 1:1. David went there after Samuel's death (1 Sam 25:1). According to the surrounding passage, Hadad the Edomite and his men passed through it from Midian on their way to Egypt (1 Kgs 11:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the et-Tih plateau of northeastern Sinai, west of the Arabah. The rough location shown here lies farther south, near Wadi Feiran in southern Sinai, a name often linked with Paran.

Shinar was the early Hebrew name for the lowland plain of southern Mesopotamia between the lower Tigris and Euphrates, later known as Babylonia. Genesis names it as the land where Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh, about 1822 BC by inference from context (Gen 10:10). It was also the plain where migrants from the east settled and built Babel and its tower (Gen 11:2). Amraphel king of Shinar joined the eastern kings who fought the cities of the plain (Gen 14:1, 9). The Hebrew behind the 'Babylonish garment' Achan stole is literally 'a garment of Shinar' (Josh 7:21). Later books use the name for the Babylonian realm. Temple vessels from Jerusalem were carried there (Dan 1:2), Isaiah lists it among lands of exile (Isa 11:11), and Zechariah's vision places a house there (Zech 5:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name with Sumer. The location shown here is near ancient Babylon.

Timnah was a town on the northern border of Judah's territory, near Beth-shemesh (Josh 15:10). Judah went up to Timnah (spelled Timnath in the King James Version) to shear his sheep, and Tamar waited for him by the road leading there (Gen 38:12–14). In Samson's day it was a Philistine town with vineyards. Samson saw a Philistine woman there whom he wanted to marry, and a young lion roared at him near its vineyards (Judg 14:1–5). In the reign of Ahaz the Philistines took Timnah and its villages and settled there (2 Chr 28:18). Several places in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Timnah of Genesis may be a different town in the hill country of Judah, but this entry treats it as the same border town. Older dictionaries placed it at Tibneh, west of Beth-shemesh. The location shown here is the nearby Tel Batash in the Sorek Valley.

Topheth (also spelled Tophet) was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech (Jer 7:31). King Josiah defiled it as part of his religious reforms so that the practice would stop (2 Kgs 23:10). Jeremiah was sent there to prophesy. He announced that the place would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, that the dead would be buried there until no room was left, and that Jerusalem itself would be made unclean like Topheth (Jer 19:6–14). The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors "place of burning," while Smith's Bible Dictionary links it to the Hebrew word for a drum and suggests it was once a royal garden. It probably lay at the lower end of the Hinnom Valley, south of the Old City, which is where the location shown here places it.

The Valley of Rephaim was a valley just southwest of Jerusalem, on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. The boundary descriptions in Josh 15:8 and Josh 18:16, where the King James Version calls it "the valley of the giants," place it at the north end near the valley of Hinnom, and this entry also links it with that name. Philistine armies twice spread out in this valley to attack David after he became king, and both times he defeated them (2 Sam 5:18, 22; 1 Chr 14:9). They camped there again while David was at the cave of Adullam, at harvest time (2 Sam 23:13). Isaiah compares coming judgment to gleaning grain there, which suggests it was known as farmland (Isa 17:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west and southwest of Jerusalem and identifies it with el-Bukei'a. The location shown here matches that general area.

n: Valley of the Son of Hinnom
bio: The Valley of the Son of Hinnom was a valley beside Jerusalem, also called the valley of the children of Hinnom. It contained Topheth, a site of high places where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech and Baal (Jer 7:31; 32:35). By inference from the surrounding chapters, kings Ahaz and Manasseh sacrificed their children there (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6), and Josiah later defiled Topheth to end the practice (2 Kgs 23:10). Jeremiah was sent there to announce that it would be renamed the valley of slaughter and filled with burials (Jer 7:32; 19:2, 6). Josh 15:8 places it on Judah's northern boundary. It is usually identified with the modern Wadi er-Rababi, which curves along the west and south of Jerusalem's Old City; the location shown here follows that view. Its Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, gave rise to the later term Gehenna.

Azekah was a fortified town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, listed among Judah's towns next to Socoh (Josh 15:35). Joshua's forces pursued the defeated Amorite kings from Gibeon as far as Azekah, and hailstones fell on the fleeing army along that route (Josh 10:10–11). Before David fought Goliath, the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah (1 Sam 17:1). Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:9). It was one of the last two fortified cities of Judah, with Lachish, still holding out when Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem (Jer 34:7). Jews returning from exile resettled it and its villages (Neh 11:30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Tell Zakariya (Tell Zaqareyeh), on the north side of the Valley of Elah about 3 miles northwest of Socoh. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dug over."

Beth-aven, whose name means "house of nothingness" or "house of wickedness," was a place in the hill country of Benjamin, east of Bethel and near Ai (Josh 7:2). Its wilderness marked part of Benjamin's northern border (Josh 18:12). In Saul's time the Philistines camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven, and the battle that followed Jonathan's attack spread as far as Beth-aven (1 Sam 13:5; 14:23). Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a suggestion of Khirbet An, west of Michmash, and the location shown here lies in that area between Bethel and Michmash. In Hosea the name appears alongside Gilgal and is linked with the calves worshipped there (Hos 4:15; 5:8; 10:5). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take these passages as a mocking name for nearby Bethel, the "house of God" turned into a "house of idols."

Beth-horon was a town in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, on the route down from Gibeon toward the western lowlands. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as two villages, an upper and a lower Beth-horon, about 2 miles apart, linked by a steep ascent; Easton's explains the name as "house of the hollow" or "of the cavern." Joshua's army chased the Amorite kings from Gibeon along this road, and many fled down it and were killed by hailstones (Josh 10:10–11). It marked part of Benjamin's boundary (Josh 18:14) and was a Levitical city with its pasturelands (Josh 21:22; 1 Chr 6:68). A Philistine raiding company headed toward it in Saul's time (1 Sam 13:18), and Amaziah's dismissed soldiers raided towns as far as Beth-horon (2 Chr 25:13). The two sites are usually identified with the modern villages of Beit Ur el-Foqa and Beit Ur et-Tahta. The location shown here lies near the upper village.

Bethsaida was a town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was the hometown of Philip and also of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44), and John 12:21 calls it "Bethsaida of Galilee." Jesus fed the five thousand in a remote place belonging to the town (Luke 9:10). He sent his disciples across the lake toward it by boat (Mark 6:45), and he healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22). Along with Chorazin, it was rebuked for not repenting despite the miracles done in it (Matt 11:21; Luke 10:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of the Jordan where the river enters the lake, in the town that Philip the tetrarch enlarged and renamed Julias. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a view that there were two towns of the name, one on each side of the lake. The location shown here follows the identification with the ruins at et-Tel.

Bozrah was a leading city of Edom, home of Zerah, whose son Jobab became one of the early kings of Edom before Israel had kings (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). The prophets name it as a stronghold of Edom that would face judgment. Isaiah describes a great slaughter there, and also pictures a figure coming from Edom with garments dyed red from Bozrah (Isa 34:6; 63:1). Jeremiah says it will become a desolation and pictures an enemy spreading its wings over it like an eagle (Jer 49:13, 22). Amos speaks of fire devouring its palaces (Amos 1:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it Edom's capital and gives the name's meaning as "sheepfold". Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Busaireh (Buseirah), southeast of the Dead Sea, and the location shown here follows that identification. Other places in the Bible share the name.

Eshtaol was a town in the lowland (the Shephelah), listed among the cities of Judah (Josh 15:33) and also counted within the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Josh 19:41). It is almost always named together with neighboring Zorah. Between the two towns lay the "camp of Dan," where the Spirit of the LORD first began to move Samson. His family later buried him there, in the burial place of his father Manoah (Judg 13:25; 16:31). Eshtaol was also one of the home towns of the Danites who sent out five spies and then six hundred armed men in search of new territory (Judg 18:2, 8, 11). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "narrow pass." It notes two proposed sites: the modern Eshwa (Ashu'a), a short distance east of Zorah, and Kustul, east of Kiriath-jearim. The location shown here follows the Eshwa identification.

Ezion-geber was a city and harbour on the Gulf of Aqaba, the northeastern arm of the Red Sea, always named beside Elath (Eloth) in Edomite territory. During the wilderness journey Israel camped there before moving on to Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, and later passed by it on the way toward Moab. Solomon built a fleet there, and Jehoshaphat's ships, built with the help of an ally to sail for Ophir's gold, were wrecked there before they set out. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries suggest the gulf once reached farther north, placing the city near the spring 'Ain el-Ghudyan, about 10–15 miles up the Arabah valley. The location shown here follows a different view, a site on the present shore at the head of the gulf, near modern Aqaba and Eilat. The name is traditionally explained as "giant's backbone."

Hermon is a high mountain at the northern edge of the land east of the Jordan, marking the far limit of the territory Israel took from the Amorites, which ran from Aroer on the Arnon to Hermon (Deut 4:48). The Sidonians called it Sirion and the Amorites Shenir (Deut 3:9), and it is also called Sion (Deut 4:48). Hivites lived beneath it in the land of Mizpeh (Josh 11:3). Poets drew on it as an image: its dew stands for blessing (Ps 133:3), it is paired with Tabor (Ps 89:12), and it appears beside Lebanon and Amana (Song 4:8). The plural 'the Hermonites' in Ps 42:6 probably refers to its several summits, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains. It is identified with Jebel esh-Sheikh, the snow-capped southern end of the Anti-Lebanon range, about 9,200 feet high. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was the scene of the transfiguration.

The Jabbok is a river east of the Jordan, which it joins roughly midway between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea. It is generally identified with the modern Zarqa River (Nahr ez-Zerqa, "blue river") in Jordan. Jacob crossed its ford by night with his wives, servants and eleven sons on his way back to Canaan (Gen 32:22). The following verses, Gen 32:24–30, place his wrestling with a mysterious figure there. The river later served as a boundary. The Amorite kingdom of Sihon stretched from the Arnon north to the Jabbok, which marked the border of the Ammonites (Num 21:24; Josh 12:2). Israel took this land but kept away from Ammonite territory along the river (Deut 2:37). It was given to Reuben and Gad (Deut 3:16). Centuries later the king of Ammon claimed the land between Arnon and Jabbok, and Jephthah disputed that claim (Judg 11:13, 22).

Kiriath-arba was the earlier name of Hebron, a town in the hill country of Judah. The name means "city of Arba," and Josh 14:15 explains that Arba was a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there, and Abraham mourned her (Gen 23:2). Jacob later came there to his father Isaac at Mamre, where Abraham and Isaac had lived (Gen 35:27). Under Joshua it was listed among the towns of Judah and was named one of the cities of refuge (Josh 15:54; 20:7). Judges 1:10 records that Judah attacked the Canaanites living there and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. After the exile, some people of Judah settled again in Kiriath-arba and its villages (Neh 11:25), so the old name was still in use then. The location shown here is the city of Hebron, known today as al-Khalil in the southern West Bank.

Mesopotamia, meaning "between the rivers," is the Greek name for the land between the Euphrates and Tigris, largely in modern Iraq. In the Old Testament it translates the Hebrew Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean chiefly the northwestern part, near the great bend of the Euphrates. Abraham's servant traveled there to the city of Nahor to find a wife for Isaac (Gen 24:10). Stephen recalled that God appeared to Abraham there before he lived in Haran (Acts 7:2). Balaam came from Pethor in Mesopotamia (Deut 23:4). Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, ruled Israel for eight years until a judge, named Othniel in Judg 3:9, defeated him, about 1418 BC by inference from context (Judg 3:8–10). The Ammonites hired chariots from there against David (1 Chr 19:6), and its residents were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). The location shown here marks a general point within the region.

Mount Hermon is a prominent mountain marking the northern limit of the land Israel took east of the Jordan, which stretched "from the river Arnon unto mount Hermon" (Deut 3:8; Josh 12:1). Og, king of Bashan, ruled in Mount Hermon (Josh 12:5), and Baalgad "under mount Hermon" marked the northern reach of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17; 13:5). The half tribe of Manasseh later spread as far as Hermon (1 Chr 5:23). STEPBible Proper Names notes the alternative names Senir and Sirion (compare Deut 3:9) and links Baal-hermon and Baal-gad with it. It is generally identified with the modern Jabal al-Shaykh on the Syria–Lebanon border, the region's highest peak. The Gospels place the Transfiguration on an unnamed high mountain after Jesus' visit to Caesarea Philippi. Some locate it on Hermon, others on Mount Tabor. This entry follows the Hermon view.

Nebo was a town east of the Jordan, on the plateau north of the Dead Sea, distinct from Mount Nebo and from the Nebo in Judah, though it probably took its name from the nearby mountain. It is listed among the towns of the former Amorite territory that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses for. Reuben rebuilt it and gave it a new name (Num 32:3, 38), and the Reubenite Bela lived as far as Nebo (1 Chr 5:8). Israel camped in the Abarim mountains "before Nebo" (Num 33:47). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it belonged to Moab, and both prophets name it in oracles of mourning and ruin (Isa 15:2; Jer 48:1, 22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that King Mesha of Moab claimed to have captured it from Israel. The location shown here follows the identification with Khirbet el-Mukhayyat, near Mount Nebo.

Taanach was a Canaanite royal city on the southwestern edge of the plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel), almost always named alongside nearby Megiddo. Its king was among those defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:21). Although it lay within Issachar's territory, it was counted to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29), and it was given to the Levites from the half tribe of Manasseh, spelled "Tanach" in Josh 21:25. Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Judg 1:27). The Song of Deborah places the battle against the kings of Canaan "in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo" (Judg 5:19). Under Solomon it belonged to the district of Baana son of Ahilud (1 Kgs 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears in Egyptian records. It is identified with the modern Ta'annek, about five miles southeast of Megiddo, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tekoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem on the edge of the wilderness that runs down toward the Dead Sea. Joab brought a wise woman from Tekoa to persuade David, through a staged plea, to allow Absalom to return (2 Sam 14:2–9). Rehoboam fortified it along with Bethlehem and Etam (2 Chr 11:6). Jehoshaphat's army went out into the wilderness of Tekoa before facing an invasion (2 Chr 20:20), and Jeremiah called for a trumpet to be blown there as a warning of disaster coming from the north (Jer 6:1). The prophet Amos was one of the herdsmen of Tekoa (Amos 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Khirbet Tequ'a, about 6 miles (10 km) south of Bethlehem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Zin was a desert region on the southern edge of Canaan, usually called the wilderness of Zin. Kadesh lay within it (Num 20:1; 33:36), and the Israelites camped there during their wanderings. Miriam died and was buried at Kadesh in Zin. It was also where the dispute at the waters of Meribah took place, which is given as the reason Moses and Aaron could not enter the land (Num 27:14; Deut 32:51). The spies sent from Kadesh explored the land starting from Zin (Num 13:21). Zin also marked the southern boundary of the promised land and of Judah's territory, next to Edom (Num 34:3; Josh 15:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between the Arabah and the plateau of et-Tih, south of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the uplands north and northwest of the wilderness of Paran, in the modern Negev. It is distinct from the wilderness of Sin.

Zoan was an ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt, known to the Greeks as Tanis and probably the modern village of San el-Hagar. The location shown here follows that identification. Num 13:22 notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan. The Psalms set God's wonders in Egypt in "the field of Zoan," which ties the city or its surrounding plain to the events of the exodus. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take this to mean that Pharaoh held court there during his dealings with Moses. Both also link Zoan with the Hyksos capital Avaris, and Easton's with the city of Rameses. Isaiah speaks of the "princes of Zoan" as Pharaoh's foolish counsellors and mentions Judah's envoys there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this by the city's role as a royal capital around 800 to 700 BC. Ezekiel foretells that Zoan will be set on fire.

Ar, also called Ar of Moab, was a leading city or district of Moab on the border near the Arnon valley. During Israel's wilderness journey, God told Moses not to fight the Moabites, because Ar had been given to Lot's descendants (Deut 2:9). Israel passed through the region of Ar, and the Moabites living there were among those who dealt with Israel on the way (Deut 2:18, 29). An old song recalls the streams running down toward Ar, and another describes Sihon's forces from Heshbon burning it (Num 21:15, 28). Isaiah's oracle against Moab opens with Ar laid waste in a single night (Isa 15:1). Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at Rabba, between Kerak and the Wadi Mujib. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a ruin on the floor of the Arnon valley, and notes a view that Ar was a district rather than a city. The location shown here follows the Arnon valley identification.

Arabia was the broad desert region south and east of Israel, roughly the Arabian Peninsula and the Syrian desert to its north. In the Old Testament it is tied to kings and nomadic peoples. The kings of Arabia brought gold and silver to Solomon (2 Chr 9:14). Isaiah addresses an oracle to Arabia that mentions the travelling caravans of Dedan (Isa 21:13). Jeremiah lists its kings among the nations facing judgment (Jer 25:24). Ezekiel names Arabia and Kedar as traders in lambs, rams and goats with Tyre (Ezek 27:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word strictly means the Arab people rather than a country. In the New Testament, Paul went into Arabia after his conversion before returning to Damascus (Gal 1:17), and he places Mount Sinai in Arabia (Gal 4:25). The location shown here is a general point in the northwestern Arabian Peninsula.

Aroer was a city east of the Jordan built by the tribe of Gad (Num 32:34). Joshua 13:25 describes it as "before Rabbah," the Ammonite capital, marking the edge of Gad's territory toward Ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the Aroer from which Jephthah struck the Ammonites as far as Minnith (Judg 11:33). Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to David's census, whose officers camped at Aroer (2 Sam 24:5). Several places share this name, so some passages are uncertain. The Reubenite home in 1 Chr 5:8 may be the Aroer on the Arnon. Smith's thinks "the cities of Aroer" in Isa 17:2 lie farther north. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no matching name has been found near Rabbah, the modern Amman. The location shown here is only a rough estimate near Rabbah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "heath" or "tamarisk."

Arpad was a city in northern Syria, always mentioned in the Bible alongside Hamath. Its name also appears as Arphad. In the Rabshakeh's speech to Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day, the Assyrians cited Arpad, its gods and its king as examples of peoples who could not withstand Assyria (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 36:19; 37:13). Isaiah uses it in a list of cities conquered by Assyria (Isa 10:9), and Jeremiah's oracle about Damascus pictures Hamath and Arpad dismayed at bad news (Jer 49:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary says Arpad fell to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser after a three-year siege, dating this to 742 BC, and identifies it as Tell Erfud. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as apparently dependent on Damascus. The location shown here is a mound north of Aleppo, probably the site known today as Tell Rifaat.

Ashtaroth was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, where Og king of Bashan lived and ruled alongside Edrei (Deut 1:4; Josh 12:4; Josh 13:12). Israel's defeat of Og under Moses was remembered as a well-known victory, and the Gibeonites mentioned it when they sought a treaty with Joshua (Josh 9:10). After the conquest the city was assigned to half of the clan of Machir son of Manasseh (Josh 13:31). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levite family of Gershom (1 Chr 6:71). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Beeshterah in the parallel Levitical list (Josh 21:27) as a shortened form of the same name. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the city was named after the goddess Ashtoreth. Easton's identifies it with Tell Ashterah in the Hauran region of southern Syria, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Babylonia was the region of southern Mesopotamia, the alluvial plain watered by the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, with Babylon as its chief city. It lies in what is now central and southern Iraq. In the verses shown here, the King James text says simply "Babylon," but the sense is the wider land where the exiles from Judah lived. Ezra 7:16 calls it "the province of Babylon," a district of the Persian Empire by that time. Sheshbazzar brought the temple vessels from there to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:11). Under Darius, the royal archives kept in Babylon were searched for an earlier decree (Ezra 6:1). Later Ezra the scribe led a group back from Babylonia to Jerusalem in the reign of Artaxerxes, a journey of about four months (Ezra 7:6, 9; 8:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the land as a fertile, canal-irrigated plain bounded by Assyria, Elam, the southern marshes and the Syrian desert.

Bahurim was a village east of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, on the road down toward the Jordan valley. Here Abner sent back Michal's husband, who had followed her weeping as she was returned to David (2 Sam 3:16). When David fled from Absalom, Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim from the family of Saul, came out and cursed him (2 Sam 16:5). He later came down to meet David at the Jordan, and David spared him (2 Sam 19:16; 1 Kgs 2:8). David's messengers Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well in a courtyard there (2 Sam 17:18). Azmaveth "the Barhumite," one of David's warriors, was probably also from Bahurim (2 Sam 23:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the Talmud's identification with modern Almit, near Anata. The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement east of Jerusalem.

Beeroth, whose name means "wells," was a city north of Jerusalem. It was one of four cities, with Gibeon, Chephirah and Kirjath-jearim, whose people made a peace treaty with Joshua after Israel's arrival. The wider passage identifies them as Hivites who won the treaty by deception (Josh 9:17). The city was later assigned to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh 18:25; 2 Sam 4:2). It was the home of Rimmon, whose sons Baanah and Rechab served as captains under Saul's son Ish-bosheth, and of Naharai, armourbearer to Joab (2 Sam 23:37). Men of Beeroth were among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:25; Neh 7:29). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Bireh, about 10 miles north of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a site northwest of Gibeon instead. The location shown here follows the el-Bireh identification.

Corinth was a Greek city on the isthmus joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece, about 48 miles west of Athens according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The location shown here is the site of ancient Corinth, near the modern town. Its harbors made it a major trading center, and the city of Paul's day was a Roman colony rebuilt after its destruction in 146 BC. Paul came there from Athens (Acts 18:1) and founded a church, to which he later wrote 1 and 2 Corinthians, the second also addressed to believers throughout Achaia (2 Cor 1:1). Apollos later worked there (Acts 19:1), Paul delayed a return visit to spare the church (2 Cor 1:23), and Erastus stayed there (2 Tim 4:20). By inference, 1 and 2 Thessalonians were written from Corinth during Paul's first stay, dated here to about AD 49. Easton's places his arrival in AD 51 or 52.

Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa, west of Egypt, in the region Acts 2:10 calls the parts of Libya around Cyrene. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Greek colonists founded it about 630 BC and that it later had a large Jewish population. Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was coming in from the country when Roman soldiers forced him to carry Jesus' cross. Jews and proselytes from the area around Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost, and Acts 6:9 mentions a Jerusalem synagogue of Cyrenians. Men of Cyprus and Cyrene later preached about Jesus to Greeks at Antioch, and Lucius of Cyrene was among the prophets and teachers of the church there. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries link the city with the Tripoli region. The location shown here is the site of its ruins near modern Shahhat in eastern Libya.

Dedan was an Arabian people and region known for trade, according to the STEPBible Proper Names.
