Ezekiel lists the men of Dedan among the merchants of Tyre, bringing ivory tusks and ebony and trading in saddlecloths for riding (Ezek 27:15, 20). It is also paired with Sheba as a trading people (Ezek 38:13). The prophets include Dedan in judgements on neighbouring nations. Jeremiah names it alongside Tema and Buz (Jer 25:23) and warns its people to flee when disaster comes on Edom (Jer 49:8). Ezekiel says Dedan will fall by the sword along with Edom, from Teman onward (Ezek 25:13). Genesis names a Dedan both among the descendants of Cush and among Abraham's descendants through Keturah, and the people are probably named after one of them. The location shown here is the oasis of Al-Ula in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the usual identification of ancient Dedan.

East, in the phrases "the children of the east" and "the men of the east," refers to the peoples of the desert lands east of Israel rather than to a single town. In Judges they joined the Midianites and Amalekites in raiding Israel after the crops were sown. They gathered in the valley of Jezreel with camels "without number," and in the account of Gideon's campaign 120,000 of them fell, leaving about 15,000 with Zebah and Zalmunna at Karkor (Judg 8:10). In Ezekiel, God declares that Ammon will be handed over to the men of the east as a possession. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains that the Hebrew term (kedem) means "in front" and covers the lands just east of Palestine: Arabia, Mesopotamia and Babylonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies these people as Arab nomad tribes. The location shown here is a rough point east of the Jordan, near modern Amman, and marks a general region rather than an exact site.

Engedi was a town in the wilderness of Judah on the western shore of the Dead Sea, listed among Judah's cities in Josh 15:62. Its name means "fountain of the kid" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries), and it is identified with the spring and oasis of modern Ein Gedi (Ain Jidy), which the location shown here matches. David hid in strongholds in the wilderness of Engedi while Saul pursued him. In Jehoshaphat's reign, invaders from Ammon, Moab and Mount Seir gathered there, and 2 Chr 20:2 equates it with Hazazon-tamar, the Amorite settlement attacked by Chedorlaomer in Gen 14:7. The Song of Songs mentions its vineyards and henna blossoms. In Ezekiel's vision of the healed Dead Sea, fishermen spread their nets from Engedi to Eneglaim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes its warm springs, palm groves and cliff-side caves.

Galatia was a region in central Asia Minor, in modern Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that its name comes from Gaulish (Celtic) settlers who arrived about 280 BC, and that it became a Roman province in 25 BC. Paul passed through "the region of Galatia" with Phrygia on his second journey (Acts 16:6). He later went through it again, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:23). He wrote to "the churches of Galatia" (Gal 1:2) and directed them about a collection for the saints (1 Cor 16:1). Crescens later went there (2 Tim 4:10), and Peter addressed scattered believers in Galatia and neighboring provinces (1 Pet 1:1). Scholars differ over whether the name means the old Gaulish territory around Ankara in the north or the larger Roman province, which also included southern cities such as Iconium and Lystra. The location shown here, in the south near Iconium, fits the wider provincial sense.

Iconium was a city in south-central Asia Minor, modern Konya in Turkey, where Paul and Barnabas preached on the first missionary journey. They came there after being driven out of Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51). In the synagogue at Iconium, a great number of Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1). Opposition then forced the missionaries on to Lystra, and Jews from Antioch and Iconium followed them there and stirred up a crowd that stoned Paul (Acts 14:19). Paul and Barnabas later returned through Iconium to strengthen the believers (Acts 14:21). Timothy was well spoken of by the believers there (Acts 16:2), and 2 Tim 3:11 recalls Paul's sufferings in the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the capital of Lycaonia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some ancient writers counted it as Phrygian and places it in the Roman province of Galatia.

Jarmuth was a Canaanite city in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. Its king, Piram, joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem and the kings of Hebron, Lachish and Eglon in attacking Gibeon after it made peace with Israel. Joshua defeated the five kings, and they were later brought out of the cave where they had hidden. The surrounding narrative says they were put to death. Jarmuth appears among the cities whose kings Joshua defeated and was later allotted to Judah, listed with Adullam, Socoh and Azekah. After the exile, people of Judah settled there again. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet el-Yarmuk (Tel Yarmut), about 8 miles north-northeast of Beit Jibrin, and the location shown here follows that identification. Another Jarmuth, in Issachar, is a separate place.

Laodicea was a city of the Roman province of Asia in the Lycus valley, near Colossae and Hierapolis. Writing to the Colossians, Paul speaks of his concern for those at Laodicea who had not seen him in person (Col 2:1) and of Epaphras's zeal for them (Col 4:13). He greets the believers there, along with Nymphas and the church in his house. He asks that his letter be read in Laodicea and that the Colossians read "the epistle from Laodicea" (Col 4:15–16). That letter's identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes Ussher's view that it was the circular letter known as Ephesians. Laodicea is the last of the seven churches of Asia addressed in Revelation (Rev 1:11; 3:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says Antiochus II founded it, naming it after his wife Laodice. Its ruins, shown here, lie near modern Denizli, Turkey.

Luz was the earlier name of the Canaanite city that became Bethel, in the hill country north of Jerusalem. Jacob named the place Bethel after his dream there, though the city was first called Luz (Gen 28:19). He later returned there with his household (Gen 35:6) and told Joseph that God Almighty had appeared to him and blessed him at Luz (Gen 48:3). In Joshua, Luz marks the boundary between Joseph's descendants and Benjamin (Josh 16:2; 18:13), and the house of Joseph scouted it before taking it (Judg 1:23). Because Josh 16:2 speaks of going 'from Bethel to Luz,' some treat them as separate places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Bethel first named a nearby sanctuary whose name eventually replaced the town's. The location shown here places Luz at Bethel, probably near modern Beitin. A different Luz was later founded in the land of the Hittites (Judg 1:26).

Lystra was a city of Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, where Paul and Barnabas fled after being threatened at Iconium (Acts 14:6). There Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth (Acts 14:8). According to the wider chapter, the crowd took Barnabas and Paul for the gods Jupiter and Mercury and tried to offer sacrifices to them. Soon afterward Jews from Antioch and Iconium stirred up the people, and Paul was stoned and left for dead. After going on to Derbe, the missionaries came back through Lystra to strengthen the disciples (Acts 14:21). On a later journey Paul found Timothy there, a disciple well spoken of by the believers (Acts 16:1–2). Paul later recalled his sufferings at Lystra (2 Tim 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary placed it at the ruins of Bin-bir-Kilisseh. The location shown here follows the identification with a mound near Hatunsaray, south of modern Konya, Turkey.

Machpelah was a cave, together with the field around it, near Hebron in Canaan, described as lying "before Mamre" (Gen 23:17, 19). The name is usually taken to mean "double," and the Greek Septuagint calls it the "double cave" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Abraham bought the field and cave from Ephron the Hittite as a family burial place and buried Sarah there (Gen 23:9, 19). His sons Isaac and Ishmael later buried Abraham there, about 1821 BC by inference from context (Gen 25:9). Jacob asked to be buried there, noting that Isaac, Rebekah and Leah already lay there (Gen 49:30–31), and his sons carried his body from Egypt to the cave (Gen 50:13). Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition places the cave beneath the massive walled enclosure known as the Haram in Hebron, which some date to Herod's time (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The location shown here follows that identification.

Mamre was a place near Hebron in Canaan, closely tied to Abraham and his family. Genesis even equates it with Hebron, also called the city of Arbah (Gen 23:19; Gen 35:27). The cave of Machpelah, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a family burial place, lay in a field described as "before Mamre," meaning facing it or east of it. Sarah, Abraham and later Jacob were buried there (Gen 23:17–19; Gen 25:9; Gen 49:30; Gen 50:13). Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, where Abraham and Isaac had lived. By inference from the surrounding account, Isaac died there, about 1716 BC by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as the "oak grove" of Mamre, named after Abraham's Amorite ally. Proposed sites include Ballatet Selta west of Hebron, er-Rameh, and Khirbet Nimreh north of it. The location shown here lies a short distance north of Hebron.

Mareshah was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It is listed with Keilah and Achzib among the towns allotted to the tribe (Josh 15:44). Rehoboam later fortified it as one of his defensive cities (2 Chr 11:8). When Zerah the Ethiopian advanced with a vast army as far as Mareshah, King Asa met him in battle in the nearby valley of Zephathah (2 Chr 14:9–10). The prophet Eliezer son of Dodavah, who condemned Jehoshaphat's shipbuilding alliance with Ahaziah, came from Mareshah (2 Chr 20:37). Micah addresses its inhabitants in his lament over the towns of Judah (Mic 1:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the ruin el-Mer'ash near Beit Jibrin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, drawing on excavations, locates it at Tell Sandahannah, about a mile south of Beit Jibrin. The location shown here follows the Tell Sandahannah identification.

Migdol, meaning “tower,” is the name of a place on Egypt’s eastern frontier. During the Exodus the Israelites camped before Pihahiroth, “between Migdol and the sea,” facing Baalzephon (Exod 14:2; Num 33:7). Jeremiah names a Migdol as one of the Egyptian towns where Jews lived after the fall of Jerusalem, listing it with Tahpanhes and Noph (Memphis) (Jer 44:1; 46:14). In Ezek 29:10 and 30:6 the KJV reads “the tower of Syene,” but Easton’s Bible Dictionary takes the phrase as “from Migdol to Syene,” meaning from Egypt’s northern border to its southern one. Smith’s Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguish two places: an Exodus campsite near the head of the Red Sea, and a fortified town about 12 miles from Pelusium. The location shown here follows the northern frontier site near Pelusium.

Millo was a fortification within ancient Jerusalem, closely linked with the City of David. It already existed when David took the city, since he built "from Millo and inward" (2 Sam 5:9; 1 Chr 11:8). Solomon raised forced labor to build it alongside the temple, his palace and the city wall, and his work on it is mentioned in the context of Jeroboam's revolt. Hezekiah later repaired it while strengthening Jerusalem's defenses. The name probably means "filling," which suggests an earth-filled rampart or terrace. The Greek Septuagint translates it "Akra," meaning citadel. Its exact position is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the north side of the city, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it on the southeastern hill south of the temple, and G. A. Smith suggested a site near Ophel's south end. The location shown here follows a site at the northern end of the City of David ridge, just south of the Temple Mount.

Mizpah was a place in Gilead, east of the Jordan, named when Laban and Jacob parted and set up a heap of stones as a witness between them, with Laban saying, "The LORD watch between me and thee" (Gen 31:49). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "watchtower." In the time of the judges the Israelites camped at Mizpah against the Ammonites. There the people made Jephthah their leader, and he repeated his terms before the LORD. Jephthah lived at Mizpah, and his daughter came out of his house to meet him when he returned from battle (Judg 11:34). Hosea later named Mizpah, alongside Tabor, as a place where Israel's leaders had been "a snare." Several places share this name. Easton's Bible Dictionary equates this one with Ramath-mizpeh. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is in northern Jordan near modern Ramtha.

Netophah was a town in Judah, closely linked with Bethlehem. It is best known through the men called Netophathites. Two of David's mighty men came from there: Maharai and Heleb (or Heled) the son of Baanah (2 Sam 23:28–29; 1 Chr 11:30). Maharai, of the Zerahite clan, also commanded the division of David's army that served in the tenth month (1 Chr 27:13). After the exile, 56 men of Netophah returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:22). Nehemiah's parallel list counts the men of Bethlehem and Netophah together, which suggests the two towns were near each other (Neh 7:26). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible link with Nephtoah and an echo of the name at Beit Nettif in the Shephelah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Conder place the town at Khirbet Umm Toba, northeast of Bethlehem. The location shown here follows the Umm Toba identification.

Nob was a city of priests near Jerusalem in the time of Saul. David came there alone while fleeing Saul and was met by the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub (1 Sam 21:1). Doeg the Edomite saw this and reported it to Saul, who summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of Nob. Afterward the city was put to the sword, its men, women, children and livestock alike (1 Sam 22:9, 11, 19). Nob is later listed beside Anathoth among towns resettled after the exile (Neh 11:32). In Isaiah it is the last halt of an advancing army, a place from which Jerusalem could be seen (Isa 10:32). Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions el-Isawiyeh, the northern summit of the Mount of Olives, and Nebi Samwil. The location shown here follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which places it just north of Jerusalem near the Mount Scopus ridge.

Philistia was the land of the Philistines, the coastal plain along the Mediterranean in southwest Canaan. The Hebrew name, Pelesheth, appears in the King James Version as "Philistia" in the Psalms and as "Palestina" in Exod 15:14 and Isa 14:29–31. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a fertile plain about 40 miles long, between Gerar and Joppa, lying on the main route between Egypt and Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia names its five chief cities as Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. In the Song of Moses its inhabitants are said to tremble at Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Psalms 60 and 108 name it among the neighbouring nations God will triumph over, and Ps 87:4 lists it among the nations whose people are counted as born in Zion. Isaiah warns all Philistia not to rejoice that the rod that struck it is broken.

Saron is the Greek form of Sharon used by the King James Version in Acts 9:35. It names the broad coastal plain between the central hill country and the Mediterranean, the district in which Lydda stood. After Peter healed the paralysed Aeneas at Lydda, the people living there and in Saron turned to the Lord. In the Old Testament, Sharon was grazing land. Royal herds under Shitrai the Sharonite fed there in David's time (1 Chr 27:29), and Isaiah pictures it as a fold for flocks (Isa 65:10). The plain was known for its fertility and beauty. It is paired with Lebanon and Carmel (Isa 33:9; 35:2) and recalled in the 'rose of Sharon' (Song 2:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a separate Sharon east of the Jordan (1 Chr 5:16). The location shown here points to the coastal plain in general rather than a single site.

Sepharvaim was a city whose people the king of Assyria resettled in the cities of Samaria after the Israelites were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). The Sepharvites burned their children in fire to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech (2 Kgs 17:31). Sennacherib's officials later named it among the cities whose gods and king had failed to stand against Assyria, as a warning to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 36:19; 37:13). Its location is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Sippar on the Euphrates, southwest of modern Baghdad, and read the name as "the two Sipparas." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that its place in the lists, after Hamath, could point to Syria, and mentions a suggested link with Sibraim near Hamath. The location shown here is a rough placement in central Mesopotamia, following the Babylonian identification.

Shephelah is a Hebrew name meaning "lowland." It refers to the region of low, rolling hills between the Judean mountains to the east and the coastal plain to the west. The King James Version translates it variously as "vale," "low plains" and "low country." The sycamore-fig trees that grew there in abundance became a byword for plenty, and Solomon was said to make cedars as common as those trees (1 Kgs 10:27; 2 Chr 1:15). David appointed an overseer for its olive and sycamore trees (1 Chr 27:28), and Uzziah kept herds there (2 Chr 26:10). Under Ahaz the Philistines invaded its towns, including Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Socho and Timnah (2 Chr 28:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes hills of soft limestone, usually 500 to 800 feet high, crossed by valleys that gave access from the plain. It notes debate over whether the Philistine plain was included. The location shown here marks the general region.

Shur, meaning "wall," was a desert region on Egypt's northeastern edge, between Egypt and southern Canaan. The angel found the fleeing Hagar at a spring "in the way to Shur" (Gen 16:7), and Abraham later lived between Kadesh and Shur (Gen 20:1). It often marks a boundary. Ishmael's descendants lived from Havilah to Shur, "before Egypt" (Gen 25:18). Saul struck the Amalekites as far as Shur (1 Sam 15:7), and David raided peoples living toward it (1 Sam 27:8). After crossing the Red Sea, Israel went three days through the wilderness of Shur without water (Exod 15:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary equates this with the wilderness of Etham. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to an Egyptian frontier wall. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the desert east of the Gulf of Suez. The location shown here, in northwestern Sinai, follows the view of a desert just east of Egypt's border.

Teman was a region, and probably also a town, in Edom, in what is now southern Jordan. The prophets name it alongside Bozrah and "the mount of Esau," sometimes as a stand-in for Edom itself (Amos 1:12; Obad 1:9). Jeremiah asks whether wisdom has vanished from Teman, which suggests it was known for its wise men (Jer 49:7). Eliphaz "the Temanite" in Job probably came from there. Gen 36:11 names a Teman as Esau's grandson, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the region to be named after him. The name means "south." Several prophets announce its desolation, while Habakkuk pictures God coming from Teman (Hab 3:3). Its exact site is unknown. Eusebius placed a town of that name about 15 miles from Petra. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries place it in southern Edom, and the ISBE argues for the north. The location shown here, near modern Ma'an, follows the southern placement.

Thessalonica was a major city of Macedonia at the head of the Thermaic Gulf, today the Greek city of Thessaloniki. Paul came there on his second missionary journey after passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, and preached in its Jewish synagogue (Acts 17:1). The uproar that followed, about AD 48 by inference from context, drove him on to Berea. The Bereans were contrasted favourably with the Thessalonian Jews, and some of those Jews followed Paul to Berea to stir up the crowds (Acts 17:11, 13). Aristarchus, Paul's companion on the voyage to Rome, was a Macedonian from Thessalonica (Acts 27:2). The Philippian church sent Paul support more than once while he was there (Phil 4:16), and Demas later left Paul to go there (2 Tim 4:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the city was named after Cassander's wife Thessalonica and was a provincial capital under Rome.

Troas was a port city on the Aegean coast of Mysia in northwest Asia Minor, a few miles south of ancient Troy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its full name as Alexandria Troas and notes it was a Roman colony. Paul came down to Troas on his second journey, and from there he sailed straight to Samothrace and Neapolis, bringing the gospel to Macedonia (Acts 16:8, 11). By inference from context, this is where he saw the vision of the man of Macedonia. On a later journey his companions waited for him at Troas, and he stayed there seven days (Acts 20:5–6). The parallel narrative in Acts 20 places the raising of Eutychus there. Paul also describes a door opened for preaching at Troas (2 Cor 2:12), and he left his cloak, books and parchments there with Carpus (2 Tim 4:13). Its ruins, known as Eski Stamboul, lie on the Turkish coast near the location shown here.

Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Carmel and Juttah among the towns of Judah's tribal territory (Josh 15:55). It is best known from David's flight from Saul. David stayed in strongholds and a wood in the nearby wilderness of Ziph, and Saul searched for him there day after day (1 Sam 23:14–15). On a later occasion Saul brought three thousand chosen men into the same wilderness to hunt him (1 Sam 26:2). Rehoboam later fortified Ziph as one of the defended cities of Judah (2 Chr 11:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Zif, a prominent hill about 4–5 miles southeast of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with at least one other town in Judah, which is a separate place.

Abarim was a mountainous region east of the Jordan, in the land of Moab, facing Jericho. The name means "regions beyond" or "the parts across," probably because, seen from Canaan, these highlands lay across the Jordan and the Dead Sea. Israel camped in "the mountains of Abarim, before Nebo" and then went down to the plains of Moab by the Jordan (Num 33:47–48). God told Moses to climb this range to Mount Nebo and view the land promised to Israel (Num 27:12; Deut 32:49). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Nebo as one of its summits. In Jer 22:20 the King James Version translates the word as "the passages," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it there as the name Abarim, a region listed alongside Lebanon and Bashan. How far north the name reached is uncertain. The location shown here is in the hills near Mount Nebo, in present-day Jordan.

Admah was one of the cities of the plain, always named alongside Zeboim and grouped with Sodom and Gomorrah. Gen 10:19 lists it at the edge of Canaanite territory. In Abraham's time its king, Shinab, joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar) in battle against an alliance of eastern kings in the Vale of Siddim (Gen 14:2, 8). Deut 29:23 says the LORD overthrew it in his anger together with Sodom, Gomorrah and Zeboim, leaving a land of brimstone and salt. Hos 11:8 uses Admah and Zeboim as examples of total destruction. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that it is the Adam of Josh 3:16, near the Damieh ford of the Jordan. The location shown here follows a placement near the southern end of the Dead Sea. The name probably means "red" or "earthy."

Aram was the land of the Arameans, the highland region stretching from northeast of Israel toward the Euphrates, which the King James Version often translates as "Syria." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "highlands" and notes that it roughly matches the Syria and Mesopotamia of Greek and Roman times. Balaam was brought from Aram, "out of the mountains of the east" (Num 23:7). Jacob fled there and kept sheep to win a wife (Hos 12:12), which Genesis places at Laban's home in Paddan-aram. The name also covered smaller Aramean states. David put garrisons in "Syria of Damascus" (2 Sam 8:6), Absalom stayed at "Geshur in Syria" (2 Sam 15:8), and Geshur and Aram took towns from the descendants of Machir (1 Chr 2:23). Because the term covers a wide area, the location shown here is only a rough central point in the Syrian interior toward the Euphrates.

Athens was the leading city of Attica in Greece, described in Easton's Bible Dictionary as the most celebrated city of the ancient world and a seat of Greek literature and art. It is the same city as modern Athens, the capital of Greece. Paul arrived there after being escorted from Berea and sent word for Silas and Timothy to join him quickly (Acts 17:15). While he waited, he was troubled to see the city full of idols (Acts 17:16). He spoke to the Athenians on Mars' Hill, the Areopagus, opening with the remark that they were very religious (Acts 17:22). From Athens he went on to Corinth (Acts 18:1). Paul later wrote that he had chosen to stay behind at Athens alone (1 Thess 3:1). The visit is placed about AD 48, an estimate inferred from context, during what Easton's calls his second missionary journey.

Beth-shean was a Canaanite city at the eastern end of the Jezreel Valley, west of the Jordan. It lay within the territory of Issachar but was assigned to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29). Its inhabitants had iron chariots, which the tribes of Joseph gave as a reason they could not take the valley (Josh 17:16), and Manasseh did not drive them out (Judg 1:27). In Solomon's time it gave its name to an administrative district under Baana son of Ahilud (1 Kgs 4:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a shortened form, Beth-shan, in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, where the Philistines fastened the bodies of Saul and his sons to its walls. It says the city was later called Scythopolis. It is identified with modern Beisan (Beit She'an), about 12 miles south of the Sea of Galilee, and the location shown here follows that identification.

The Corner Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem, probably near a corner of the city's defenses, as its name suggests. When Jehoash king of Israel defeated and captured Amaziah king of Judah, he broke down 400 cubits (roughly 180 meters) of Jerusalem's wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate (2 Kgs 14:13; 2 Chr 25:23). Since the Ephraim Gate faced north, the Corner Gate is usually placed at the northwest corner of the city, though its exact site is uncertain. Uzziah later built and fortified towers at the Corner Gate (2 Chr 26:9). The prophets used it as a landmark: Jeremiah foresaw the city rebuilt from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate (Jer 31:38), and Zechariah included it among the boundaries of a restored Jerusalem (Zech 14:10). The location shown here marks a general point within Jerusalem, not a precisely identified site.

Crete is a large, mountainous island in the Mediterranean that closes off the Aegean Sea to the south. The ship carrying Paul to Rome struggled against the wind past Cnidus and then sailed along Crete's southern side, in the lee of the island, rounding Cape Salmone on its eastern tip (Acts 27:7). Because the harbor where they had stopped was poorly suited for wintering, most of those aboard wanted to reach Phenice, another Cretan harbor, and they set out along the coast when a gentle south wind blew (Acts 27:12–13). A violent storm then drove them off course, and Paul later told them they should have listened to him and stayed at Crete (Acts 27:21). In his letter to Titus, Paul says he left Titus on Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every city (Titus 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the island was once known for its "hundred cities."

Elealeh was a town east of the Jordan, in the pastoral highlands north of the Dead Sea, always mentioned alongside nearby Heshbon. It was among the places in the land taken from the Amorites that Reuben and Gad asked for because it suited their livestock (Num 32:3), and the Reubenites rebuilt it (Num 32:37). By the time of Isaiah and Jeremiah it was held by Moab. In their oracles against Moab, Heshbon and Elealeh cry out so loudly that they are heard as far as Jahaz, and the joyful shouts over their summer fruit and harvest fall silent (Isa 15:4; 16:9; Jer 48:34). The name probably means "God has ascended." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruin el-'Al, about a mile north or northeast of Heshbon (modern Hesban, Jordan), and the location shown here follows that identification.

Gibbethon was a town in the territory of the tribe of Dan, listed with Eltekeh and Baalath (Josh 19:44) and given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary specifies the Kohathite clan. By the time of the divided kingdom it belonged to the Philistines. Nadab king of Israel was besieging it when Baasha conspired against him and killed him there (1 Kgs 15:27). Later, Israel's army was again camped against Gibbethon when Zimri seized the throne in Tirzah. The troops made their commander Omri king (1 Kgs 16:16), and he marched from Gibbethon to besiege Tirzah. The name probably means "height" or "hill." Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Kibbiah, modern Qibya, about 16 miles southeast of Jaffa. Others favor Tell el-Melat near Gezer. The location shown here follows the Qibya identification.

Gihon was a spring just outside Jerusalem, below the City of David. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet, with Benaiah and the royal guard, brought Solomon there on King David's mule and anointed him king. The crowd's rejoicing as they came back up was heard throughout the city (1 Kgs 1:33, 38, 45). King Hezekiah later blocked its upper outlet and channeled the water straight down to the west side of the City of David (2 Chr 32:30). Manasseh built an outer wall west of Gihon, in the valley (2 Chr 33:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring called the Virgin's Fountain in the Kidron Valley, which a tunnel links to the Pool of Siloam. The location shown here follows that identification. The same name is also given to a river of Eden (Gen 2:13).

Gozan was a region in northern Mesopotamia where the king of Assyria settled Israelites deported after the fall of Samaria. They were placed in Halah, in Habor by "the river of Gozan," and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11). 1 Chr 5:26 names Reubenites, Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh among those taken there. Sennacherib's envoys also listed Gozan with Haran, Rezeph and Eden as nations whose gods had not saved them from Assyria (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates it with Assyrian Guzana, Ptolemy's Gauzanitis, west of Nisibis. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the Habor, the modern Khabur River, a tributary of the Euphrates. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the "river of Gozan" with the Kizil Ozan. The location shown here follows the Khabur identification, near Tell Halaf in northeastern Syria.

Greece is the land and people of the Greeks, called Javan in Hebrew, whose name the King James Version renders as "Grecia" or "Greece." In Daniel's visions the rough goat stands for the king of Grecia, and its great horn for the first king (Dan 8:21). A prince of Grecia follows the prince of Persia (Dan 10:20), and a rich Persian king stirs up all against the realm of Grecia (Dan 11:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary reads these as a sketch of Alexander and his successors, and Zech 9:13, which sets Zion's sons against Greece's sons, as a prophecy of the Maccabean wars. In Acts 20:2 Paul reaches Greece after passing through Macedonia, so the name there probably means the southern province of Achaia. Paul probably wrote Romans during that stay, about AD 54 by inference from context. The location shown here is a general point in the Greek peninsula.

Hazeroth was a stopping place of the Israelites in the wilderness after they left Mount Sinai. They traveled to it from Kibroth-hattaavah and stayed there for a time (Num 11:35; Num 33:17). When they left, they camped in the wilderness of Paran, or at Rithmah in the itinerary of Num 33 (Num 12:16; Num 33:18). The account in Num 12, set during this stay, tells how Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses and Miriam was struck with leprosy. Hazeroth is also one of the landmarks used to place Moses' speeches in Deut 1:1. The name probably means "enclosures" or "settlements." Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring of 'Ain Hudhera (Ain Khadra), about 30 to 40 miles northeast of the traditional Mount Sinai. The location shown here follows that identification.

Jahaz was a city east of the Jordan, north of the Arnon River, where Sihon king of the Amorites gathered his army and fought Israel when he refused to let them pass through his land (Num 21:23; Deut 2:32). Israel won the battle and took his territory, an event Jephthah later recalled (Judg 11:20). Other passages call the town Jahaza, Jahazah or Jahzah, place it in Reuben's territory, and assign it to the Merarite Levites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha's inscription claims he drove Israel's king out of Jahaz. By the prophets' time it was a Moabite town, named in oracles against Moab (Isa 15:4; Jer 48:34). Its site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the suggestion, reported by that encyclopedia, that it was at the ruins of Umm er-Rasas, north of Dibon.

Jebus was the city of the Jebusites, identified in the Bible with Jerusalem (Judg 19:10; 1 Chr 11:4). In Joshua's allotment it appears as "Jebusi, which is Jerusalem" among the cities of Benjamin (Josh 18:28). In Judges a Levite traveling home with his concubine passed by Jebus late in the day but refused to lodge in a city of foreigners (Judg 19:10–11). Its inhabitants later told David he could not enter, but he captured the stronghold of Zion, which became the city of David (1 Chr 11:4–5). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a naturally strong fortress and calls its capture one of David's great achievements. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name Jerusalem is attested centuries before David, so Jebus was probably an alternate name taken from the Jebusites rather than the city's original name. The location shown here is ancient Jerusalem.

Kibroth-hattaavah, meaning "graves of craving" or "graves of lust," was an Israelite camp in the wilderness and their first stop after leaving the desert of Sinai (Num 33:16). It was named for the people buried there "that lusted" (Num 11:34). The surrounding chapter tells how the Israelites grew tired of manna and demanded meat, then received a great flight of quails and were struck by a plague. From there they moved on to Hazeroth (Num 11:35; 33:17). Moses later listed it with Taberah and Massah as places where Israel provoked the LORD (Deut 9:22). Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably in the Wady Murrah, about 30 miles northeast of Sinai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it near the Gulf of Aqaba. The location shown here, in the eastern Sinai Peninsula, follows this general identification and is approximate.

Kir is the name of a place, meaning "wall" or "enclosure," used in the Bible for what appear to be two different sites. Most mentions refer to a distant land where the Assyrian king took the people of Damascus captive after capturing the city and killing Rezin (2 Kgs 16:9), as Amos had foretold (Amos 1:5). Amos 9:7 also names it as the land the Syrians originally came from. Isaiah lists it with Elam as supplying soldiers (Isa 22:6). Its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a link with Susiana near Elam, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals in Media or Armenia. Isaiah 15:1 separately speaks of "Kir of Moab," a Moabite stronghold, probably the same as Kir-hareseth. The location shown here follows that Moabite identification, probably the modern town of al-Karak in Jordan.

Kiriathaim (King James Version also "Kirjathaim") was a city east of the Jordan in the uplands of Moab. The Reubenites rebuilt it along with Heshbon and Elealeh, and it was listed in Reuben's territory beside Sibmah. Later it was a Moabite town again: Jeremiah lists it among the Moabite cities facing judgment, and Ezekiel names it with Beth-jeshimoth and Baal-meon as "the glory of the country." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha claimed to have fortified it, and connects it with Shaveh-kiriathaim in Gen 14:5. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with el-Kureiyat, about 11 miles southwest of Medeba near ancient Ataroth, and the location shown here follows that identification. The ISBE suggests a site north of the Wadi Zerqa Ma'in instead. The name was also used for other places, including a town in Naphtali.

Kishon (also spelled Kison) was a river in northern Israel. It was the scene of Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, who gathered his nine hundred iron chariots there (Judg 4:7, 13). Deborah's song says the river "swept them away," calling it "that ancient river" (Judg 5:21), and Ps 83:9 recalls that defeat. Later Elijah brought the prophets of Baal down to the brook Kishon and killed them there (1 Kgs 18:40), probably close below the spot on Carmel where his sacrifice took place, as Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern Nahr el-Muqatta (the Kishon River). It is a seasonal stream that drains the plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel) and enters the Mediterranean near Haifa. When rains flood its deep bed and turn the plain to mud, it would have trapped heavy chariots.

Lebanon, in this entry, refers to the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a large hall Solomon built as part of his palace complex in Jerusalem. The location shown here is Jerusalem. It measured 100 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high, and rested on four rows of cedar pillars with cedar beams (1 Kgs 7:2). Its name probably comes from its rows of cedar columns, which suggested a forest, and from the cedar timber brought from the Lebanon mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes those mountains as the lofty range of Syria famous for its cedars. Solomon placed 300 shields of beaten gold in the hall (1 Kgs 10:17; 2 Chr 9:16), and all its vessels were pure gold, since silver was thought of little value in his day (1 Kgs 10:21; 2 Chr 9:20).

Medeba was a city east of the Jordan on the high tableland north of the Arnon River. It first appears in a victory song over the Amorite kingdom of Heshbon, where it marks the limit of the land laid waste (Num 21:30). In the division of land east of the Jordan, the level plain around it, "the plain of Medeba," fell within Reuben's territory (Josh 13:9, 16). In David's time the Ammonites' hired allies, including the king of Maachah, camped before Medeba to fight Israel (1 Chr 19:7). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Joab defeated them there. By Isaiah's day it was a Moabite city, mourned in his oracle against Moab (Isa 15:2). Its name may mean "waters of quiet," though the sense is uncertain. It is generally identified with modern Madaba in Jordan, south of Heshbon, which matches the location shown here.

Meshech was a people and land on the far northern edge of the biblical world, named after Meshech son of Japheth (Gen 10:2). Ezekiel lists Meshech with Javan and Tubal as merchants who traded slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13). His prophecy against Gog calls Gog the "chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). In Ps 120:5 the psalmist laments living in Meshech and among the tents of Kedar. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as a way of describing distant, hostile foreigners. Easton's identifies Meshech with the Moschi, who lived in the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas. Others link the name with the Mushki of Assyrian records, in central or eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey). The location shown here follows the general region between the Black and Caspian Seas.

Mount Carmel is a mountain ridge in northern Israel. The location shown here is on the ridge that runs northwest to the Mediterranean coast near modern Haifa. At Elijah's request, King Ahab gathered all Israel there, together with 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the groves who ate at Jezebel's table, for a contest between Elijah and these prophets (1 Kgs 18:19–20). Afterward Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel and bowed to the ground with his face between his knees while Ahab went off to eat and drink (1 Kgs 18:42). Carmel was later linked with Elisha. He went there after leaving Bethel and then returned to Samaria (2 Kgs 2:25). The Shunammite woman traveled to him at Mount Carmel after her son died, which suggests he sometimes stayed there (2 Kgs 4:25). STEPBible's Proper Names describes it as a mountain range.

Mount Ebal is a mountain in central Canaan, standing north of Mount Gerizim with the valley of Shechem between them. It is probably the modern Jebel Eslamiyeh beside Nablus, and the location shown here matches that site. Moses instructed that once Israel entered the land, the blessing was to be placed on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal (Deut 11:29). Six tribes, Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali, were to stand on Ebal for the curses. Large plastered stones were also to be set up there, which the surrounding passage says were for writing the law (Deut 27:4, 13). Joshua later built an altar to the LORD on Ebal and gathered all Israel, half facing each mountain, to carry out this command (Josh 8:30, 33). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its height as about 3,076 feet. STEPBible's proper-name index also links it with Mount Zalmon.

Mount Gilboa is the mountain where Israel was defeated by the Philistines and King Saul died, about 1056 BC by inference from context. The Israelites fled before the Philistines and fell dead on its slopes. The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the bodies, they found Saul and his three sons lying there (1 Sam 31:1, 8; the parallel account in 1 Chr 10:1, 8). A young man who brought the news to David, identified later in the chapter as an Amalekite, said he had happened upon Saul on the mountain, leaning on his spear as chariots and horsemen closed in (2 Sam 1:6). In the lament that follows, David calls on the "mountains of Gilboa" to have no dew or rain (2 Sam 1:21). The site is generally identified with the ridge still called Mount Gilboa in northern Israel, on the southeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here lies on that ridge.

Naioth was a place in or near Ramah, Samuel's hometown, where David and Samuel stayed together after David escaped from Saul (1 Sam 19:18). Saul learned where David was and sent men after him, then came himself. On the way the Spirit of God came on him, and he prophesied until he reached Naioth (1 Sam 19:22–23). From there David fled again and went to Jonathan (1 Sam 20:1). The nearby verse 1 Sam 19:20 describes a company of prophets there, led by Samuel. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take Naioth to be the dwellings of a prophetic community, and they give the name's meaning as "dwellings" or "habitations." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as uncertain. The site of Ramah itself is debated. The location shown here is approximate, near Nebi Samwil northwest of Jerusalem, one proposed site for Samuel's Ramah.

Ono was a town in the coastal lowland, regularly named alongside Lod (Lydda). According to 1 Chr 8:12, Shamed, a descendant of Benjamin through Elpaal, built Ono and Lod with their surrounding towns. After the exile, people from Lod, Hadid and Ono returned with Zerubbabel, numbering 725 in Ezra 2:33 and 721 in Neh 7:37, and Benjamites later settled there. Nehemiah 11:35 lists Lod and Ono with "the valley of craftsmen," which Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests may be the same as "the plain of Ono." In that plain Sanballat and Geshem proposed a meeting with Nehemiah, but he understood they meant him harm. Easton's Bible Dictionary says they asked four times and intended to seize him. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Ono with Kefr 'Ana, northwest of Lydda, near present-day Or Yehuda. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ophel was a fortified part of ancient Jerusalem, on the narrow ridge running south from the temple mount between the Tyropoeon and Kidron valleys, according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. The name is usually explained as "hill" or "mound", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes an argument for "fortress." King Jotham built extensively on the wall of Ophel. Manasseh later enclosed it with an outer wall and raised it to a great height. After the exile, the Nethinim, the temple servants, lived there under Ziha and Gispa. Nehemiah places Ophel near the Water Gate on the east and "the tower that lieth out", and the Tekoites repaired the wall up to it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Chronicler used Ophel for the older stronghold called Zion or the City of David. The location shown here lies on that hill just south of the temple area.

Ophrah was a town of the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh and the home of Gideon. An angel of the LORD appeared there under an oak belonging to Gideon's father Joash, while Gideon threshed wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites (Judg 6:11). Gideon built an altar there called Jehovah-shalom (Judg 6:24). After his victory he placed in Ophrah an ephod made from the spoils, which became a snare to him and his family (Judg 8:27). He was buried there in his father's tomb (Judg 8:32). Later his son Abimelech killed seventy of his brothers there on one stone, and only Jotham escaped (Judg 9:5). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Ferata near Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it nearer the Jezreel plain, and the location shown here follows that view, near modern Afula. A different Ophrah lay in Benjamin.

Pamphylia was a coastal region in the middle of the southern shore of Asia Minor, lying between Lycia to the west and Cilicia to the east, in what is now the area around Antalya in southern Turkey. People from Pamphylia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). On their first missionary journey, Paul and his company sailed from Paphos on Cyprus to Perga in Pamphylia, and there John Mark left them and went back to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). Paul and Barnabas passed through Pamphylia again on their return from Pisidia (Acts 14:24). Mark's departure in Pamphylia later led Paul to refuse to take him on another journey (Acts 15:38). Years afterward, the ship carrying Paul to Rome sailed across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia to Myra in Lycia (Acts 27:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that in Paul's time it was a Roman province.

Pathros was a region of Egypt, generally identified as Upper Egypt, the southern Nile valley above Memphis. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as the Hebrew form of an Egyptian term meaning "the South land," and Easton's Bible Dictionary contrasts it with Lower Egypt in the north. Isaiah lists it among the distant lands from which a scattered remnant of God's people would be brought back (Isa 11:11). After the fall of Jerusalem, Jews lived there alongside communities at Migdol, Tahpanhes and Noph (Memphis), and Jeremiah addressed them about worshipping other gods (Jer 44:1, 15). Ezekiel calls it Egypt's land of origin, where the Egyptians would return as a lowly kingdom, and also foretells its desolation (Ezek 29:14; 30:14). The Pathrusim of Gen 10:14 are probably its people. The location shown here is a point in the Nile valley standing for the region as a whole.

Penuel was a city east of the Jordan River, near Succoth and the Jabbok River, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Its name means "face of God," and it is also spelled Peniel. Jacob was passing Penuel at sunrise, limping on his thigh, after wrestling through the night (Gen 32:31). The surrounding passage explains that he named the place because he had seen God face to face. Later, when Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings, the men of Penuel answered him as Succoth had. The preceding verses show this was a refusal to give his troops bread. Gideon threatened to break down their tower, and on his return he did so and killed the men of the city (Judg 8:8–9, 17). After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam built Penuel, probably fortifying it (1 Kgs 12:25). The location shown here follows a common identification with Tulul edh-Dhahab on the Jabbok, the modern Zarqa River in Jordan.

Pisgah was a mountain ridge or summit in Moab, east of the Jordan and facing Jericho. Its top marked a stage in Israel's march, overlooking Jeshimon, the desert (Num 21:20). King Balak brought Balaam to the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah and built seven altars there (Num 23:14). Moses was told to climb it and look in every direction at the land he would not enter (Deut 3:27). Deut 34:1 equates the top of Pisgah with Mount Nebo, where he was shown the land. The springs or slopes of Pisgah bordered the plain above the Dead Sea (Deut 4:49). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Pisgah as the range at the western edge of the Moab plateau, with Nebo as its summit. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Jebel Siaghah, and the location shown here follows that identification, in present-day Jordan.

Rephidim was a campsite of the Israelites on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. They reached it after leaving the wilderness of Sin, by way of Alush, and found no water to drink there (Exod 17:1; Num 33:14). The surrounding chapter tells how Moses brought water from a rock, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the spot was therefore also called Massah and Meribah. At Rephidim the Amalekites attacked Israel, the first battle after the Exodus (Exod 17:8). From there the people moved on to the wilderness of Sinai and camped before the mountain (Exod 19:2; Num 33:15). The name probably means "rests" or "resting places." The exact site is uncertain. Most older dictionaries place it in Wadi Feiran in southern Sinai, while some prefer Wadi esh-Sheikh. The location shown here follows Easton's Bible Dictionary, which puts it in Wadi Feiran near its junction with Wadi esh-Sheikh.

The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake in northern Israel, fed by the Jordan River. John also calls it the Sea of Tiberias (John 6:1), and STEPBible's proper-names index notes that it is the lake called Chinnereth in the Old Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as oval, about 12½ miles long and up to 7½ miles wide, lying about 682 feet below the Mediterranean, and full of fish. Jesus was walking along its shore when he saw the fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew casting their net (Matt 4:18; Mark 1:16). He returned to it from the region of Tyre and Sidon by way of the Decapolis (Mark 7:31), went up a mountain near it (Matt 15:29), and crossed it by boat (John 6:1). Easton's also links the lake with Capernaum, the calming of a storm, and Jesus' appearance to his disciples after the resurrection (John 21).

Sibmah was a town east of the Jordan in the former territory of Moab, rebuilt by the tribe of Reuben and assigned to it in Joshua's division of the land (Num 32:38; Josh 13:19). It is spelled Shibmah in Num 32:38 and probably appears as Shebam in Num 32:3. The town was famous for its vineyards. Isaiah and Jeremiah, in their laments over Moab, mourn the ruined "vine of Sibmah," whose branches had spread as far as Jazer and beyond. They link it with nearby Heshbon, Elealeh and Jazer, which suggests that by then it was again a Moabite town. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ruin of Sumieh near Heshbon, where rock-cut winepresses have been found. The location shown here is approximate and places it close to Heshbon.

Tabor (Mountain) is a prominent, isolated mountain in Lower Galilee, rising from the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley (the plain of Esdraelon). It is identified with the modern Jebel et-Tur (Mount Tabor), about 1,843 feet high according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, and the location shown here follows that identification. Josh 19:22 names it on the border of Issachar's territory. The Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna killed Gideon's brothers at Tabor (Judg 8:18). The earlier account in Judg 4:6–14 has Barak gather his forces there before defeating Sisera. Poets and prophets used it as a landmark. Ps 89:12 pairs it with Hermon, Jer 46:18 points to how it stands out among the mountains, and Hos 5:1 speaks of Israel's leaders as a net spread upon Tabor. A Christian tradition traced to the fourth century places the transfiguration of Jesus on this mountain.

Tahpanhes was a city in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt. After Jerusalem fell to Babylon and the governor Gedaliah was murdered, a group of Judeans fled there and took the prophet Jeremiah with them, against his warning (Jer 43:7). At Tahpanhes Jeremiah was told to bury large stones in the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh's house, which shows the town had a royal building (Jer 43:8–9). Jews were still living there later (Jer 44:1). Jeremiah also names it with Migdol and Noph (Memphis) in a warning of coming war against Egypt (Jer 46:14). Other passages spell the name Tahapanes and Tehaphnehes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Tell Defenneh, the Greek Daphnai, on the old caravan route to Palestine, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tarsus was the chief city of Cilicia, in southeastern Asia Minor, and the birthplace of the apostle Paul. Paul described himself as a Jew born in Tarsus, "a citizen of no mean city," though he was brought up in Jerusalem under Gamaliel (Acts 21:39; 22:3). When he was converted, the Lord directed Ananias to look for "Saul, of Tarsus" in Damascus (Acts 9:11). Later, when his life was threatened in Jerusalem, believers took him to Caesarea and sent him home to Tarsus, and Barnabas went there to find him and bring him to Antioch (Acts 9:30; 11:25). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as a wealthy commercial city on the river Cydnus, famous for its schools, which Strabo compared to those of Athens and Alexandria. The location shown here is the modern city of Tarsus in southern Turkey, about 10 to 12 miles from the Mediterranean coast.

Thebes was a major city of ancient Egypt, called "No" in the King James Version. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains that its Hebrew name, No-amon, means the abode of the god Amon, and that it long served as the capital of Upper Egypt. It stood on both banks of the Nile, at the site of modern Luxor and Karnak. The location shown here follows that identification. Jeremiah and Ezekiel name it among the Egyptian cities facing judgment. They speak of punishing "the multitude of No" along with Pharaoh and Egypt's gods (Jer 46:25), and of No being "rent asunder" (Ezek 30:14–16). Nahum warns Nineveh by pointing to "populous No," a city set among rivers with water as its defence, which had nonetheless fallen (Nah 3:8). This probably refers to the Assyrian sack of Thebes in the seventh century BC.

Tubal was a region and people in the far north, as seen from Israel. Gen 10:2 names Tubal as a son of Japheth, and the STEPBible Proper Names index treats the nation as his descendants. In Ezekiel, Tubal appears with Javan and Meshech as trading partners of Tyre, dealing in slaves and bronze vessels (Ezek 27:13). It is also listed with Meshech as one of the peoples ruled by Gog, 'the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal,' against whom Ezekiel prophesies (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Isaiah includes Tubal among distant nations that will hear of God's glory (Isa 66:19). Tubal is usually linked with the Tabal of Assyrian records in central Anatolia, or with the Tibareni, whom Greek writers place near the southern Black Sea coast. The location shown here, in northeastern Turkey near the Black Sea, matches the Tibareni identification and is approximate.

The Valley of Achor was a valley near Jericho where Joshua and the Israelites brought Achan, his family, his livestock and the goods he had taken, and stoned them. They raised a great heap of stones over him, and the place kept its name from that event. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "trouble." The valley later marked part of the northern border of Judah's territory, which ran up from it toward Debir and Gilgal. Isaiah and Hosea both mention it in promises of restoration, as a resting place for herds and as "a door of hope." Easton's suggests the name had become proverbial for trouble, so these passages picture trouble turned to blessing. Its exact location is uncertain. Proposals include the Buqeia plain west of the Dead Sea and the Wadi Qelt, which Easton's names. The location shown here follows the Wadi Qelt identification, southwest of Jericho.

Zeboiim was one of the cities of the plain, almost always named alongside Admah and grouped with Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis 10:19 lists it among the places marking the edge of Canaanite territory. It had its own king, Shemeber, who joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Bela (Zoar) in battle against an alliance of eastern kings in the Vale of Siddim. Deuteronomy 29:23 counts it among the cities the LORD overthrew, leaving the land barren, and Hosea 11:8 uses it as a byword for that destruction. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "deer" or "goats." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it should not be confused with Zeboim in 1 Sam 13:18. The site has never been identified. Scholars place the cities of the plain near either the northern or southern end of the Dead Sea, and the location shown here follows the southern view.

Ain (meaning "spring" or "eye") was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev region. It is listed among the southernmost cities of Judah's territory (Josh 15:32) and was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon, whose land lay within Judah's (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). It was also one of the towns, with their surrounding pasturelands, assigned to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:16). Because Ain is repeatedly named immediately beside Rimmon, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that the two names may form a single place, En-rimmon (Ain-Rimmon). STEPBible's Proper Names takes the same view. The location shown here, north of Beersheba, follows that En-rimmon identification. The name Ain is also used for at least one other place in the Bible, so references need to be read in context.

Antioch (Pisidia) was a city in the interior of Asia Minor, distinct from Antioch in Syria. Paul and Barnabas came there from Perga on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context, and spoke in its synagogue on the sabbath (Acts 13:14). Later in the chapter, opposition forced them to leave. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then followed Paul to Lystra, where he was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Afterward the missionaries passed back through Antioch on their way home (Acts 14:21), and Paul later recalled the persecutions he endured there (2 Tim 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary says Seleucus Nicator founded the city, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it became a Roman colony in the province of Galatia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the modern Yalvaç (Yalobatch) in Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Arad was a Canaanite city in the Negev, the dry south country of Canaan. When Israel approached near the end of the wilderness journey, the king of Arad attacked them and took some prisoners (Num 21:1; Num 33:40). The King James Version reads these verses as naming a king called Arad, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Arad as the city's name, with the ruler being its king. Arad later appears among the cities whose kings Joshua defeated, listed next to Hormah (Josh 12:14). The Kenite relatives of Moses' father-in-law settled with the people of Judah in the wilderness south of Arad (Judg 1:16). The ISBE also notes that the Egyptian king Shishak listed the city among his conquests. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE identify it with Tel Arad, about 17 to 20 miles south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Argob was a region in Bashan, east of the Jordan, belonging to the kingdom of Og. When Israel conquered Og it took all of Argob's sixty cities (Deut 3:4). Moses gave the region, with the rest of Bashan, to the half tribe of Manasseh (Deut 3:13), and Jair son of Manasseh took the whole area as far as the borders of Geshur and Maacah, naming it after himself (Deut 3:14). Under Solomon, Argob's sixty great cities, with walls and bronze bars, were administered by the son of Geber from Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:13). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries identify Argob with the later Trachonitis, the rugged volcanic Lejah south of Damascus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the location is uncertain and suggests other fertile districts of Bashan. The location shown here follows the Lejah identification.

Ashan, a name meaning "smoke" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was a town in the lowland of Judah, listed with Libnah and Ether among Judah's cities (Josh 15:42). It was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon inside Judah's territory (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). It also appears among the towns with their pasturelands given to the priestly descendants of Aaron, alongside Beth-shemesh (1 Chr 6:59). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Ain" in the parallel list at Josh 21:16 is a copying variant of Ashan, and that Chor-ashan (1 Sam 30:30), probably a reservoir site in southwestern Judah, is the same place. The site has not been firmly identified, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Asshur is the Hebrew name for Assyria, the Mesopotamian power on the Tigris, and for its original capital city. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name probably comes from Asshur son of Shem and that the old capital stood at Kalah Sherghat on the west bank of the Tigris, before the capital moved to Nineveh. In Balaam's oracle, Asshur will carry the Kenites away captive, and ships from Chittim will later afflict Asshur (Num 24:22, 24). Psalm 83 lists Assur among the nations allied with the children of Lot, meaning Moab and Ammon, against Israel (Ps 83:8). Ezekiel names Asshur among the trading partners of Tyre (Ezek 27:23). In these verses the name points to the nation more than to a single city. The location shown here is near Nineveh, opposite modern Mosul, and stands for the Assyrian heartland rather than the older city site farther south.

Beth-horon, here Lower Beth-horon ("Bethhoron the nether"), was a town on the border between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Benjamin. It had a twin, Upper Beth-horon, and this name is shared by both towns. Lower Beth-horon marked a point on Ephraim's southern boundary as it ran west toward Gezer and the sea (Josh 16:3). A hill south of it was a landmark on Benjamin's northern border (Josh 18:13). Solomon rebuilt it along with Gezer, and he fortified both Beth-horons with walls, gates and bars (1 Kgs 9:17; 2 Chr 8:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the two towns stood about 2 miles apart on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa. The pass between them was the ascent of Beth-horon, where Joshua chased the Amorite kings. The lower town is generally identified with the modern village of Beit Ur et-Tahta, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-jeshimoth, meaning "house of the wastes" or "deserts" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, was a town east of the Jordan near the northeastern shore of the Dead Sea, in the plains of Moab. Israel's last camp before crossing the Jordan stretched from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (Num 33:49). It also marked a point on the border of the territory of Sihon, king of the Amorites, along the way toward the Dead Sea (Josh 12:3). It was later listed among the towns given to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:20). By Ezekiel's time it belonged to Moab and was named with Baal-meon and Kiriathaim as one of the frontier cities that were "the glory of the country" (Ezek 25:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was Khirbet es-Suweimeh, about 3 miles east of the mouth of the Jordan. The location shown here matches that area.

Beth-peor, meaning "house of Peor," was a place east of the Jordan in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean a temple of Baal-peor, the god whose worship led Israel astray in Num 25:3. Israel camped in the valley facing Beth-peor while Moses gave the speeches of Deuteronomy. The area had belonged to Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, whom Israel defeated. Moses was buried in a valley in Moab facing Beth-peor, though no one knew where his grave was. Later the town was assigned to the tribe of Reuben, listed alongside the slopes of Pisgah. Its exact site is uncertain. Eusebius placed it near Mount Peor, about six miles from Livias. Conder suggested el-Mareighat, an ancient worship site with standing stones, and the location shown here appears to follow that area, on the heights south of Mount Nebo.

Bezer was a city of the tribe of Reuben east of the Jordan, described as lying "in the wilderness, in the plain country," the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. It was one of three cities of refuge set apart east of the Jordan, along with Ramoth in Gilead and Golan in Bashan (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8). It was also given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites, and the surrounding passage (Josh 21:34) shows these were the Merarite families. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the ruins of Burazin, about 12 miles north of Heshbon, and Kasur-el-Besheir near Dibon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested link with Bozrah. The location shown here follows a Bozrah identification and places Bezer at Bosra in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "vine branches."

Brook Eshcol, also called the valley of Eshcol, was a valley in the hill country of Canaan explored by the twelve spies Moses sent ahead of Israel. There they cut a single cluster of grapes so large that two men carried it on a pole, along with pomegranates and figs, as samples of the land's produce. The place was named for that cluster, since Eshcol means "cluster." The spies' discouraging report after visiting the valley turned the Israelites against entering the land. Because the preceding verse, Num 13:22, says the spies came to Hebron, many place the valley near that city. Easton's Bible Dictionary, following Palmer, suggests the grape-growing valleys farther south near Beersheba, perhaps Wadi Hanein. The location shown here follows the identification near Hebron.

Cana, called "Cana of Galilee" in the Bible, was a village in Galilee where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding. His mother was there, and John 2:11 calls it the beginning of his miracles. He later returned to Cana, where a nobleman asked him to heal his son, who was sick at Capernaum. It was also the home of the disciple Nathanael. The New Testament mentions it only in John's Gospel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that "of Galilee" set it apart from Kanah in Asher. Its site is disputed. Church tradition places it at Kefr Kanna, about 4 miles northeast of Nazareth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 9 miles north of Nazareth on the edge of the Beit Netofa plain, whose name may mean "place of reeds." The location shown here follows the Khirbet Qana identification.

Chephirah was a city in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, one of the four Gibeonite cities whose people tricked Israel into making a treaty with them (Josh 9:17). It was later counted among the towns given to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh 18:26). After the exile in Babylon its people returned and resettled it. The lists in Ezra and Nehemiah count them together with the men of Kirjath-jearim and Beeroth, 743 in all (Ezra 2:25; Neh 7:29). The name is often taken to mean "hamlet" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "little lioness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Kefireh, southwest of Gibeon, on high ground with many ancient remains. The location shown here follows that identification, the site known as Khirbet el-Kafira.
The inhabitants of Gadara, in Revised Version “Gerasenes” (Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26, 37). In Matt. 8:28 they are called Gergesenes, Revised Version “Gadarenes.”

Derbe was a city of Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, mentioned only in Acts. Paul and Barnabas fled there with Lystra after a threat at Iconium (Acts 14:6), and Paul went on to Derbe the day after he was stoned at Lystra (Acts 14:20). On a later journey Paul came again to Derbe and Lystra, where he met Timothy (Acts 16:1). Gaius of Derbe was one of Paul's travelling companions (Acts 20:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a frontier customs town on a Roman road toward the Cilician Gates, and says its coins honor the emperor Claudius. Its exact site was long uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary notes the modern town Divle, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Ramsay's choice of Gudelisin. The location shown here follows a later identification with the mound of Kerti Hüyük, north of modern Karaman in Turkey.

Dor was an ancient Canaanite royal city on the Mediterranean coast. Its king is listed among those Joshua defeated, and Josh 12:23 places it "in the coast of Dor." Dor and its surrounding towns lay within the areas of Issachar and Asher but were assigned to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29). Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, who went on living there (Judg 1:27). Other passages call the area Naphath-dor, the heights or coast of Dor (Josh 11:2), and 1 Kgs 4:11 names it as one of Solomon's supply districts. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the most southern Phoenician settlement on that coast and identifies it with Tantura, about 8 miles (13 km) north of Caesarea. Smith's Bible Dictionary agrees, citing Jerome's placement of Dor nine miles from Caesarea. The location shown here follows this identification, at the ancient mound near modern Tantura.

The Dung Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day, called the "dung port" in the King James Version at Neh 2:13. Nehemiah passed it during his night inspection of the ruined walls and burned gates. It stood 1,000 cubits (about 450 meters) along the wall from the Valley Gate. It was rebuilt, with doors, locks and bars, by Malchiah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccerem (Neh 3:13–14). At the dedication of the restored wall, one of the two thanksgiving processions marched along the wall toward it (Neh 12:31). Its name probably reflects its use for carrying refuse out of the city, as the STEPBible names data suggests. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the southern part of the city, facing the valley where rubbish was dumped. Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is approximate.

Elim was an oasis where the Israelites camped during their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. It came after Marah, the camp of bitter water, and stood out for its twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Exod 15:27; Num 33:9). From Elim the people moved on and camped by the Red Sea, then entered the wilderness of Sin, which lay between Elim and Sinai. They reached Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt (Exod 16:1; Num 33:10). The name is usually linked to large trees such as terebinths or palms. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Elim with Wadi Gharandel, on the western side of the Sinai Peninsula about halfway down the Gulf of Suez, where palms and good water are still found. The location shown here follows that traditional identification.

En-rogel was a spring just outside Jerusalem that marked a point on the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin (Josh 15:7; Josh 18:16). The boundary ran down the valley of Hinnom past the south side of the Jebusite city to reach it. During Absalom's revolt, Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited at En-rogel so they would not be seen entering the city. A servant girl brought them news, which they carried to David (2 Sam 17:17). Later, Adonijah held a sacrificial feast by the stone of Zoheleth near the spring and invited the king's sons and the men of Judah (1 Kgs 1:9). The name is often explained as "fuller's spring." Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Gihon spring ("Fountain of the Virgin"). Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Bir Ayyub ("Job's well"), below the meeting of the Kidron and Hinnom valleys. The location shown here follows the Bir Ayyub identification.

Etham was the Israelites' second camp after leaving Egypt, reached by a march from Succoth and described as being "in the edge of the wilderness" (Exod 13:20; Num 33:6). From there they turned back toward Pi-hahiroth, before Baal-zephon, and camped before Migdol (Num 33:7). After crossing the sea they traveled three days through the "wilderness of Etham" to Marah (Num 33:8), so the name also covered desert land east of the sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Exod 15:22 calls this stretch the wilderness of Shur. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may come from the Egyptian Khetam, "fortress," on Egypt's eastern frontier. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here follows the view that it lay near the north end of the Bitter Lakes, south of modern Ismailia. The stop dates to about 1491 BC, by inference from context.

Ethiopia is the English rendering, through Greek, of the Hebrew name Cush, a land lying south of Egypt along the Nile. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it from Syene at the First Cataract to beyond the meeting of the White and Blue Nile, roughly corresponding to modern Sudan. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds Nubia and northern Abyssinia in its widest sense. The location shown here is in the Nile valley of northern Sudan. In Gen 2:13 the Gihon, a river of Eden, is said to surround the whole land of Ethiopia. Because that passage is set in Eden, the identity of this Cush is uncertain, and it may not be the same African region. In Esther, Ethiopia marks one edge of the empire of Ahasuerus, which stretched from India to Ethiopia over 127 provinces (Esth 1:1; 8:9). Job 28:19 mentions the topaz of Ethiopia as a costly stone.

Gaash was a hill in the hill country of Ephraim. Joshua was buried on its north side, within his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which Judg 2:9 calls Timnath-heres (Josh 24:30). The "brooks of Gaash" were the home of one of David's mighty warriors, named Hiddai in 2 Sam 23:30 and Hurai in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:32. These are probably two spellings of the same man's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that these brooks, better understood as seasonal streambeds or wadis, lay at the foot of the hill. The name is often explained as meaning "shaking" or "earthquake." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no likely identification of the site has been proposed, so the location shown here is only approximate, placed near Timnath-serah in Ephraim.

The Gate of Benjamin was a gate of Jerusalem in the time of Jeremiah. Its name probably comes from the fact that it faced the tribal territory of Benjamin, which lay north of the city. The passage suggests this, since Jeremiah was arrested there by the guard captain Irijah while leaving the city and was accused of deserting to the Babylonians (Jer 37:13). Jer 20:2 calls it the "high gate of Benjamin" beside the house of the LORD, where the priest Pashur put Jeremiah in the stocks. The king, Zedekiah by inference from context, was sitting in this gate when Ebedmelech came to plead for Jeremiah (Jer 38:7). Zech 14:10 uses it as a landmark marking the extent of a restored Jerusalem. Its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the north side of the city near the Temple area.

Golan was a city in Bashan, east of the Jordan, in the territory of the half-tribe of Manasseh. Moses set it apart as one of three cities of refuge east of the river, alongside Bezer of Reuben and Ramoth in Gilead of Gad, where a person who had killed someone accidentally could flee (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite families of the Levites (Josh 21:27; 1 Chr 6:71). Scripture says nothing more about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it later gave its name to the district of Gaulanitis, roughly the modern Jaulan (the Golan region). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the exact site as unknown. The location shown here is east of the Sea of Galilee in southern Syria, near the village of Sahem el-Jolan, a site often proposed for ancient Golan.

Havvoth-jair was a group of villages east of the Jordan. The name means "tent villages of Jair," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, captured the towns during Israel's conquest and named them after himself (Num 32:41). Deut 3:14 links them with the region of Argob in Bashan, reaching to the borders of Geshur and Maacah. Judg 10:4 says the thirty sons of Jair the judge held thirty cities called Havvoth-jair in Gilead. Whether this is the same Jair or a later namesake is uncertain. 1 Chr 2:23 counts the towns of Jair among sixty cities connected with the sons of Machir, the father of Gilead. The exact area is uncertain, with Bashan and Gilead both suggested. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors northern Gilead. The location shown here, which is approximate, follows a placement in Gilead.

Hazar-enan was a town marking the northeastern corner of the land promised to Israel. In Numbers it is where the northern border ends after Ziphron, and the point from which the eastern border begins, running to Shepham (Num 34:9–10).
