Ezekiel's vision of the restored land also uses it as a northern boundary point, near the borders of Damascus and Hamath (Ezek 47:17), and places the tribe of Dan's portion at the far north beside it (Ezek 48:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "village of fountains" and mentions two identifications: Ayan ed-Dara in the Anti-Lebanon range, or, more probably, Kuryetein, about 60 miles east-northeast of Damascus. The location shown here follows the second view, the modern town of Al Qaryatayn in Syria.

Hazar-shual was a town in the Negev, in the far south of Judah, always listed near Beersheba. It appears among the southern cities of Judah's allotment (Josh 15:28) and again among the towns given to Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh 19:3). The Simeonites were living there in the time of David, as their genealogy in 1 Chr 4:28 notes. After the return from Babylonian exile, people of Judah settled there again (Neh 11:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "village" or "enclosure of the jackal," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a wolf's house." Easton's identifies it with the ruins of Saweh, halfway between Beersheba and Moladah. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here, east of Beersheba, fits that general area.

Horesh was a place in the wilderness of Ziph in Judah where David hid while Saul was hunting him. There Saul's son Jonathan came to David, encouraged him, and the two made a covenant before the LORD before Jonathan returned home (1 Sam 23:15–18). The Ziphites then reported to Saul at Gibeah that David was hiding in strongholds there, near the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon (1 Sam 23:19). The King James Version does not treat the Hebrew word as a name and translates it "in the wood." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word means "forest" elsewhere and favors that reading, while the Septuagint renders it "in the New." This entry treats Horesh as a place name, as STEPBible's proper-name index does. The location shown here, south of Hebron near Ziph, probably matches the ruin Khirbet Khoreisa, which is often identified with Horesh.

Horonaim was a city of Moab named only in the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah against Moab. It appears with Zoar, Luhith, Heshbon, Elealeh and Jahaz as a place where cries of destruction would be heard as Moab's people fled (Isa 15:5; Jer 48:3, 34). The texts speak of "the way of Horonaim" and "the going down of Horonaim" (Jer 48:5), which suggests it lay on a road descending from the Moabite plateau toward the Dead Sea and the Arabah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south of the Arnon on raised ground, and the name is usually explained as "two caverns" or "two hollows." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified but notes a proposal linking it to ruins near Wadi Kerak. The location shown here, near the eastern side of the southern Dead Sea, fits that general area.

Italy was the peninsula of southern Europe stretching from the Alps to the strait facing Sicily, the home region of Rome and the heart of the Roman Empire. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that by New Testament times the name covered this whole peninsula, though it had earlier referred only to the far south. Aquila and Priscilla had recently come from Italy to Corinth after the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). When it was decided that Paul should be sent to Italy as a prisoner, he was placed in the custody of a centurion named Julius, who later put him aboard an Alexandrian ship bound there (Acts 27:1, 6), the start of his journey to Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. The letter to the Hebrews passes on greetings from "they of Italy" (Heb 13:24), probably Christians living in or from Italy.

Jattir was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Shamir and Socoh in the territory allotted to the tribe (Josh 15:48). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the descendants of Aaron the priest as one of the Levitical cities, alongside Eshtemoa and Hebron (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57). After defeating the Amalekites, David sent part of the spoil from Ziklag to the people of Jattir, among other towns of Judah (1 Sam 30:27). The name is usually taken to mean "pre-eminent" or "excellent." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Khirbet 'Attir, a ruin full of caves at the southern edge of the Judean hills, about ten miles south of Hebron. The ISBE links it with the "very large village Jethira" described by Eusebius. The location shown here matches that general area.

Jeshimon, meaning "the waste" or "desolation," was a barren wilderness in Judah near Ziph. In 1 Samuel it serves as a landmark during Saul's pursuit of David. The hill of Hachilah, where David hid and where Saul later camped, lay south of or "before" Jeshimon (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1, 3), and the wilderness of Maon lay to its south (1 Sam 23:24). The Hebrew word is also an ordinary noun for desert, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may simply mean "the waste" below the plateau of Ziph rather than a proper name. The same term appears in Num 21:20 and 23:28 near Pisgah and Peor, possibly for a district east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which place it in the dry, chalky hills west of the Dead Sea, between the Judean highlands and the shore.

Kedemoth was a town east of the Dead Sea, in the land north of the Arnon that Israel took from Sihon, king of the Amorites. Before the conquest, Moses sent messengers "out of the wilderness of Kedemoth" to Sihon at Heshbon with an offer of peace (Deut 2:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the town gave its name to this stretch of open pasture land. Kedemoth was later listed among the towns given to the tribe of Reuben, next to Jahaz and Mephaath (Josh 13:18). It became one of the cities assigned with their pasture lands to the Levites of the family of Merari (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:79). The name probably means "eastern parts" or "beginnings." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that it was the ruins of Umm er-Rasas. The location shown here lies north-east of Dibon, which fits Easton's Bible Dictionary.

Kiriath-sepher was the earlier name of Debir, a Canaanite town in the hill country of Judah. Both Josh 15:15 and Judg 1:11 say plainly that Debir was formerly called Kiriath-sepher. Caleb, advancing against the town's inhabitants, promised his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever attacked and captured it. The verses that follow in both accounts name Othniel as the man who took it. The name is often rendered "town of books," and the Greek translation took it that way, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other proposed meanings such as "border-town" or "toll-town." The site is uncertain. The same encyclopedia records a frequent identification with edh-Dhaheriyeh, southwest of Hebron, and a suggestion by Sayce that it lay west of Gath. The location shown here follows the edh-Dhaheriyeh identification.

Laish was a city in the far north of the land, which the tribe of Dan captured and renamed Dan. Five Danite spies found its people living quietly and securely, like the Sidonians, with no ruler to trouble them, far from Sidon and without ties to anyone (Judg 18:7). The Danites later came with the idols and priest they had taken from Micah, struck down the inhabitants, burned the city, rebuilt it, and named it after their ancestor Dan (Judg 18:27, 29). Joshua 19:47 calls the city Leshem. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near the sources of the Jordan, about 4 miles from Paneas (Banias), and identifies it with Tell el-Qadi, the modern Tel Dan. The location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a lion."

Lod was a town in the lowland west of the hill country, associated with the tribe of Benjamin. 1 Chr 8:12 credits its building, along with Ono and their surrounding villages, to Shamed, a Benjamite descended from Elpaal. After the Babylonian exile, the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono returned together. They numbered 725 in Ezra 2:33 and 721 in Neh 7:37. Neh 11:35 lists Lod and Ono among places resettled by Benjamites and links them with "the valley of craftsmen." The same town appears in the New Testament under its Greek name Lydda, where Peter healed Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it under that name. It is identified with modern Lod in Israel, southeast of Tel Aviv, which the location shown here matches. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "nativity" or "generation."

Lud was a people and land named in the prophets, known especially for their archers. Isaiah lists Lud, "that draw the bow," among distant nations to which survivors would be sent to declare God's glory (Isa 66:19). In Jeremiah, the Lydians who "handle and bend the bow" march with Ethiopians and Libyans in Egypt's army (Jer 46:9). Ezekiel names men of Lud as soldiers serving Tyre (Ezek 27:10) and Lydia among Egypt's allies who would fall by the sword (Ezek 30:5). Where Lud was is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to the Ludim descended from Mizraim (Gen 10:13), an African people west of Egypt. Others connect it with Lud son of Shem (Gen 10:22) or with Lydia in Asia Minor. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Lod. The location shown here follows Easton's African identification and places it in eastern Libya, near Cyrene, so it is only approximate.

Maacah was a small Aramean (Syrian) kingdom near Geshur, northeast of Israel. When the Ammonites had offended David, they hired Syrian forces that included the king of Maacah and a thousand men (2 Sam 10:6). The parallel account says the king came with his people and camped before Medeba (1 Chr 19:7). In the battle, Maacah's troops stood apart in the open field while the Ammonites lined up at their city gate (2 Sam 10:8), and the narrative goes on to describe Joab defeating them. Eliphelet, one of David's mighty men, was the son of Ahasbai, called 'the Maachathite' (2 Sam 23:34), so his family probably came from this region. Its exact extent is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of the Hauran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it between Geshur and Mount Hermon, probably bordered by the Jordan. The rough location shown here, east of Hermon and south of Damascus, is closer to Easton's view.

Maon was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Carmel, Ziph and Juttah among the towns assigned to the tribe (Josh 15:55). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "habitation" and says the town gave its name to the surrounding wilderness. David and his men hid in the wilderness of Maon, south of Jeshimon, when the people of Ziph reported him to Saul, and Saul pursued him there (1 Sam 23:24–25). Maon was also the home of a wealthy man whose flocks grazed at nearby Carmel, where he sheared his sheep (1 Sam 25:2). The following verse names him as Nabal, husband of Abigail. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Maon with Tell Ma'in, a conical hill about seven miles (11 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Massah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites, lacking water, quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD by asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" Moses named it Massah, meaning "testing" or "temptation," and also Meribah, meaning "quarreling" (Exod 17:7). The surrounding narrative places the episode at Rephidim, before Israel reached Sinai, when water came from a struck rock. That happened during the wilderness wanderings, about 1491 BC by inference from context. Deuteronomy later recalls Massah as a warning not to test God (Deut 6:16) and lists it with Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel provoked the LORD (Deut 9:22). Moses' blessing on Levi also mentions it (Deut 33:8). Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is approximate, in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, following the traditional southern route of the Exodus.

Mephaath was a city east of the Jordan in the territory given to the tribe of Reuben, listed with Jahazah and Kedemoth among the towns of the tableland (Josh 13:18). It was one of the four Reubenite cities assigned, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Merarite clan of the Levites (Josh 21:37; 1 Chr 6:79). Centuries later, Jeremiah names it among the towns of the 'plain country' on which judgment falls in his prophecy against Moab, which suggests the area was then under Moabite control (Jer 48:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius and Jerome knew it as the site of a Roman garrison. The location is uncertain. Proposed sites include Tell Jawa, south of modern Amman, and Umm er-Rasas further south. The location shown here follows the Tell Jawa identification.

Meribah (of Kadesh) was a spring at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin. There the Israelites quarreled with the LORD over a lack of water, and water was provided from a rock, near the end of the desert wanderings. The name means "strife" or "quarrel" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Moses and Aaron were told that, because they rebelled against God's word at the water of Meribah, they would not enter the promised land (Num 20:24; Num 27:14). The surrounding account in Numbers 20 describes Moses striking the rock. Smith's Bible Dictionary distinguishes this place from the Massah and Meribah of Exodus 17 near Rephidim, and calls it Meribah-kadesh. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some think one place carried both names. Ps 81:7 could refer to either. This entry treats the Kadesh spring as its own place. The location shown here is approximate, in the Kadesh region of northeastern Sinai.

Moladah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of Judah, listed among the cities of Judah's southern district (Josh 15:26). It was then given to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah (Josh 19:2), and Simeon's descendants are recorded living there (1 Chr 4:28). After the return from exile in Babylon, people of Judah settled there again (Neh 11:26). It is always mentioned close to Beersheba. The name probably means “birth.” Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with el-Milh (Tel Malhata), about 10 miles east of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Malatha, a town Josephus mentions, but notes that Eusebius and Jerome placed Malatha near Jattir, which would point elsewhere. The location shown here follows the general identification east of Beersheba in the eastern Negev.

Mount Gerizim is a mountain in the hill country of Samaria, facing Mount Ebal across the valley of Shechem, near modern Nablus. Before Israel entered Canaan, Moses commanded that the blessing be set on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal (Deut 11:29). Six tribes, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin, were to stand on Gerizim to bless the people (Deut 27:12). Joshua 8:33 records this ceremony, with half of Israel facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal around the ark. Later, Jotham stood on its top and called out his parable to the men of Shechem (Judg 9:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its height as about 3,000 feet and, citing Josephus, says the Samaritans built a rival temple there. The Samaritan woman's mention of "this mountain" as a place of worship (John 4:20) is usually taken to mean Gerizim. A small Samaritan community still worships there.

Mount of Esau is a name used only in the book of Obadiah for the mountainous homeland of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. It stands in parallel with Edom in Obad 1:8, where the LORD threatens to destroy the wise men of Edom and understanding from the mount of Esau, and with Teman, an Edomite district, in Obad 1:9. Obadiah says its inhabitants will be cut off by slaughter. He also foretells that people from the south will take possession of it (Obad 1:19) and that deliverers on Mount Zion will judge it (Obad 1:21), setting Esau's mountain against Zion. The name probably refers to the whole highland region of Edom rather than one peak, a view shared by the STEPBible Proper Names index. That region is the high country of southern Jordan, east of the Arabah. The location shown here marks a point in that area.

Oboth was a camp of the Israelites during their wilderness journey, reached shortly before they came to the borders of Moab. In Num 21:10–11 it is their next stop after the episode of the bronze serpent, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the first camp after that event. The fuller itinerary in Num 33:43–44 places it between Punon and Ijeabarim; counting from that list, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it the third camp after Mount Hor. From Oboth the people moved on to Ijeabarim, on the edge of Moab toward the east. The name is usually explained as meaning "water-skins" or "bottles." The exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably south of the Dead Sea, near the boundary of Moab and Edom. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea.

On was an ancient city of Lower Egypt, later known by its Greek name Heliopolis ("city of the sun"). In Genesis it appears only as the home of Potipherah, priest of On. Pharaoh gave Potipherah's daughter Asenath to Joseph as his wife, and she bore him Manasseh and Ephraim before the years of famine (Gen 41:45, 50; 46:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the city as the great center of Egyptian sun-worship, once filled with obelisks. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "Aven" in Ezek 30:17, named with Pibeseth in a prophecy against Egypt, has the same Hebrew consonants as On and is almost certainly the same city. Both dictionaries also connect it with Beth-shemesh in Jer 43:13. The location shown here is the ancient site of Heliopolis, on the northeastern edge of modern Cairo, in the area of present-day Matariya.

Peor was a mountain peak in Moab. It was the last of the heights to which King Balak brought Balaam so that he could curse Israel (Num 23:28). The verse says it "looketh toward Jeshimon," the wasteland below. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the Abarim range near Pisgah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records Eusebius's statement that it lay between Livias and Heshbon, and Buhl's identification of it with Jebel el-Mashaqqar. The location shown here is a rough position in that area, northeast of the Dead Sea. In other passages "Peor" is short for Baal-peor, the god worshipped there. "The matter of Peor" refers to Israel's idolatry with the Moabites and Midianites, which Num 31:16 links to Balaam's counsel. It brought a plague on the congregation and was still remembered in Joshua's day (Num 25:18; Josh 22:17). The name is often taken to mean "opening" or "cleft."

Philippi was a city in eastern Macedonia, described in Acts 16:12 as a leading city of that district and a Roman colony. Paul and his companions stayed there for some days on his first journey into Europe. The events located here include Lydia's conversion, the casting out of a spirit from a fortune-telling slave girl, and the imprisonment and release of Paul and Silas along with the conversion of their jailer. Paul later recalled the shameful treatment he had suffered there (1 Thess 2:2). He passed through Philippi again and sailed from it after the days of unleavened bread (Acts 20:6). He also wrote to the believers there, together with their overseers and deacons (Phil 1:1). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain that the city was named after Philip II of Macedon and that it lay inland from its port, Neapolis (modern Kavala). Its ruins are in northeastern Greece.

Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim. It was the home and burial place of Abdon son of Hillel, one of the judges of Israel, who was buried there "in the mount of the Amalekites" (Judg 12:15). It was also the hometown of Benaiah the Pirathonite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:30; 1 Chr 11:31). He served as captain of the division of 24,000 men on duty in the eleventh month and is described as an Ephraimite (1 Chr 27:14). Its site is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Fer'on, about 10 miles southwest of Shechem. Smith's Bible Dictionary favors Fer'ata, south of the road from Jaffa to Nablus. The location shown here follows the identification with the modern village of Far'un, near Tulkarm.

Rameses was a city and district in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt. Genesis calls the area where Joseph settled his father and brothers, at Pharaoh's command, "the land of Rameses," described as the best of the land. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take this to be Goshen, or part of it. The city was the starting point of the Exodus. Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, with about six hundred thousand men on foot besides children. It is probably the same as Raamses, one of the store cities the Israelites built (Exod 1:11). Its site is debated. Easton's identifies it with Zoan (Tanis), and Smith's also notes Tell Ramsis near Belbeis. The location shown here follows the identification with the Egyptian royal city Pi-Ramesses, near modern Qantir.

Rehob was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher in northern Israel. It is listed among Asher's towns in Josh 19:30, and it was one of the cities, with its surrounding pastureland, given to the Levites (Josh 21:31; 1 Chr 6:75). The Gershonite Levites received it, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Judges 1:31 names Rehob among the towns whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out. Several places share the name, which means "breadth" or "open space" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts two separate Rehobs in Asher and suggests that the Levitical city and the one left to the Canaanites may not be the same town. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the site unknown. The location shown here is approximate, in the hills of western Galilee east of Acco, the modern Acre.

Rimmon, a name meaning "pomegranate," was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev. It is listed among Judah's southernmost cities (Josh 15:32) and was later assigned to the tribe of Simeon (Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32, spelled "Remmon" in the King James Version of Joshua 19:7). In each list it appears next to Ain, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the two names may form one place, Ain-Rimmon, "spring of the pomegranate." That would make it probably the En-rimmon of Neh 11:29. Zechariah uses it to mark the southern limit of the land, "from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem" (Zech 14:10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Umm er-Rumamin, about 13 miles (21 km) southwest of Hebron. Several other biblical places share the name Rimmon.

The Rock was a rocky height in the wilderness of Maon, in the hill country of Judah south of Hebron, where David took refuge while Saul was hunting him. After the people of Ziph told Saul where David was, David and his men moved into the wilderness of Maon. There he came down to the rock and stayed. Saul followed, and the connected verses (1 Sam 23:26–28) describe the two forces on opposite sides of the mountain. Saul then broke off the chase when news came of a Philistine raid. The place was therefore named Sela-hammahlekoth, usually translated "Rock of Escape" or "Rock of Divisions." Maon itself was a town of Judah near Carmel and Ziph. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement near Maon, probably the modern Tell Ma'in.

Salecah (spelled Salchah or Salcah in the King James Version) was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan River, belonging to the kingdom of Og. It is always named as a boundary point, the far edge of Bashan, as in the phrase "all Bashan unto Salcah" (Deut 3:10; Josh 13:11). Joshua 12:5 lists it among the places where Og reigned. After Israel conquered the region, the territory up to Salecah went to the tribes settled east of the Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary assigns it to the half tribe of Manasseh, and 1 Chr 5:11 says the tribe of Gad lived in Bashan as far as Salchah. Easton's also gives the name's meaning as "wandering" and identifies the city with Salkhad, about 56 miles east of the Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification with modern Salkhad, in the Jebel al-Druze area of southern Syria.

Salem was the city ruled by Melchizedek, king and priest of the most high God, who brought out bread and wine to Abraham as he returned from defeating the kings and blessed him (Gen 14:18; Heb 7:1). Hebrews explains the name as meaning "peace," so that Melchizedek was "King of peace" (Heb 7:2). Ps 76:2 sets Salem in parallel with Zion as God's dwelling place, which is why Salem is commonly taken as an older or poetic name for Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note this view, which Jewish tradition, Josephus and early Christians held. Other traditions place Melchizedek's Salem elsewhere. The Samaritans linked it with Salim east of Nablus, and Jerome placed it near Scythopolis (Beth-shean), as Smith's Bible Dictionary reports. The location shown here follows the Jerusalem identification.

Senir (also spelled Shenir) is a mountain name linked with Mount Hermon, at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon range. Deut 3:9 says it was the Amorite name for Hermon, which the Sidonians called Sirion. Other passages list Senir alongside Hermon as though they were separate: the half tribe of Manasseh spread from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon (1 Chr 5:23), and Song 4:8 pairs the peaks of Shenir and Hermon. Ezek 27:5 says the ship planks of Tyre were made from fir trees of Senir. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore suggests Senir may have named a particular part of the range, and notes that medieval Arab geographers used Jebel Sanir for the Anti-Lebanon between Damascus and Homs. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the central of Hermon's three summits. The location shown here follows the identification with Mount Hermon itself.

Sheep Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah. Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt it, hung its doors and consecrated it, along with the wall as far as the towers of Meah and Hananel (Neh 3:1). Nehemiah's account of the repairs begins and ends at this gate, with goldsmiths and merchants restoring the stretch between the upper corner and the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:32). At the wall's dedication, one procession passed it before halting at the prison gate (Neh 12:39). The name probably reflects sheep being brought through it toward the nearby temple. In John 5:2, the KJV's "sheep market" beside the Pool of Bethesda is rendered "Sheep Gate" in many modern translations. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it in the eastern wall, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it near the northeast corner. The location shown here places it generally near the temple area.

Shittim, meaning "the acacias" and also called Abel-shittim (Num 33:49), was the last camp of the Israelites east of the Jordan before they entered Canaan. It lay on the plains of Moab across the river from Jericho. While Israel stayed there, the people began to commit sexual immorality with Moabite women (Num 25:1). From Shittim Joshua secretly sent two spies to view the land and Jericho, and they lodged with Rahab (Josh 2:1). The whole people then moved from Shittim to the Jordan and camped before crossing (Josh 3:1). Micah later recalled the events "from Shittim unto Gilgal," connecting it with Balak and Balaam (Mic 6:5). Josephus placed the camp near Abila, a place of palm trees. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Khirbet el-Kefrain, an area with many acacias, and the location shown here follows that identification, near Tell Kefrein in the Jordan Valley.

Sin was a wilderness region between Elim and Mount Sinai where the Israelites camped on their journey out of Egypt. They arrived on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt (Exod 16:1). Numbers places the stop after a camp by the Red Sea and before Dophkah (Num 33:11–12). Exodus has them leave Sin for Rephidim, where they found no water (Exod 17:1). The rest of Exodus 16 describes the people complaining about food here and receiving quails and the first manna. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the region to be probably the narrow coastal plain of el-Markha, along the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez in the western Sinai Peninsula. Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise places it between the gulf coast and Wadi Feiran. The location shown here follows this coastal identification. It is a different place from the Egyptian city of Sin mentioned in Ezekiel.

Succoth was the first camping place of the Israelites after they left Rameses during the exodus from Egypt (Exod 12:37; Num 33:5). The name means "booths" or "tents." From Succoth they moved on to Etham, at the edge of the wilderness (Exod 13:20; Num 33:6). The departure is dated to about 1491 BC, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Succoth was reached at the end of the first day's march. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the lower Wadi Tumilat, the valley running east from the Nile Delta, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Succoth as another name for Pithom. The location shown here follows the Wadi Tumilat identification, placing it near the valley's eastern end close to Lake Timsah, near modern Ismailia. This Succoth in Egypt is distinct from other places of the same name, such as the Succoth east of the Jordan.

Thyatira was a city in western Asia Minor, in the Roman province of Asia. It was the home city of Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who heard Paul's preaching and responded to it (Acts 16:14). By the context of that chapter, they met at Philippi, where she was evidently trading. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that Thyatira was famous for its dyeing industry and its trade guilds, which fits Lydia's business. Thyatira was also one of the seven churches of Asia to which the book of Revelation was sent (Rev 1:11). The message to its church is introduced as coming from the Son of God (Rev 2:18). It addresses separately those in Thyatira who had not accepted a certain teaching (Rev 2:24). The city is identified with modern Akhisar in western Turkey, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Tower, the Tower of Hananel ("Hananeel" in the King James Version), was a tower in the wall of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "God has graciously given." In Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall, the priests under Eliashib the high priest repaired the section from the Sheep Gate as far as the Tower of Meah and the Tower of Hananel (Neh 3:1). At the dedication of the wall, one procession passed the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of Meah on its way to the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). These passages place it on the north side of the city, near the Temple area. Jeremiah and Zechariah use it as a boundary marker in prophecies of a rebuilt Jerusalem (Jer 31:38; Zech 14:10). Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate point in Jerusalem's northern wall area.

Ur of the Chaldees was the city where Terah's family lived before setting out for Canaan. Haran, Abram's brother, died there, in the land of his birth, before his father Terah (Gen 11:28). Terah then left Ur with Abram, Sarai and Lot, heading for Canaan, but settled in Haran (Gen 11:31). Later passages describe the LORD as having brought Abram out of Ur (Gen 15:7; Neh 9:7). By inference it was also the birthplace of Abram and his brother Nahor, with Abram's birth placed about 1996 BC, also by inference from context. Its site has long been debated. Ancient tradition placed it at Urfa (Edessa) in northern Mesopotamia, and the Talmud at Erech (Warka). The location shown here follows the identification favoured by Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia: the ruins of Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq, near the Euphrates, an ancient center of moon-god worship.

The Valley of Salt was a valley near the border between Judah and Edom where two Israelite kings won battles against the Edomites. In David's reign, 18,000 men were struck down there. 2 Sam 8:13 says they were Syrians, while the parallel account in 1 Chr 18:12 says they were Edomites and credits the victory to Abishai son of Zeruiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some interpreters therefore take the 2 Samuel text to refer to Edom as well. The heading of Ps 60 links Joab with a victory over Edom there. Later, King Amaziah of Judah killed 10,000 Edomites in the valley and then captured Selah, which he renamed Joktheel. Easton's places the valley in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, while others identify it with Wadi el-Milh east of Beersheba. The location shown here follows the southern Dead Sea identification.

The Water Gate was a landmark on the east side of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Neh 3:26 places it opposite the area of Ophel where the temple servants (the Nethinim) lived, near a projecting tower. Its name probably reflects a route down to the Gihon Spring in the Kidron Valley below, though the text does not say so. In front of it was an open square, where the people gathered and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law of Moses. He read it aloud there from morning until midday to men, women and all who could understand. During the Feast of Tabernacles that followed, people built booths in this same square. Neh 12:37 mentions it again in the procession at the dedication of the wall. The location shown here places it on the eastern slope of the City of David.

Zarephath was a Phoenician town belonging to Sidon, on the coast between Tyre and Sidon. During the drought in Elijah's time, God sent the prophet there, saying a widow had been commanded to feed him. At the city gate he found her gathering sticks and asked her for water (1 Kgs 17:9–10). The following verses of the chapter tell how her flour and oil did not run out and how Elijah raised her son. Jesus referred to this episode in Luke 4:26, where the town appears under its Greek name, Sarepta, and is noted as a non-Israelite city to which Elijah was sent. Obadiah names Zarephath as the northern limit of Canaanite land that returning Israelite exiles would possess (Obad 1:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with modern Sarafand in Lebanon, about 8 miles south of Sidon, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Abel was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, near Dan, where Sheba son of Bichri took refuge after his revolt against David. In 2 Sam 20:14–15 it is also called Abel of Bethmaachah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the short form as an abridgment of the fuller name Abel-beth-maacah. The name means "meadow." Joab's forces besieged the city, built a siege ramp against it and battered its wall. A wise woman of the city then spoke with Joab, recalling an old saying that people would "ask counsel at Abel" to settle disputes, which suggests the town had a long reputation for wisdom. According to the rest of the chapter, the townspeople handed over Sheba's head and the siege ended. The city is usually identified with Tel Abel Beth Maacah (Abil el-Qamh), near present-day Metula, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Abel-meholah, meaning "meadow of dancing," was a town in the Jordan Valley and the home of the prophet Elisha son of Shaphat. God told Elijah to anoint Elisha from there as his successor (1 Kgs 19:16). The following verses describe Elijah finding him plowing, probably near the town. Earlier, the Midianite army routed by Gideon fled toward the border of Abel-meholah (Judg 7:22). Under Solomon, the town marked a limit of Baana's district, which ran from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah (1 Kgs 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius and Jerome placed it about ten Roman miles south of Beth-shean. It links the site with the area where Wadi el-Malih or Wadi Helweh enters the valley, and Easton's Bible Dictionary names 'Ain Helweh. Some scholars place it east of the Jordan instead. The location shown here follows the west-bank identification south of Beth-shean.

Achshaph was a Canaanite royal city in northern Canaan. Its king was one of the rulers Jabin king of Hazor summoned to join a coalition against Joshua and Israel (Josh 11:1). He later appears in the list of kings Joshua defeated (Josh 12:20). The city was then named among the border towns of the tribe of Asher (Josh 19:25). The name is usually explained as meaning "sorcery" or "fascination." Its exact site is uncertain, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that explorers have not agreed on an identification. Other proposals include Tell Keisan. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Achshaph with the ruined village of Kesaf or Yasif, northeast of Acco, and the location shown here follows that view, near modern Kafr Yasif in the western Galilee.

Ahava was a river, or possibly a town or district that a river flowed toward, in Babylonia. Ezra gathered the exiles there before leading them back to Jerusalem. The company camped in tents for three days while Ezra reviewed the people and priests. He found no Levites among them (Ezra 8:15) and sent for some. He also proclaimed a fast there to ask God for a safe journey for the families and their goods. The group left the river on the twelfth day of the first month and reached Jerusalem safely. The phrase "the river that runneth to Ahava" suggests the name may belong to a place rather than the stream itself. The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it was probably one of Babylonia's many canals, while Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries mention the modern town of Hit on the Euphrates. The location shown here follows the Hit identification.

Akrabbim, meaning "scorpions", was an ascent or mountain pass on the southern edge of the land of Israel. It always appears with the word for "ascent", and Josh 15:3 gives the full form Maaleh-acrabbim, "Scorpion Pass". It was one of the landmarks on the southern border of the promised land, running toward the wilderness of Zin and Kadesh-barnea (Num 34:4), and it also marked the southern border of the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:3). Judg 1:36 names it as a point on the border of the Amorites. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place it between the southern end of the Dead Sea and Zin and explain the name by the scorpions common in the district. Easton's links it with the pass of es-Sufah. The exact pass is uncertain. The location shown here lies in the Negev, southwest of the Dead Sea.

Alexandria was a major Egyptian port on the Mediterranean, founded by Alexander the Great about 332 BC and still a large city with the same name today. Apollos, an eloquent Jew well versed in the scriptures, was born there before he came to Ephesus (Acts 18:24). Alexandrian ships twice carried Paul toward Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. At Myra a centurion put the prisoners aboard one bound for Italy (Acts 27:6). After the shipwreck they sailed on in another that had wintered at the island, bearing the sign of Castor and Pollux (Acts 28:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the city one of Rome's chief grain ports, which fits the wheat cargo mentioned in Acts 27:38. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes its large Jewish community, its famous library, and that the Greek Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible was made there.

Aphek was a Canaanite royal city whose king was among those defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:18). Later the Philistines camped there before the battle near Ebenezer (1 Sam 4:1), and they gathered all their armies at Aphek before the battle in which Saul died, while Israel camped by a spring in Jezreel (1 Sam 29:1). Several places in the Bible share this name, so it is uncertain whether all three passages refer to the same town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this Aphek in Issachar near Jezreel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads Josh 12:18 as "Aphek in Sharon" and suggests that 1 Sam 29:1 may describe only a Philistine rallying point before they moved north toward Jezreel. The location shown here follows the Sharon identification. That places Aphek near later Antipatris, probably the modern Tel Aphek (Ras el-Ain) at the source of the Yarkon River, northeast of present-day Tel Aviv.

Aphek was a city east of the Jordan where the Syrian (Aramean) king Benhadad gathered his army to fight Israel in the year after an earlier defeat (1 Kgs 20:26). When the Syrians were beaten, the survivors fled into the city, where a wall fell on 27,000 of them, and Benhadad hid in an inner room (1 Kgs 20:30). Later the dying Elisha told King Joash of Israel that he would defeat the Syrians at Aphek (2 Kgs 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this may be the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it on the road from Damascus into Israel and identify it with modern Fik (Afiq), about six miles east of the Sea of Galilee, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several other biblical places share the name Aphek, which means "strength" or "fortress."

The Areopagus, meaning "hill of Ares" and called Mars' Hill in the King James Version, is a rocky hill in Athens just northwest of the Acropolis, above the ancient marketplace. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe it as the meeting place of Athens' oldest and most respected council, which still existed under Roman rule. In Acts 17, Athenians curious about Paul's "new doctrine" brought him to the Areopagus, where he stood and addressed the "men of Athens" (Acts 17:19, 22). Readers differ on whether he spoke before the council itself or simply on the hill. Smith's dictionary pictures the philosophers bringing him up from the marketplace to hear him more easily, and the location shown here is the hill. Among those who believed afterward was Dionysius "the Areopagite," probably a member of the council, along with a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:34).

Ariel is a poetic name Isaiah uses for Jerusalem, identified in Isa 29:1 as "the city where David dwelt." In that oracle the prophet announces woe on Ariel despite its continuing round of yearly feasts and sacrifices. God will bring distress, heaviness and sorrow on the city (Isa 29:2). Yet the multitude of nations that fight against Ariel and its fortifications will vanish "as a dream of a night vision" (Isa 29:7). The meaning of the name is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as "lion of God" when applied to the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the related Hebrew word in Ezek 43:15–16 for the altar hearth of burnt offering, and that sense may lie behind the phrase "it shall be unto me as Ariel" in Isa 29:2. The location shown here is Jerusalem.

Arimathea was the home town of Joseph, the rich man and disciple of Jesus who asked Pilate for Jesus' body after the crucifixion and took it for burial (Matt 27:57; Mark 15:43; John 19:38). Mark describes Joseph as an honorable council member who was waiting for the kingdom of God. John says he was a secret disciple out of fear. Luke 23:51 calls Arimathea a city of the Jews (Smith's Bible Dictionary renders this as "a city of Judea"). The town is mentioned only in connection with Joseph, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary thinks it was probably Ramathaim, the birthplace of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1). Others place it at Ramleh, which Smith's Bible Dictionary favors, or at Ramah in Benjamin. The location shown here is a hilltop just northwest of Jerusalem associated with Samuel, which matches the Ramathaim identification.

Azmon was a place on the southern border of the land promised to Israel, later the southern border of Judah. The boundary ran from the ascent of Akrabbim past Zin and Kadesh Barnea to Hazar Addar and on to Azmon. From there it turned toward the river of Egypt and ended at the Mediterranean Sea (Num 34:4–5; Josh 15:4). It was therefore probably the last named point before the border reached the river of Egypt, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to be the Wadi el-Arish. Smith's left the site unidentified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports H. Clay Trumbull's identification with Ain el-Qaseimeh, northwest of Kadesh Barnea. The location shown here also lies northwest of Kadesh Barnea, near the modern border between Israel and Egypt, but the exact site remains uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bone of a bone" or "our strength."

Baal-gad was a Canaanite city "in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon," marking the northern limit of Joshua's conquests (Josh 11:17; 12:7). The land he took stretched from Mount Halak near Seir in the south to Baal-gad in the north. Josh 13:5 also names it as the starting point of territory still unconquered, running from Baal-gad to the entrance of Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "lord of fortune" and says it probably comes from the worship of Baal. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's identifies it with Banias near the source of the Jordan and equates it with Baal-hermon, and notes that some have linked it to Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the valley west or northwest of Hermon, distinct from Baal-hermon, and notes Conder's suggestion of Ain Jedeideh. The location shown here is a general point at Mount Hermon rather than any one of these sites.

Baal-meon was a city east of the Dead Sea, in the tableland north of the Arnon. The Reubenites rebuilt it along with Nebo and Shibmah, and Num 32:38 notes that these towns were renamed. A Reubenite family line under Bela is said to have lived from Aroer as far as Nebo and Baal-meon (1 Chr 5:8). By Ezekiel's day it belonged to Moab and was named among the frontier cities, "the glory of the country," that would be laid open to invaders (Ezek 25:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears as Beon, Beth-baal-meon and Beth-meon, and that the Moabite king Mesha claimed on his inscription to have fortified it. The site is usually identified with modern Ma'in, southwest of Madaba in Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Baal-peor was the name of a Moabite god, the "Baal of Peor," and is treated here as the place where he was worshipped. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name from Mount Peor, where this cult was practised, and gives its meaning as "lord of the opening." The three verses here recall how Israel "joined" itself to Baal-peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead (Ps 106:28). They also recall that the men who followed him were destroyed (Deut 4:3), and Hosea calls the episode a shameful turning away (Hos 9:10). The event itself is narrated in Num 25, set while Israel was camped at Shittim in the plains of Moab. Because the name can mean either the god or his sanctuary, the exact place is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough point in the hills of Moab northeast of the Dead Sea, in present-day Jordan, near where Mount Peor is usually placed.

Baal-zephon was a place in Egypt near the sea, mentioned only as a landmark for the Israelite camp just before they crossed the Red Sea. The Israelites turned back from Etham and camped before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. There Pharaoh's chariots and army overtook them (Exod 14:2, 14:9; Num 33:7). By inference from context, this was about 1491 BC. The name means "lord of the north," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a god called Baali-Zapuna appears in an Egyptian papyrus, so the place was probably a shrine or town dedicated to that deity. Its exact position is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the western shore of the Gulf of Suez, possibly at Jebel Deraj or Kulalah, while other scholars consider the site unknown. The location shown here follows a placement near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez.

Baalah was a city on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, identified in the text itself as another name for Kirjath-jearim (Josh 15:9; 1 Chr 13:6). The boundary description runs from the spring of Nephtoah to Baalah, then turns west toward mount Seir, Chesalon, Beth-shemesh and Timnah (Josh 15:10). David and all Israel went to Baalah, described as belonging to Judah, to bring the ark of God up from there (1 Chr 13:6). The name is often taken to mean "mistress" or "possessor" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several places in the Bible share this name, so this entry covers only the Judahite city. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kuriet-el-Enab, or, as some think, with 'Erma. The location shown here is rough and lies nearer the 'Erma site, in the hills west of Jerusalem.

Besor was a brook or seasonal stream in the far south of Judah, named only in the account of David's pursuit of the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. David set out with six hundred men, but two hundred were too exhausted to cross the brook and stayed behind while the other four hundred went on (1 Sam 30:9–10). On his return with the recovered people and goods, David met the men waiting at the Besor and greeted them (1 Sam 30:21). The following verses record his ruling that those who stayed with the supplies would share the spoil equally. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Wadi esh-Sharia south of Gaza. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the Wadi Ghazza, which reaches the sea southwest of Gaza and into which the Sharia drains. The location shown here follows the Wadi esh-Sharia identification.

Beth-arabah, meaning “house of the Arabah” or “house of the desert,” was a town in the Jordan valley on the boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Judah's northern border passed Beth-hoglah and then ran along the north side of Beth-arabah toward the stone of Bohan (Josh 15:6). It is listed among Judah's towns “in the wilderness” with Middin and Secacah (Josh 15:61). It also appears among the towns of Benjamin, alongside Zemaraim and Bethel (Josh 18:22). That fits a site lying right on the shared border. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the “Arabah” of Josh 18:18 to be the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified and that the Judahite and Benjamite names may refer to different towns. This entry treats them as one town. The location shown here is a rough placement in the lower Jordan valley near the north end of the Dead Sea.

Beth-hoglah was a town in the Jordan Valley near the northern end of the Dead Sea, on the boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Judah's northern border ran up to Beth-hoglah and passed north of Beth-arabah (Josh 15:6). Benjamin's southern border passed along its north side before ending at the north bay of the Salt Sea, where the Jordan enters it (Josh 18:19). The town is listed among Benjamin's cities together with Jericho (Josh 18:21), so it probably belonged to Benjamin while marking Judah's edge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "house of the partridge." It identifies the site with a spring between Jericho and the Jordan, near the ruins of a medieval Greek monastery called Kasr Hajlah, and notes that the area now lies several miles inland from the sea. The location shown here follows that identification, southeast of Jericho.

Beth-shan was a city where the Philistines displayed the bodies of King Saul and his sons after defeating them on Mount Gilboa. They put Saul's armour in the temple of Ashtaroth and fastened the bodies to the city wall. The brave men of Jabesh-gilead marched all night, took the bodies down and burned them at Jabesh (1 Sam 31:10–12). Later David recovered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them from the street of Beth-shan (2 Sam 21:12). Other passages spell the name Beth-shean and place it in the territory assigned to Manasseh, near the Jordan Valley. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "house of the tooth," "of ivory," or "of sleep." The site is generally identified with Tel Beth-shean, beside modern Beit She'an in northern Israel, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Beth-zur, meaning "house of rock" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Halhul and Gedor among the tribe's towns (Josh 15:58). King Rehoboam fortified it as one of the defensive cities of Judah (2 Chr 11:7). After the exile, Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall near the tombs of David (Neh 3:16). In the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:45, Maon is called the father of Beth-zur, which links the town with that clan. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it commanded the main road from Hebron to Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes its importance as a fortress during the Maccabean wars. The location shown here is the site near the modern village of Beit Sur, a few miles north of Hebron.

Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem and close to Bethany. It appears only in the accounts of Jesus' approach to Jerusalem. As he and his disciples drew near the city and reached Bethphage, he sent two disciples ahead (Matt 21:1; Mark 11:1; Luke 19:29). The following verses describe them fetching the animal he rode into the city. Mark and Luke name it together with Bethany. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary place it on the road between Jericho and Jerusalem. Easton's adds that it lay at the limit of a Sabbath-day's journey from the city. The name is usually explained as "house of unripe (or early) figs." The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the village of Kefr et-Tur on the summit. Abu Dis has also been suggested. The location shown here is on the Mount of Olives east of Jerusalem.

Caphtor was the land from which the Philistines originally came, according to Deut 2:23, Jer 47:4 and Amos 9:7. Deuteronomy says the Caphtorim, who came out of Caphtor, destroyed the Avims living in settlements as far as Azzah (Gaza) and took their place. Jeremiah calls the Philistines "the remnant of the country of Caphtor," and Amos sets God's bringing the Philistines from Caphtor alongside Israel's exodus from Egypt and the Syrians' migration from Kir. The Bible does not say where Caphtor was. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it is commonly taken to be Crete, since the Philistines seem to be linked with the "Cherethites" (1 Sam 30:14). It also mentions a possible location in Egypt's northern Delta, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in or near Egypt. The location shown here follows the Crete identification.

Carchemish was an ancient city on the west bank of the Euphrates River, which commanded a main crossing of the river. Isaiah lists it with Calno, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria and Damascus as cities that had fallen to Assyria (Isa 10:9). It was the scene of a decisive battle. Pharaoh Necho of Egypt marched there to fight, and Josiah king of Judah went out to oppose him on the way (2 Chr 35:20). Later, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon defeated Necho's army at Carchemish (Jer 46:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this battle to about 605 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a very old Hittite city and identifies it with Jerablus. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries place it at or near Hierapolis (Mabug). The location shown here follows the Jerablus identification, on the modern border between Turkey and Syria.

Daberath was a city in Lower Galilee, at the western foot of Mount Tabor. Its name probably means "pasture," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. It appears on the line of Zebulun's border, which ran from Sarid past Chisloth-tabor to Daberath and up to Japhia (Josh 19:12). It lay on the boundary between Zebulun and Issachar and belonged to Issachar. It was one of the towns from Issachar given with its pasturelands to the Levites. Joshua 21:28 spells it Dabareh. The surrounding passages assign these towns to the Gershonite clan of Levites, which suggests Daberath went to the Gershonites (Josh 21:28; 1 Chr 6:72). Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Daburiyya (Deburieh) on the lower western slopes of Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification.

Decapolis, Greek for "ten cities," was a region mostly east and southeast of the Sea of Galilee, home to a league of largely Greek cities in Roman times. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the Roman writer Pliny, list them as Scythopolis (Beth-shean, the only one west of the Jordan), Hippos, Gadara, Pella, Philadelphia (modern Amman), Gerasa (Jerash), Dion, Canatha, Raphana and Damascus. People from the Decapolis were among the crowds who followed Jesus (Matt 4:25). A man Jesus freed from demons went there to tell what had been done for him (Mark 5:20). Jesus later passed through the region on his way back to the Sea of Galilee (Mark 7:31). By inference from the accounts that follow, he healed a crowd and fed four thousand people near there. The region had no fixed borders, and the location shown here marks Damascus, the northernmost city.

Ebenezer, meaning “stone of help,” was the name Samuel gave to a memorial stone he set up between Mizpeh and Shen after Israel defeated the Philistines, saying, “Hitherto hath the LORD helped us” (1 Sam 7:12). The name also appears earlier as the place where Israel camped against the Philistines at Aphek before the battle in which the ark of God was captured and taken to Ashdod (1 Sam 4:1; 5:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these earlier uses as naming the spot in advance, so the defeat and the later victory happened in the same area. The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no identification is yet possible. Easton's records two proposals: Beit Iksa, a prominent height northwest of Jerusalem, or Deir Aban, east of ‘Ain Shems. The location shown here is a rough one near Mizpah and Beit Iksa.

Elath was a city at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, an arm of the Red Sea, near Ezion-geber. Moses recalls that Israel passed by way of Elath and Ezion-geber on the route around Edom toward the wilderness of Moab (Deut 2:8). Under the plural form Eloth it appears beside Ezion-geber in Solomon's time (1 Kgs 9:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary says it later broke away from Judah. King Azariah (Uzziah), named in the preceding verse, rebuilt it and restored it to Judah (2 Kgs 14:22). In the reign of Ahaz, Rezin king of Syria took it back and drove out the Jews, and the Syrians settled there (2 Kgs 16:6). Some translations read "Edom" and "Edomites" here instead. Easton's identifies it with the Greek and Roman Elana and the ruin of Aila. The location shown here is at modern Aqaba in Jordan.

Eloth was a town on the shore of the Red Sea in the land of Edom, at the northern tip of what is now the Gulf of Aqaba. It is another spelling of Elath, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Solomon built a fleet of ships at nearby Ezion-geber, described as lying beside Eloth, and he visited both places (1 Kgs 9:26; 2 Chr 8:17). Later Uzziah king of Judah rebuilt Eloth and brought it back under Judah's control after his father Amaziah died (2 Chr 26:2). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 14:22 records the same event under the name Elath, and 2 Kgs 16:6 says Judah later lost the town in the days of Ahaz. Its exact site is uncertain. It is usually placed near modern Aqaba in Jordan or nearby Eilat in Israel. The location shown here follows the Aqaba identification.

En-dor was a town in the territory of Issachar whose inhabitants and surrounding towns were allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, though Manasseh did not drive out its Canaanite population (Josh 17:11). On the eve of his final battle with the Philistines, King Saul had his servants find a woman there who was a medium, so that he could consult her (1 Sam 28:7). Psalm 83 recalls En-dor as the place where enemies of Israel perished. The previous verse names Sisera and Jabin, linking it with the victory of Deborah and Barak near the Kishon (Ps 83:10). The name probably means 'spring of Dor.' Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Endur on the northern slope of the Hill of Moreh, south of Mount Tabor and near Nain and Shunem. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ephrath was the ancient name of the town later called Bethlehem, in the hill country south of Jerusalem. Genesis twice adds the note "which is Bethlehem" to explain the older name, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the early name of Bethlehem-judah. Jacob's family was traveling south from Bethel and was only a short distance from Ephrath when Rachel went into a hard labor. She gave birth to Benjamin and died, and Jacob buried her beside the road to Ephrath. This was about 1739 BC, by inference from context. Near the end of his life, Jacob recalled burying her there. Some read 1 Sam 10:2 as placing Rachel's tomb farther north, near the border of Benjamin. The location shown here follows the Genesis identification with Bethlehem and matches the modern town of that name.

Esau, used as a place name, stands for the land and people of Edom, the territory settled by the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Esau driving the Horites out of Mount Seir and settling there as a powerful chief in Edom. Gen 36:40 lists the chiefs (dukes) who came from Esau "after their places," tying his name to the districts they held. The prophets use "Esau" as a name for this land and nation. Jer 49:10 says Esau will be stripped bare and his hiding places uncovered, and Obad 1:18 pictures the house of Esau as stubble burned by the house of Jacob. The region lay south-east of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan. The location shown here marks the surrounding area, near ancient Bozrah (modern Buseirah), rather than a single town.

Eshtemoa was a town in the hill country of Judah. It was one of the cities given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57). After David defeated the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag, he sent gifts from the spoil to his friends in Eshtemoa, among other towns where he and his men had moved about (1 Sam 30:28). Josh 15:50 lists it in a shorter form, Eshtemoh, among the towns of Judah's mountain district. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of es-Semu'a, about 7 or 8 miles south of Hebron, where ancient remains survive. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "obedience." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same name is used of a person in a genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 4:17, 19).

Ezem was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev region, that was later given to the tribe of Simeon. The King James Version spells it Azem in Joshua. It appears in the list of Judah's southernmost towns near the border with Edom (Josh 15:29), again among the towns of Simeon's inheritance, which lay within Judah's territory (Josh 19:3), and among the places where Simeon's descendants lived (1 Chr 4:29). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a bone." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify Ezem with Azmon, a point on Judah's southern border. The text gives no further details, and the exact site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement.

Field, the "fuller's field" (ESV "Washer's Field"), was a spot just outside Jerusalem where fullers washed and bleached cloth, an activity that needed a steady water supply. It lay beside a highway near the conduit of the upper pool. There Isaiah and his son Shearjashub were sent to meet King Ahaz (Isa 7:3). Years later the Assyrian officials Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh, sent from Lachish with an army, stood at the same place to confront King Hezekiah's men (2 Kgs 18:17; Isa 36:2). Its exact position is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west of the city, near the upper pool at the head of the Hinnom Valley. Others place the upper pool north of the city or near the Gihon spring to the east. The rough location shown here follows the western placement near the Hinnom Valley.

The Fish Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. Its name probably comes from a fish market nearby, perhaps where traders from the coast sold their catch, as Neh 13:16 describes Tyrians doing. King Manasseh, who is the "he" of 2 Chr 33:14 by context, built an outer wall west of Gihon that ran as far as the Fish Gate. After the exile, the sons of Hassenaah rebuilt it, setting its beams, doors, locks and bars. Zephaniah foretold a cry of distress rising from it on the day of the LORD. Nehemiah's account of the rebuilding moves west from the Sheep Gate, so the Fish Gate is usually placed on the city's north side, the direction from which attackers most often approached. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is approximate.

The Gate of the Fountain (Fountain Gate in modern translations) was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. It stood near the king's pool and the pool of Siloah (Siloam), by the king's garden and the stairs leading down from the city of David. That places it toward the southern end of the city, probably near the southeast corner where the Kidron and Tyropoeon valleys meet. During his night inspection of the ruined walls, Nehemiah reached this gate and found so much rubble that his animal could not get through (Neh 2:14). Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of part of the Mizpah district, rebuilt it, fitting its doors, locks and bars, and repaired the nearby wall of the pool (Neh 3:15). At the dedication of the wall, one procession passed by it and went up the stairs of the city of David toward the Water Gate (Neh 12:37).

Gath-rimmon was a city in the territory of the tribe of Dan, listed with Jehud and Bene-berak in Dan's allotment (Josh 19:45). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Kohathite clan (Josh 21:24). The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:69 names it alongside Aijalon but places it in a passage about Ephraim's cities. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "press of the pomegranate." Gath-rimmon was apparently in the coastal plain not far from Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that its exact site is not identified. The location shown here places it east of modern Tel Aviv. The name is shared by another Levitical city in Manasseh (Josh 21:25), which this entry does not describe.

Gebal was a Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast, known to the Greeks as Byblos and probably the modern town of Jbeil in Lebanon, north of Beirut. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre says the elders and skilled men of Gebal worked as caulkers on Tyre's ships (Ezek 27:9). In 1 Kgs 5:18 the word the King James Version renders "stonesquarers" is, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the Hebrew term for men of Gebal (Gebalites), who helped prepare stone and timber for Solomon's temple. Josh 13:5 also mentions their land. Gebal appears in Ps 83:7 among peoples allied against Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Gebal to be a separate hill district southeast of the Dead Sea, near Edom. The location shown here follows the Phoenician coastal city. The name probably means "border" or "limit."

Gederah was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the fourteen cities of that district in Josh 15:36. The name means "wall" or "fortified place." In 1 Chr 4:23 the King James phrase "among plants and hedges" probably translates two place names, Netaim and Gederah, where potters of the tribe of Judah lived and worked for the king. Josabad "the Gederathite," one of the warriors who joined David (1 Chr 12:4), is likely named after this town or a place of similar name. Because he appears in a group with Benjamite links, some think his home was a different Gederah in Benjamin. STEPBible's name index also links Baal-hanan, one of David's overseers, to Gederah. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with Jedireh, a ruin near Zorah. The location shown here lies farther west, near the modern Israeli town of Gedera.

Gennesaret was a district, and by some accounts a town, on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. After Jesus fed the five thousand and walked on the water, he and his disciples crossed the lake and landed in "the land of Gennesaret" (Matt 14:34; Mark 6:53), where the Healing in Gennesaret took place. Luke calls the Sea of Galilee itself "the lake of Gennesaret" (Luke 5:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to Chinnereth, a town of Naphtali named in Josh 19:35. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the land of Gennesaret with the fertile plain now called el-Ghuweir. It runs a little over three miles from Magdala (el-Mejdel) in the south toward Khan Minyeh in the north and is about a mile wide. Josephus praised its fruitfulness. The name is often explained as "garden of the prince." The location shown here lies on that western shore.

Gilboa was a mountain range in northern Israel, on the eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon) above the Jordan valley. It is known almost entirely for one event. Saul camped there with the army of Israel while the Philistines gathered at Shunem, across the valley (1 Sam 28:4). The Philistines killed Saul and Jonathan on Gilboa and hung their bodies on the wall of Beth-shan. The men of Jabesh-gilead later took the bodies away, and David afterward recovered the bones (2 Sam 21:12). In his lament over Saul and Jonathan, David called for no dew or rain to fall on the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul's shield was thrown away (2 Sam 1:21). The name is usually explained as "bubbling spring" (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). The range is identified with the modern Jebel Faqu'a, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Golgotha was the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. The Gospels explain the name as "the place of a skull" (Matt 27:33; Mark 15:22), and John notes that Jesus carried his own cross there (John 19:17). The word comes from Aramaic for "skull." Its Latin equivalent gives the familiar name Calvary. Smith's Bible Dictionary offers two explanations of the name: it was a place of executions, or a bare, rounded mound shaped like a skull. Connected passages place it near the city and outside its gate (Heb 13:12), with a garden and tomb close by (John 19:41). The exact site is uncertain. Long tradition places it at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors the skull-like hillock above Jeremiah's Grotto, north of the city. The location shown here is approximate and only places it within Jerusalem, without choosing between these sites.

Goshen was a district in southern Canaan, distinct from the better-known Goshen in Egypt where Jacob's family settled. It appears in the summaries of Joshua's conquests as "the country of Goshen", listed with lands stretching from Kadesh-barnea and Gaza to Gibeon (Josh 10:41), and alongside the hills, the south country, the valley and the plain (Josh 11:16). A town named Goshen is also listed among the cities of Judah's southern hill country (Josh 15:51). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the district probably took its name from this town or was linked to it. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the district in the maritime plain of Judah, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a separate region whose exact site is unknown. The location shown here follows the hill country view and places it southwest of Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "drawing near".

Habor was a river in Assyria, and probably also the district around it, where the king of Assyria settled Israelites deported from the northern kingdom. 2 Kgs 17:6 and 2 Kgs 18:11 place the exiles in Halah and in Habor "by the river of Gozan" after the fall of Samaria in Hoshea's ninth year. 1 Chr 5:26 records that Pul and Tiglath-pileser carried the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read Habor as the river of Gozan itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that another river called Khabur flows into the Tigris, but identifies the biblical Habor with the Khabur (ancient Chaboras), a tributary of the Euphrates in modern northeastern Syria. The location shown here follows that Euphrates-tributary identification.

Hachilah was a hill in the wilderness of Judah, near Ziph, where David hid while Saul was pursuing him. The text places it "on the south of Jeshimon" and "before Jeshimon," meaning at the edge of the barren wasteland that falls away toward the Dead Sea (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1). Twice the people of Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah to report that David was hiding there. On the second occasion Saul camped on the hill by the road, while David stayed out in the wilderness nearby (1 Sam 26:3). The surrounding chapter tells how David then entered Saul's camp at night and took the king's spear and water jug. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Hachilah with the ridge of Dhahret el-Kolah (Zahrat al Kula) east of Ziph, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hadid was a town named with Lod (Lydda) and Ono in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon. Ezra 2:33 counts 725 people from Lod, Hadid and Ono together, and the parallel list in Neh 7:37 gives 721. Neh 11:34 includes Hadid among the places resettled by people of Benjamin after the return, so it was probably a Benjamite town. The name is usually taken to mean "sharp" or "pointed." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Adida, a town fortified by Simon Maccabeus according to 1 Maccabees. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that in Eusebius's time a town called Aditha stood east of Lydda. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE place Hadid at modern el-Haditheh, about 3 miles (5 km) east or northeast of Lydda, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Halah was a region where the king of Assyria resettled Israelites taken captive from the northern kingdom. After Samaria fell in the ninth year of King Hoshea, the deportees were placed in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11). Chronicles says Tiglath-pileser had earlier carried Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:26). Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it along the upper Khabur River in present-day northeastern Syria and, like Smith's Bible Dictionary, links it with the district Ptolemy called Chalcitis. Another view connects it with an Assyrian district near Nineveh. The location shown here follows the upper Khabur identification, near the Gozan river named alongside it.

Harosheth-hagoyim, called "Harosheth of the Gentiles" in the King James Version, was the home of Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin, the Canaanite king who reigned in Hazor (Judg 4:2). Sisera gathered his nine hundred iron chariots and his troops from there and marched to the Kishon River to fight Israel (Judg 4:13). After Barak defeated him, Barak chased the chariots and the army all the way back to Harosheth, and Sisera's whole force was killed (Judg 4:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "the smithy of the nations" and suggests that Jabin's chariots may have been made there. It places the city at the pass leading from the plain of Acre into the Jezreel Valley, at the foot of Mount Carmel, and identifies it with el-Harithiyeh. Some scholars instead treat the name as a district rather than a town. The location shown here follows the el-Harithiyeh identification, near the Kishon.

Hena was a city named in the Assyrian taunts sent to King Hezekiah of Judah during Sennacherib's invasion. The Rabshakeh's speech (2 Kgs 18:34) and Sennacherib's letter (2 Kgs 19:13; Isa 37:13) list it with Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim and Ivah as places whose gods and kings could not withstand Assyria, implying it had already been conquered. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Anah on the Euphrates, not far from Sepharvaim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary also suggests Anah. The location shown here follows that identification, in present-day western Iraq. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other views: that the text may be corrupt, that "Hena and Ivah" may be a Hebrew phrase meaning "he has driven away and overturned," or that the words may be divine names. Its exact identity therefore remains uncertain.

Ibleam was a Canaanite city with its surrounding towns, lying within the territory of Issachar or Asher but assigned to the tribe of Manasseh (Josh 17:11). Manasseh did not drive out its inhabitants, and the Canaanites went on living there (Judg 1:27). Ibleam later appears in Jehu's revolt. When Jehu killed King Joram of Israel, King Ahaziah of Judah fled and was struck in his chariot "at the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam." He escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). The name probably also appears as Bileam in 1 Chr 6:70. The site lay near modern Jenin, but identifications differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Jelamah, north of Jenin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it at the ruin of Bel'ameh, just south of Jenin. The location shown here follows the Bel'ameh identification.

Ijon was a fortified town in the far north of Israel, in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It was among the cities struck by the commanders of Ben-hadad of Syria, whom King Asa of Judah had paid to attack Baasha of Israel (1 Kgs 15:20; 2 Chr 16:4). Later, in the days of Pekah king of Israel, the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser captured it along with Abel-beth-maacah, Kedesh, Hazor and the rest of Naphtali, and deported its people to Assyria (2 Kgs 15:29).
