Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name to the Merj Ayun ("meadow of springs"), a fertile plain northwest of Dan in present-day southern Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at el-Khiam, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Tell Dibbin at the north of the plain. The location shown here lies near el-Khiam.

Ivvah was a city named by the Assyrian king Sennacherib's officials in their threats against Hezekiah of Judah. They listed it with Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim and Hena as places whose gods and kings had been unable to resist Assyria, so Jerusalem should not expect rescue either (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). It is often taken to be the same as Avva, one of the places from which the Assyrians resettled people in Samaria (2 Kgs 17:24). Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Euphrates between Sepharvaim and Hena, and some have linked it with Hit on the Euphrates or with Imm near Aleppo. Others have read Hena and Ivvah as names of gods rather than cities. The rough location shown here follows the Euphrates view, placing it on the middle Euphrates in modern Iraq.

Jokneam was a Canaanite royal city whose king appears in the list of kings defeated by Joshua, where it is called "Jokneam of Carmel" (Josh 12:22). It lay on the edge of Zebulun's territory, whose border reached "the river that is before Jokneam," probably the Kishon (Josh 19:11). Zebulun later gave the city and its surrounding pasturelands to the Merarite families of the Levites (Josh 21:34). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Tell Kaimon (Tell Qeimun, today Tel Yokneam), a steep mound at the eastern end of Mount Carmel above the Kishon valley, about 12 miles southwest of Nazareth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed it on the road from Legio to Acre, which supports that site. The location shown here follows this identification. The same encyclopedia notes that the "Jokneam" of 1 Kgs 4:12 in the King James Version is better read as Jokmeam, a different place.

Jotbathah was a desert campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Numbers lists it between Hor-hagidgad and Ebronah (Num 33:33–34). Deuteronomy calls it Jotbath and describes it as "a land of rivers of waters," a place with streams (Deut 10:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "goodness." Because the Numbers itinerary soon reaches Ezion-geber on the Gulf of Aqaba (Num 33:35), the site was probably in the southern Arabah valley, north of the gulf. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the exact site is unknown. A common suggestion links it to the springs of the southern Arabah, near modern Yotvata in Israel, whose name echoes the biblical one. The location shown here is only approximate and follows that southern Arabah identification, north of the Gulf of Aqaba.

Kabzeel was a city in the far south of Judah's territory, listed first among the tribe's "uttermost cities" toward the border of Edom in the Negeb (Josh 15:21). It was the hometown of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, one of David's mighty men, remembered for killing two champions of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day (2 Sam 23:20; 1 Chr 11:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it to be the same place as Jekabzeel, which was resettled by people of Judah after the exile (Neh 11:25). The name is usually explained as "gathered by God" or "God gathers." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negeb, consistent with the description in Joshua.

Lehi, meaning "jawbone," was a place in Judah where Samson fought the Philistines. The Philistines camped in Judah and spread out in Lehi, demanding that Samson be handed over. When the men of Judah brought him there bound, the cords fell from his arms and he struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Afterward, thirsty, he received water from a hollow place, and he named the spring En-hakkore. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the phrase in Judg 15:19 is better read, as in the Revised Version, "the hollow place that is in Lehi." The nearby verse Judg 15:17 calls the site Ramath-lehi. Its exact location is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Beit-Likiyeh near upper Beth-horon. The location shown here is a rough placement in the western hills of Judah, near Samson's home region along the Sorek Valley.

Lo-debar was a town east of the Jordan River in Gilead, home of Machir son of Ammiel. In the context of 2 Sam 9, Jonathan's son Mephibosheth was living in Machir's house there until King David brought him to his court. Later, when David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, the same Machir of Lo-debar was among those who met him there, alongside Shobi of Rabbah and Barzillai of Rogelim. That grouping suggests Lo-debar lay not far from Mahanaim. The name is often explained as meaning "no pasture." Easton's Bible Dictionary places it north of the Jabbok and takes it as probably the same place as Debir in the boundary list of Josh 13:26. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a village called Ibdar, about 6.5 miles (10 km) east of Umm Qeis in northern Jordan, as a possible match, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Lydda was a town in the coastal plain of Judea, near Joppa. Peter visited the believers living there during a tour of the region (Acts 9:32). There he healed Aeneas, a man paralyzed for eight years, and the residents of Lydda and Saron (Sharon) turned to the Lord (Acts 9:35). Because Lydda was close to Joppa, the disciples there sent two men to bring Peter after Dorcas died, and he raised her to life (Acts 9:38). By context these events date to about AD 38. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Lydda with Old Testament Lod (1 Chr 8:12; Ezra 2:33) and place it about nine miles from Joppa on a road to Jerusalem. Easton's says it was later rebuilt under the name Diospolis. It is identified with the modern city of Lod in Israel, which matches the location shown here.

Magog is a region or people named in Ezekiel's prophecy as "the land of Magog," whose ruler Gog is called the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal (Ezek 38:2). God declares he will send fire on Magog (Ezek 39:6). In Rev 20:8 "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations from the four corners of the earth that are gathered for battle, as numerous as the sand of the sea. Elsewhere, Gen 10:2 and 1 Chr 1:5 list Magog as the second son of Japheth, which suggests the people took their name from him. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be a Scythian or Tartar people, citing Jerome, who placed such nations beyond the Caucasus and near the Caspian Sea. Another suggestion links the name to the Assyrian "land of Gugu." The rough location shown here follows the Caucasus and Caspian view.

Marah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites camped soon after crossing the sea out of Egypt. They reached it after a three days' journey through the wilderness of Etham, and found that its water was too bitter to drink, which is why the place was called Marah, meaning "bitterness" (Exod 15:23; Num 33:8). The following verses in Exodus, not quoted here, tell how the people complained and Moses threw a tree into the water, which made it drinkable. From Marah they moved on to Elim, a site with twelve springs and seventy palm trees (Num 33:9). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary mention the common identification with 'Ain Hawarah, a bitter spring about 47 miles from 'Ayun Musa on the western side of the Sinai Peninsula. The location shown here follows that identification.

Meribah-kadesh was the place in the wilderness of Zin where, according to Deut 32:51, Moses and Aaron failed to honor God as holy before Israel. That failure is the reason given for Moses not entering the promised land. The name joins Meribah, meaning “strife” or “quarreling,” with Kadesh. It recalls the episode in Num 20, where the people complained about having no water at Kadesh and Moses struck the rock. Ezekiel calls the same spot “the waters of strife in Kadesh” and uses it as a point on the ideal southern border of the restored land, running from Tamar to Kadesh and then along the brook to the Mediterranean (Ezek 47:19; 48:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Kadesh with Kadesh-barnea at ‘Ain el-Kadeis. The rough location shown here, in northeastern Sinai near the springs of that area, follows this identification.

Miletus was a seaport on the west coast of Asia Minor, near the mouth of the Meander River, about 36 miles south of Ephesus (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Paul reached it by ship on his voyage toward Jerusalem, sailing past Chios, Samos and Trogyllium (Acts 20:15). This was about AD 54, by inference from context. From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church, who came to hear his farewell address (Acts 20:17). Later Paul wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus, called Miletum in the King James Version (2 Tim 4:20). According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Miletus was once a leading Ionian Greek trading city that founded many colonies, then declined after its capture by the Persians. River silt has since pushed the coastline miles away from its ruins, which lie in modern Turkey and include a large theater.

Mount Tabor is a mountain in northern Israel where Barak gathered his army before the battle against Sisera. The prophet Deborah summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and told him to march to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun (Judg 4:6). When Sisera, commander of the Canaanite forces, learned that Barak had gone up the mountain, he moved his army against him (Judg 4:12). At Deborah's command Barak then came down from Tabor with his ten thousand men and defeated Sisera (Judg 4:14). The location shown here is the isolated, dome-shaped hill rising from the eastern edge of the Jezreel Valley, southwest of the Sea of Galilee, still called Mount Tabor today. Its height and position overlooking the plain probably made it a natural rallying point for the tribes.

Nebo was a town in Judah whose people returned from the Babylonian exile. The lists of returnees record fifty-two "children of Nebo" (Ezra 2:29), and Nehemiah calls it "the other Nebo" (Neh 7:33), probably to tell it apart from the better-known Nebo in Moab. Ezra 10:43 names seven "sons of Nebo" among the men who, by the context of that chapter, had married foreign wives. The name appears in the lists next to Bethel and Ai, but the verses give no clue to where it was. Reference works suggest different sites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Beit Nuba, northwest of Jerusalem, or Nuba, south-southeast of Adullam. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at a village about 7 miles northwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Nuba identification, between Adullam and Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that speaks or prophesies."

Perga was a city of Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey. Paul and his companions reached it after sailing from Paphos on Cyprus during the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. At Perga, John (Mark) left the group and went back to Jerusalem, while Paul and Barnabas travelled inland to Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:13–14). On their return journey they preached in Perga and then went down to the port of Attalia, from which they sailed back to Antioch in Syria (Acts 14:25). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the capital of Pamphylia and places it on the river Cestrus, about 7 miles from the sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was known for the worship of a local goddess identified with Artemis. The location shown here is the ruined site near modern Aksu, east of Antalya.

Phenicia (Phoenicia in modern spelling; also written Phenice in the King James Version) was the coastal region along the Mediterranean north of Israel, roughly modern Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a narrow strip about 120 miles long, running from the Eleutherus River in the north to Mount Carmel in the south. Its chief cities included Tyre and Sidon, and its people were famous seafarers and traders. The name appears only in Acts. Believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen's death travelled there, preaching only to Jews (Acts 11:19). Paul and Barnabas later passed through Phenicia and Samaria on their way to Jerusalem, reporting that Gentiles had been converted (Acts 15:3). At the end of his third journey, Paul boarded a ship bound for Phenicia (Acts 21:2) and landed at Tyre, according to the following verse.

Phrygia was a region in the interior of Asia Minor, in present-day west-central Turkey. People from Phrygia were among the Jews and converts gathered in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). On his second journey Paul and his companions went through Phrygia and the region of Galatia after being prevented from preaching in Asia (Acts 16:6). At the start of his third journey he again passed through Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:23). Its borders were never sharply fixed. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it an ethnic rather than a political term, since its territory was divided among several Roman provinces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes a Galatian Phrygia, which included Antioch and Iconium, from a larger Asian Phrygia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Colosse, Hierapolis and Laodicea within it. Because the region was so loosely defined, no single location is shown here.

Pi-hahiroth was the place in Egypt where the Israelites camped by the sea just before crossing it during the Exodus. God told Moses to have the people turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exod 14:2). There Pharaoh's chariots and army caught up with them (Exod 14:9). The list of camps in Numbers places it after Etham (Num 33:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "place where sedge (or reeds) grows." The site is uncertain, partly because the Suez isthmus has changed since ancient times. Easton's notes that some identify it with Ajrud, a fortress between Etham and Suez. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the old shoreline within about ten miles of modern Suez. The location shown here follows this general placement near Suez, close to Ajrud.

Pontus was a region and Roman province in northern Asia Minor, stretching along the southern coast of the Black Sea, in what is now northern Turkey. Its name comes from the Greek name for that sea, the Pontus Euxinus. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries compare it roughly to the later province of Trebizond. It appears three times in the New Testament. People from Pontus were among the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Aquila, the Jewish husband of Priscilla whom Paul met in Corinth, was born there (Acts 18:2). Peter addresses his first letter to the scattered believers living in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Pet 1:1). Together these passages point to a significant Jewish population in the region, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a resort of many Jews of the Dispersion. The location shown here marks the general area of the region rather than a single site.

Put was a people and land in Africa closely tied to Egypt. Nahum 3:9 lists Put alongside Lubim (the Libyans) as helpers of Thebes, together with Ethiopia and Egypt. In Jer 46:9 the King James Version's "Libyans" probably renders the same Hebrew name. There Put's shield-bearers march with Egypt's army against Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Gen 10:6 names Phut as a son of Ham, between Egypt and Canaan. It adds that Ezek 27:10 and 30:5 describe men of Put as mercenaries serving Tyre and Egypt, and that a fragment of Nebuchadnezzar's annals mentions "Phut of the Ionians." The exact location is uncertain. Some identify Put with Libya west of Egypt, and others with Punt on the Red Sea coast of East Africa. The location shown here follows the Libyan identification and is placed in Cyrenaica, in modern eastern Libya.

Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt used in the Psalms and Isaiah, distinct from Rahab of Jericho, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it to mean "the proud one" or "insolence." In Ps 87:4 Rahab is listed with Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia among nations whose people will come to know the LORD. In Ps 89:10 and Isa 51:9 God is praised for having broken or cut Rahab in pieces. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads these as references to the defeat of Egypt at the exodus. In Isa 51:9 Rahab stands alongside "the dragon," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also sees in the name an ancient image of a sea monster that became an emblem of Egypt. The location shown here is a general point in Egypt's Nile Delta region, matching the identification with Egypt.

Ramoth, called "Ramoth in Gilead," was a city east of the Jordan in the territory of the tribe of Gad. Its name means "heights" or "high places" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Moses set it apart as one of three cities of refuge east of the Jordan, alongside Bezer and Golan (Deut 4:43). Under Joshua it was confirmed as a city of refuge and given to the Levites (Josh 20:8; 21:38). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the place usually called Ramoth-gilead, where King Ahab was mortally wounded fighting the Syrians (1 Kgs 22) and where Jehu was later anointed king (2 Kgs 9). Its site is uncertain. Easton's mentions Reimun near Jerash and a site northeast of es-Salt. The location shown here follows another proposed identification, probably Tell er-Rumeith near modern Ramtha in northern Jordan. Several other places in the Bible share the name Ramoth.

Rimmon, called "the rock of Rimmon" or "the rock Rimmon," was a stronghold toward the wilderness to which the tribe of Benjamin fled after its defeat by the other Israelite tribes in the war over the crime at Gibeah. During the flight, thousands of Benjamites were cut down along the roads. Six hundred men reached the rock and stayed there for four months (Judg 20:47). Later the assembly of Israel sent messengers to these survivors at the rock to make peace with them (Judg 21:13). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "pomegranate" or "exalted." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the site with the modern village of Rammun, northeast of Jerusalem and east of Bethel, on the edge of the hill country above a steep drop toward the Jordan valley. The location shown here follows that identification. Several other places in the Bible share the name Rimmon.

Sardis was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, and the home of one of the seven churches to which the book of Revelation was addressed (Rev 1:11). The message to its church says it had a name for being alive but was dead, though a few people there had not defiled their garments and would walk in white (Rev 3:1, 3:4). According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, it had been the capital of the kingdom of Lydia, standing at the foot of Mount Tmolus beside the river Pactolus, and was the seat of the wealthy king Croesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 17. Its ruins lie at the village of Sart, near Salihli in western Turkey, which is the location shown here. The STEPBible proper-names index suggests that Sepharad in Obad 1:20 may also refer to Sardis.

Sela, a name meaning "rock," was an Edomite stronghold in the rugged mountains south of the Dead Sea. The King James Version uses it as a name in Isa 16:1, where Moab is told to send lambs from Sela to Zion. Elsewhere it renders the word as "the rock," as in Judg 1:36 and Isa 42:11. According to 2 Kgs 14:7, King Amaziah of Judah captured Sela and renamed it Joktheel. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Petra, the later Nabatean city in modern southern Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places the rock of Judg 1:36 and Amaziah's conquest at a fortified cliff near the Ascent of Akrabbim, south-west of the Dead Sea. It allows that Isaiah's references may point to Petra. Which site each passage means remains uncertain.

Shechem (tower) was a fortified place belonging to the city of Shechem, where the people sheltered during Abimelech's attack on the city. After he had taken and destroyed Shechem itself (Judg 9:45), the men of the tower heard what had happened and gathered in the stronghold of the temple of the god Berith, probably the Baal-berith of Judg 9:4. When Abimelech learned of this, he and his followers each cut a branch, piled the branches against the stronghold, and set it on fire, killing about a thousand men and women. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts the tower, with Beth-millo and the temple of El-berith, among the strongest parts of Shechem's defences. Whether it was a citadel inside the city or a separate stronghold nearby is uncertain. The location shown here places it within Shechem, generally identified with Tell Balata near modern Nablus.

Shunem was a town on the border of the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed with Jezreel and Chesulloth (Josh 19:18). Before the battle of Gilboa the Philistines camped there while Saul's army camped on Mount Gilboa across the valley (1 Sam 28:4). The prophet Elisha regularly stopped at Shunem, where a wealthy woman gave him meals (2 Kgs 4:8). The surrounding chapter tells how she later gave him a room and how he raised her son. Abishag, who served the aged King David, is called a Shunammite in 1 Kgs 1:3. Eusebius placed a village called Sulem 5 Roman miles south of Mount Tabor, and this points to the modern village of Sulam on the slope of the Hill of Moreh. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a possible alternative site for Elisha's Shunem nearer Samaria.

Siloam was a pool, and evidently also a district, at the southern end of ancient Jerusalem. John explains the name as meaning "Sent" (John 9:7). Jesus put clay on the eyes of a blind man and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. He did so and came back able to see (John 9:7, 9:11). Jesus also mentioned eighteen people killed when a tower in Siloam fell on them (Luke 13:4). The pool is probably the same as the Shiloah of Isa 8:6 and the Siloah of Neh 3:15. Easton's Bible Dictionary says it was fed by a winding rock-cut tunnel from the spring now called the Gihon or Fountain of the Virgin. A Hebrew inscription describing how the tunnel was dug was found there in 1880 and is probably from Hezekiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name survives in the Arabic Silwan. The location shown here is at the southern tip of the City of David.

Sirion was the name the Sidonians (Phoenicians) used for Mount Hermon, while the Amorites called it Shenir (Deut 3:9). The name probably means "breastplate" or "body armor," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Psalm 29 pairs Sirion with Lebanon as mountains made to leap like a young wild ox at the voice of the Lord (Ps 29:6). There the Hebrew spelling is slightly different (Shirion). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may refer to the whole Hermon range as seen from the Phoenician coast, not to one part of it. Jer 18:14 is also linked to Sirion, probably because the snowy rock described there is taken to be Hermon, although the King James wording does not name it. The location shown here is the summit of Mount Hermon, on the modern border of Lebanon and Syria.

South is a term the King James Version uses for a region lying to the south, and in these verses it points to two different areas. In Zech 7:7 it describes the populated land around Jerusalem in earlier, prosperous times, when people lived in "the south and the plain". This is probably the Negev, the dry southern district of Judah, paired with the lowland foothills to the west. In Matt 12:42 and Luke 11:31, Jesus speaks of "the queen of the south" who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom. By comparison with 1 Kgs 10:1–13, she is the queen of Sheba, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Her land is commonly placed in southern Arabia, while Ethiopian tradition places it in Ethiopia. No single location is shown for this entry.

Syene was a city on Egypt's southern frontier, on the east bank of the Nile, identified with modern Aswan, which is the location shown here. Ezekiel uses it in prophecies against Egypt to mark the country's full extent. Egypt would be made desolate "from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia" (Ezek 29:10), and its allies would fall by the sword there (Ezek 30:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as Egypt's southern frontier town, as Migdol was in the north-east, and notes its quarries of red granite, called "syenite." On that reading, many translators take Ezekiel's phrase as "from Migdol to Syene," meaning from one end of Egypt to the other. Some interpreters also connect "the land of Sinim" in Isa 49:12 with Syene, a distant place from which scattered people return. This entry notes that view without settling it.

Tappuah was a city in the central hill country of Canaan whose name means "apple" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It stood on the border between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, and the boundary ran west from it to the brook Kanah and on to the Mediterranean (Josh 16:8). The surrounding "land of Tappuah" went to Manasseh, but the town itself belonged to Ephraim (Josh 17:8). Josh 17:7 calls the place En-tappuah, probably referring to a nearby spring. A king of Tappuah also appears among the Canaanite kings defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this royal city may or may not be the same border town. Several other places share the name. Its site is uncertain. Khirbet Atuf northeast of Nablus has been suggested. The location shown here follows the view placing it south-southwest of Nablus, probably at Sheikh Abu Zarad near Yasuf.

Tema was an oasis town and tribal territory in northern Arabia, known for its caravans. Genesis traces the tribe to Tema, a son of Ishmael, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and others take the place to be named after him. Job 6:19 pictures the caravans of Tema and Sheba looking in vain for water at dried-up streams. In an oracle about Arabia, Isaiah calls on the people of the land of Tema to bring water and bread to fugitives (Isa 21:14). Jeremiah names Tema with Dedan and Buz among the distant peoples who must drink the cup of God's judgment (Jer 25:23). It is generally identified with the modern oasis of Tayma in northwestern Saudi Arabia, on the old caravan route between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Aqaba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the ruins of its ancient city wall. The location shown here follows that identification.

Uz was a region east of the Jordan, best known as the homeland of Job (Job 1:1). Jeremiah lists "all the kings of the land of Uz" among the peoples made to drink the cup of God's wrath, which suggests it was a territory with several local rulers (Jer 25:20). Lamentations addresses the "daughter of Edom" as living in Uz, linking it with Edom or with land under Edomite control (Lam 4:21). Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east or south-east of Israel and north of Edom. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to the north-east, citing Josephus, who connects Uz with Trachonitis and Damascus, and Arab tradition, which places Job in the Hauran of southern Syria. The location shown here follows the view that places it near Edom, in what is now southern Jordan.

The Vale of Siddim was a valley where the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (Zoar) gathered and fought the invading eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer (Gen 14:3, 8). The text identifies it with the Salt Sea, the Dead Sea, which suggests the valley later came to lie under its waters or beside them. It was full of slime pits, probably pits of bitumen or asphalt. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell into them as they fled, and the survivors escaped to the hills (Gen 14:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary places the valley at the south end of the Dead Sea, between Engedi and the cities of the plain. It notes that some locate the cities of the plain at the north end instead. The location shown here follows the southern identification, near the southern basin of the Dead Sea.

The Valley of Elah was the valley where Saul and the army of Israel camped and lined up for battle against the Philistines (1 Sam 17:2, 19). It was the scene of David's fight with Goliath. Later the priest at Nob reminded David that he had killed Goliath there and gave him Goliath's sword, which had been kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod (1 Sam 21:9). According to 1 Sam 17:1, the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah in Judah, which places the valley in the Shephelah, the low hills southwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the modern Wadi es-Sunt and connects the name Elah ("terebinth") with the large terebinth trees that still grow there. The location shown here follows that identification.

The Valley of Hinnom, also called the valley of the son of Hinnom, was a valley just south of Jerusalem, which Joshua identifies with the Jebusite city. It formed part of the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, running past the southern side of the Jebusite city, below the mountain facing it to the west, and down to En-rogel (Josh 15:8; 18:16). After the exile it marked the northern limit of Judah's settlements, which stretched from Beersheba to this valley (Neh 11:30). Other passages, such as 2 Kgs 23:10 and Jer 7:31, place Topheth, a site of child sacrifice, in this valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a deep, narrow ravine below Mount Zion and notes that its name, shortened in Greek to Gehenna, later came to stand for the place of the wicked. It is generally identified with the modern Wadi er-Rababi, which curves around the west and south of Jerusalem's Old City. The location shown here follows that identification.

The Valley of Jezreel was a valley in northern Israel that took its name from the town of Jezreel. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as an offshoot of the Plain of Esdraelon, running east toward the Jordan between Mount Gilboa and the hill of Moreh, the area now often called the Harod Valley. The name was later applied to the whole plain. The location shown here is a rough point near the town itself. Its Canaanite inhabitants had iron chariots, which the tribes of Joseph gave as a reason they could not take the lowlands (Josh 17:16). The Midianites, Amalekites and peoples of the east camped there before Gideon defeated them (Judg 6:33). Easton's also places Saul's death in battle against the Philistines in this area (1 Sam 31). Hosea foretold that God would break Israel's bow in the valley (Hos 1:5).

Zanoah was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It appears in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:34), grouped with Eshtaol and Zorah. After the return from exile, Jews settled again in Zanoah and its villages, alongside towns such as Adullam, Lachish and Azekah (Neh 11:30). When Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt, Hanun and the people of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate, hung its doors, fitted its locks and bars, and rebuilt a thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern ruin of Zanu'a, about 10 miles west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification. Another town of the same name stood in the hill country of Judah, so the name refers to more than one place.

Abdon was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher that was assigned, together with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (Josh 21:30; 1 Chr 6:74). The surrounding passages place it among the towns given to the Gershonite clan of Levites, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries say the same. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it is probably the same town as Ebron ("Hebron" in the King James Version) in Asher's boundary list in Josh 19:28, where some manuscripts read Abdon. The name may mean "service" or "servile." The site is generally identified with the ruins of Abdeh (Khirbet Abdeh), about 8 to 10 miles northeast of Acco in northern Israel, a few miles inland from the Mediterranean. The location shown here follows that identification. Abdon is a different person from the judge Abdon and the other men of that name.

Abel-beth-maacah, meaning "meadow of the house of Maacah," was a fortified city in the far north of Israel, in Naphtali near Ijon and Dan. When King Asa of Judah persuaded Benhadad of Damascus to turn against Israel, Benhadad's forces struck it with other northern towns (1 Kgs 15:20). The parallel account in 2 Chr 16:4 names Abel-maim instead. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as another name for the same city, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows it may be a nearby place. In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured the city and deported its people (2 Kgs 15:29), about 734 BC according to Easton's. In 2 Sam 20, Joab besieged the rebel Sheba there. A wise woman called the city "a mother in Israel," and the townspeople ended the siege by executing Sheba. It is generally identified with Abil el-Qamh, a few miles west of Dan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Abronah was one of the places where Israel camped during the wilderness journey. It lay between Jotbathah and Ezion-geber, the station just before Ezion-geber at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba (Num 33:34–35). The King James Version spells the name "Ebronah," while the Revised Version uses "Abronah," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the march from Sinai toward Kadesh. Its exact site is unknown. Because Ezion-geber was near the head of the gulf, Abronah was probably somewhere in the Arabah valley a short distance north of modern Eilat and Aqaba. The location shown here is a rough estimate in that area.

Achzib was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It is listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah, grouped with Keilah and Mareshah (Josh 15:44). The prophet Micah mentions it in a lament over the towns of Judah, saying that "the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel" (Mic 1:14). This is a play on the name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take to mean "lying" or "false." Easton's and Smith's dictionaries probably identify it with Chezib, the place where Judah's son Shelah was born (Gen 38:5). Easton's places it at Ain Kezbeh. The location shown here lies in the western foothills southwest of Jerusalem, in that general area. A different Achzib lay on the coast in the territory of Asher.

Achzib was a coastal city in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It is named near the end of Asher's boundary description, where the border runs to the sea "from the coast to Achzib" (Josh 19:29). Judges records that Asher did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants, along with those of nearby Accho and Sidon (Judg 1:31). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a Phoenician city that its original people always kept, known in Greek as Ecdippa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears in Assyrian inscriptions as Aksibi, among the Phoenician towns Sennacherib took. It is generally identified with es-Zib (ez-Zib) on the Mediterranean coast, about 8 to 9 miles north of Acre, and the location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with another Achzib in Judah, which is a separate place.

Adummim was a hill pass, called "the going up to Adummim," on the road climbing from the Jordan valley near Jericho to Jerusalem. It appears only as a landmark on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin. Josh 15:7 places it opposite Gilgal and south of the stream, and Josh 18:17 uses it again when describing Benjamin's southern border. The name probably means "red ones," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it to red streaks in the local rock. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify the ascent with the road along the south side of the Wadi Qelt gorge, at a spot called Tal'at ed-Dumm, roughly halfway between Jerusalem and Jericho. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia add that this stretch of road is traditionally taken as the setting of the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:30–37.

Akeldama, meaning "Field of Blood" in Aramaic, was a plot of land near Jerusalem connected with the death of Judas. Matthew says the chief priests used the thirty pieces of silver Judas returned to buy "the potter's field" as a burial place for strangers. He adds that it was therefore called the field of blood "unto this day" (Matt 27:6–8). Acts gives a related account: the field Judas acquired with his reward, where he fell and died, became known to the people of Jerusalem by the Aramaic name Akeldama (Acts 1:18–19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition going back to about the 4th century that places the field on a level terrace on the southern slope of the Valley of Hinnom, near where it meets the Kidron Valley. A ruined charnel house long stood there. The location shown here follows that traditional identification, given only roughly.

Almon-diblathaim was a city in Moab, east of the Dead Sea, and one of the last camps of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey. They came to it from Dibon-gad and went on from it to the mountains of Abarim, opposite Mount Nebo (Num 33:46–47). The name may mean "Almon of the double fig-cake," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the site was named for two hills that looked like lumps of pressed figs. That work also notes the Hebrew may be read "Almon toward Diblathaim." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Beth-diblathaim, named in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab (Jer 48:22). Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here lies on the Moabite plateau between Dibon and the Nebo range, which fits the order of the itinerary.

Alush was a desert campsite of the Israelites on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. It appears only in the itinerary of Num 33, where the people traveled from Dophkah to Alush and then moved on to Rephidim, where there was no water to drink (Num 33:13–14). That makes it the last recorded stop before Rephidim. The shorter account of this stretch in Exodus 17:1 does not name Alush, so nothing else is known of it. Its location is not certainly known, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably on the shore of the Red Sea. The location shown here is a rough placement in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, between the proposed sites of Dophkah and Rephidim. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a crowd of men," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mingling together."

Anab was a town in the hill country of Judah. Joshua drove the Anakim out of it, along with Hebron, Debir and the other mountain towns of Judah and Israel, and destroyed them and their cities (Josh 11:21). It was later listed among the hill-country towns given to the tribe of Judah, named in the same group as Eshtemoh and Anim (Josh 15:50). The name is usually explained as meaning "grapes" or "grape-town." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the site still keeps its ancient name and lies among the hills about 10 miles south-southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about twelve miles southwest of Hebron, a short distance southwest of Debir, and identifies it with the ruin called Khirbet 'Anab. The location shown here follows that identification in the southern Judean hills.

Aphek was a city on the northern edge of Israel's promised land, one of several places in the Bible with this name. Joshua 13:4 names it as a point on the boundary of the land not yet conquered, near the Sidonians and "the borders of the Amorites." Joshua 19:30 lists an Aphek among the cities allotted to the tribe of Asher, and Judg 1:31 probably refers to the same town as Aphik, whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two Joshua references as one place and identifies it with classical Aphaca, modern Afqa, near the source of the Nahr Ibrahim (the ancient Adonis River) in Lebanon. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes a temple ruin there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accepts Afqa but notes it lies farther north than expected. The location shown here follows the Afqa identification.

Ararat is a mountainous region in western Asia. Genesis says Noah's ark came to rest "upon the mountains of Ararat" as the flood waters went down. The plural points to a range of mountains rather than one peak. In Jer 51:27, Ararat is one of the kingdoms, along with Minni and Ashchenaz, called to attack Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Urartu of Assyrian records, a kingdom on the Armenian plateau around Lake Van. The same Hebrew name is translated "Armenia" in the KJV at 2 Kgs 19:37 and Isa 37:38. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE both suggest the ark's resting place was probably in the Kurdish range south of Armenia, and Kurdish tradition points to Jebel Judi. The location shown here marks the region at the peak now called Mount Ararat, in eastern Turkey near the Armenian and Iranian borders.

Arvad was a small island city off the coast of Syria, named in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre. Ezekiel describes its people as rowers or sailors for Tyre, alongside the men of Zidon (Ezek 27:8), and as soldiers who manned Tyre's walls with its army (Ezek 27:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the island of Ruad (modern Arwad), two or three miles off Tartus on the Phoenician coast, and the location shown here follows that identification. Smith's also links it with the Arvadites, listed among the descendants of Canaan with Zidon and Hamath in Gen 10:18 and 1 Chr 1:16. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "wandering" and notes that it appears as Aruada or Arada in the Tell el-Amarna tablets.

Ashnah was the name of a town, or probably two separate towns, in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. One Ashnah appears in the same group as Eshtaol and Zoreah (Zorah) in Josh 15:33, which places it in the northern lowland, west of Jerusalem. Another appears with Jiphtah and Nezib in Josh 15:43, in a group of towns farther south. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat these as two different places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the small ruin of Aslin, between Eshtaol and Zorah, may preserve the name of the northern town, and calls the southern site unknown. The location shown here is approximate and follows the northern town near Eshtaol and Zorah. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "change."

Assos was a seaport city in the district of Mysia in the Roman province of Asia, on the northern shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium, facing the island of Lesbos. During Paul's journey from Troas toward Miletus, his companions sailed ahead to Assos while Paul, by his own arrangement, travelled there on foot. They took him on board at Assos and sailed on to Mitylene (Acts 20:13–14). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the overland road from Troas was about 20 miles, compared with about 30 miles by sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the city as built on a steep rock about 700 feet high, with a temple of Athena at its summit, and notes that Aristotle lived there for three years. The site is the modern village of Behramkale on the Aegean coast of Turkey, which matches the location shown here. This entry dates the voyage to about AD 54, by inference from context.

Ataroth was a town east of the Jordan River. It was one of the places named by the tribes of Gad and Reuben when they asked Moses for the land of Jazer and Gilead as pasture for their livestock (Num 32:3). The Gadites afterward built, or fortified, Ataroth along with Dibon and Aroer (Num 32:34). The name means "crowns." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it seems to have lain in the area assigned to Reuben, even though Gad built it. It identifies the site with Khirbet Attarus, near Jebel Attarus in present-day Jordan, a mountain that keeps the ancient name, northwest of Dhiban (ancient Dibon). The location shown here follows that identification, east of the Dead Sea. Several other places in the Bible share the name Ataroth, and this entry covers only the town in this passage.

Ataroth, a name meaning "crowns" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a town on the border of the territory given to the descendants of Joseph. Joshua lists it twice. In Josh 16:2 the boundary runs from Bethel to Luz, past the Archites, to Ataroth. In Josh 16:7 it runs down from Janohah to Ataroth and Naarath, then to Jericho and the Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats both as one town on the Ephraim–Benjamin border, also called Ataroth-adar (Josh 16:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Ataroth of Josh 16:7 as a separate, unidentified place on Ephraim's eastern frontier in the Jordan valley. Several places in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate. It lies west of Bethel, matching the southern-border town rather than a Jordan-valley site.

Avith was the city of Hadad son of Bedad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings. Hadad succeeded Husham and is remembered for defeating Midian in the country of Moab (Gen 36:35; 1 Chr 1:46). Nothing else is said about the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "ruins," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "wicked, perverse." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the name as Getthaim and that its site cannot be identified. Its location is therefore unknown. The point shown here is only an approximate placement in the Edomite highlands south-east of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. It reflects the city's link with Edom rather than an identified site.

Azmaveth was a town near Jerusalem. Forty-two of its people are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:24). The parallel list in Neh 7:28 calls the town Beth-azmaveth. Later, at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall, singers came from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, where they had built villages around the city (Neh 12:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the tribe of Judah. STEPBible's proper-names data places it in Benjamin, which fits its mention alongside the Benjamite town of Geba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with el-Chizma, a village a little north of Anathoth, today known as Hizma, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strong death."

Baal-perazim was the place where David defeated the Philistines early in his reign over all Israel. After the victory David said the LORD had broken through his enemies like a breaking flood of water, and the place was named for this. The name means roughly "lord of breakings through" (2 Sam 5:20; 1 Chr 14:11). The surrounding passages place the battle in or near the Valley of Rephaim, close to Jerusalem, where the Philistines had gathered. The Mount Perazim of Isa 28:21 is probably the same site. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Jebel Aly, west of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the heights just south of Jerusalem, near the so-called Mount of Evil Counsel, overlooking the valley often taken as Rephaim. The location shown here follows this second view and is only approximate.

Baalath was a city that Solomon built or fortified as part of his building program. It appears in a list with Tadmor in the wilderness (1 Kgs 9:18). The preceding verse also names Gezer and lower Beth-horon. The parallel account places it alongside Solomon's store cities, chariot cities and cities for horsemen (2 Chr 8:6). Its location is uncertain, and the name is shared by several places in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the town of Baalath in the territory of Dan (Josh 19:44) and mentions a suggested site at Bel'ain in Wadi Deir Balut. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Beth-horon and suggests it may be the same as a nearby border town. STEPBible suggests it may have been in the Lebanon region. The location shown here follows the Danite identification and is only approximate, west of the hill country near Beth-horon.

Babel was a city in the land of Shinar, named in Gen 10:10 as the first of the cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Erech, Accad and Calneh. Gen 11:9 explains the name: there the LORD confused the language of all the earth and scattered people across it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "confusion" or "mixture." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Babylon is the Greek form of Babel, and the city is generally taken to be the early Babylon on the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the tower of Gen 11 with the ruins of Birs Nimrud at ancient Borsippa, while others link it with a temple mound within Babylon itself. The location shown here follows the identification with the site of ancient Babylon, near the modern town of Hillah.

Bamoth was a stopping place of the Israelites on their journey through the land east of the Dead Sea, reached after Mattanah and Nahaliel and before the top of Pisgah (Num 21:19–20). Num 21:20 places it by a valley in the country of Moab. The name means "heights," and Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the forty-seventh station of the Israelites' journey. It is probably the same place as Bamoth-baal, mentioned later in Num 22:41 and Josh 13:17 as a height in this region, though the two names are not explicitly linked. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, on the plateau northeast of the Dead Sea near the Pisgah and Mount Nebo range, which fits its place in the itinerary just before Pisgah.

Bamoth-baal, meaning "heights of Baal," was a place in Moab east of the Jordan. The King James Version translates the name in Num 22:41, where the Moabite king Balak brought the prophet Balaam up to "the high places of Baal" so he could see the edge of Israel's camp. Later, Josh 13:17 lists Bamoth-baal among the towns near Heshbon and Dibon given to the tribe of Reuben. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same as Bamoth, a stopping place on Israel's journey, and is also mentioned in Isaiah 15:2. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on or near the Arnon River. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one on the plateau near Mount Nebo, northeast of the Dead Sea in modern Jordan. That position fits a height overlooking the plains where Israel camped.

The Beautiful Gate was a gate of the temple in Jerusalem. A man who had been lame from birth was carried there every day to beg for alms from people entering the temple (Acts 3:2). Peter and John met him there and he was healed. Afterward the people recognized him as the beggar who used to sit at the Beautiful Gate, and they were amazed (Acts 3:10). The event is dated about AD 30, by inference from context. Its exact position in the temple complex is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the common view that it led from the Court of the Gentiles into the Court of the Women, and that it was a massive gate covered with plates of Corinthian brass. Others have placed it at an outer entrance to the temple. The location shown here is a point within the temple area rather than a precise identification.

Beer-lahai-roi was a well in the wilderness of the Negev, the dry south country of Canaan. Its name is usually explained as "well of the Living One who sees me." Genesis 16:7–14 presents it as the spring where the angel of the Lord met Hagar as she fled from Sarah, and places it between Kadesh and Bered on the way to Shur. Isaac was coming from this well when Rebekah first arrived to marry him, since he was living in the south (Gen 24:62). After Abraham's death, Isaac settled beside it (Gen 25:11). The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention its identification with 'Ain Muweileh (Moilahi), southwest of Beersheba and about 12 miles west of Kadesh-barnea. The location shown here follows that identification.

Bela was an older name for the city of Zoar, one of the five cities of the plain near the Dead Sea. Genesis explains the name as it goes: "Bela, which is Zoar" (Gen 14:2, 8). Its king, who is not named, joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim against an alliance of four eastern kings, and they fought in the vale of Siddim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note that later in Genesis this city, as Zoar, was the only one of the five spared when the others were destroyed, because Lot asked to flee there (Gen 19:20–23). Its exact site is uncertain. Some scholars place the cities of the plain north of the Dead Sea, others to its south. The location shown here follows the southern view, placing Zoar southeast of the Dead Sea in the area of the modern Ghor es-Safi in Jordan.

Bene-jaakan was a camp of the Israelites during their wilderness journey, reached after leaving Moseroth and followed by Hor-hagidgad (Num 33:31–32). The name means "sons of Jaakan," and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as a tribe whose name was attached to certain desert wells. Deut 10:6 calls the place Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, "the wells of the sons of Jaakan." Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as one place. That passage places it before Mosera rather than after, so the camp may have been visited more than once or the route recorded differently. Jaakan is probably the descendant of Seir the Horite named in Gen 36:27 (as Akan) and 1 Chr 1:42, which would place the site near Edom. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Arabah, in the region of Edom.

Berea was a city in Macedonia where Paul and Silas went after the believers in Thessalonica sent them away by night. On arrival they went into the Jewish synagogue to preach (Acts 17:10). When Jews from Thessalonica heard that Paul was preaching there, they came to Berea and stirred up the people against him (Acts 17:13). The surrounding passage says Paul then left for the coast and sailed to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. This visit is dated about AD 48, by inference from context. Acts 20:4 names Sopater of Berea as one of Paul's later travelling companions, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably converted during this visit. Easton's also identifies the city with modern Veria in northern Greece, which matches the location shown here. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists it under the spelling Beroea.

Beth-anath was a fortified city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali in northern Galilee. It appears among Naphtali's nineteen cities with their villages, alongside Horem and Beth-shemesh (Josh 19:38). Judges 1:33 records that Naphtali did not drive out the Canaanites living in Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh. The Israelites lived among them instead, and these inhabitants were later made to pay tribute. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "house" or "temple" of Anath, a Canaanite goddess, while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "house of response." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both tentatively identify the site with the modern village of 'Ainata, a few miles west of Kedesh, in what is now southern Lebanon. The location shown here follows that identification, though the exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-eked was a place on the road between Jezreel and Samaria. The King James Version translates its name as "the shearing house"; the Hebrew name may mean "house of binding." Jehu passed it on his way to Samaria after overthrowing the house of Ahab. There he met forty-two relatives of Ahaziah, king of Judah, whom the surrounding passage (2 Kgs 10:13) describes as his brothers on their way to visit the royal family. Jehu ordered them taken alive. They were then killed at the pit of Beth-eked, and none were spared. Its exact site is uncertain. It is often identified, by inference from Jehu's route, with the modern village of Beit Qad near Jenin, at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here is approximate and places it in that general area.

Beth-haccherem, meaning "house of the vineyard," was a place in Judah near Jerusalem. After the exile it was the center of a district whose ruler, Malchiah son of Rechab, repaired the Dung Gate of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Neh 3:14). Earlier, Jeremiah named it alongside Tekoa as a spot for raising a signal fire to warn of an invasion from the north (Jer 6:1), which suggests a high, visible site south of Jerusalem. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favor ‘Ain Karim, west of Jerusalem, where ancient cairns on a nearby ridge may once have served as beacons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Jerome's remark that he could see the village daily from Bethlehem, which has led some to suggest the Herodium hill near Tekoa. The location shown here follows the Herodium identification.

Beth-maacah was a city in the far north of Israel, closely linked with the town of Abel. Its name may mean "house of Maacah." In 2 Sam 20:14 the rebel Sheba son of Bichri passed through the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and Joab's forces then besieged him in "Abel of Beth-maacah," building a siege ramp and battering the wall (2 Sam 20:15). Whether Beth-maacah was a separate place next to Abel or simply part of that town's fuller name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under Abel-beth-maacah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places that city in Naphtali near Dan and Ijon and identifies it with the modern village of Abil el-Qamh, about 6 miles west-northwest of Dan. The location shown here matches that identification, near the Israel–Lebanon border.

Beth-marcaboth, meaning "house of chariots", was a town in the far south of Judah that was allotted to the tribe of Simeon. It is listed next to Ziklag and Hazar-susah (Josh 19:5), and 1 Chr 4:31 counts it among the Simeonite towns held until the reign of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the parallel list of Judah's southern towns in Josh 15:31 has Madmannah in its place, and Tyndale House's STEPBible names list treats the two as the same town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the site had not been identified and mentions Guérin's suggestion of Khan Yunis, southwest of Gaza. It also links the name with the chariot cities Solomon later built. The location shown here follows the identification with Madmannah, in the northern Negev north-northeast of Beersheba. The exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-millo, meaning "house of Millo," was a place or community associated with Shechem, translated "the house of Millo" in the King James Version. Its people joined the men of Shechem in making Abimelech king beside the pillar at Shechem (Judg 9:6). Jotham, in his fable from Mount Gerizim, called for fire to come from Abimelech and devour the men of Shechem and the house of Millo, and for fire from them to devour Abimelech, foreshadowing their later conflict (Judg 9:20). "Millo" probably refers to a rampart or earthwork fortification. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a rampart in Shechem, probably the same as the "tower of Shechem" mentioned later in the chapter (Judg 9:46, 49). It is distinct from the Millo in Jerusalem. The location shown here places it at or near ancient Shechem, by Tell Balata near modern Nablus.

Beth-nimrah was a fortified town east of the Jordan River, rebuilt by the tribe of Gad after the defeat of Sihon king of Heshbon. It was one of the fenced cities the Gadites built, alongside sheepfolds for their flocks (Num 32:36). In the allotment it is listed among the towns "in the valley" of the Jordan with Betharam, Succoth and Zaphon, part of the former kingdom of Sihon assigned to Gad (Josh 13:27). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that it is probably the place called simply Nimrah in Num 32:3, and possibly the "waters of Nimrim" of Isa 15:6. The name means "house of leopards" (Hitchcock's gives "house of rebellion"). It is generally identified with Tell Nimrin, near the Wadi Nimrin in the Jordan Valley northeast of Jericho, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-pelet was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negeb region toward the border of Edom. It appears in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:27), where the King James Version spells it Bethpalet, and again among the places resettled by people of Judah after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh 11:26), spelled Bethphelet. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "house of escape" and places it among "the uttermost cities" of Judah toward Edom, following the heading of the list in Joshua 15:21. It also describes the site as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negeb, near the other towns named with it, such as Moladah and Heshmon.

Beth-rehob was an Aramean (Syrian) town and small kingdom in the far north of Israel. Judges 18:28 places Laish, the city the tribe of Dan captured and rebuilt, "in the valley that lieth by Bethrehob," far from Sidon. In David's time, the Ammonites hired Syrian soldiers from Beth-rehob, along with troops from Zobah, Maacah and Ish-tob, to fight Israel (2 Sam 10:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as probably the same as the Rehob that marked the northern limit of the spies' journey in Num 13:21. The site is uncertain. Robinson, cited in Smith's Bible Dictionary, identified it with Hunin, west of Banias, while others favor Banias itself. The location shown here follows the Hunin identification, in the hills above the Huleh Valley near Dan.

Beth-shemesh, meaning "house of the sun," was a city in the tribal territory of Naphtali in Galilee. It is one of several places with this name, and it should not be confused with the better-known Beth-shemesh in Judah. It appears among the fortified cities assigned to Naphtali (Josh 19:38). Judges 1:33 records that Naphtali did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants. Instead the tribe lived among them, and the people of Beth-shemesh and nearby Beth-anath were made to pay tribute. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Mount Tabor and the Jordan and identifies it with Khurbet Shema near Safed, while also suggesting it may be the same as the Beth-shemesh on Issachar's border. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Upper Galilee, somewhat north of Safed.

Beth-togarmah, meaning "house of Togarmah," was a northern region or people that Ezekiel mentions twice. In his lament over Tyre, the house of Togarmah traded horses, horsemen and mules in Tyre's markets (Ezek 27:14). In his prophecy against Gog, it appears among Gog's allies, described as coming "of the north quarters" alongside Gomer and its forces (Ezek 38:6). The name probably goes back to Togarmah, listed in Gen 10:3 as a son of Gomer, which would explain why the two are named together. Its exact location is uncertain. Some connect it with the ancient city of Tegarama (Til-garimmu) in eastern Anatolia, and others with Armenia, a region long known for breeding horses. The location shown here follows the Armenian identification, placing it in the highlands of modern Armenia.

Bethel (of Judah) was a town in the south of Judah, distinct from the better-known Bethel north of Jerusalem. Its name means "house of God" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. In 1 Sam 30:27 it heads the list of towns whose people received a share of the spoil David sent after recovering the captives taken from Ziklag. It is grouped there with south Ramoth and Jattir, which places it in the southern hill country and the Negev. Easton's Bible Dictionary also takes the king of Bethel in Josh 12:16, listed beside the king of Makkedah among the defeated Canaanite rulers, as belonging to this southern town, though that verse may refer to the northern Bethel instead. Many interpreters identify it with Bethul or Bethuel, a town of Simeon (Josh 19:4; 1 Chr 4:30). Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Bezek was a Canaanite town where the tribe of Judah defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites after the death of Joshua, killing ten thousand men (Judg 1:4). It was the home of its ruler, Adoni-bezek, whose name means "lord of Bezek." Judah found him there and fought against him (Judg 1:5). By context it lay within the territory allotted to Judah. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the hill country not far from Jerusalem and probably at the modern Bezkah, southeast of Lydda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively links it with Bezqah, northeast of Gezer. The location shown here follows the Bezqah identification. The name is shared by more than one place: a different Bezek appears as the site where Saul mustered Israel (1 Sam 11:8).

Bithynia was a Roman province in northwestern Asia Minor, along the southern shores of the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, in what is now northwestern Turkey. On Paul's second missionary journey, after reaching Mysia, Paul and his companions tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them (Acts 16:7). Bithynia is later one of the regions named in the greeting of 1 Peter, addressed to scattered believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia (1 Pet 1:1), which suggests Christian communities had formed there early. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Roman governor Pliny, who ruled the province in the early second century, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking how to deal with the many Christians brought before him. Smith's Bible Dictionary names Nicaea as its chief town. The location shown here marks the general region rather than a single site.

Bochim, meaning "weepers," was the place where an angel of the LORD, coming up from Gilgal, spoke to Israel early in the period of the judges. He reminded them that he had brought them out of Egypt and would never break his covenant with them (Judg 2:1). In the verses that follow (Judg 2:2–4) he rebukes them for making agreements with the people of the land, and the people weep aloud. They named the place Bochim for this and offered sacrifices there (Judg 2:5). No later place name resembling it has been found, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may not have lasted. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably at the head of a valley between Gilgal and Shiloh. Many, following the Greek Septuagint, identify it with Bethel. The location shown here follows the Bethel identification, near the modern village of Beitin north of Jerusalem.

Bozkath was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It appears in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, named between Lachish and Eglon (Josh 15:39). It is mentioned again as the home of Adaiah, whose daughter Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:1). The King James Version spells it "Boscath" there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "rocky height," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "stony." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only approximate, placed near Lachish because of the town's position in the Joshua list.

The Broad Wall was a section of Jerusalem's city wall that was repaired after the return from exile under Nehemiah. In the list of rebuilders, Uzziel, one of the goldsmiths, and Hananiah, son of one of the perfume makers, restored the stretch of wall leading up to it (Neh 3:8). At the dedication of the rebuilt walls, one of the two thanksgiving processions, with Nehemiah following it, walked along the top of the wall from the Tower of the Furnaces as far as the Broad Wall (Neh 12:38). Its name probably refers to the wall's unusual thickness. Its exact course is uncertain, but the surrounding passages place it on the western side of the city. Many scholars connect it with a very thick wall uncovered by excavations in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, usually dated to the late 8th century BC. The location shown here follows that identification.

Brook Kidron, called the brook Cedron in John's Gospel and the Kidron Valley in modern versions, was the stream and ravine running below the eastern wall of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "the black torrent." The stream flowed mainly in the rainy season, and the valley lies between the city and the Mount of Olives. During Hezekiah's Passover, the people removed the altars and incense altars that stood in Jerusalem and threw them into the Kidron (2 Chr 30:14). After speaking with his disciples on the night of his arrest, Jesus crossed the brook Cedron with them to a garden on the far side (John 18:1). By inference from other Gospel accounts, this was Gethsemane, on the slopes of the Mount of Olives. The location shown here is the valley immediately east of Jerusalem's Old City.

Caesarea Philippi was a city at the foot of Mount Hermon, about 20 miles north of the Sea of Galilee, beside one of the main sources of the Jordan. It is the modern village of Banias. In its region Jesus asked his disciples who people said he was. That question led to Peter's confession of him as the Christ and to Jesus' first plain prediction of his death and resurrection (Matt 16:13; Mark 8:27). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as the northern limit of Jesus' travels. They say Herod Philip enlarged it and named it after the emperor and himself, which set it apart from the coastal Caesarea. Its earlier name was Paneas, after a cave linked with the Greek god Pan. Both dictionaries mention that some identify it with the Old Testament Baal-gad, though this remains uncertain.

Calah was one of the ancient cities of Assyria named in the table of nations. Genesis 10:11 says that from the land of Shinar "Asshur" went out and built Nineveh, Rehoboth and Calah. The verse can also be read as Nimrod going out into Assyria, as the Revised Version and Easton's Bible Dictionary take it, which is why Calah is connected here with the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom. Resen lay between Nineveh and Calah, and the phrase "the same is a great city" (Gen 10:12) may refer to the whole group. Calah is probably the ancient Kalhu, the ruins now called Nimrud on the east bank of the Tigris near where it meets the Greater Zab, south of Mosul in Iraq. The location shown here follows that identification. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt it about 880 BC, and it then served as a royal capital of Assyria.

Calneh was a city in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), named in Gen 10:10 as one of the four cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Babel, Erech and Accad. This beginning is dated here to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Amos 6:2 also names Calneh, along with Hamath and Gath, as kingdoms Israel should look at and compare with itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Calneh with Calno (Isa 10:9) and Canneh (Ezek 27:23), a town that traded with Tyre. Other interpreters take the Calneh of Amos and Isaiah to be a separate city in northern Syria. Its location is uncertain. The location shown here follows the identification with the mound of Niffer, ancient Nippur, east of the Euphrates and about 60 miles south-southeast of Babylon. Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note this view.

Cappadocia was a large region in eastern Asia Minor, in what is now central Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the largest province of Asia Minor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as mostly high, rather barren uplands bounded by the Taurus mountains to the south and the Euphrates to the east, with Caesarea Mazaca as its chief city. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it was good grain and grazing country. Cappadocia came under Roman rule in AD 17. The New Testament mentions it twice. People living in Cappadocia were among those in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). It was also one of the regions, along with Pontus, Galatia, Asia and Bithynia, whose scattered believers Peter addressed in his first letter (1 Pet 1:1). This implies that Christianity reached the region early. The location shown here marks the general area of the region.

Cenchreae was the eastern harbour of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf side of the isthmus. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 9 miles from the city and calls it Corinth's outlet for trade with the eastern Mediterranean, while Lechaeum served as the western port. At the end of his long stay in Corinth, Paul had his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow, then sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. This marked his return from the second missionary journey, about AD 50 by inference from context (Acts 18:18). Romans 16:1 shows that a church existed there, and Paul commends Phoebe as a servant of that church. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she carried the letter to Rome. The site is generally identified with the ruins at modern Kechries, near Corinth, which the location shown here follows.

Cherith was a brook or seasonal stream in a ravine where the prophet Elijah hid at God's command after announcing a drought to King Ahab (1 Kgs 17:3, 5). The same chapter says that ravens brought him food there and that he drank from the brook until it dried up for lack of rain. The text places it "before Jordan," which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to mean that it opened toward the river and flowed into it. The exact site is uncertain. Easton's notes that some identify it with the Wadi el-Kelt behind Jericho, west of the Jordan. Easton's, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also point to a ravine east of the Jordan in Gilead, since Elijah was told to turn eastward. The location shown here follows the eastern view, roughly where a stream from the Gilead hills meets the Jordan valley.

Cherub was a place in Babylonia named among the towns from which some exiles returned to Judea after the Babylonian captivity. It is listed with Telmelah, Tel-harsha, Addan and Immer (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61). The people who came from these places could not prove their family line or show that they were descended from Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary links this group with the return led by Zerubbabel, which fits the setting of the list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified and notes that the parallel passage in 1 Esdras 5:36 seems to garble these place names. Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Mesopotamia. The place name is spelled the same in English as the winged figures called cherubim, but these verses use it only as the name of a town.

Chinneroth was a region in northern Israel around the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. It is the plural form of Chinnereth, the name of a fortified town by the lake. Easton's Bible Dictionary places that town a little south of Tiberias and suggests it gave its name to the surrounding district. In Josh 11:2, the plains south of Chinneroth are among the areas whose kings joined the northern alliance against Joshua. In 1 Kgs 15:20, Benhadad of Syria, answering King Asa of Judah's appeal, struck Israel's northern cities, including "all Cinneroth" along with the land of Naphtali. That pairing suggests the district lay within or beside Naphtali's territory. The lake itself is also called the Sea of Chinnereth or Chinneroth, later known as Gennesaret or the Sea of Tiberias. The location shown here marks the general area near the lake's northwestern shore.

Chorazin was a town in Galilee, named in the Bible only in Jesus' woe against it. He paired it with Bethsaida and said that if the mighty works done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes (Matt 11:21; Luke 10:13). Matthew sets the saying alongside a similar rebuke of Capernaum, so Chorazin was probably one of the lakeside towns where Jesus often worked. Eusebius placed it 2 miles from Capernaum, and Jerome put it on the lake shore. Smith's Bible Dictionary treated the site as uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Kerazeh, in the hills north of Capernaum (Tell Hum). The location shown here follows the Kerazeh identification.

Dibon-gad was a camping place of the Israelites during their journey toward the plains of Moab, reached after Iim and left for Almon-diblathaim (Num 33:45–46). The name probably means "Dibon of Gad." By inference from Num 32:34, where the tribe of Gad is said to have built Dibon, it is usually taken to be the town of Dibon east of the Dead Sea, which Gad occupied before it later passed to Reuben and then to Moab. The location shown here follows the common identification with modern Dhiban in Jordan, a little north of the Arnon River (Wadi Mujib). The famous Moabite Stone of King Mesha was found there in 1868. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "great understanding" or "abundance of sons."

Dinhabah was the city of Bela son of Beor, the first king listed among those who reigned in Edom before any king ruled over Israel (Gen 36:32; 1 Chr 1:43). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it Bela's capital and probably his birthplace. Nothing else is said about it in the Bible.
