Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "robbers' den," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he gives judgment." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the modern Dibdiba, a little northeast of Petra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible likeness in the name Hodbat et-Teneib, about 8 miles east of Heshbon, though that lies in Moab, and it adds that no satisfactory identification has been proposed. The location shown here, near Petra in southern Jordan, roughly follows Easton's identification and is only approximate.

Dophkah was a place where the Israelites camped on their journey from Egypt to Mount Sinai. The list of stopping places in Numbers 33 records that they moved there from the wilderness of Sin and then went on to Alush (Num 33:12–13). It is not mentioned anywhere else. The narrative in Exod 17:1 says only that the people travelled from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim in stages, so Dophkah was probably one of those unnamed stages. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, near the eastern shore of the Gulf of Suez, somewhere in the Wadi Feiran area. Others have linked it with the Egyptian mining district around Serabit el-Khadim. The location shown here is a rough one in southwestern Sinai, close to Easton's placement. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a knocking."

Dothan was a town in the hill country north of Shechem, set among good pasture land. Joseph followed his brothers there while they were grazing their father's flocks and found them at Dothan (Gen 37:17). The surrounding chapter tells how they threw him into a pit and sold him to Ishmaelite traders. Centuries later the prophet Elisha was staying in Dothan when the king of Syria learned where he was and sent troops to seize him (2 Kgs 6:13). The name is usually explained as "two wells" or "two cisterns." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell Dothan, on the southern edge of the Jezreel plain about 5 miles southwest of modern Jenin. The site lay near an old trade route running from Gilead toward the coast and Egypt. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ellasar was a kingdom ruled by Arioch, one of four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam who fought against five kings of the Jordan plain, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:1, 9). Its alongside Shinar and Elam places it somewhere in Mesopotamia, but the Bible gives no further detail. Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Larsa, an old Babylonian city on the east bank of the Euphrates between Ur and Erech, now the ruins of Senkereh in southern Iraq. Another view places it in northern Mesopotamia. The location shown here follows the northern view and marks the region around ancient Urkesh, probably modern Tell Mozan in northeastern Syria.

Eltolad was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the Negev toward the border of Edom in Josh 15:30. It was later assigned to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay inside Judah's allotment (Josh 19:4). Both lists place it beside Hormah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same place as Tolad in 1 Chr 4:29, with the first part of the name dropped. Smith's Bible Dictionary, reading that passage, says Simeon held the town until the time of David. The name is usually explained as "kindred of God" or, in Hitchcock's Bible Names, "the generation of God." The actual site has not been identified, so any location given for it, including the location shown here, is only approximate.

En-gannim, meaning "spring of gardens," was a city in the territory of the tribe of Issachar. It is listed among Issachar's towns in Josh 19:21. It was one of four cities in Issachar given, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh 21:29). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:73 has Anem in its place, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the two as the same town. A different En-gannim lay in the lowlands of Judah. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries identify this town with modern Jenin, at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley (the plain of Esdraelon), where the road climbs into the central hill country. The location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary also links it with the "garden house" toward which King Ahaziah fled from Jehu in 2 Kgs 9:27.

En-shemesh, meaning "spring of the sun," was a spring that marked part of the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin. Joshua 15:7 traces Judah's northern border past "the waters of Enshemesh" toward En-rogel, and Josh 18:17 traces Benjamin's southern border the same way, from En-shemesh toward Geliloth near the ascent of Adummim. Because it lay between the ascent of Adummim and En-rogel, it was east of Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the spring known as Ain Haud, about a mile east of Bethany, the last spring on the road down to Jericho. Christians call it the "Apostles' Fountain" because of a tradition from the 15th century that the apostles drank there. The location shown here matches that identification.

Enaim was a town in Judah where Tamar, dressed as a veiled woman, sat beside the road to Timnah and waited for her father-in-law Judah, because she had not been given to his son Shelah as promised (Gen 38:14). When Judah's friend, the Adullamite named in the surrounding passage, came back to pay her, he asked the local men where the woman by the roadside at this place was. They told him there had been no such woman there (Gen 38:21). The King James Version translates the name as "an open place" and "openly" rather than treating it as a place name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "place of a fountain." Easton's Bible Dictionary and that encyclopedia both take it to be probably the same as Enam (Josh 15:34), a town in the Shephelah lowland between Adullam and Timnah. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement near Timnah.

Ephrathah (spelled Ephratah in the King James Version) is an older name for Bethlehem in Judah. In Ruth 4:11 the elders at the gate bless Boaz with parallel wishes to prosper in Ephratah and be famous in Bethlehem, treating the two names as one place. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that other passages also link the names, such as Gen 35:19 and the form “Bethlehem Ephratah” in Mic 5:2. In Ps 132:6 the psalmist says “we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood,” referring to the ark. Easton's reads this as David hearing of the ark in his hometown of Bethlehem and later finding it at Kirjath-jearim, the “forest town.” Some interpreters instead take Ephratah here as the district around Kirjath-jearim. The location shown here follows the Bethlehem identification, about 9 km (5 miles) south of Jerusalem.

Erech was an ancient city in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), named in Gen 10:10 as one of the cities where Nimrod's kingdom began, along with Babel, Accad and Calneh. Easton's Bible Dictionary links Ezra 4:9's "Archevites", people settled in Samaria who wrote against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, with Erech, probably as its former inhabitants. The city is the Sumerian and Babylonian Uruk, identified with the ruins of Warka near the Euphrates in southern Iraq, about 120 miles southeast of Babylon. The location shown here matches that site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Uruk was among the oldest cities of Babylonia, home of the hero-king Gilgamesh and of a major temple to Ishtar. This entry dates the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Etam was a rocky height in the territory of Judah where Samson went to live after killing many Philistines in revenge for the burning of his wife and her father. Samson stayed at "the top of the rock Etam" (Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "cleft"). Three thousand men of Judah came to him there, fearing Philistine reprisals, and asked what he had done. Easton's describes the place as a natural stronghold and identifies it with Beit 'Atab, west of Bethlehem near Zorah and Eshtaol, where a long tunnel under the village may be the cleft. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that a cavern called 'Arak Isma'in, high on the cliffs of the Wady Isma'in, fits the story better. The location shown here is in the hills west of Jerusalem, near both suggested sites. Other places in the Bible share the name Etam.

Ether was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in the same district as Libnah and Ashan (Josh 15:42). It appears again among the towns given to the tribe of Simeon, whose territory lay within Judah's (Josh 19:7). In that list it is grouped with Ain, Remmon and Ashan as "four cities and their villages." Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Khirbet el-'Atr, an ancient site with cisterns and foundations near Beit Jibrin, whose name is spelled the same way. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Shephelah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "abundance," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "talk."

The Forest of Ephraim was a wooded region where David's troops fought and defeated the army of Israel that had rallied behind his son Absalom (2 Sam 18:6). The fighting spread across the whole countryside, and the text says the forest itself killed more men that day than the sword did (2 Sam 18:8). The surrounding chapter adds that twenty thousand fell and that Absalom was caught by his head in an oak there, where Joab killed him. Because David was at Mahanaim and Absalom had camped in Gilead (2 Sam 17:24–26), the forest probably lay east of the Jordan, even though the tribe of Ephraim's own territory was west of it. How it got the name is uncertain. Some place it west of the Jordan within Ephraim. The location shown here follows the Gilead identification, in the wooded hills of what is now northern Jordan.

Galeed was the name Jacob gave to a heap of stones that he and Laban set up as a witness to the agreement between them when they parted (Gen 31:47–48). The name is Hebrew and means "heap of witness." Laban called the same heap Jegar-sahadutha, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the Aramaic equivalent, reflecting the language of Laban's family in Mesopotamia. Laban declared that the heap would stand as a witness between the two men. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the cairn on Mount Gilead, where the surrounding narrative sets the meeting, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the story may hint at how the name Gilead came to be applied to that region. The exact site is not known. The location shown here places it in the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan in present-day northern Jordan.

Gallim was a town, probably in the territory of Benjamin north of Jerusalem. It was the home of Phalti son of Laish, to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, while David was a fugitive (1 Sam 25:44). The same man is called Paltiel in 2 Sam 3:15. Gallim appears again in Isaiah's description of an Assyrian army advancing on Jerusalem, where it is named alongside Laish (Laishah) and Anathoth as towns crying out in alarm (Isa 10:30). Smith's Bible Dictionary connects this passage with Sennacherib's approach. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary says there is no clue to its position. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many link it with the Gilgal on Judah's northern border. The location shown here follows the view of Easton's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House that it lay in Benjamin, placing it near Anathoth. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "heaps."

The Gate of Ephraim was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. When Jehoash (also called Joash), king of Israel, defeated and captured Amaziah, king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh, he came to Jerusalem and broke down a 400-cubit stretch of the city wall, about 600 feet (180 m), from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate (2 Kgs 14:13; 2 Chr 25:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the side of the city facing the territory of Ephraim, which is the north side. That fits its name, which probably refers to the road leading out toward Ephraim. A gate of the same name appears in Nehemiah's account of the restored city (Neh 8:16; 12:39), probably the same gate, though this is not certain. Its exact position is unknown. The location shown here places it within the northern part of ancient Jerusalem.

The Gate of Ephraim was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's day. It was probably on the north side of the city and was likely named for the road leading north toward the territory of Ephraim. An open street or square lay beside it, and during the Feast of Tabernacles people built booths there along with other public spaces (Neh 8:16). At the dedication of the rebuilt wall, one of the thanksgiving processions passed above this gate on its way past the Old Gate, the Fish Gate and the towers of Hananeel and Meah to the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). A gate of the same name appears in earlier accounts of King Jehoash of Israel breaking down Jerusalem's wall (2 Kgs 14:13). Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is only an approximate point within Jerusalem.

The Gate of the Valley, called the Valley Gate in modern translations, was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem. Nehemiah left the city through it at night to inspect the broken walls and burned gates, going past the Dragon Well toward the Dung Gate (Neh 2:13). He then went up along the brook and came back in through the same gate (Neh 2:15). STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) also connects it with King Uzziah, who built towers at the Valley Gate (2 Chr 26:9), and with the rebuilding under Nehemiah, when the gate was repaired along with a stretch of wall reaching to the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Its name suggests it opened onto one of the valleys around the city, usually taken to be the Tyropoeon or the Hinnom Valley. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the western side of the old City of David.

Gath-hepher was a town on the border of the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee. In Josh 19:13 the King James Version spells it Gittah-hepher, in a list of points marking Zebulun's boundary. It is best known as the hometown of the prophet Jonah son of Amittai, who foretold Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25). The name is usually explained as "winepress of the pit" or "winepress of the well." Jerome described it as a small village near Sepphoris where Jonah's tomb was shown, and a long local tradition places that tomb at the same spot. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify Gath-hepher with el-Meshhed, a hilltop village with ancient ruins near Kafr Kanna, a few miles northeast of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Gederoth was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It appears in the list of Judah's lowland towns, alongside Beth-dagon, Naamah and Makkedah (Josh 15:41). Its name probably means "sheepfolds" or "walls," as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. During the reign of Ahaz, the Philistines invaded the lowland and the south of Judah. They captured Gederoth, along with Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Socho, Timnah and Gimzo, and settled there (2 Chr 28:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia cites Eusebius, who places a large village called Gedrom 10 Roman miles from Lydda on the road to Eleutheropolis. That points to Katrah (Qatra), southeast of Yebnah. The encyclopedia also suggests a possible link with the Kidron of 1 Maccabees. The location shown here, near modern Gedera, follows the Katrah identification and is approximate.

Gedor was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed in Josh 15:58 with Halhul and Beth-zur among the towns given to the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it a few miles north of Hebron, at Khirbet Jedur, about halfway between Bethlehem and Hebron. The location shown here follows that identification. 1 Chr 12:7 names Joelah and Zebadiah, "the sons of Jeroham of Gedor," among the warriors who joined David. The surrounding passage links that group with Saul's tribe of Benjamin, so Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this Gedor to be a town apparently in Benjamin, probably the same as Geder. Whether the two verses refer to one place or two is uncertain. Several other places in the Bible share the name.

Gethsemane was a place across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem, at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Jesus went there with his disciples after the Last Supper and told them to sit while he went on to pray (Matt 26:36; Mark 14:32). The surrounding accounts show it was also where Judas betrayed him and he was arrested, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew and Mark call it simply a “place.” John 18:1 calls it a garden across the Kidron, and Luke 22:39 places it on the Mount of Olives and says Jesus often went there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia derives the name from the Aramaic for “oil press,” which suggests an olive grove. A tradition dating from the 4th century identifies a walled garden of old olive trees just east of the Kidron. Some writers quoted in Easton's Bible Dictionary preferred a more secluded spot farther up the valley. The location shown here roughly follows the traditional site.

Gibeah, a name meaning "hill," was a town in the hill country of Judah. Joshua 15:57 lists it with Cain and Timnah in a district of ten towns, a group that also includes Maon, Carmel and Ziph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore place it in the uplands southeast of Hebron. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is approximate. 2 Chr 13:2 names Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, as the mother of King Abijah of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this as probably the same town, and this entry follows that view, though the verse does not say which Gibeah is meant. Because several places in the Bible share this name, this Gibeah should be kept distinct from others, such as the Benjaminite town.

Gilgal was a place associated with the prophets Elijah and Elisha, distinct from the better-known Gilgal near Jericho in the Jordan valley. Elijah set out from Gilgal with Elisha on the journey that ended with his being taken up into heaven by a whirlwind (2 Kgs 2:1). Elisha later returned there during a famine, when a group of prophets, called the sons of the prophets, were sitting before him and he had his servant cook a stew for them (2 Kgs 4:38). The next verse says the two prophets "went down" to Bethel, so this Gilgal probably lay in the hill country rather than in the low Jordan plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Jiljilia, on a hill north of Bethel. The location shown here follows that identification. The name means "circle" or "rolling."

Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the same group as Debir and Eshtemoa (Josh 15:51). It was the home of Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counsellor. Absalom summoned him from Giloh while offering sacrifices as his rebellion against David gained strength (2 Sam 15:12). According to 2 Sam 17:23, when Absalom rejected his advice, Ahithophel went home to his city and hanged himself. 2 Sam 23:34 names his son Eliam, also called a Gilonite, among David's mighty men. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that the original form of the name was Gilon. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the site with the ruins of Khirbet Jala, about 7 miles (11 km) north of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Gittaim was a town to which the people of Beeroth fled, living there as resident foreigners "until this day" (2 Sam 4:3). The verse comes in the account of Rechab and Baanah, Beerothites who killed Saul's son Ish-bosheth. Nehemiah lists Gittaim with Hazor and Ramah among the towns Benjamites settled after the exile (Neh 11:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two mentions are probably the same place, since the Beerothites' refuge need not have lain outside Benjamin. Easton's Bible Dictionary also places it probably in Benjamin and gives the name's meaning as "two winepresses." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, in the lowland west of the Benjamin hill country, near modern Ramla.

Gob was a place where David's warriors fought two battles against the Philistines. It appears only in 2 Sam 21:18–19. In the first battle Sibbechai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of the giant. In the second, Elhanan son of Jaareoregim of Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam. The name is usually explained as meaning "pit" or "cistern." Its identity is uncertain. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:4 names the place Gezer, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries note. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions that some manuscripts read Nob, while the Syriac and Septuagint versions read Gath, and it favours Gath. The location shown here follows the Gezer identification, at or near Tel Gezer in the low hills between Jerusalem and the coastal plain.

Hammath was one of the fortified cities in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali. It is listed alongside Ziddim, Zer, Rakkath and Chinnereth (Josh 19:35). The name means "hot springs." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the warm baths on the shore of the Sea of Galilee just south of Tiberias. Smith's also suggests that the Levitical city Hammoth-dor in Josh 21:32 is the same place. The location shown here does not follow that identification. It places the city farther northwest, near the present Israel–Lebanon border, so the site remains uncertain. The same Hebrew name appears in 1 Chr 2:55, where the King James Version spells it Hemath and calls it "the father of the house of Rechab." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Hemath as a person, an ancestor of the Kenites, rather than this city.

Hammon was a city named in the list of towns on the border of the tribe of Asher, alongside Rehob and Kanah and reaching toward Sidon (Josh 19:28). The name probably means "glowing" or "warm," and Smith's Bible Dictionary connects it with warm springs. A Hammon is also listed among the towns with surrounding pasturelands given to the Levites from the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chr 6:76). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names list take this Naphtali town to be the same as Hammath or Hammoth-dor in Joshua, which would make it a different place from the Asher town. For the Asher town, Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests 'Ain Hamul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Umm el-'Amud on the coast about 10 miles south of Tyre, where an inscription to Baal Hammon was found. The location shown here follows that coastal identification.

Haradah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where the people moved to it from Mount Shapher and then on to Makheloth (Num 33:24–25). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the twenty-fifth station of the journey, and the name is usually taken to mean "fear" or "fright." Nothing else is recorded about the place, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its position is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough estimate, placing it in the highlands east of the Arabah in present-day southern Jordan, near the Petra region.

Harod was a spring where Gideon and his army camped early one morning before routing the Midianites, whose camp lay to the north by the hill of Moreh in the valley (Judg 7:1). The name is usually taken to mean "trembling" or "fear." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Gideon's test of his men by how they drank also happened here. The common identification is Ain Jalud, modern Ein Harod, a large spring at the foot of the northern cliffs of Mount Gilboa on the edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows that view. Some scholars have looked instead for the spring near Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with the spring in Jezreel where Saul camped (1 Sam 29:1). Two of David's mighty men, Shammah and Elika, are called Harodites (2 Sam 23:25). This probably refers to a place named Harod, but whether it is the same place is uncertain.

Hashmonah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The itinerary in Numbers 33 lists it between Mithcah, where they came from, and Moseroth, where they went next (Num 33:29–30). Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as “fatness,” counts it as the thirtieth halting place, and places it not far from Mount Hor. Moseroth, the next stop, is probably the same as the Mosera where Deut 10:6 says Aaron died, which fits a location in that area. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the region east of the Arabah valley, south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan.

Hauran was a region east of the Sea of Galilee, named only in Ezekiel's vision of the future boundaries of Israel. There it marks part of the northern border, where Hazar-hatticon lies "by the coast of Hauran" (Ezek 47:16). It is also the starting point for measuring the eastern border, which runs from Hauran, Damascus and Gilead down along the Jordan to the Dead Sea (Ezek 47:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "cave-land" and describes Hauran as one of the ancient divisions of Bashan and a very fertile area. Both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with the Greek and Roman province of Auranitis and with the modern Hauran, a plain in southern Syria on the edge of the desert. The location shown here is a general point east of the Sea of Galilee within that wider area.

Havilah (of Arabia) was a region marking one end of the territory of Ishmael's descendants, who lived "from Havilah unto Shur," the area east of Egypt (Gen 25:18). The same phrase reappears when King Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur (1 Sam 15:7), suggesting Havilah was a known boundary on the desert fringe southeast of Israel. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in southern Arabia and links it with the tribes named Havilah among the descendants of Cush (Gen 10:7) and of Joktan (Gen 10:29). It cites Kalisch's view that these are one vast country stretching from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea. The location shown here follows a narrower placement in northwestern Arabia, near the Arabah south of the Dead Sea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that suffers pain; that brings forth."

Hazazon-tamar was a place near the Dead Sea where Amorites lived in the time of Abraham. In Gen 14:7 the eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer struck the Amalekite country and the Amorites living there on their return from Kadesh. Centuries later, in 2 Chr 20:2, messengers told King Jehoshaphat that a great army from beyond the sea was at Hazazon-tamar, which the verse identifies with En-gedi. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "Hazazon of the palm trees" and takes it to be the older name of En-gedi, possibly preserved in Wady Husasah northwest of Ain Jidy. The same work notes another view placing it at Thamara, perhaps the ruin Kurnub southwest of the Dead Sea on the road from Hebron to Elath. The location shown here follows the En-gedi identification, on the western shore of the Dead Sea. The King James Version spells it Hazezon-tamar in Genesis.

Helam was a place east of the Jordan River where David fought and defeated the Syrian (Aramean) army. Hadarezer, king of Zobah, brought Syrian forces from beyond the river, probably the Euphrates, and they gathered at Helam under his army commander Shobach (2 Sam 10:16). David assembled all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and met them there in battle (2 Sam 10:17). The next verse, 2 Sam 10:18, reports that the Syrians fled and Shobach was killed. The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown and notes proposals placing it between Damascus and Hamath, or at Aleppo. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with Alamatta near Nicephorium on the Euphrates. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead, in present-day Jordan.

Helkath was a city on the border of the tribe of Asher, listed first among the boundary towns in Josh 19:25, along with Hali, Beten and Achshaph. It was later one of the cities given, with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (Josh 21:31). By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Gershonite clan, who received four cities from Asher. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "smoothness" and places the town on Asher's eastern border. It also notes that the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:75 calls it Hukok, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as a copyist's variant of the same name. The site's exact identification is uncertain, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here places it in western Galilee, inland and northeast of the plain of Acco.

Hepher was a Canaanite town whose king appears among the rulers Joshua defeated west of the Jordan, listed next to the king of Tappuah (Josh 12:17). Under Solomon, "all the land of Hepher" formed part of the third administrative district, along with Sochoh, under the son of Hesed based at Aruboth (1 Kgs 4:10). That suggests the town gave its name to a surrounding district, probably in the Sharon plain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) treats both the town and the district as unidentified. Many later scholars place Hepher at Tell el-Ifshar (Tel Hefer) on the coastal plain north of modern Netanya, and the location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a digger."

Hethlon was a place on the northern border of the land in Ezekiel's vision of the restored Israel. Ezekiel describes that border as running from the Mediterranean ("the great sea") along "the way of Hethlon" toward Zedad and Hamath, and he uses the same line to mark the northern edge of Dan's portion (Ezek 47:15; 48:1). The site is not mentioned anywhere else. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take "the way of Hethlon" to be the pass at the northern end of Lebanon leading to the plain of Hamath, probably the same route as the "entrance of Hamath" in Numbers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions an identification with 'Adlun on the Qasmiyeh River, and also one with Heitala northeast of Tripoli, which would place the route in the Eleutherus valley between the coast and Homs. The location shown here follows that northern, Eleutherus valley identification.

Highway, called the King's Highway in modern translations, was a main road east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. During their journey toward Canaan the Israelites asked permission to use it. Moses first asked the king of Edom (Num 20:17), and later Israel asked Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:22). Each time they promised to keep to the road, not to turn aside into fields or vineyards, and not to drink from the wells until they had crossed the king's territory. The surrounding chapters show that both requests were refused. STEPBible's proper-names index (Tyndale House) describes the King's Highway as an ancient trade route through Edom and Moab. It is generally taken to have run north and south along the high ground east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here is a rough point in that region, in what is now Jordan.

Holon was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in a group with Goshen and Giloh (Josh 15:51). It was later assigned with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites, the descendants of Aaron, and is named alongside Debir (Josh 21:15). The parallel list of Levitical towns in 1 Chr 6:58 gives the name as Hilen, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary take to be the same place. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the ruins of Beit 'Alam, northwest of Hebron, and the location shown here is in that area. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sandy." The name Holon is also used of a different town in Moab (Jer 48:21), which should not be confused with this one.

Hor-haggidgad was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. The itinerary in Numbers places it between Bene-jaakan and Jotbathah: the people moved there from Bene-jaakan and went on from it to Jotbathah (Num 33:32–33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list both identify it with Gudgodah in Deut 10:7, where the same sequence of places appears in a different order. The site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only approximate. It places the camp in the Arabah region south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan, which fits its position in the itinerary before Ezion-geber.

Horse Gate was a gate in the wall of Jerusalem near the temple. During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls, priests repaired the section from above the Horse Gate, each working opposite his own house (Neh 3:28). This suggests the priests' homes stood close to the temple. Jeremiah mentions "the corner of the horse gate toward the east" as one of the boundaries of a restored city that would be holy to the Lord, alongside the Kidron Valley (Jer 31:40). That points to a position on the eastern side of the city. Many interpreters also link it with the "horses' entry" to the royal palace where Queen Athaliah was killed (2 Kgs 11:16; 2 Chr 23:15), though this is an inference. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the west end of a bridge leading from Zion to the temple. The location shown here is within Jerusalem, by the temple area.

Immer was a place in the land of exile from which some Jews returned to Judah after the Babylonian captivity. It appears only in the parallel lists of Ezra 2:59 and Neh 7:61, alongside Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub and Addan (or Addon). The people who came from these places could not prove their family descent or show that they were of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Immer as a place in Babylonia, but its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in northern Mesopotamia, near modern Mosul in Iraq. The same name is also borne elsewhere by a priestly family, which is a separate use of the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "saying" or "a lamb."

Iye-abarim was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. They reached it after leaving Oboth. It is described as lying "in the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising" (Num 21:11) and "in the border of Moab" (Num 33:44). That places it east of the land along Moab's frontier, before Israel moved on toward the Zered Valley. The name probably means "the heaps (or ruins) of the Abarim," after the Abarim range of highlands east of the Dead Sea. The King James Version spells it Ije-abarim. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the shorter name Iyim (Iim) in Num 33:45 refers to the same place. It also notes that the biblical descriptions are too general to fix the site, and no exact identification is known. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea on the edge of Moab.

Jahzah was a town east of the Jordan, in the territory of the tribe of Reuben, that was given with its pasturelands to the Levites. By context, it went to the Merari clan named in the surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:78). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Jahaz, also spelled Jahaza and Jahazah. Connected passages tie Jahaz to the battle in which Israel defeated Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:23). Jeremiah later lists Jahazah among the towns of the Moabite plateau facing judgment, alongside Holon and Mephaath (Jer 48:21). This suggests the town had passed into Moabite hands by his time. Its exact site is uncertain, and several ruins north of the Arnon River have been proposed. The location shown here is on the plateau east of the Dead Sea in modern Jordan, east of Dhiban.

Janoah (spelled Janohah in the King James Version) was a city on the boundary of Ephraim's territory. Joshua 16 traces the border east from Michmethah past Taanath-shiloh to Janohah, then down to Ataroth and Naarath, reaching Jericho and ending at the Jordan (Josh 16:6–7). The name probably means "resting place" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Its location is debated. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place this border town at Yanun (Khirbet Yanun), southeast of Nablus, near the Jordan valley. The location shown here is Yanouh in southern Lebanon, a site often connected with another Janoah in Naphtali that Tiglath-pileser captured (2 Kgs 15:29). This entry follows the Yanouh identification. Because several places in the Bible share this name, which references belong to which town is not always certain.

Javan is a distant land named among the nations in Isaiah and Ezekiel. In Isa 66:19 it appears with Tarshish, Pul, Lud and Tubal among faraway peoples, near "the isles afar off," to whom survivors would be sent to declare God's glory. In Ezek 27:13 Javan, Tubal and Meshech are traders who supplied Tyre's market with slaves and bronze vessels. The name is generally taken to mean the Greeks, especially the Ionians of the Aegean coast of Asia Minor. It is probably connected with Javan, son of Japheth, in the table of nations (Gen 10:2). The location shown here is in Ionia, near ancient Ephesus in western Turkey, and represents the wider region rather than one exact site. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "deceiver" or "one who makes sad."

Jogbehah was a town east of the Jordan in Gilead. It appears in the list of towns that the tribe of Gad built or fortified after settling the region (Num 32:35); the preceding verse names Gad as the builder. Later, when Gideon pursued the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, he went up "by the way of them that dwelt in tents" east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck their camp while it felt secure (Judg 8:11). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the ruins of Ajbeihat, about 7 miles northwest of Amman on the road toward es-Salt, at roughly 3,470 feet above sea level. The name survives in Jubeiha, now a district of north Amman, Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Juttah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Carmel and Ziph among the towns given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:55). It was later one of the nine cities that Judah and Simeon gave to the Levites, together with its surrounding pasturelands (Josh 21:16). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chronicles 6 does not name it. Juttah is generally identified with the modern town of Yatta (Yutta), about 5.5 miles (9 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition that Juttah was the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth and the birthplace of John the Baptist, linking it with the "city of Judah" in the hill country mentioned in Luke 1:39. The name is usually explained as meaning "extended" or "stretched out."

Kain was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the ten cities of a district in the tribe's territory in Josh 15:57, where the King James Version spells it "Cain." The Hebrew word behind it, qayin, is also the name of the Kenite clan. In Balaam's oracle at Num 24:22, the King James Version translates it "the Kenite," while the Revised Version reads "Kain." For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the town to be a Kenite settlement and connects it with the Kenites' "nest" set in the rock in Balaam's words. The site is usually identified with modern Yaqin (Yukin), on a high hill southeast of Hebron overlooking the wilderness of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this identification as uncertain. The location shown here follows the Yaqin identification.

Kanah was a stream, called "the river Kanah" in the King James Version, that marked part of the boundary between the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Ephraim's border ran westward from Tappuah to the Kanah and on to the Mediterranean Sea, with Ephraim's land to the south of the stream and Manasseh's to the north (Josh 16:8; 17:9). The Hebrew word usually means a wadi or seasonal torrent bed, and the name means "of reeds." Several other biblical places share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the modern Wadi Qanah, which rises southwest of Shechem and joins the Yarkon (Auja) before reaching the sea north of Jaffa. Easton's Bible Dictionary also mentions a reedy stream entering the sea between Joppa and Caesarea. The location shown here follows the Wadi Qanah identification.

Kehelathah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their years in the wilderness after leaving Mount Sinai. It appears only in the list of camps in Numbers 33, where the people moved there from Rissah and then went on to Mount Shapher (Num 33:22–23). The name means "assembly" or "gathering," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about the place, and its site is unknown, as both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. The location shown here is only a rough estimate based on its place in the route. It puts the camp in the highlands of present-day southern Jordan, east of the Arabah valley.

Kenath was a city east of the Jordan, in the region of Bashan. Num 32:42 says that Nobah captured Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed the city Nobah after himself. The surrounding chapter places this among the conquests of Manasseh's descendants east of the Jordan. 1 Chr 2:23 lists Kenath and its towns among sixty cities belonging to the sons of Machir, the father of Gilead. In the King James wording an unnamed "he" takes Geshur and Aram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the verse as Geshur and Aram retaking Kenath from the Israelites. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "possession." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Kenath with Qanawat (Kanawat), on the slopes of Jebel al-Druze in southern Syria, a site with extensive Roman remains. Some scholars question this identification, but the location shown here follows it.

Kerioth was a city of Moab, east of the Dead Sea. Jeremiah names it with Bozrah among the Moabite cities facing judgment (Jer 48:24), and Amos announces that fire will devour "the palaces of Kerioth" (Amos 2:2), which suggests it was a prominent town. The name means "the cities," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Moabite king Mesha's inscription mentions a sanctuary of the god Chemosh at Kerioth. Its location is uncertain. It may be the modern Khirbet el-Qureiyat, between Dhiban and Ataroth. Others take it as another name for Ar of Moab, or identify it with Kir of Moab (modern Kerak). The location shown here follows the Qureiyat identification. Some readers link it to Judas Iscariot, but his Kerioth is usually placed in Judah rather than Moab.

Kir-hareseth was a fortified city of Moab. In 2 Kgs 3:25 it is the one stronghold left standing when the armies of Israel, Judah and Edom overran Moab, wrecking its cities, fields, wells and trees. Even so, slingers surrounded and attacked it. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Mesha king of Moab took refuge there, and from its wall he offered his eldest son as a burnt offering, after which the invaders withdrew (2 Kgs 3:26–27). Isaiah's oracle against Moab later mourns the city's ruined foundations (Isa 16:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the forms Kir-haresh and Kir-heres (Isa 16:11; Jer 48:31, 36) as names for the same place, and identifies it with modern Kerak in Jordan, a town on a steep hill east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the Kerak identification.

Kiriath-baal, meaning "town of Baal," is an alternative name for Kiriath-jearim, a town of Judah. Both verses that use the name explain it this way. Josh 15:60 lists it with Rabbah among the towns of Judah's hill country. Josh 18:14 places it at the end of a stretch of Benjamin's boundary, where the border with Judah ran west of Jerusalem, and calls it "a city of the children of Judah." Elsewhere the same town is called Baalah (Josh 15:9) and Baale of Judah (2 Sam 6:2). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under Kiriath-jearim. The Baal name probably reflects an older Canaanite association that was later replaced. The town is usually identified with a site near modern Abu Ghosh, about 13 km (8 miles) west of Jerusalem. The location shown here is only approximate.

Kishion was a town in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed among the cities of Issachar's allotment (Josh 19:20). It was later given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Gershonite Levites (Josh 21:28). The King James Version spells the name "Kishon" in that second passage, though it is the same town and not the Kishon River. The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:72 has "Kedesh" in its place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the original form may have been something like Kidshon and notes Conder's proposal to identify the site with Tell Abu Kedes, near Taanach on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows that identification. The name is usually explained as meaning "hardness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Kittim (spelled Chittim in the King James Version) is a coastal land across the sea from Israel, mentioned for its ships. In Balaam's oracle, ships from the coast of Kittim come to afflict Asshur and Eber (Num 24:24). In Daniel's vision, the ships of Kittim oppose a northern king, who then turns back in anger against the holy covenant (Dan 11:30). Many interpreters read this as Roman intervention against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, though the text does not name either. The name is usually linked with Citium, an ancient town on Cyprus, and Kittim is also listed as a descendant of Javan in Gen 10:4, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. In later use the term could extend to the western coastlands more broadly. The location shown here follows the identification with Cyprus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "breaking" or "bruising small."

Kue is a place from which Solomon obtained horses, mentioned in 1 Kgs 10:28 and the parallel 2 Chr 1:16. The King James Version does not show the name. It translates the Hebrew word as "linen yarn," so the verses speak of horses and linen yarn brought from Egypt. Many later translations read the same word as a place name and render the verses as horses imported "from Egypt and from Kue," with the king's merchants buying them from Kue. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) treats Kue as a place in this way. Kue is usually identified with Cilicia, the coastal plain of what is now south-eastern Turkey, an area known in the ancient world for horse breeding. The location shown here follows that identification and marks the Cilician plain near modern Adana in general terms rather than a specific site.

Libnah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. The list of stations in Numbers 33 records that they moved from Rimmon-parez to Libnah, and from Libnah went on to Rissah (Num 33:20–21). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the stretch of the journey between the wilderness of Sinai and Kadesh. The name probably means "whiteness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Laban, mentioned in Deut 1:1. The name Libnah is also borne by other places, including a town in Judah, and this wilderness camp should be kept distinct from them. Its actual site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough approximation.

Libya was the region of North Africa west of Egypt, along the Mediterranean coast. In Ezek 30:5 it is named with Ethiopia, Lydia and other peoples allied with Egypt, who are foretold to fall by the sword with Egypt. The Hebrew name behind this translation is Put, a people usually linked with North Africa. In Acts 2:10, Jews and proselytes from “the parts of Libya about Cyrene” were among the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost. By the context of the chapter, they heard the apostles speak in their own languages. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a large tract along the Mediterranean west of Egypt, with Cyrene as one of its five cities. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Greek and Roman writers used the name for the African continent generally, usually excluding Egypt. The location shown here marks the general region west of the Nile, broadly the eastern part of modern Libya.

City of the Lord is a title given to Jerusalem in Isaiah 60:14, where the prophet says that those who once oppressed and despised the city will come bowing before it and will call it "The city of the LORD, The Zion of the Holy One of Israel." The pairing with Zion shows that Jerusalem is meant. The chapter describes a future restoration of the city. Its closing verse promises that "a little one shall become a thousand, and a small one a strong nation," and that the Lord will bring this about in his time (Isa 60:22). The same phrase is used of Jerusalem in Psalms such as Ps 48:8 and Ps 101:8. The location shown here is Jerusalem, at the Temple Mount.

Luhith was a place in Moab, known for its ascent or climbing road, named only in the parallel prophecies against Moab in Isa 15:5 and Jer 48:5. In both passages, fugitives fleeing destruction go up the ascent of Luhith weeping, while a cry of destruction is heard on the road of Horonaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Zoar and Horonaim. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Eusebius and Jerome still knew the site, between Areopolis (Rabbath-moab) and Zoar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was a route by which refugees could climb from the low ground near the Dead Sea to the Moabite plateau, perhaps the road through Wadi Bene Hammad, though the site cannot be identified with certainty. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea in that general area. The name is often explained as meaning "made of boards."

Madmannah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of Judah, listed among the tribe's southern towns between Ziklag and Sansannah (Josh 15:31). In the genealogy of Caleb, Shaaph, a son of Caleb's concubine Maacah, is called "the father of Madmannah" (1 Chr 2:49). This probably means he founded or led the town's settlers rather than that he had a son of that name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Beth-marcaboth, in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (Josh 19:5), stands for the same place. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "dunghill." The site is uncertain. Smith's and Easton's identify it with el-Minyay, south-southwest of Gaza. The Palestine Exploration survey proposed Umm Deimneh, about 12 miles northeast of Beersheba. The location shown here follows the Umm Deimneh identification.

Madon was a Canaanite royal city in the north of the land. Its king, Jobab, was one of the rulers Jabin king of Hazor summoned into a coalition against Joshua (Josh 11:1). The following verses of that chapter describe the allied kings gathering at the waters of Merom and being defeated. Madon's king appears in the list of kings Joshua defeated (Josh 12:19). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "strife" and suggests the ruin Madin, near Hattin, about 5 miles (8 km) west of Tiberias. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Hebrew letters for "d" and "r" were confused and that the name should read "Maron," which it identifies with Meiron, northwest of Safed. The location shown here follows the identification near Hattin, west of the Sea of Galilee.

Mahaneh-dan, meaning "camp of Dan," was a place in the lowlands west of Jerusalem linked with the tribe of Dan. Judg 13:25 places it between Zorah and Eshtaol and says this is where the Spirit of the LORD began to move Samson. Judg 18:12 explains the name: the six hundred Danites who set out from Zorah and Eshtaol to seize Laish camped "behind" Kirjath-jearim in Judah, and the spot was called Mahaneh-dan from then on. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "behind" to mean west of Kirjath-jearim. Some have thought the two descriptions point to different places, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Sorek Valley area west of Kirjath-jearim, where Zorah and Eshtaol stand, fits both. No site with a matching name has been found. The location shown here follows that view and places it between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Makheloth was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their journey through the wilderness after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of encampments in Numbers 33, where the people moved to Makheloth from Haradah and then went on to Tahath (Num 33:25–26). Nothing else is said about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "assemblies" or "congregations." Its actual site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement, in the region east of the Arabah valley in present-day southern Jordan, inferred from its position in the sequence of wilderness stations.

Masrekah was a place in Edom, the home of Samlah, who became king of Edom after the death of Hadad (Gen 36:36; 1 Chr 1:47). Both verses come from the list of Edomite kings who reigned before any king ruled over Israel. Nothing more is said about the town, and its site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "vineyard of noble vines," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "place of choice vines." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "whistling" or "hissing." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing shows where the place should be sought. The location shown here is only a rough placement within Edomite territory, south of the Dead Sea in present-day southern Jordan.

Mattanah was a stopping place of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey, on the route toward the land east of the Jordan. Numbers 21 says they went to Mattanah from the wilderness, right after the song about the well the princes dug at Beer, and then moved on to Nahaliel and Bamoth (Num 21:18–19). The name means "gift." Because of this, some have linked it with the well just described. Its site is unknown, and reference works place it differently. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it in the Wadi Waleh, between the desert and the borders of Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it southeast of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no clue to its location now remains. The location shown here is only approximate, east of the northern Dead Sea, and follows the general view that it lay in the region north of the Arnon on the edge of Moab.

Meribah (of Horeb) was the name Moses gave, along with Massah, to the place near Rephidim where the Israelites quarreled with him over lack of water and tested the LORD by asking, "Is the LORD among us, or not?" (Exod 17:7). The surrounding account in Exodus 17 says water came from a rock at Horeb when Moses struck it, so the site is described as a spring. The name means "quarrel" or "dispute." Moses later recalled the episode in his blessing of the tribe of Levi (Deut 33:8). It belongs to the wilderness wanderings, about 1491 BC by inference from context. It is distinct from the later Meribah at Kadesh in Numbers 20. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Wady Feiran near Mount Serbal, and the location shown here is a rough placement in that part of southern Sinai.

Merom, or "the waters of Merom," was a body of water in northern Canaan where a coalition of kings gathered to fight Israel (Josh 11:5). Joshua made a sudden attack on them there and routed them (Josh 11:7). The surrounding chapter names Jabin king of Hazor as the leader of the alliance and says the pursuit went as far as Sidon. The name is usually explained as "height" or "high place." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Lake Huleh, a small lake in the upper Jordan Valley about ten miles north of the Sea of Galilee, once ringed by papyrus marsh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions other views: Josephus places the allied camp at Beroth near Kedesh in upper Galilee, and Conder proposed a stream west of Nazareth. The location shown here follows the Lake Huleh identification.

Michmas is the spelling of Michmash used in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon, where the men of Michmas number 122 (Ezra 2:27; Neh 7:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as another form of that name. Michmash was a town of Benjamin. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Bethel on the road toward Jerusalem (Isa 10:28), on the north side of a steep ravine called "the passage of Michmash" (1 Sam 13:23), facing Geba on the other side. It was the scene of Saul's battle against the Philistines. Easton's identifies it with the modern village of Mukhmas, northeast of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site.

Michmethath was a town on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Manasseh. It appears only in the boundary lists of Joshua. Ephraim's northern border ran to Michmethath and then turned east toward Taanath-shiloh and Janohah (Josh 16:6), and Manasseh's border ran from Asher to Michmethath, which is described as lying "before Shechem," meaning facing or near that city (Josh 17:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the northern border of Ephraim and Manasseh, not far west of the Jordan, and gives the meaning of the name as "hiding-place." Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here puts it just south of Shechem, near modern Nablus. That fits the description of it lying before Shechem and matches suggested identifications with ruins in the plain east and southeast of the city.

Migron was a place in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. In 1 Sam 14:2, Saul stayed with about six hundred men under a pomegranate tree at Migron, on the outskirts of Gibeah, while the Philistines held Michmash. Isaiah 10:28 names Migron in a poetic description of an Assyrian army advancing on Jerusalem: after Aiath it passes Migron, then stores its baggage at Michmash. Because that route seems to place Migron north of Michmash, Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these as two separate places, with the town in Samuel lying to the south. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others take them as possibly one locality. The location shown here, given only roughly, follows the setting near Gibeah in 1 Samuel. The exact site of either is uncertain. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "precipice" or "landslip."

Minnith was a town east of the Jordan, named as the limit of Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites. He struck them from Aroer as far as Minnith, twenty cities, and on to the "plain of the vineyards" (Judg 11:33). Ezekiel mentions "wheat of Minnith" among the goods Judah and Israel traded to Tyre (Ezek 27:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat this as the same place, an Ammonite town known for its wheat. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some readers do not take the word in Ezekiel as a place name at all. The site is uncertain. Eusebius' Onomasticon mentions a Maanith about 4 Roman miles from Heshbon on the road to Rabbah (modern Amman), and the location shown here follows that identification, placing Minnith near Heshbon on the plateau of modern Jordan.

Mishal was a town in the territory of the tribe of Asher. It appears in the list of Asher's towns, where the King James Version spells it Misheal (Josh 19:26). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites (Josh 21:30). Smith's Bible Dictionary specifies the Gershonite clan of Levites, and the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:74 calls the town Mashal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "parables" or "governing." The site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient writer Eusebius placed it near Carmel by the sea, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the coastal site Misalli near Carmel. The location shown here is only a rough placement farther north, in western Galilee near Abdon, the town listed next to it in Josh 21:30.

Misrephoth-maim was a place in northern Canaan near the coast, the point to which Israel chased the kings allied with Jabin after Joshua defeated them. The pursuit ran to great Sidon, to Misrephoth-maim, and to the valley of Mizpeh to the east (Josh 11:8). It later appears as a boundary of land still to be taken, the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, which is linked with the Sidonians (Josh 13:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burning of waters," perhaps referring to salt-pans, lime-kilns or glass-works, and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "hot waters." Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Musheirifeh at the headland of Ras en-Naqura, about 11 miles north of Acre. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Zarephath near Sidon instead. The location shown here follows the Ras en-Naqura identification, near modern Naqoura in southern Lebanon.

Mithkah (spelled Mithcah in the King James Version) was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where the people moved from Tarah to Mithcah and then on to Hashmonah (Num 33:28–29). The name means "sweetness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was given because of sweet pasture or water at the site. Nothing else is recorded about the camp, and its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the desert region south of the Dead Sea, in what is now southern Jordan, by inference from its position in the sequence of stations.

Moreh (Shechem) was a landmark at the place of Shechem, in the hill country of central Canaan, where Abram first stopped after entering the land (Gen 12:6). The King James Version calls it the "plain of Moreh," but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Hebrew is better rendered "oak" or "terebinth of Moreh," probably meaning "terebinth of the teacher." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Moreh may have been a Canaanite who gave his name to the spot. According to the next verse, Gen 12:7, the Lord appeared to Abram here and he built an altar. The arrival is dated about 1921 BC, by inference from context. Deut 11:30 mentions the "plains of Moreh" near Mounts Ebal and Gerizim. Some treat that as a separate site linked with Gilgal, but this entry follows the view that it is the same place. The exact spot is unknown. The location shown here is near Shechem, by the modern city of Nablus.

Moresheth was the hometown of the prophet Micah, a town in Judah. It does not appear by name in these verses but is implied by Micah's title, "the Morasthite," meaning a man of Moresheth. Micah prophesied there during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Mic 1:1). A century later, elders recalled him by this title when they defended Jeremiah, quoting his warning that Jerusalem would become heaps (Jer 26:18). Micah 1:14 mentions a "Moresheth-gath," probably the same town, which suggests it lay near the Philistine city of Gath in the Shephelah, the low hill country west of Judah's highlands. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and fits the common identification with Tell el-Judeideh (Tel Goded), near modern Beit Guvrin.

Moseroth was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. They came to it from Hashmonah and moved on from it to Bene-jaakan (Num 33:30–31). The name is usually taken to mean "bonds." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Mosera (Moserah) in Deut 10:6, where Aaron is said to have died and been buried. In that passage, though, the order is reversed, with Mosera coming after Bene-jaakan. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the region south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan, and should be treated as approximate.

Mount Halak was a mountain marking the southern limit of the land Joshua conquered. It is described as the mountain "that goeth up to Seir," meaning it rises toward Seir, the hill country of Edom to the southeast. Its northern counterpart was Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon under Mount Hermon (Josh 11:17; 12:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "smooth" or "bald" and suggests it was a conspicuous landmark visible from a distance. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's notes that some have identified it with Jebel el-Madura, on Judah's southern frontier near the south end of the Dead Sea. Others link it to a hill called Jebel Halaq, whose Arabic name preserves the biblical one. The location shown here follows a site in the central Negev highlands, probably that Jebel Halaq identification.

Mount Hor was a mountain marking the northern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:7–8 the line runs from the Mediterranean ("the great sea") to Mount Hor, then on to the entrance of Hamath and Zedad. It is mentioned nowhere else and is a different place from the Mount Hor on the border of Edom where Aaron died. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be one of the peaks of Lebanon. Others have proposed Mount Hermon or a peak in the coastal mountains farther north. The location shown here is a rough one in the mountains of northwestern Syria, which fits a border running inland from the sea toward Hamath, probably modern Hama.

Mount Nebo was a mountain in the land of Moab, facing Jericho across the Jordan, and part of the Abarim range. God told Moses to climb it and look at the land of Canaan that Israel would possess (Deut 32:49). Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, and the Lord showed him the whole land, from Gilead as far as Dan (Deut 34:1). Moses died there. By inference from context, this was about 1452 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Nebo with Jebel Nebah, near the northern end of the Dead Sea on its eastern side, about 5 miles southwest of Heshbon. It describes the mountain as the summit of the Pisgah ridge, about 2,643 feet high, with a commanding view of western Palestine. The location shown here matches that identification, the modern Jebel Nebo in Jordan.

Mount Paran is a mountain or highland named only in two poetic passages, both describing God coming from the south to his people. In Moses' blessing the LORD comes from Sinai, rises from Seir and shines forth from Mount Paran (Deut 33:2). Habakkuk's prayer similarly has the Holy One coming from Mount Paran, alongside Teman in Edom (Hab 3:3). The name is probably connected with the wilderness of Paran, where Israel camped after leaving Sinai. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was the hilly upland on the north side of the Paran desert, near the southern edge of the Promised Land. Others place it farther south in the Sinai Peninsula, where the name Wadi Feiran may echo Paran. The location shown here is a rough point in the western Sinai Peninsula, which fits the southern Sinai view.

Mount Shapher (spelled Mount Shepher in some modern translations) was a mountain where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey after leaving Egypt. It appears only in the list of camping places in Numbers 33, where Israel moved there from Kehelathah and then left it to camp at Haradah (Num 33:23–24). Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "brightness." Its exact location is unknown, and none of the neighbouring stations has been firmly identified. The location shown here is only a rough estimate, placing it in the mountainous region of what is now southern Jordan, east of the Arabah valley.

Mysia was a region in the northwest of Asia Minor, in what is now northwestern Turkey. Paul and his companions reached it on the journey that took them through Phrygia, Galatia and Asia, dated here to about AD 47 by inference from context. From Mysia they tried to go northeast into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them (Acts 16:7). They then passed by Mysia and came down to the coastal city of Troas (Acts 16:8). The verses record no preaching there. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Mysia's boundaries were always vague. It stretched roughly from the Sea of Marmara and the Hellespont south toward Lydia, and after 190 BC it formed part of the Roman province of Asia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the name as referring to a people and region rather than an official province. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Troas as its chief port. The location shown here is approximate.

Nahalal was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It appears in the list of Zebulun's towns, where the King James Version spells it Nahallal (Josh 19:15). It was later given, with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites (Josh 21:35). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia specify the Merarite clan of Levites, as the surrounding passage indicates. Both dictionaries and Easton's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as Nahalol, where, according to Judg 1:30, Zebulun did not drive out the Canaanite inhabitants. The name is usually taken to mean "pasture." Its site is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's identify it with Malul, west of Nazareth in the Plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel Valley). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also offers 'Ain Mahil, about 3½ miles northeast of Nazareth. The location shown here follows the 'Ain Mahil identification.

Nephtoah was a spring that marked part of the boundary between the tribal territories of Judah and Benjamin. The boundary descriptions call it "the fountain of the water of Nephtoah" and "the well of waters of Nephtoah." The line ran from the hill near Jerusalem to this spring, then on to the cities of Mount Ephron and to Kirjathjearim (Josh 15:9). Benjamin's southern border is traced in the reverse direction, from Kirjathjearim to the same spring (Josh 18:15). Its location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the spring at Lifta, about 2 miles (3 km) northwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes another view, based on a Talmudic tradition linking Nephtoah with Etam, which places it at 'Ain 'Atan southwest of Bethlehem. The location shown here follows the 'Ain 'Atan identification.

The New Gate was a gate of the temple ("the LORD's house") in Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Jeremiah. When Jeremiah was accused for prophesying against the temple and the city, the princes of Judah came up from the king's palace and sat at the entry of this gate to hear the case (Jer 26:10). It later served as the setting where Jeremiah's scribe Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll to the people from the chamber of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, in the upper court at the entry of the New Gate (Jer 36:10). That description suggests it opened from the higher inner court of the temple. Its name implies it had been built or rebuilt fairly recently. Some interpreters identify it with the upper gate of the temple that King Jotham built (2 Kgs 15:35), though this is uncertain. The location shown here places it within the temple area in Jerusalem.

Nimrim, called "the waters of Nimrim," was a stream or spring in Moab. It appears only in two prophetic oracles against Moab, which foretell that its waters will be desolate. Isa 15:6 describes the hay withered, the grass failing and nothing green left. Jer 48:34 places it in the same list as Zoar and Horonaim. That pairing suggests a location southeast of the Dead Sea. The name may mean "pure" or "wholesome water"; Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "stream of the leopards." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed a town of this name near Zoar. It also links the name to Wadi Numeira, which opens onto the Dead Sea. Easton's identifies it as Wady en-Nemeirah, a fertile spot at the southeastern end of the sea. The location shown here follows the Numeira identification on the southeastern shore.

Nobah was a town east of the Jordan, named after Nobah, a man who captured Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed it after himself (Num 32:42). The surrounding chapter places this among the conquests of the eastern half-tribe of Manasseh. Nobah appears again in Gideon's pursuit of the Midianites, who went up by the route of the tent-dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and struck their army (Judg 8:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats both mentions as the same place, the renamed Kenath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Nobah of Judges, being paired with Jogbehah, may have been a separate town further south, perhaps northeast of modern Amman, though no matching site has been found. The location shown here follows the Kenath identification, probably the modern Qanawat in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that barks or yelps."

Ophrah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin, listed alongside Avim and Parah (Josh 18:23). It is a different place from the Ophrah in Manasseh that is linked with Gideon. In Saul's time, Philistine raiding parties left their camp in three groups, and one of them took the road toward Ophrah and the land of Shual (1 Sam 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons that this group went north, because Saul held the passes to the south. Eusebius and Jerome place Ophrah about five Roman miles east of Bethel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the ISBE both identify it with the hilltop village of et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Beitin (Bethel), and the location shown here follows that identification. The ISBE also suggests it may be the same place as Ephron (2 Chr 13:19) and Ephraim (John 11:54). The name is usually taken to mean "fawn."

Paphos was a city on the west coast of Cyprus, visited by Barnabas and Saul (Paul) on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. After crossing the island from Salamis, they met a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-jesus there (Acts 13:6). The next verses (Acts 13:7–12) place the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, which fits Easton's Bible Dictionary's description of it as the island's capital and the governor's residence. From Paphos, Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia, where John left them and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). Ancient writers used the name for two towns: Old Paphos (modern Kouklia), famous for its temple of Aphrodite, and New Paphos, its harbor about ten miles northwest. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the city in Acts to be New Paphos, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Pekod was a people or district of Babylonia named in two prophetic passages. In Jer 50:21 God orders an attack on the land of Merathaim and on the inhabitants of Pekod, as part of the judgment announced against Babylon. In Ezek 23:23 Pekod appears alongside the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, Shoa, Koa and the Assyrians among the horsemen and nobles whom God would bring against Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a place in Babylonia. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as a name applied to the Chaldeans. Because the word can mean "visitation" or "punishment," some read it in Jeremiah as a symbolic name for Babylon as the city marked for judgment, a wordplay paired with Merathaim. Its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here places it in central Babylonia, near the site of Babylon.

Pelusium is the Greek name for the Egyptian city that Ezekiel calls Sin. In his prophecy against Egypt, Ezekiel names Sin as "the strength of Egypt" and says it will suffer fury, fire and great pain, alongside No (Thebes) and Noph (Memphis) (Ezek 30:15–16). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that both the Hebrew and Greek names mean "clayey" or "muddy," from the clay found there. It takes the phrase "the strength of Egypt" to mean an important fortified city, which fits a stronghold on Egypt's northeastern frontier. Easton's identifies the site with the modern Tineh, where a few red granite columns survive. The ruins are usually located near the eastern edge of the Nile Delta, southeast of modern Port Said, at a site also known as Tell el-Farama. The location shown here is an approximate placement in the surrounding region rather than the exact site.

Pergamum (spelled Pergamos in the King James Version) was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor. It was home to one of the seven churches to which John was told to send what he saw (Rev 1:11), and it receives its own message from the one "which hath the sharp sword with two edges" (Rev 2:12). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, the letter that follows says that "Satan's seat" was there. It also rebukes the church for holding the teachings of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, and it names Antipas as a faithful martyr killed in the city. Easton's describes Pergamum as the chief city of Mysia, standing near the Caicus River about 20 miles from the sea, and notes that parchment took its name from the city. The location shown here is the modern Turkish town of Bergama.
