Pethor was the home town of Balaam son of Beor, the man Balak king of Moab sent for to curse Israel (Num 22:5). It is described as lying "by the river" in the land of Balaam's people, and Deut 23:4 places it in Mesopotamia (Aram-naharaim). "The river" most likely means the Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Pethor with Pitru, a town mentioned by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser. Pitru stood on the west bank of the Euphrates near its meeting with the Sajur River, a few miles south of Carchemish. That would put it about 400 miles from Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the site as unknown. The location shown here follows the Pitru identification, at a site in northern Syria near the Sajur–Euphrates junction, probably modern Tell Aushariye.

Philadelphia was a city in the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, and one of the seven churches addressed in the Book of Revelation (Rev 1:11). Its message begins with Christ described as holy and true, the one who holds "the key of David" and opens and shuts doors that no one else can (Rev 3:7). The name means "brotherly love." Smith's Bible Dictionary says it stood on the lower slopes of Mount Tmolus, about 25 miles southeast of Sardis, and was built by Attalus II, king of Pergamum. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that it lay on a highway into the interior and was rebuilt after an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was repeatedly damaged by earthquakes. The site is the modern town of Alaşehir in western Turkey, and the location shown here matches it.

Pisidia was a mountainous district in southern Asia Minor, north of Pamphylia, in what is now south-central Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Taurus range runs through it. Paul and Barnabas crossed it during the First Missionary Journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. After leaving Perga they came to "Antioch in Pisidia" and spoke in the synagogue there (Acts 13:14). On the return leg they passed through Pisidia again before reaching Pamphylia (Acts 14:24), heading back toward Antioch in Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that Antioch actually lay in the Phrygian part of the Roman province of Galatia, near Pisidia's northern border. It was called "Pisidian" because of that closeness and to tell it apart from other cities named Antioch. Pisidia's borders were never sharply defined, so the location shown here is only approximate.

Place, more fully the Place of a Skull, is the meaning given in the Gospels for Golgotha, the site where Jesus was brought to be crucified (Matt 27:33; Mark 15:22). Both writers translate the Aramaic name for Greek readers. Luke 23:33 calls it simply "the place which is called Calvary," from the Latin word for skull, and John 19:17–20 adds that it was near Jerusalem, outside the city. Why it bore this name is not stated. Suggestions include a skull-shaped rise of ground or a place of execution. Its exact location is uncertain. A tradition going back to the fourth century places it at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and some identify it with Gordon's Calvary near the Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough placement at Jerusalem and does not settle between these views.

Plain refers here to the low, flat country of the lower Jordan Valley around Jericho, just north of the Dead Sea. In Deut 34:3 "the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees" is one of the regions Moses viewed before his death, a view that, by the surrounding chapter, he had from Mount Nebo. The view stretched as far south as Zoar. Deut 34:8 uses the related phrase "the plains of Moab" for the lowland on the eastern side of the Jordan, across from Jericho, where Israel mourned Moses for thirty days. The two phrases probably describe opposite sides of the same broad valley floor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this term to its entry on the Cities of the Plain, the Jordan lowland associated in Genesis with Sodom and Zoar. The location shown here is the valley near Jericho.

The Plain of Jordan (ESV: Jordan Valley) is the well-watered lowland along the Jordan River that Lot chose when he and Abraham separated. Looking from the hill country near Bethel, Lot saw that it was watered everywhere, like the garden of the LORD and like the land of Egypt, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 13:10). He took the whole plain for himself and moved east (Gen 13:11). The separation is dated to about 1920 BC, by inference from context. Because the passage links the plain with Sodom, Gomorrah and Zoar, many place it at the southern end of the valley near the Dead Sea. Others take it to mean the broader valley floor north of the Dead Sea. The location shown here is in the central Jordan Valley, roughly between Jericho and the point where the Jabbok joins the Jordan.

Punon was one of the camps where the Israelites stopped during the last stage of their wilderness journey. Numbers lists it between Zalmonah and Oboth (Num 33:42–43), and the verse just before shows Zalmonah was the first stop after Mount Hor, so Punon was the second camp after leaving Mount Hor. The text says nothing more about it. Eusebius and Jerome identified it with Phaeno, or Phinon, a village between Petra and Zoar known for copper mines worked by convicts, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. That site is usually taken to be modern Feinan in southern Jordan. The location shown here is only a rough placement east of the Dead Sea and does not mark the Feinan site. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "precious stone", and Smith's gives "darkness".

Ramah, in this entry, is the town where King Joram (Jehoram) of Israel, son of Ahab, was wounded by the Syrians while fighting Hazael king of Syria. He went back to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah king of Judah (called Azariah in 2 Chr 22:6) went down to visit him there. Several places in the Bible are called Ramah, a name meaning "height." Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take this Ramah as a shortened form of Ramoth-gilead, and the verse just before, 2 Kgs 8:28, names Ramoth-gilead as the scene of this battle. The site of Ramoth-gilead east of the Jordan has been placed at several locations. The location shown here follows the identification near modern Ramtha in northern Jordan, by the nearby mound of Tell er-Rumeith.

Ramoth, a name meaning "heights" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a city in the territory of Issachar given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Gershonite Levites. It is listed with Anem in 1 Chr 6:73. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same town called Remeth (Josh 19:21) and Jarmuth (Josh 21:29) in the parallel lists of Joshua. The encyclopedia suggests it may be er-Rameh, southwest of Jenin. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement within Issachar's territory near the eastern Jezreel Valley. Several biblical places share the name. This one should not be confused with Ramoth in Gilead, the Levitical city of the tribe of Gad named a few verses later (1 Chr 6:80).

Rehob was a town or district in the far north of Israel. It marked the northern limit of the land searched by the twelve spies, who went from the wilderness of Zin "unto Rehob, as men come to Hamath" (Num 13:21). In David's time Syrians of Rehob were among the troops the Ammonites hired against Israel, drawn up in the field apart from the Ammonite army (2 Sam 10:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Beth-rehob, the Syrian place named in 2 Sam 10:6 and near the city of Dan in Judg 18:28. The name means "breadth" or "space" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's Bible Dictionary, following Robinson, puts it near Tell el-Kady (Dan) and Banias. Easton's links it with the castle of Hunin, southwest of Dan, and the location shown here follows that identification. Several other places in the Bible share this name.

Rehoboth was the home city of Saul (or Shaul), who succeeded Samlah as one of the early kings of Edom, reigning before Israel had kings (Gen 36:37; 1 Chr 1:48). It is called "Rehoboth by the river," and the name means "wide places" or "open spaces." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take "the river" to mean the Euphrates, as the phrase often does in the Bible, and place the city there. Others look for it within or near Edom, with the river being a local stream. The location shown here follows the Edom identification, in present-day southern Jordan, and is only approximate. This place should not be confused with the well called Rehoboth dug by Isaac near Gerar (Gen 26:22) or with Rehoboth-Ir in Assyria (Gen 10:11), which share the name.

Rezeph was a city named in the Assyrian king Sennacherib's taunting message to Hezekiah, delivered during the threat to Jerusalem. It is listed with Gozan, Haran and "the children of Eden" in Telassar as places destroyed by earlier Assyrian kings, whose gods had not saved them (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The point of the list was that Jerusalem's God would not save it either. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Rezeph with the Rasappa of Assyrian records, a provincial center under Assyrian governors and probably an important trade town. It places the city at Rusafa (Resafa) in northern Syria, northeast of Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a fortress near Haran, probably west of the Euphrates. The location shown here follows the Resafa identification, a site south of the Euphrates in present-day Syria.

Rimmon-perez (spelled Rimmonparez in the King James Version) was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt to Canaan. It is named only in the list of stations in Numbers 33. The Israelites arrived there from Rithmah and moved on to Libnah (Num 33:19–20). Nothing else is recorded about it, and the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives two explanations of the name. Following Gesenius, "rimmon" means "pomegranate," so the place may have been named for an abundance of pomegranates. Following Conder, the word comes from a root meaning "to be high," giving the sense "cloven height." The second element, "perez," means "breach."

Rissah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt toward Canaan. It appears only in the list of camping stations in Numbers 33. The people came to Rissah after leaving Libnah and moved on from there to Kehelathah (Num 33:21–22). Nothing else is recorded about it, and its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the mountainous region east of the Arabah, in present-day southern Jordan, near the area later associated with Edom. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heap of ruins" or "dew," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "watering," "distillation," or "dew."

Rithmah was a place where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey from Egypt toward Canaan. It appears only in the list of stations in Numbers 33, where Israel moved there from Hazeroth and went on to Rimmon-parez (Num 33:18–19). The name means "broom," after the white desert broom shrub, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a "valley of broom bushes" near Kadesh and suggests it may be the place of Israel's first encampment in that region. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably northeast of Hazeroth. Its exact location is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

Rogelim was a town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and the home of Barzillai the Gileadite. When David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, Barzillai came from Rogelim with Shobi of Rabbah and Machir of Lodebar to help him. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) list the food and bedding they brought. After the rebellion ended, Barzillai came down from Rogelim again and crossed the Jordan with David to see him over the river. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "fullers" and places the town probably near Mahanaim, while Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it in the highlands east of the Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a foot or footman." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Gilead hills east of the Jordan valley.

Sarid was a town on the southern border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Joshua 19 uses it as the starting point for tracing Zebulun's boundary. From Sarid the border ran eastward toward Chisloth-tabor, then on to Daberath and up to Japhia (Josh 19:10, 12). Smith's Bible Dictionary concludes from this that it lay west of Chisloth-tabor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may originally have read "Sadid." On that reading it follows Conder in placing the town at Tell Shaddu (Tel Shadud), an artificial mound with good springs in the Jezreel Valley, about 5 miles west of Iksal. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "remaining."

The Sea of Chinnereth is an Old Testament name for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Lake of Gennesaret or Sea of Tiberias. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same body of water, and the location shown here matches it, at the modern Lake Kinneret in northern Israel. In Num 34:11 the lake serves as a landmark on the eastern boundary of the land promised to Israel, which runs down to its eastern shore. In Josh 13:27 it marks the northern limit of the territory given to the tribe of Gad in the Jordan Valley. That territory covered the remainder of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, along the east side of the Jordan up to the edge of the lake. The name is probably linked to the nearby town of Chinnereth.

Sea of the Plain is a name used in the King James Version for the body of water at the southern end of the Jordan Valley, which the ESV calls the Sea of the Arabah. Joshua 3:16 identifies it with the Salt Sea. It is the lake known today as the Dead Sea, and the location shown here lies there. When Israel crossed the Jordan opposite Jericho, the water flowing down toward this sea was cut off while the water upstream piled up near the city of Adam (Josh 3:16). It later served as a boundary marker. Jeroboam II restored Israel's territory from the entrance of Hamath in the north to the Sea of the Plain in the south, as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai had foretold (2 Kgs 14:25). The name comes from the Arabah, the deep rift valley in which the sea lies.

The Sea of Tiberias is a name used in John's Gospel for the Sea of Galilee. John 6:1 makes the link explicit, describing Jesus crossing "the sea of Galilee, which is the sea of Tiberias." The name probably comes from the city of Tiberias on its western shore, which was founded in the first century and named after the Roman emperor Tiberius. This is an inference from the name, since the verses do not explain it. Elsewhere the same lake is called the Sea of Galilee, the Lake of Gennesaret and, in the Old Testament, the Sea of Chinnereth. John 21:1 places one of Jesus' appearances to his disciples after his resurrection beside this sea. It is the freshwater lake in northern Israel fed by the Jordan River, and the location shown here marks its centre. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under the entry for the Sea of Galilee.

The Second Quarter was a district of Jerusalem where the prophetess Huldah, wife of Shallum the keeper of the wardrobe, lived when King Josiah's officials, led by Hilkiah the priest, went to consult her (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). The King James Version renders the Hebrew word mishneh as "the college," following Jewish commentators who took it as a place of instruction. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the word properly means "second." It suggests the district may be the lower city, built after the part on Mount Zion and enclosed by a second wall. Tyndale House's STEPBible names also link it to the "second" district in Zeph 1:10. Its exact boundaries are uncertain. The location shown here places it within the city, just west of the Temple Mount.

The Rock of Escape was a rock or cliff in the wilderness of Maon, in Judah southeast of Hebron. There David took refuge while Saul was hunting him (1 Sam 23:25). The surrounding narrative describes Saul and David moving along opposite sides of the same mountain. Just as Saul was closing in, he was called away to fight the Philistines, so he broke off the chase. For that reason the place was named Selahammahlekoth (1 Sam 23:28). The Hebrew name can be understood as "rock of escape" or "rock of divisions" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the latter), perhaps referring to the two forces being parted there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name survives in Wadi Malaki, a steep gorge between Carmel and Maon. The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here places it in that area of the Maon wilderness.

Shaalbim was a town in the lowland hills west of Jerusalem, in the area allotted to the tribe of Dan. Judg 1:35 says the Amorites held on there, along with Mount Heres and Aijalon, until the house of Joseph grew strong enough to make them pay tribute. Under Solomon it belonged to the administrative district of the son of Dekar, together with Makaz, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kgs 4:9). It is probably the same place as Shaalabbin in Josh 19:42. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with Shaalbon, the home of Eliahba the Shaalbonite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:32). Eusebius placed it at Salaba near Samaria. Conder identified it with Selbit, northwest of Aijalon. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Salbit.

Shaaraim was a city in the Shephelah, the western lowland of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to Judah in Josh 15:36, where the King James Version spells it Sharaim. After David killed Goliath, the defeated Philistines fled from the Elah Valley area toward Gath and Ekron, and their wounded fell along the road to Shaaraim (1 Sam 17:52). The name means "two gates." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in this verse the "two gates" might instead refer to the two Philistine cities themselves, as the Greek Septuagint suggests. The exact site is uncertain. Proposals include Tell Zakariya, Khirbet Sa'ireh and, more recently, Khirbet Qeiyafa above the Elah Valley. The location shown here is approximate and places it generally in that western Elah Valley region. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the Shaaraim of Simeon (1 Chr 4:31) as a different place.

Shamir was a town in the hill country of Ephraim where Tola, son of Puah and a man of the tribe of Issachar, lived while he judged Israel after Abimelech. Tola judged for twenty-three years, then died and was buried at Shamir (Judg 10:1–2). Its exact site is uncertain, and other places in the Bible share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a proposal to identify it with Sanur, a strongly placed town on the road from Nablus to Jenin, while noting that Sanur probably lay outside Issachar's territory. The same work observes that one manuscript of the Greek Septuagint, Codex Alexandrinus, reads "Samaria" here instead of Shamir. The location shown here follows the Sanur identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "thorn" or "bush."

Shepham was a landmark on the eastern border of the land promised to Israel, as described in Num 34:10–11. The border ran from Hazar-enan to Shepham, then went down from Shepham to Riblah on the east side of Ain, and continued toward the Sea of Chinnereth (Galilee). The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Hazar-enan and a site near Mount Hermon, probably on one of the bare ridges of the Anti-Lebanon range. It explains the name as meaning a "naked" place, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "treeless." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fruitful" instead. The same encyclopedia suggests that Zabdi the Shiphmite, David's officer over the vineyards, may have come from here. The location shown here is a rough one in northern Lebanon, near the Riblah on the Orontes River, and it reflects the uncertainty about the site.

Shihor (spelled Sihor in the King James Version) is a body of water named in connection with Egypt. Josh 13:3 uses it as the southwestern starting point of the unconquered Philistine territory, describing it as lying "before Egypt." Isa 23:3, in an oracle about Tyre, speaks of "the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river" as Tyre's revenue, probably meaning Egyptian grain shipped by sea. Identifications differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shihor in Isaiah (and Jer 2:18) as the Nile, and in Joshua as the "river of Egypt," the Wadi el-Arish. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following Naville, identifies it with an ancient eastern Nile canal called Shi-t-Hor, "the stream of Horus." The STEPBible proper names list treats it as the Brook of Egypt, marking the southwestern boundary of the Promised Land. The location shown here follows the Wadi el-Arish identification in northern Sinai.

Shimron was a Canaanite city whose king was summoned by Jabin king of Hazor to join a northern alliance against Joshua (Josh 11:1). It was later listed among the twelve cities, with their villages, allotted to the tribe of Zebulun (Josh 19:15). The list of defeated kings in Josh 12:20 names a king of Shimron-meron, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to be the city's fuller name. The name is often explained as meaning "watch-post" or "watch-height." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no identification is certain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and others place it at Semuniyeh, a site about 5 miles (8 km) west of Nazareth on the northern edge of the Jezreel plain, linked with the Simonias of Josephus. A site near Acre, Es-Semeiriyeh, has also been suggested. The location shown here follows the Semuniyeh identification.

Smyrna was a city on the western coast of Asia Minor, about 40 miles north of Ephesus, and the second of the seven churches in the province of Asia to which the book of Revelation was sent (Rev 1:11). The message to its church opens with Christ described as "the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive" (Rev 2:8). The wider message (Rev 2:8–11) speaks of the church's hardship and poverty. The name means "myrrh." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Smyrna as a busy harbor and trading center that rivaled Ephesus and Pergamos in Roman times. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle John, later led the church there and was martyred in the second century. The city is the modern Izmir in Turkey, which is where the location shown here is placed.

Solomon's Portico, also called Solomon's Porch, was a covered colonnade in the temple complex at Jerusalem. After Peter and John healed a man lame from birth, the man held on to them there while a crowd ran together in amazement, and Peter used the occasion to address the people (Acts 3:11). Later the apostles regularly gathered there 'with one accord' while many signs and wonders were done among the people (Acts 5:12). These events are dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. John 10:23 also describes Jesus walking there at the Feast of Dedication. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a cloister, probably on the eastern side of the temple, and notes that it is not mentioned with Solomon's first temple, though Josephus mentions a porch of that name in Herod's temple. The location shown here places it within the temple area.

Spain was the Roman region occupying the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, roughly the area of modern Spain and Portugal. It is named in the Bible only in Paul's letter to the Romans, where he tells the believers in Rome that he plans to visit them on his way to Spain. He hopes they will help send him on from there, once he has delivered the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (Rom 15:24, 28). The New Testament does not record whether he ever made the journey. Easton's Bible Dictionary finds no evidence that he did. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it probable that he went after being released from his first imprisonment, pointing to Clement of Rome's statement that Paul reached "the extreme limit of the West." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the older name Tarshish may have referred to the same region. The location shown here marks the central part of the peninsula.

Taberah was a place in the wilderness where the Israelites camped after leaving Mount Sinai. Its name means "burning" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It was given that name because "the fire of the LORD burnt among them" there (Num 11:3). The surrounding verses in Num 11:1–2 say the people complained, fire broke out at the edges of the camp, and it died down when Moses prayed. Later, Moses listed Taberah with Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah as places where Israel provoked the LORD to anger (Deut 9:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the wilderness of Paran. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as another name for Kibroth-hattaavah, the next site in Numbers 11, while Deut 9:22 names the two separately. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is a rough estimate in the Sinai Peninsula, northeast of the traditional Mount Sinai.

Tahath was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. Numbers lists it as the stop after Makheloth and before Tarah (Num 33:26–27). Nothing else is recorded about it, and it appears only in this itinerary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the Hebrew name as "below." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fear" or "going down." The site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough estimate. It places Tahath in the desert region south of the Dead Sea, in what is now southern Jordan, by inference from its place in the sequence of camps. Tahath is also the name of several people in the Bible, but this entry concerns only the campsite.

Tamar was a place marking the southeastern corner of the land in Ezekiel's vision of Israel's future borders. From Tamar the southern boundary was to run to the waters of strife at Kadesh, then along the river (the Brook of Egypt) to the Mediterranean (Ezek 47:19; 48:28). Its name means "palm tree," and several biblical places share it. Because the Dead Sea forms the eastern border in the same passage, Tamar probably lay southwest of the Dead Sea. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be Hazazon-tamar, the old name of En-gedi, or a Thamar mentioned by Eusebius a day's journey south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Thamara, a Roman fortress on the road from Hebron to Elath. The location shown here follows the New Bible Dictionary, which identifies it with Kurnub (ancient Mampsis) in the northern Negev.

Tel-harsha was a town or village in Babylonia, listed among the places from which some Jewish exiles returned to Judah after the exile. The King James Version spells it Telharsa in Ezra 2:59 and Telharesha in Neh 7:61. Both lists name it alongside Tel-melah, Cherub, Addan (or Addon) and Immer, and say that the people who came from these places could not prove their family descent or show that they were of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this return under Zerubbabel and notes that 1 Esdras 5:36 calls the place Thelersas. The name begins with "tel," a mound marking an old settlement. The actual site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the lowlands of southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq.

Tel-melah was a town in Babylonia, the home of some Jewish exiles who returned to Judah after the exile. It appears only in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:59 and Neh 7:61, alongside Tel-harsa, Cherub, Addan and Immer. The people who came from these places could not prove their family descent, so they could not show whether they belonged to Israel. The name probably means "hill of salt" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "heap of salt" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it may have stood on the low, salty ground near the Persian Gulf, and that 1 Esdras 5:36 calls it Thermeleth. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Mesopotamia.

Telassar (spelled Thelasar in 2 Kgs 19:12) was a place where "the children of Eden" lived. Sennacherib's messengers name it in their warning to Hezekiah, listing it with Gozan, Haran and Rezeph as peoples his forefathers had destroyed and whose gods had failed to save them (2 Kgs 19:12; Isa 37:12). The name is usually taken to mean "hill of Asshur," or possibly "hill of Assar," a name of the Babylonian god Merodach. Its location is uncertain. Because it appears alongside cities of western Mesopotamia, some link it with Bit Adini (Beth-eden) between the Euphrates and the Balikh. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in southeastern Assyria, probably in Babylonia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with Til-Assuri, mentioned in Assyrian inscriptions, which may have lain near the western border of Elam. The location shown here follows that Elam identification and is only approximate.

Terah (spelled Tarah in the King James Version) was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. It appears only in the list of stopping places in Numbers 33, where the people moved from Tahath to Tarah and then on to Mithcah (Num 33:27–28). Nothing else is recorded about the site, and its location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in present-day southern Jordan. It is inferred from its position in the itinerary, which runs between Sinai and the later camps near Ezion-geber and Kadesh. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "stopping" or "station," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "to breathe" or "scent."

Thebez was a town attacked by Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) who had made himself king at Shechem. Judg 9:50 says he camped against Thebez and took it. By inference from its placement right after the destruction of Shechem, Thebez had probably joined Shechem's revolt against him, as Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests. The following verses (Judg 9:51–54) tell how the townspeople fled to a strong tower inside the city. When Abimelech came near to burn it, a woman dropped a piece of millstone on his head from the wall, and he died there. The incident was remembered long afterward. In 2 Sam 11:21, Joab expects David to cite it as a warning against going too close to a city wall. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Thebez with the village of Tubas, northeast of Nablus, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hiddekel is the Hebrew name of the river known as the Tigris. Gen 2:14 lists it as the third of the four rivers flowing out of Eden, describing it as the river that runs east of Assyria, alongside the Euphrates. In Dan 10:4 Daniel was standing beside "the great river, which is Hiddekel" when he received a vision. The Greek Septuagint translates the name as Tigris, and Smith's Bible Dictionary links "Dekel" with Digla, a name the river has carried through the ages, preserved in the modern Arabic Dijleh. The Tigris rises in the mountains of eastern Turkey and flows southeast through Iraq, past the site of Nineveh, to join the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf. The location shown here is a rough point on the modern Tigris in northern Iraq. The river's course in the Eden account may have differed from its present one.

Timnath-serah was the city in the hill country of Ephraim that the Israelites gave to Joshua at his request, as the LORD had directed, once the land had been divided among the tribes. Joshua rebuilt it and lived there (Josh 19:50). When he died, about 1424 BC by inference from context, he was buried within the border of his inheritance there, on the north side of the hill of Gaash (Josh 24:30). Judg 2:9 gives the name as Timnath-heres. There are two main proposed sites. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at Kefr Haris, about 10 miles south-west of Shechem, which matches Jewish and Samaritan traditions of Joshua's tomb there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers Tibneh, north-east of Lydda, where rock-cut tombs were linked with Joshua as early as Eusebius. The location shown here follows the Kefr Haris (Kifl Haris) identification.

Tob, "the land of Tob", was a district east of the Jordan where Jephthah went after his half-brothers drove him out of his family home. There he gathered a band of "vain men", worthless or reckless followers, who went out raiding with him (Judg 11:3). When the Ammonites made war on Israel, the elders of Gilead came to Tob to bring him back as their commander (Judg 11:5). The story implies that Tob lay not far from Gilead. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others take the "men of Ish-tob" who joined the Ammonites against David (2 Sam 10:6, 8) to be men of this same region. The name means "good". Its location is uncertain. The Talmud links it with the district of Hippos east of the Sea of Galilee, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favour et-Taiyibeh, south of Gadara. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification.

Tower here refers to the Tower of Meah, a tower in the wall of Jerusalem whose name means "the Hundred" (so the ESV calls it the Tower of the Hundred). Why it had that name is not explained, and suggestions such as its height or a company of a hundred soldiers remain guesses. When Nehemiah rebuilt the walls, Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate and consecrated the wall as far as this tower and on to the Tower of Hananeel (Neh 3:1). At the dedication of the walls, one of the thanksgiving processions passed by the Tower of Hananeel and the Tower of Meah toward the Sheep Gate (Neh 12:39). These passages place it on the north side of the city, near the temple area, between the Sheep Gate and the Tower of Hananeel. The location shown here follows that northern placement. The same word "tower" is also used for several other towers in the Bible.

Tower, called the "tower of the furnaces" in the King James Version and the Tower of the Ovens in modern translations, was a tower in the wall of Jerusalem. During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the city walls, Malchijah son of Harim and Hashub son of Pahath-moab repaired a section of the wall along with this tower (Neh 3:11). At the dedication of the completed wall, one of the two thanksgiving choirs, with Nehemiah following, passed along the wall from beyond this tower to the Broad Wall (Neh 12:38). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the north-western angle of Jerusalem's second wall. It suggests the tower was probably named for being near the bakers' street mentioned in Jer 37:21. The exact site is not known, and the location shown here is an approximate point within the city. Several other towers in the Bible share the general name Tower.

Ulai was a river beside Shushan (Susa), the royal city in the province of Elam, in what is now southwestern Iran. Daniel saw himself standing by the Ulai in his vision of the ram and the goat (Dan 8:2), and there he heard a man's voice "between the banks of Ulai" telling Gabriel to explain the vision to him (Dan 8:16). Greek and Roman writers called it the Eulaeus. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the eastern branch of the Choaspes, the modern Karkheh, which once split into two streams about 20 miles above Susa. They read "between the banks" as the land between those two streams. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies the Ulai with the Karkheh itself and notes that the river once ran at the foot of Susa's citadel before shifting its bed westward. The location shown here places the river at Susa.

Uzza was a garden in Jerusalem where two kings of Judah were buried. Manasseh was laid to rest "in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Uzza" (2 Kgs 21:18), and his son Amon was buried in his own tomb in the same garden (2 Kgs 21:26). These burials fall in about 642 BC and 640 BC, dates estimated from context. Unlike most earlier kings of Judah, neither is said to have been buried in the city of David. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the garden was probably near the royal palace or part of its grounds. It notes that the name means "strength," and that Manasseh may have acquired the garden from someone called Uzza. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here simply places it within Jerusalem.

The Valley of Hamongog, meaning "valley of the multitude of Gog," is a place named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog. Ezekiel says that God would give Gog a burial ground in Israel, in "the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea." There Gog and all his army would be buried, and the place would then be called Hamongog (Ezek 39:11). Travelers passing through the land who found a human bone were to set up a marker beside it until the buriers carried it to this valley (Ezek 39:15). The text does not give a clear location. Many take "the sea" to be the Dead Sea, and some link "the passengers" (Hebrew 'obrim) with the Abarim region east of it. Others read "the sea" as the Mediterranean. The location shown here is a rough one on the eastern side of the Dead Sea, following the Dead Sea reading.

The Valley of Jehoshaphat is the place where, in Joel's prophecy, God says he will gather all nations to judge them for scattering his people Israel and dividing his land (Joel 3:2, 12). The name means "the LORD judges," which fits the scene, and the same passage calls it "the valley of decision" (Joel 3:14). The Bible gives no geographical details, and views differ on whether it was a real place. Some take the name as symbolic. Others connect it with the Valley of Berachah, where King Jehoshaphat celebrated a victory (2 Chr 20:26). A long-standing Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition identifies it with the Kidron Valley, between Jerusalem's Temple Mount and the Mount of Olives, where many graves have been placed in expectation of the final judgement. The location shown here follows the Kidron Valley identification.

The Valley of Jiphthahel (Iphtahel in some modern translations) was a valley in lower Galilee that marked part of the boundary between the tribes of Zebulun and Asher. It appears only in the boundary lists of Joshua. Zebulun's northern border ran past Hannathon and ended at this valley (Josh 19:14). Asher's border, running eastward, reached Zebulun and the valley, north of Beth-emek and Neiel, before going on to Cabul (Josh 19:27). It was therefore a meeting point of the two tribal territories. Its exact identification is uncertain. Because Hannathon lies nearby, it is often taken to be one of the wadis draining westward from the hills of lower Galilee. Some identify it with Wadi el-Malik (Nahal Zippori), and others with a stream near the Beit Netofa plain. The location shown here is in that area, northwest of Nazareth.

The Valley of Lebanon was a valley beneath Mount Hermon where the town of Baal-gad stood. It marked the northern limit of the land Joshua conquered, which stretched south to Mount Halak on the way up to Seir (Josh 11:17; 12:7). The kings of this territory west of the Jordan were defeated, and the land was divided among the tribes of Israel. The verses give no further detail. It is commonly taken to be the southern end of the broad valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, now called the Beqaa in Lebanon. Some place it more narrowly in a side valley along Hermon's western slopes, such as the Wadi et-Teim. The location shown here sits in the Hermon area, matching the valley's description as lying under the mountain.

The Valley of Shaveh, also called the King's Dale (ESV King's Valley), was a valley where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram after Abram defeated Chedorlaomer and his allied kings (Gen 14:17). The following verse has Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing out bread and wine at the same meeting, so the valley was probably near Salem, usually understood as Jerusalem. Centuries later, Absalom set up a pillar for himself in the King's Dale because he had no son to carry on his name, and it became known as Absalom's place (2 Sam 18:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the valley with the Kidron, beside Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that view, placing it in the Kidron Valley east of the Old City. It should not be confused with Shaveh Kiriathaim, a different place named in the same chapter.

Valley of Slaughter is the name Jeremiah said would replace the names Tophet and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, the valley just outside Jerusalem. In two nearly identical prophecies (Jer 7:32; Jer 19:6), the LORD declares that the days are coming when the place will no longer be called by its old names but by this new one, because so many dead will be buried at Tophet that no room will remain. It is therefore not a separate location but a prophetic renaming of the Hinnom Valley. That valley is generally identified with the Wadi er-Rababi, which curves along the western and southern sides of Jerusalem's Old City, and the location shown here lies in that area. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name together with its entries on the Valley of Hinnom and Topheth.

The Valley of Succoth was a valley east of the Jordan River, named after the town of Succoth. It appears only in a poetic oracle repeated in Ps 60:6 and Ps 108:7, where God declares that he will divide Shechem and measure out the valley of Succoth. The pairing probably sets a place west of the Jordan beside one to the east, together standing for the land being allotted. The town itself, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, is where Jacob built a house and shelters for his cattle after meeting Esau. It is also the town whose leaders refused to help Gideon, and the area near where bronze work for Solomon's temple was cast. Easton's identifies it with Tell Deir Alla, a mound in the plain north of the Jabbok River, and the location shown here matches that site. The valley is probably the surrounding stretch of the Jordan Valley.

Zaanannim was a place on the border of the tribe of Naphtali, listed among the boundary points of that tribe's territory in Josh 19:33. It is probably the same place as the "plain of Zaanaim" near Kedesh, where Heber the Kenite, who had separated from the rest of the Kenites, pitched his tent (Judg 4:11). Later in the same chapter Sisera flees to the tent of Heber's wife Jael. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "as far as the oak" of Zaanaim instead of "plain." It places the site north-west of Lake Merom (the Huleh basin), near Kedesh. Easton's also records another view, based on the Septuagint and the Talmud, that reads the name as Bitzanaim and identifies it with ruins called Bessum between Tiberias and Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows the identification near Kedesh in upper Galilee, and it is only approximate.

Zalmonah was one of the places where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey. It was the first stop after Mount Hor, where Aaron died, and the stop before Punon (Num 33:41–42). The Bible gives no other details about it. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the east side of Edom, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name points to a gloomy valley leading up to the Edomite plateau. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the highlands east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually explained as meaning "shady" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "gloomy" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Zaphon was a town in the Jordan Valley east of the Jordan, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Gad. It was part of the rest of the former kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, named alongside Beth-aram, Beth-nimrah and Succoth (Josh 13:27). The name means "north." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in Judg 12:1, where the KJV says the men of Ephraim "went northward" to confront Jephthah, the Hebrew can be read as "to Zaphon," which would make the town the meeting place. The ISBE identifies Zaphon with Amathus, the modern Tell 'Amateh, near the Jabbok. Another view places it at Tell el-Qos, in the Jordan Valley north of the Jabbok. The location shown here follows the Tell el-Qos identification. The same Hebrew word also appears elsewhere as a general term for the north.

Zarethan was a town in the Jordan Valley, spelled Zaretan and Zartanah in the King James Version. When Israel crossed the Jordan opposite Jericho, the river's waters piled up far upstream at the city of Adam, which lay beside Zarethan (Josh 3:16). In the list of Solomon's districts, it helps mark the territory of Baana son of Ahilud, where Beth-shean is described as lying by Zartanah below Jezreel (1 Kgs 4:12). According to 1 Kgs 7:46, Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. The parallel account in 2 Chr 4:17 reads Zeredah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been positively identified, and one proposal points to the peak of Kurn Sartabeh west of the river. The location shown here follows the identification with Tell es-Saidiyeh, a mound on the east side of the Jordan Valley north of the Jabbok.

Zedad was a town marking the northern border of the land of Israel. It appears in the border Moses described for the promised land, which ran from Mount Hor to the entrance of Hamath and then out to Zedad (Num 34:8). It appears again in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land, on the northern boundary running from the Mediterranean by way of Hethlon toward Zedad (Ezek 47:15). Ancient versions spell the name differently, and this has led to two proposed sites. Some scholars read it as "Zerad" and place it at Khirbet Serada in the Merj Ayun valley of southern Lebanon. Others read "Zedad" and identify it with Sadad, a village in central Syria between Riblah and Qaryatayn, northeast of Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favours Sadad. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls the identification uncertain. The location shown here follows the Sadad identification.

Zela (spelled Zelah in the King James Version) was a town in the territory of Benjamin. It is listed among the cities given to that tribe, next to Jerusalem (Josh 18:28). The family tomb of Kish, Saul's father, was there. David had the bones of Saul and Jonathan brought to this tomb and buried in it (2 Sam 21:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "slope" or "side" and suggests the town was probably Saul's birthplace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint translates the word as "side" in 2 Samuel rather than treating it as a place name. It also suggests Zela may be the Zilu mentioned in the Tell el-Amarna Letters. The site has not been identified, so the location shown here is only a rough placement in Benjamin's territory near Jerusalem.

Zered was a brook or stream valley that the Israelites crossed near the end of their journey through the wilderness, on their way past Edom and Moab. Moses records the command to cross it and notes that 38 years had passed between leaving Kadesh-barnea and crossing the Zered. By then the whole generation of fighting men had died, as the LORD had sworn (Deut 2:13–14). Num 21:12 mentions Israel camping in the valley of Zared, probably the same place. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with the Wadi el-Hasa, which flows into the Dead Sea near its southeastern end and lay between Moab and Edom. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places it among the streams feeding Wadi Kerak, farther north. The location shown here follows the Wadi el-Hasa identification.

Zin was a point on the southern border of the promised land, later the southern boundary of Judah's territory. Both border descriptions place it between the ascent of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea (Num 34:4; Josh 15:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a town in the far south of Judah, on the line dividing it from Edom, and notes that its exact site has not been found. It probably lay somewhere between Wadi el-Fiqra and Ain Qadis, the likely sites of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea. The location shown here is a rough placement along that route. The name is shared with the wider Wilderness of Zin. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes that wilderness as the southeastern corner of the desert et-Tih and distinguishes it from the Wilderness of Sin. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "buckler" or "coldness."

Abana was one of the two "rivers of Damascus" that Naaman, the Aramean army commander, named with the Pharpar when Elisha told him to wash in the Jordan to be cured of his skin disease. Naaman protested that these rivers were better than all the waters of Israel and left in anger (2 Kgs 5:12). The Hebrew margin gives the name as Amanah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it to mean "perennial" or "stony." Both dictionaries identify the Abana with the modern Barada River, which the Greeks called the Chrysorrhoas, or "golden stream." It rises in the Anti-Lebanon range about 23 miles northwest of Damascus and flows through the city and across its plain, making that land fertile. The location shown here follows this Barada identification.

Abel-keramim was a town in the region of Ammon, east of the Jordan River. Its name means "meadow of vineyards," and the King James Version translates it as "the plain of the vineyards" rather than treating it as a proper name. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version gives it as a place name. It appears only once, in Judg 11:33, as the furthest point of the campaign in which Jephthah (the "he" of the verse, by context of the chapter) struck the Ammonites from Aroer to Minnith, taking twenty cities, until Ammon was subdued before Israel. The exact site is unknown, and several locations in the hills of Ammon have been proposed. The location shown here is a rough one in the area of modern Amman, Jordan.

Abel-maim was a town in the far north of Israel, in the territory of Naphtali. Its only mention is in 2 Chr 16:4. There, Ben-hadad of Damascus, persuaded by King Asa of Judah, sent his army against Israel and struck Abel-maim along with Ijon, Dan and the store cities of Naphtali. The name is usually understood as "meadow of waters," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mourning of waters." The parallel account in 1 Kgs 15:20 names Abel-beth-maacah in its place. For this reason Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Abel-maim as another name for that city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that it may instead be a separate town nearby. The location shown here follows the identification with Abel-beth-maacah, at modern Abil al-Qamh. The site lies on a height a few miles west of Dan, near the sources of the Jordan.

Abel-shittim, meaning "meadow of the acacias," was a place on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River and roughly opposite Jericho. Israel camped there in the last stage of the wilderness journey, along a stretch of the Jordan running from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (Num 33:49). This full name appears only in this verse, but Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with the place more often called simply Shittim, the camp where the episode with Moab occurred, from which Joshua sent out the spies, and the last stop before the crossing of the Jordan (Num 25:1; Josh 2:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus knew a later town there called Abila, and that scholars of its time placed the site near Kefrein, at the mouth of the wadi of that name. The location shown here follows the Kefrein identification.

Abiezer is the name of a clan of the tribe of Manasseh, used here for the clan's home district west of the Jordan. In Judg 8:2 Gideon, himself an Abiezrite, calms the angry men of Ephraim with a proverb: Ephraim's 'gleaning', its capture of the Midianite princes, was worth more than Abiezer's whole 'vintage', his own clan's victory. Elsewhere, Josh 17:2 lists Abiezer among the families of Manasseh, and Judg 6:11, 24 and 34 place Gideon's town of Ophrah among the Abiezrites and show the clan rallying to him. The district's exact extent is not given. The location shown here lies near modern Afula at the edge of the Jezreel Valley, one proposed site for Ophrah, though other sites have also been suggested. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'father of help.'

Abilene was a district on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon mountains, northwest of Damascus. It appears in the Bible only in Luke 3:1, where it is named as the tetrarchy of Lysanias in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the year John the Baptist began preaching. The region took its name from its chief town, Abila. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, Abila stood about 18 miles from Damascus in the gorge of Suk Wady Barada, beside the Barada River. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Greek inscription found there that mentions a "freedman of Lysanias the tetrarch." The same work records that Abilene was later granted to Agrippa I and afterward to Agrippa II. The location shown here follows the identification with the Suk Wady Barada area.

Accad was a city in the land of Shinar, named in Gen 10:10 as one of the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom, along with Babel, Erech and Calneh. This is its only mention in the Bible. This entry dates the start of that kingdom to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Shinar is generally understood as southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. The STEPBible proper-names index takes Accad to be the ancient city of Akkad, which gave its name to the Akkadian people and language. The exact site of that city has not been found. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls its position quite uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with the mounds of Akker Kuf, north of Babylon, and places the city near the Euphrates, opposite Sippar. The location shown here is a general placement in central Iraq, south of modern Baghdad.

Acco was a coastal city on the Mediterranean, a few miles north of Mount Carmel on the northern side of the bay now shared with Haifa. It lay within the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher, but Judg 1:31 records that Asher did not drive out its inhabitants, listing it with Sidon, Achzib and other towns that stayed in Canaanite or Phoenician hands. Its harbour and its position on the coast road gave it lasting importance. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, it was later renamed Ptolemais after the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt. Under that name it is probably the port where Paul stopped on his last journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:7). During the Crusades it became known as Acre. The location shown here is the modern city of Acre (Arabic Akka) in northern Israel.

Adadah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe's southernmost district alongside Kinah and Dimonah (Josh 15:22). It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Its location is uncertain. The older copies of the Greek translation read "Arouel" here, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars adopt this reading and place the town at Ararah, about seven miles southeast of Beersheba. This is probably the site often linked with the Aroer of 1 Sam 30:28. Others identify it with a site eight or nine miles southeast of Arad. The location shown here follows the Ararah identification southeast of Beersheba, and its coordinates are only approximate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "testimony of the assembly". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "festival" or "boundary".

Adam was a city in the Jordan Valley, mentioned once in the Bible. It was the point upstream where the Jordan's waters stopped and 'rose up upon an heap' when the Israelites crossed the river opposite Jericho under Joshua. Downstream, the flow toward the Dead Sea was cut off (Josh 3:16). The verse places Adam 'beside Zaretan', probably the same place as Zarethan. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the west bank of the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the name with the Damieh Ford, near where the Jabbok joins the Jordan, about twenty miles above Jericho. That work notes that the river's narrow gorge there could easily be blocked, and cites an Arab historian who reported a landslide damming the Jordan at that spot around AD 1265. The location shown here follows the Damieh identification, at the modern Tell ed-Damiyeh. The name may mean 'red' or 'earthy'.

Adamah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, listed between Chinnereth and Ramah, just before Hazor (Josh 19:36). The list it belongs to opens in Josh 19:35 with the words "the fenced cities," so Adamah is understood to have been a fortified town. It is mentioned nowhere else. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red earth." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Damieh, west of the Sea of Galilee, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers 'Admah, a ruin on the plateau about 10 miles north of Beisan (Beth-shean). The location shown here is only approximate. It places Adamah in the hills of lower Galilee southwest of the Sea of Galilee, between these two proposed sites, and does not settle the question.

Adami-nekeb was a town on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, named once in the description of that border (Josh 19:33). The King James Version prints it as two names, "Adami" and "Nekeb." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that scholars have long debated whether one place or two is meant, and that most Greek texts read two names. It gives the meaning as "the ground of the pass." The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary favors Seiyadeh, a ruin between Tiberias and Mount Tabor. Others place Adami at Damieh, northwest of the Sea of Galilee. The survey maps cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia put Adami at Khurbet Adamah, several miles south of where the Jordan leaves the lake. The location shown here follows that southern identification.

Addar (spelled "Adar" in the King James Version) was a place on the southern border of the tribe of Judah's territory. Joshua 15:3 traces the boundary from Maale-acrabbim past Zin and Kadesh-barnea, then on to Hezron, up to Addar, and around to Karkaa. Addar therefore lay somewhere in the dry region near Kadesh-barnea, on the edge of the Negev and the Sinai. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hazar-addar, which appears at the same point in the parallel description of Israel's southern border in Num 34:4. There, Hazar-addar seems to combine Hezron and Addar into one name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "high" or "eminent." The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough estimate.

Adithaim was a town allotted to the tribe of Judah, named only once in the Bible, between Sharaim and Gederah, in Josh 15:36. That verse closes a list of fourteen towns with their villages. By inference from the start of the list (Josh 15:33), the group lay in the lowland, or Shephelah, the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "double ornament," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "assemblies" or "testimonies." The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Adida, a town near Lod. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the western Shephelah near the other towns of the same list, not at Adida.

Adoraim was a town in Judah that King Rehoboam fortified after the kingdom divided. It appears in a list of his defensive cities alongside Lachish and Azekah (2 Chr 11:9). The surrounding passage presents these as cities built up for defence. The name is usually explained as "pair of mounds" or "two knolls" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strength of the sea." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take it to be the Adora mentioned in 1 Maccabees and Josephus. Smith notes that Adora might instead be Dor on the coast. Both works identify Adoraim with the village of Dura, about five miles west-southwest of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Adramyttium was a port city on the northwest coast of Asia Minor, in the region of Mysia within the Roman province of Asia. It stood at the head of a gulf facing the island of Lesbos. It appears in the Bible only once, when Paul, travelling as a prisoner to Rome, boarded a ship that belonged to this city (Acts 27:2). From the surrounding narrative, he boarded it at Caesarea. The ship planned to sail along the coast of Asia, and Aristarchus of Thessalonica went with him. The following verses show that Paul stayed on this ship only as far as Myra in Lycia, where he moved to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy. The voyage dates to about AD 56, by inference from context. The name survives in the modern Turkish town of Edremit, slightly inland from the ancient harbor, and the location shown here matches that area.

Adria, called the Adriatic Sea in modern translations, is the sea across which the ship carrying Paul to Rome was driven by a storm. On the fourteenth night of being tossed about there, the sailors sensed around midnight that they were nearing land, shortly before the shipwreck (Acts 27:27). Today the name refers to the sea between Italy and the Balkan coast. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary, in Paul's time it covered a much wider area, the whole central Mediterranean between Greece and Italy, reaching south from Crete to Sicily. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient writers extended the name as far as the waters between Crete and Malta. Since the ship approached the shore of Malta (Acts 28:1), the storm was probably in this southern part. The location shown here is a point in the modern Adriatic.

Aenon was a place near Salim where John the Baptist was baptizing because there was much water there, and people came to him to be baptized (John 3:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "springs." The surrounding passage suggests it lay west of the Jordan, unlike Bethabara where John first baptized. It was here, probably around AD 27 by inference from context, that John spoke about his role in relation to Jesus. Its exact site is uncertain. Eusebius's Onomasticon places it eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this to springs near Umm el-'Amdan in the Jordan Valley. Easton's suggests the springs at the head of Wadi Far'ah, near Mount Ebal. The location shown here follows the Jordan Valley identification south of Beth-shean.

Ahlab was a town in the territory of the tribe of Asher whose Canaanite inhabitants the Israelites did not drive out. It appears only once, in a list of coastal and northern towns, including Accho, Zidon and Achzib, that Asher failed to conquer (Judg 1:31). The name probably means "fatness" or "fertile," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention its common identification with Giscala (Gush Halab), the modern village of el-Jish in upper Galilee, northwest of the Sea of Galilee. Others place it nearer the coast close to Tyre, a site sometimes linked with Helbah in the same verse. The location shown here follows the el-Jish identification.

Ai was a city in Ammonite territory, named only in Jeremiah's prophecy against the Ammonites. There Heshbon is told to wail because Ai has been plundered, and the daughters of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, are told to put on sackcloth because their king, priests and princes will go into captivity (Jer 49:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to have been closely linked with Heshbon. It is a different place from the better-known Ai near Bethel west of the Jordan. The name probably means "the ruin" or "heap." Some scholars, as noted in Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, think the text originally read Ar or "the city" rather than a place-name. This entry treats it as an Ammonite town. Its site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement east of the Jordan.

Aiath was a town north of Jerusalem, named once in Isaiah's poetic description of an invading army, understood from the surrounding chapter to be Assyria, advancing on Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:28 says the invader reaches Aiath, passes on to Migron, and leaves his baggage at Michmash. The name is a feminine form of Ai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Aiath to be the same place as Ai, the city Joshua captured. The similar name Aija in Neh 11:31, also listed near Michmash, probably refers to the same town. Ai is commonly identified with et-Tell, east of Bethel, though other nearby sites have been proposed. The location shown here follows the et-Tell identification.

Aija was a town where people of the tribe of Benjamin lived after the return from exile in Babylon. It appears only in Neh 11:31, listed with Michmash, Bethel and their villages. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Aija, like Aiath in Isa 10:28, as another form of the name Ai. That city stood near Bethel and is best known from Joshua's conquest in Josh 7–8. The pairing with Bethel supports this, as does Ezra 2:28, which counts returned exiles from "Bethel and Ai." Ai is commonly placed at et-Tell, a mound east of Bethel north of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that site. Whether the town settled after the exile stood on exactly the same spot as the older city is uncertain.

Ain was a landmark on the northeastern boundary of the land of Canaan as described to Moses, mentioned only in Num 34:11. The border was to run down from Shepham to Riblah "on the east side of Ain" and then descend to the eastern side of the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). The name means "spring" or "eye" in Hebrew, so the place was probably named for a notable spring. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with 'Ain el-'Asy, the main source of the Orontes River, southwest of Riblah in present-day Lebanon. The ISBE also notes a view that, because the border reaches the Sea of Chinnereth, this Riblah and Ain lay farther south. The location shown here follows the Orontes-spring identification. This Ain is distinct from other places with the same name.

Alemeth was a city in the territory of Benjamin, given with its surrounding pasture lands to the priestly descendants of Aaron. It is listed alongside Geba and Anathoth among the thirteen cities assigned to the priestly families (1 Chr 6:60). The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:18 names the same town Almon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as one place. Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Almit, about a mile northeast of ancient Anathoth, northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives several possible meanings for the name, including "hiding" and "youth." A man named Alemeth also appears in Benjamite genealogies, and the town may share his name, though the text does not connect them.

Allammelech was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It appears only once, in the list of Asher's boundary towns in Josh 19:26, where it is named together with Amad and Misheal, just before the border runs west to Carmel and to Shihorlibnath. The King James Version spells it Alammelech. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "oak of a king" and says its location is not known. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the inland hills of western Galilee, east of Acco. It is inferred from the town's place in the boundary list among Asher's towns rather than from any identified site.

Allon-bacuth, meaning "oak of weeping," was an oak tree below Bethel where Deborah, the nurse of Rebekah, was buried (Gen 35:8). The name probably recalls the mourning for her death. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the narrative implies that Deborah was living with Jacob's household after his return from Paddan-aram, while they were staying at Bethel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that large trees were rare enough in the land to serve as landmarks, and it suggests this tree may be the same as the "palm tree of Deborah" mentioned in Judg 4:5, though that Deborah was a different woman. The exact spot is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near Bethel, which is usually identified with modern Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

Almon was a city in the territory of Benjamin that, along with its surrounding pasturelands, was assigned to the priests. It is named in Joshua 21:18 beside Anathoth as the last of four Benjamite cities given to the descendants of Aaron. The surrounding verses name the other two as Gibeon and Geba. The name means "hidden" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with Alemeth, the name used for the same priestly city in the parallel list at 1 Chr 6:60. Almon is probably the modern ruin of Khirbet Almit, a short distance northeast of Anata (ancient Anathoth), northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here matches that identification.

Amad was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher when Joshua divided the land. It is named only once, in the list of Asher's towns, between Alammelech and Misheal, in a passage tracing the tribe's boundary toward Mount Carmel on the west and Shihor-libnath (Josh 19:26). Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as unknown, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the ruin called Amud near Accho (modern Acre). The location shown here, in western Galilee northeast of Acre, follows that suggested identification. Older name lists give differing meanings for the name: Smith's offers "enduring," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "people of witness" or "a prey."

Amam was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the allotment of the land. It appears only once in the Bible, in Josh 15:26, where it is named alongside Shema and Moladah in the group of towns lying toward the border of Edom. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gathering place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified, and no other passage mentions it. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, south of Hebron, based on the town's position in Judah's southern list rather than on an identified site.

Amana was a mountain named once in the Bible, in a love poem where the bridegroom calls his bride to come with him from Lebanon and look from the tops of Amana, Shenir and Hermon, a wild region of lions' dens and leopards' mountains (Song 4:8). The verse pairs it with peaks of the Lebanon and Hermon ranges, so it was probably a summit in that area. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the southern part of the Anti-Lebanon range, near the sources of the Abana, the river of Damascus mentioned in 2 Kgs 5:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a possible link with Mount Amanus in far northern Syria. The location shown here follows the Anti-Lebanon identification, near the headwaters of the modern Barada River. The name probably means "firm" or "constant."

Amaw was the land where Balaam son of Beor lived, in the town of Pethor "by the river," taken to mean the Euphrates. Balak king of Moab sent messengers there to summon Balaam to curse Israel (Num 22:5). The name does not appear in the King James Version, which translates the Hebrew phrase as "the land of the children of his people." Some modern translations read the same words as a place name, "the land of Amaw." STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) follows that reading and describes Amaw as a place near the Euphrates where Balaam lived. The area is otherwise unknown, and its location is only approximate. The location shown here places it on the upper Euphrates in what is now northern Syria, the region usually associated with Pethor.

Ammah was a hill near Gibeon in the territory of Benjamin. It is mentioned once, in 2 Sam 2:24, as the place Joab and his brother Abishai reached at sunset while chasing Abner after the battle at the pool of Gibeon. The verse places it "before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon," but Giah is otherwise unknown, and the exact site of the hill has not been identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Gibeon, and the rough location shown here follows that view. The Hebrew word can mean "cubit," "mother" or "beginning." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word forms part of Metheg-ammah in 2 Sam 8:1, though that is probably a different place.

Amphipolis was a city of Macedonia that Paul and Silas passed through on their way from Philippi to Thessalonica, along with Apollonia (Acts 17:1). The verse only mentions it as a stop on the journey, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the wording suggests they did not stay long. According to that work, the city stood on a terraced hill on the east bank of the Strymon River (the modern Struma), about three miles from its mouth. It was an important station on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across Macedonia, and after 168 BC it served as capital of the first district of Roman Macedonia. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it about 33 Roman miles from Philippi. The location shown here matches the ancient site near the modern village of Amfipoli, in northern Greece.

Anaharath was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar when the land was divided under Joshua. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns at Josh 19:19, alongside Hapharaim and Shion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the eastern part of the Jezreel Valley and identifies it with the modern village of en-Na'ura, where it holds the old name to have survived. The location shown here follows that identification, near the Hill of Moreh in northern Israel. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gorge or pass," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dryness, burning, wrath." The text records nothing about the town beyond its place in the tribal list.

Ananiah was a town of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible. It appears in the list of places resettled by Benjamites after the return from exile in Babylon, alongside Anathoth and Nob (Neh 11:32). The following verse names Hazor next, so Ananiah lay among these towns north of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "protected by the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "Yah has covered." Both works identify the town with the modern village of Beit Hanina, about three to four miles north-northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows that identification, though the placement is approximate. Nothing else about the town is recorded.

Anem was a city in the tribe of Issachar, listed with Ramoth among the towns given with their surrounding pasturelands to the Levites (1 Chr 6:73). By inference from the surrounding list, it went to the Levite clan descended from Gershom. The name is usually taken to mean "two springs." The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:29 names En-gannim ("spring of gardens") where Chronicles has Anem, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the two as the same place, the modern town of Jenin at the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also records other suggestions: Eusebius linked it with Aner, and the explorer Conder proposed a village called Anim in the hills west of the plain of Esdraelon. The location shown here follows the Jenin identification.

Aner was a city in the territory of the western half-tribe of Manasseh. It was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites of the Kohathite family, together with Bileam (1 Chr 6:70). It is mentioned only once. The parallel list of Levitical towns in Josh 21:25 names Taanach and Gath-rimmon from the same half-tribe, so many scholars, Gesenius among them, treat Aner as another form of Taanach, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. That encyclopedia adds that there is no agreement about the site. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it west of the Jordan. The location shown here follows the Taanach identification, probably the modern Tell Ta'annek on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley. The town should not be confused with Aner the Amorite, an ally of Abram.

The Angle was a point on the wall of Jerusalem where the wall turned, rendered in the King James Version as "the turning of the wall." The Hebrew word means a corner or angle. According to 2 Chr 26:9, King Uzziah built towers there, as well as at the Corner Gate and the Valley Gate, and fortified them. STEPBible's proper names index, from Tyndale House, treats the Angle as a fortified tower that Uzziah built. The same Hebrew term appears in Nehemiah's account of rebuilding the wall, where "the turning of the wall" marks sections repaired near the armoury and the king's house (Neh 3:19–20, 24–25). That passage probably refers to the same angle or to a nearby one, but this is an inference. The exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it within the ancient city of Jerusalem, and that placement is approximate.

Anim was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the allotment recorded in Josh 15:50, where it is named alongside Anab and Eshtemoh.
