The Bible mentions it only in this list and records nothing else about it. The name is usually taken to mean "springs" or "fountains" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the double ruin of el-Ghuwein, south of es-Semu'a (ancient Eshtemoa) and roughly 10 miles south-west of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the visible remains there are Byzantine and that a Christian town called Anem stood on the site in the 4th century, though the site appears to be much older. The location shown here follows the el-Ghuwein identification.

Antipatris was a city on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea. Roman soldiers brought Paul there by night after a plot against his life was uncovered in Jerusalem, on the way to sending him to the governor Felix (Acts 23:31), about AD 56 by inference from context. The next verses say the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem from there while the horsemen took Paul on to Caesarea. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia say Herod the Great built the city and named it after his father, Antipater. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its earlier name as Capharsaba and links it with the village of Kefr-Sabba. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it at Ras el-Ain, at the springs of the Aujeh (Yarkon) River northeast of Jaffa. The location shown here follows the Ras el-Ain identification.

Aphekah was a town in the territory of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns in Joshua 15:53 between Beth-tappuah and Humtah. The surrounding list places it in the hill country of Judah, in the group of towns around Hebron (Josh 15:48, 15:54). Its name probably means "strength" or "stronghold." Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same place as Aphek, the Canaanite royal city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:18). The location shown here follows that link to Aphek and places it at Tel Aphek, near modern Rosh HaAyin at the source of the Yarkon River. That site lies on the coastal plain, well northwest of the Judean hill country where the list in Joshua 15 places the town.

Aphik was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. Judg 1:31 lists it among the places whose Canaanite inhabitants Asher did not drive out, alongside Accho, Zidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah and Rehob. Its name probably means "stronghold." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as the Aphek named in Asher's allotment (Josh 19:30), and Easton's also links it with the Aphek on the northern border in Josh 13:4. Its site is uncertain. One view places it on the coastal plain near Accho, at a mound such as Tel Afek. Another identifies it with Afqa in the Lebanon mountains, at the source of the Adonis River (modern Nahr Ibrahim). The location shown here follows the Afqa identification.

Apollonia was a city of Macedonia that Paul and Silas passed through, after Amphipolis, on their way to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1). The text does not say they stopped or preached there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in the district of Mygdonia, just south of Lake Bolbe (modern Lake Volvi), on the Via Egnatia, the main Roman road across the region. Smith's Bible Dictionary, citing an ancient Roman itinerary, gives its distance as about 30 Roman miles from Amphipolis and 37 from Thessalonica, roughly a day's journey from each. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that coins show the town existed by the 4th century BC, and that its name may survive in the modern village of Pollina. The location shown here fits that position near Lake Volvi in northern Greece. Its name means "belonging to Apollo."

Appii Forum ("Forum of Appius" or "Market of Appius") was a town and way station on the Appian Way, the main Roman road running south from Rome. It lay about 43 Roman miles from the city, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Christians from Rome heard that Paul was coming and travelled out along the road to meet him. Some went as far as Appii Forum, and others waited at the Three Taverns, closer to the city. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage (Acts 28:15). This happened as he arrived at Rome as a prisoner, about AD 57 by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a canal began here and ran through the Pontine Marshes, which made the town a busy stopping point. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at ruins near Treponti, south of Rome, and the location shown here matches that area.

Arab was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it appears alongside Dumah and Eshean (Josh 15:52). Nothing else is recorded about it. The name probably means "ambush," as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it. Its towns in the same group lay in the hills around and south of Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of Er-Rabiyeh, south of Hebron. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it more generally near Hebron. The location shown here is only approximate and fits a site in that area southwest of Hebron. The exact site is uncertain.

Arabah, called the Brook of the Arabah in modern versions, is a stream named in Amos 6:14, where the King James Version calls it "the river of the wilderness." Amos warns that a nation will oppress Israel "from the entering in of Hemath" in the north to this brook, which marks the opposite limit of the land. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) describes it as a boundary of King Jeroboam II's kingdom. This fits 2 Kgs 14:25, which says Jeroboam restored Israel's border from Hamath to the "sea of the plain," the Dead Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that "Arabah" refers to the deep valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea, so the brook was probably a stream running into that valley near the Dead Sea. Its exact identity is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate. Several other places in the Bible share the name.

Aram-maacah was an Aramean kingdom in Syria, called "Syriamaachah" in the King James Version. After Hanun of Ammon insulted David's messengers, the Ammonites paid a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Aram-maacah and Zobah to fight against David (1 Chr 19:6). The parallel account in 2 Sam 10:6 mentions the king of Maacah, who supplied a thousand men. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise describes it as an Aramean kingdom allied with the Ammonites against David. By inference from other mentions of Maacah alongside Geshur and Bashan, it was probably a small state near Mount Hermon, east of the upper Jordan. Its exact borders are uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Syria, south of Damascus.

Armageddon is the place named in Rev 16:16 where the kings of the world are gathered together, a site the verse says is called by this name "in the Hebrew tongue." The surrounding passage (Rev 16:14) connects the gathering with the "battle of that great day of God Almighty." The name is usually taken to mean "mount of Megiddo," and the Revised Version spells it Har-Magedon. Megiddo was an ancient city overlooking the plain of Esdraelon (the Jezreel Valley) in northern Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this plain was famous for Barak's and Gideon's victories and for the deaths of Saul and Josiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's both treat the name in Revelation as symbolic, drawing on that well-known battlefield. The location shown here follows the identification with Tel Megiddo.

Aroer was a town in the far south of Judah, one of the places to which David sent gifts from the spoil he recovered from the Amalekites after the raid on Ziklag (1 Sam 30:28). It is a different place from the better-known Aroer on the Arnon River east of the Jordan, and several places in the Bible share the name. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as the home town of two of David's warriors named in 1 Chr 11:44. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the town called Adadah in Josh 15:22 may be the same place, read as Ararah. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it at Ar'arah, a ruin with ancient cisterns about 12 to 14 miles (19 to 23 km) southeast of Beersheba. The location shown here follows that identification.

Arubboth (spelled Aruboth in the King James Version) was a place or district that served as the base of one of the twelve officers who supplied provisions for King Solomon's household. According to 1 Kgs 4:10, the son of Hesed governed from Arubboth, and his territory also included Sochoh and "all the land of Hepher." The verse is the only mention of the name, so its exact location is uncertain. Many scholars place the district in the Sharon plain or the hills of northern Samaria, where Hepher was a clan area of Manasseh and another Socoh lay near modern Tulkarm. The location shown here is only approximate and sits near Socoh in the Judean lowlands (Shephelah), linking Arubboth to that better-known Sochoh.

Arumah was a place near Shechem where Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), stayed during his conflict with the people of Shechem. According to Judg 9:41, after Abimelech defeated Gaal son of Ebed outside Shechem, he remained at Arumah, while Zebul, the ruler of the city, drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem. Judging from the narrative, Arumah was close enough to Shechem for Abimelech to attack the city again the next day. The name is usually understood to mean "height" or "lofty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its exact site is not known for certain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the ruins of El-Ormeh, about 6 miles southeast of Shechem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Ashkenaz was a kingdom that Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon summons, together with Ararat and Minni, to make war on Babylon (Jer 51:27). The KJV spells it Ashchenaz there. The name is the same as that of a son of Gomer in the table of nations (Gen 10:3), and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the people to be descended from him. Because it is named alongside Ararat and Minni, Easton's places their original homeland in Armenia and suggests a link with the Black Sea. Many scholars connect Ashkenaz with the Scythians, who were active in the region south of the Caucasus in Jeremiah's time. The exact territory is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one in the Armenian highlands, near Mount Ararat, which follows the Armenian identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a fire that spreads."

Ashteroth-karnaim was an ancient town east of the Jordan where Chedorlaomer and his allied kings defeated the Rephaim during their campaign in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:5). The name is usually explained as "Ashteroth of the two horns." Easton's Bible Dictionary links the horns to the crescent moon and suggests the town may be the same as Ashtaroth in Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that a Carnaim or Carnion in Gilead, which had a temple, appears in 1 and 2 Maccabees as a town captured by Judas Maccabeus. Smith's and Easton's identify the site with es-Sanamein, about 25 to 28 miles south of Damascus. The location shown here follows a different identification. It places the town farther south in the Bashan region of southern Syria, near Tell Ashtara, the probable site of Ashtaroth.

Ataroth-addar was a town on the boundary between the tribal territories of Ephraim and Benjamin. Joshua 16:5 names it as a point on Ephraim's southern border, which ran from Ataroth-addar to Upper Beth-horon. The description of Benjamin's border in Josh 18:13 also mentions it, placing it near the hill south of Lower Beth-horon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "crowns of Addar," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "crowns of power." The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and places it near the Beth-horon towns, northwest of Jerusalem, which fits the border descriptions. It is probably distinct from the other places called Ataroth in the Bible.

Atharim is the name of a route in the Negev along which Israel was travelling when the Canaanite king of Arad attacked them and took some of them captive (Num 21:1). The Hebrew phrase is understood in different ways. The King James Version, following the Syriac and the Targum, translates it as "the way of the spies." The Revised Version, following the Septuagint, treats Atharim as a place name, "the way of Atharim." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Dillmann's rendering, "the caravan path," from an Arabic word meaning a track or footprint. This entry follows the place-name reading. The route's exact course is unknown. By inference from the passage, it ran through the southern region near Arad's territory. The location shown here is a rough point in the Negev and should be taken as approximate.

Atroth-shophan was a town east of the Jordan that the tribe of Gad built or fortified after the land there was given to them (Num 32:35). It is named in a list of Gadite towns next to Aroer and before Jazer and Jogbehah. The King James Version prints "Atroth, Shophan" as two separate places. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both read it as a single name, Atroth-shophan, as the Revised Version does. This entry follows the single-name reading. Easton's gives the meaning of Shophan as "hidden" or "hollow." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no firm identification of the site is yet possible. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Gadite territory, in the region of modern Amman, Jordan.

Attalia was a port city on the southern coast of Asia Minor in the region of Pamphylia. Paul and Barnabas came down to it from Perga near the end of their first missionary journey, after preaching in Perga (Acts 14:25). The next verse says they sailed from there back to Antioch in Syria, so Attalia was probably their port of departure. By inference from context, this was about AD 46. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the city was founded by Attalus II Philadelphus, king of Pergamum (159–138 BC), and named after him. It stood on a limestone terrace near where the Catarrhactes River met the sea, and it long remained a main harbor for ships from Syria and Egypt. It is generally identified with modern Antalya in Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Aven, meaning "emptiness" or "wickedness," is the name Hosea uses for a center of idolatrous worship in Israel. He announces that its high places, called "the sin of Israel," will be destroyed, with thorns and thistles growing over their altars (Hos 10:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name as a shortened form of Beth-aven, Hosea's mocking name for Bethel, home of one of the northern kingdom's royal shrines (compare Hos 4:15; 10:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same word is used elsewhere for other places, such as On (Heliopolis) in Egypt in Ezek 30:17 and a valley near Damascus in Amos 1:5. The location shown here follows the Bethel identification, near modern Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

Avva (spelled "Ava" in the King James Version) was one of the places from which the king of Assyria brought people to resettle the cities of Samaria after the Israelites there were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). It is listed with Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and Sepharvaim. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same place as Ivah, which Assyrian officials named among the cities whose gods had failed to protect them (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). Easton's also notes that it has been identified with Hit on the Euphrates in modern Iraq. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one on the middle Euphrates, near modern Anah, somewhat upstream of Hit.

Avvim was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities at Josh 18:23, where it appears alongside Parah and Ophrah. That list groups towns of Benjamin's eastern district, so Avvim probably lay in the hill country north of Jerusalem, near Bethel and Ophrah. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement. Some scholars suggest the name may be another form of Ai, a town in the same area, but this remains uncertain. It should not be confused with the Avvim or Avites, a people who lived near Gaza before the Caphtorim displaced them.

Ayyah was a town named as one end of the territory held by the descendants of Ephraim, listed after Shechem in 1 Chr 7:28. The King James Version reads "Gaza" here, but the Hebrew word is closer to Ayyah, and many modern translations use that name. Its location is uncertain. Because the list describes Ephraim's lands in the central hill country, with Bethel, Naaran, Gezer and Shechem, many readers take Ayyah to be a town near Shechem, perhaps related to Ai or Aija, rather than the Philistine city of Gaza far to the southwest. Others follow the reading Gaza. The location shown here follows the Gaza identification, placing it on the southern coastal plain at modern Gaza. The verse gives no other details about the town.

Azal is a place named only once in the Bible, in Zechariah's prophecy of the day when the LORD comes to Jerusalem. Zech 14:5 says the newly formed "valley of the mountains" will reach as far as Azal, and that people will flee through it as they fled from the earthquake in the days of King Uzziah of Judah. By inference from the surrounding passage, this valley opens when the Mount of Olives splits in two, so Azal marked its far limit. The place has not been identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the word may not be a name at all and could be translated "very near." If it is a name, Easton places it near the western end of the valley, close to Jerusalem, while Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as the limit of the ravine of the Mount of Olives. The location shown here is a rough position near Jerusalem.

Aznoth-tabor was a landmark on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only in Josh 19:34, where the border turns west to Aznoth-tabor and then runs on to Hukkok. The name probably means "peaks of Tabor" (Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "the ears," possibly the summits, of Tabor). That suggests a spot near Mount Tabor on the western side of Naphtali's territory, where it met Zebulun. Smith's Bible Dictionary is unsure whether it was a town at all. Both it and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia say the exact site is unknown, while the STEPBible names list calls it a border town of Naphtali near Mount Tabor. The location shown here is a rough placement in the vicinity of Mount Tabor in Lower Galilee, not a firm identification with any known ruin.

Azotus was a city near the Mediterranean coast, named in the New Testament as the place where Philip the evangelist was found after he baptized the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza. From there he preached in all the towns along his route until he reached Caesarea (Acts 8:40). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names identify Azotus as the Greek form of Ashdod, one of the five main Philistine cities of the Old Testament, where the captured ark of God was taken (1 Sam 5:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes the name in 1 Maccabees. The old city probably lay at or near the site of Isdud, close to the modern Israeli city of Ashdod, though no exact location is shown here.

Baal was a place named as the limit of the villages belonging to the tribe of Simeon. In 1 Chr 4:33 their villages spread around their cities as far as Baal. The name means "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take it to be probably the same place as Baalath-beer, which Josh 19:8 lists among Simeon's towns and links with "Ramath of the south." On that view it lay in the southern country, the Negev, where Simeon's other towns were. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, following the link with Baalath-beer and "Ramath of the south."

Baal-hamon was the place where Solomon had a vineyard, according to Song 8:11. He leased it to keepers, and each was to bring a thousand pieces of silver for its fruit. This is the only mention of the place in the Bible, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of a multitude," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who rules a crowd." Easton's records several proposed identifications: with Baal-gad, with Hammon in the territory of Asher (Josh 19:28), or with Belamon in central Palestine near Dothan. The location shown here, near the foot of Mount Hermon in present-day southern Lebanon, follows the Baal-gad identification. Because the verse appears in poetry, some readers also take the vineyard as part of the song's imagery, but the text presents it as a real holding of Solomon's.

Baal-hazor was the place where Absalom held a sheep-shearing two full years after his sister Tamar was wronged by Amnon. It is described as "beside Ephraim," and Absalom invited all of King David's sons there (2 Sam 13:23). The following verses tell how Amnon was killed at this feast on Absalom's orders. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin and suggests it may be the same as the Hazor of Neh 11:33. Both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Tell 'Asur, a mountain about 4 to 5 miles northeast of Bethel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its height as 3,318 feet above sea level. The location shown here follows the Tell 'Asur identification.

Baal-hermon was a place near Mount Hermon that marked the northern limit of the land settled by the half tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. According to 1 Chr 5:23, that tribe grew so numerous that it spread from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir and Mount Hermon. Judg 3:3 also speaks of a "mount Baal-hermon" in the same region. The name joins the god Baal with Hermon, which suggests a site linked to Baal worship. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Baal-gad (Josh 11:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Banias, near the springs of the Jordan. The location shown here does not follow either of these. It places Baal-hermon on Mount Hermon itself, at the area of its summit.

Baal-shalishah was a town in Israel. A man from there brought Elisha, called “the man of God,” bread made from the firstfruits, including twenty barley loaves and fresh ears of grain. Elisha told him to give the food to the people so they could eat (2 Kgs 4:42). The nearby story in 2 Kgs 4:38 puts Elisha at Gilgal during a famine, so Baal-shalishah was probably not far from there. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note an identification with Khirbet Sirisia, about 13–15 miles north of Lydda, based on the ancient writer Eusebius. The encyclopedia also mentions Kefr Thilth, whose Arabic name matches Shalishah. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country near that Gilgal, north of Bethel.

Baal-tamar was a place near Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin. There the main army of Israel drew up in battle order during the war against the Benjamites, while the troops hidden in ambush broke out from their positions near Gibeah (Judg 20:33). The name means "lord of the palm tree." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to have been a sanctuary of Baal and suggests the name may recall the palm tree of Deborah (Judg 4:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it between Bethel and Gibeah, inferring this from the roads mentioned in the same campaign (Judg 20:18, 31). It notes that Eusebius knew of the place but that all trace of the name has since been lost. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Gibeah area, north of Jerusalem.

Baalah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:29 among the cities of Judah's southernmost district, near the border with Edom. The name is shared by other places, including Baalah, another name for Kiriath-jearim (Josh 15:9), and Mount Baalah on Judah's northern border (Josh 15:11). This southern Baalah should not be confused with them. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same town as Balah (Josh 19:3) and Bilhah (1 Chr 4:29), which appear in the lists of towns given to the tribe of Simeon inside Judah's territory. The STEPBible names index likewise treats it as a Simeonite town. Easton's identifies the site with Khurbet Zebalah. The location shown here is only approximate, placing it in the Negev region near Beersheba. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "her idol" or "a spouse."

Baalath was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Dan. It is listed with Eltekeh and Gibbethon among Dan's cities in Josh 19:44, its only mention in this entry's verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same Baalath that Solomon later fortified (1 Kgs 9:18; 2 Chr 8:6), though because several places share this name, that link is not certain. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention a possible identification with Bel'ain, probably the present-day village of Bil'in west of Ramallah, and the rough location shown here follows that identification. The name is related to Baal, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a rejoicing" or "our proud lord."

Baalath-beer was a town on the edge of the territory given to the tribe of Simeon, named in Josh 19:8 together with the villages around it. The verse links it with "Ramath of the south," probably another name for the same place, which would put it on a height in the Negeb, the dry country of the far south. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "lady (mistress) of the well" and connects it with "Ramoth of the south" in 1 Sam 30:27. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be probably the same as Baal, a Simeonite town in 1 Chr 4:33. Its site is unknown. Conder suggested that the shrine Kubbet el Baul may keep the old name. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negeb, following the verse's own setting.

Baale-judah, meaning "lords of Judah" or "Baals of Judah," was a town in Judah. David and his people set out from there to bring the ark of God up to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:2). The parallel account in 1 Chr 13:6 calls the place Kiriath-jearim, and Josh 15:9 says that Baalah is Kiriath-jearim. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Baale-judah as another name for that town. This fits the earlier account in 1 Sam 7:1–2, where the ark was kept at Kiriath-jearim for many years after the Philistines returned it. Kiriath-jearim is usually placed in the hills west of Jerusalem, near modern Abu Ghosh. The location shown here is only approximate.

Baharum was the hometown of Azmaveth the Baharumite, one of David's mighty warriors, listed in 1 Chr 11:33. The place itself is not described, and it is known only from this title. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:31 calls the same man "Azmaveth the Barhumite." For that reason Baharum is probably the same as Bahurim, a village near Jerusalem on the road to the Jordan Valley, which appears in the stories of David's flight from Absalom (2 Sam 16:5). The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough one, east of Jerusalem in the direction of the Jordan.

Balah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Josh 19:3, in the list of Simeon's cities, between Hazar-shual and Azem. Simeon's towns lay within Judah's allotment in the Negev, the dry southern region around Beersheba. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Balah with Bilhah in the parallel list of Simeonite towns (1 Chr 4:29) and with Baalah among the southern towns of Judah (Josh 15:29). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accepts the link with Bilhah and calls the identification with Baalah possible. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, east of Beersheba, near the other towns in the same list.

Bamah is a Hebrew word meaning "high place", used as a name in Ezek 20:29. There God, speaking through Ezekiel, asks Israel's elders what the high place is that they go to, and adds that it is still called Bamah "unto this day." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it as a general term for the hilltop sites where Israelites worshipped idols, not as the name of one town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a possible wordplay in the Hebrew ("what" is mah, "come" is ba) and suggests that a prominent high place, such as the one at Gibeon, may be meant. It points to 1 Kgs 3:4 and 1 Chr 16:39 for that site. The location shown here follows the Gibeon identification, at the modern village of el-Jib north of Jerusalem. Because the passage does not name a specific site, any location is uncertain.

Bath-rabbim was a gate of the city of Heshbon, mentioned once in the Bible. In Song 7:4 the beloved's eyes are compared to "the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim," so pools apparently lay near this gate. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take it as one of Heshbon's gates and give the meaning of the name as "daughter of many." That may refer to the crowds who passed through it, though this is only an inference from the meaning. Heshbon lay east of the Jordan, and it is generally identified with the modern site of Hesban in Jordan, southwest of Amman. The location shown here places the gate within that city. The exact position of the gate itself is unknown.

Bealoth was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negeb. It appears only in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, between Ziph and Telem (Josh 15:24). Nothing else is said about it there. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the same place as Baalath-beer, a town assigned to Simeon within Judah's territory (Josh 19:8). The name is shared by other places. In 1 Kgs 4:16, where the King James Version reads "in Aloth," the Revised Version reads "Bealoth," a district that may be a separate location. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the Judahite town as unidentified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the southern Judean region, matching its listing among the Negeb towns. The name's meaning is uncertain: Easton's gives "citizens," Smith's Bible Dictionary "ladies."

Bealoth was a place in northern Israel named in the list of Solomon's twelve district officers, who each supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. Baanah son of Hushai governed the district of Asher together with Bealoth (1 Kgs 4:16). The King James Version reads "in Aloth" here, while the Revised Version reads "Bealoth," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing more is said about it, and its exact site is unknown. Because it is paired with Asher, it was probably in or near Asher's territory in western Galilee, and the location shown here is a rough placement in that area. This entry is distinct from the town of Bealoth in the far south of Judah (Josh 15:24), which Easton's Bible Dictionary treats as probably the same as Baalath-beer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "cast under."

Beer was a stopping place of the Israelites on their journey through the region east of the Dead Sea, shortly before they entered Amorite territory. Its name means "a well," and Num 21:16 identifies it as the well where the LORD told Moses to gather the people so he could give them water. The following verses record a song the people sang there, praising a well dug by their princes and nobles with their staves. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts it as the forty-fourth station of the wanderings, in the wilderness of Moab, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it north of the Arnon River. The site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in that general region. The name is also used for at least one other place in the Bible, such as the town to which Jotham fled in Judg 9:21.

Beer was the town where Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, fled and settled out of fear of his brother Abimelech (Judg 9:21). Abimelech had killed Gideon's other sons, and Jotham had just denounced him with a parable spoken from Mount Gerizim. The name means "a well" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and several places in the Bible share it, including a well-station on Israel's wilderness route. The text gives no detail about this town's location. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that it may be the same place as Beeroth. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at Beeroth, probably near modern el-Bireh, north of Jerusalem. The site is uncertain because the passage itself names nothing nearby.

Beer-elim was a place in or on the border of Moab, named only once, in Isaiah's oracle against Moab, where the wailing of Moab is said to reach as far as Eglaim and Beer-elim (Isa 15:8). The name means "well of heroes" or "well of Elim" (Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "well of rains"). The pairing with Eglaim suggests two places at opposite edges of Moab, so the verse probably pictures mourning across the whole land. Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary connect it with Beer, the well dug by Israel's leaders in Num 21:16. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in northern Moab, opposite Eglaim in the south, and treats the link with Beer as possible but not certain. The location shown here is only approximate, in southern Moab, and does not settle the question.

Beeroth Bene-jaakan, meaning "the wells of the children of Jaakan," was a desert campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Deut 10:6 says they moved from there to Mosera, where Aaron died and was buried and his son Eleazar took over as priest. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Bene-jaakan in Num 33:31. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Numbers places this camp after Moseroth, while Deuteronomy places it before Mosera. The Jaakan clan may be the Horite family of Seir listed in 1 Chr 1:42, which would place the wells near Edom, though this is an inference. The exact site is unknown. The rough location shown here is in the hills near Petra, close to Jebel Harun, which tradition identifies as Mount Hor, where Num 20 says Aaron died.

Beeshterah was a Levitical city in Bashan, east of the Jordan. Joshua 21:27 lists it with Golan as one of two towns, each with its surrounding pasturelands, given to the Gershonite families of the Levites from the half tribe of Manasseh that settled beyond the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "house of Ashterah" and identifies it with Ashtaroth. That identification rests on the parallel list in 1 Chr 6:71, which names Golan and Ashtaroth as the Gershonite cities from eastern Manasseh. Beeshterah is probably a contracted form of Be-Ashtaroth. Ashtaroth is usually placed at Tell Ashtarah in southern Syria, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Bene-berak was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, listed with Jehud and Gath-rimmon in Josh 19:45. This is its only mention in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "sons of lightning." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Ibn Ibraq, about an hour's journey southeast of Jaffa. The location shown here is in the coastal plain east of modern Tel Aviv, near the present-day city of Bnei Brak, which takes its name from the biblical town. This fits that general area, since Jehud and Gath-rimmon, the towns named with it, also belong to the coastal part of Dan's inheritance.

Beon was a town east of the Jordan, named in Num 32:3 among the places in the land of Jazer and Gilead that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them because it suited their livestock. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as the same town called Baal-meon in Num 32:38, which Reuben rebuilt and renamed. It also identifies it with Beth-baal-meon, given to Reuben in Josh 13:17, and with Beth-meon, listed among the cities of Moab in Jer 48:23. The same work notes that Mesha, king of Moab, claimed to have fortified it. Following the early church historian Eusebius, it places the town at the ruins of Ma'in, about 4 miles southwest of Madaba in modern Jordan, though the visible remains there date only from Roman times. The location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "in affliction."

Bered was a place in the far south of Canaan, mentioned only once. Genesis 16:14 says the well Beer-lahai-roi, where the angel of the Lord found Hagar after she fled from Sarai, lay "between Kadesh and Bered." The wider story places this well on the way to Shur (Gen 16:7), so Bered was probably in the Negev or northern Sinai. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "hail." Its exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Aramaic Targums render the name with terms for Shur and Chalutsah, and links it to the large ruin of Khalasa (ancient Elusa), southwest of Beersheba. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region west of Kadesh, not a precise identification.

Berothah was a place on the northern boundary of the land of Israel described in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land. Ezek 47:16 lists it with Hamath and Sibraim, in the area between the borders of Damascus and Hamath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Berothai, a city of Hadadezer king of Zobah mentioned in 2 Sam 8:8. Its exact site is uncertain. Some have linked the name with Beirut. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the springs at Hasbeya. Others look to Wadi Brissa, north of Baalbek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the village of Bereitan, a little south of Baalbek in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley. The location shown here follows the Bereitan identification.

Berothai was a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, from which King David took a very large amount of bronze (the King James "brass") after defeating him (2 Sam 8:8). The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:8 names Cun instead of Berothai and Tibhath instead of Betah. Some connect it with Berothah on the northern border described in Ezek 47:16, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "wells" or "a cypress." Its exact site is not certain. It is often identified with the modern village of Bereitan in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, south of Baalbek, and the location shown here follows that identification. A site in this valley would fit Zobah's position north of Israel, between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges.

Betah was a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah. After David defeated Hadadezer, he took a great quantity of bronze ("brass" in the King James Version) from Betah and from Berothai (2 Sam 8:8). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "confidence." The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:8 calls the city Tibhath, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Syriac version reads the name as Tebah. That encyclopedia adds that the city may be the Tubihi named in Egyptian records alongside Kadesh on the Orontes, and that Chronicles presents this bronze as later used by Solomon for the temple furnishings. The exact site is unknown. It probably lay in the Aramean kingdom of Zobah, on or near the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon range. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Beqaa Valley region of present-day Lebanon.

Beten was a town on the border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. It is named in Josh 19:25 between Hali and Achshaph, in the list of places that marked Asher's boundary. Nothing else is recorded about it in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "belly," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "height." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius, in his Onomasticon, placed a town called Bethseten about 8 Roman miles east of Ptolemais (Acre). It suggests the site may be the modern village of el-B'aneh in western Galilee, though it adds that no certainty is possible. The location shown here follows the el-B'aneh identification.

Beth-anoth was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:59). It belongs to a group of six towns with their villages that includes Maarath and Eltekon. By the surrounding verse (Josh 15:58), the group also includes Halhul, Beth-zur and Gedor, north of Hebron. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "house of answers", Smith's Bible Dictionary "house of echo", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "house of Anath", after a deity. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruin of Beit 'Ainun, about 3 miles northeast of Hebron and near Halhul. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the visible ruins there come from later periods.

Beth-arbel was a place whose brutal destruction Hosea cites as a warning to Israel. Its fortresses would be plundered "as Shalman spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle," when mothers were dashed in pieces with their children (Hos 10:14). It is not mentioned anywhere else in Scripture, so both the place and the attacker are uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shalman to be probably Shalmaneser, king of Assyria (2 Kgs 17:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view, that he was Shalamanu, a Moabite king who paid tribute to Tiglath-pileser. It also gives two possible sites: Arbela (Irbid) in Galilee, or Irbid east of the Jordan, southeast of Gadara, which Eusebius's Onomasticon called Arbela. The location shown here follows the eastern identification with Irbid in modern northern Jordan.

Beth-azmaveth was a town in Judah or Benjamin whose men, forty-two in all, are counted among the exiles who returned from Babylon in Nehemiah's list (Neh 7:28). The parallel list in Ezra 2:24 gives the same number under the shorter name Azmaveth, so the two names refer to one place, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats them. Nehemiah 12:29 later mentions the fields of Azmaveth as a place where the temple singers had settled near Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house of death's strength." The town is commonly identified with the modern village of Hizma, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem near Anathoth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-baal-meon was a town east of the Jordan listed among the cities on the plain near Heshbon that were given to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place called Baal-meon, which Reuben rebuilt and renamed (Num 32:38), and Beon (Num 32:3). Later it appears as a Moabite city, called Beth-meon in Jer 48:23 and Baal-meon in Ezek 25:9. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Moabite king Mesha named it among the towns he fortified. The name probably refers to a local shrine of Baal. Eusebius placed it near hot springs about nine miles from Heshbon. On that basis it is usually identified with the ruins of Ma'in, about 4 miles southwest of Madaba in modern Jordan, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-barah was a place near the Jordan River, named only in Judg 7:24. After Gideon routed the Midianites, he sent messengers through the hill country of Ephraim calling the Ephraimites to seize "the waters unto Bethbarah and Jordan" ahead of the fleeing enemy, and they did so. The name is usually understood as "house of the ford" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries), and it was probably a main crossing point of the Jordan in that district. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's suggests it may be the ford Jacob used near the Jabbok and where Jephthah later killed the Ephraimites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it where the Wadi Fari'ah meets the Jordan. Smith's links it with Bethabara, where John baptized. The location shown here follows that last view, placing it at a Jordan crossing east of Jericho.

Beth-biri (spelled Bethbirei in the King James Version) was a town of the tribe of Simeon in the Negeb, the dry region of southern Judah. It appears only in 1 Chr 4:31, in a list of the towns where the Simeonites lived, which the verse says remained theirs until the reign of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) takes it to be the same place as Beth-lebaoth, which appears at the matching point in the parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6. STEPBible's proper-names index connects it instead with Bethul, another name in that list. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negeb, near Beersheba, based on the town's place among the other Simeonite settlements.

Beth-car was the place to which the men of Israel chased the Philistines after defeating them near Mizpah in Samuel's time (1 Sam 7:11). According to the surrounding chapter, the Philistines had attacked while Israel was gathered at Mizpah, and they were thrown into confusion before the pursuit began. Beth-car is mentioned nowhere else. Its name is usually explained as "house of the lamb" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names) or "sheep-house" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Its site is unknown. Easton's and Smith's place it west of Mizpah, inferring this from the direction of a Philistine retreat toward their own coastal territory. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests 'Ain Karem, west of Jerusalem, if Mizpah is Nebi Samwil. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem.

Beth-dagon was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed in Joshua's allotment of towns to the tribe alongside Gederoth, Naamah and Makkedah, in a district of sixteen cities with their villages. Its name is usually taken to mean "house of Dagon" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), probably after the Philistine god. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of corn, or of fish." Since it lay in the low country, it was probably near Philistine territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with modern Beit Dajan, about 5 miles from Lydda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Beit Dajan, southeast of Jaffa, and nearby Khirbet Dajan are candidates, but suggests the list points to a site farther southeast. The location shown here is only approximate and lies in the coastal plain in the general area of these proposals. A different Beth-dagon appears on the border of Asher (Josh 19:27).

Beth-dagon was a city on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in Josh 19:27 as a landmark where Asher's border turned east toward Zebulun and the valley of Jiphthah-el. The name probably means "house of Dagon," after the god Dagon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a Philistine colony. Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "house of corn, or of fish." The name is shared by other places, including a town in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name was widespread, which may reflect broad worship of Dagon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the coast. Easton's and Conder identify it with Tell D'auk, near the mouth of the Belus River (the modern Na'aman) in the plain of Acre. The rough location shown here follows that identification.

Beth-diblathaim was a town of Moab, east of the Dead Sea. It appears once, in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab, where it is listed with Dibon and Nebo among the cities facing judgment (Jer 48:22). The name probably means "house of fig cakes," as Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries explain it. Several reference works, including Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take it to be the same place as Almon-diblathaim, an Israelite camping site during the wilderness journey (Num 33:46). Easton's also links it with Diblath (Ezek 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that King Mesha of Moab claimed on the Moabite Stone to have fortified it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a proposed spot in the Moabite highlands between Dibon and Medeba, in present-day Jordan.

Beth-eden, meaning "house of Eden," was a place named in Amos's prophecy against Damascus, where the LORD declares he will cut off "him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden" (Amos 1:5). The King James Version translates the name rather than spelling it out. The verse links it with Damascus and the plain of Aven as a seat of Syrian (Aramean) rule, and says the people of Syria would go into captivity to Kir. Its location is uncertain. Some identify it with Bit Adini, a district on the middle Euphrates known from Assyrian inscriptions and probably the same as "the children of Eden" of 2 Kgs 19:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was perhaps in Syria near Damascus. The location shown here follows the view placing it in the Damascus area.

Beth-emek, meaning "house of the valley," was a town named once, in the description of the border of the tribe of Asher (Josh 19:27). The boundary ran east toward Beth-dagon, reached Zebulun and the valley of Jiphthah-el on the north side of Beth-emek, then went on to Neiel and Cabul. Because it lies where Asher's line meets Zebulun, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts it within Zebulun, while Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on or near Asher's border. The ISBE describes the site as unidentified but says it should be sought east of Acre, not far from Cabul (modern Kabul). The location shown here follows a later identification with Tel Bet ha-Emek, near the former village of Amqa, which may preserve the name, about 9 kilometres (6 miles) northeast of Acre in western Galilee. That identification is probable rather than certain.

Beth-ezel was a town named only once in the Bible, in Micah's lament over the towns of Judah and the lowland facing coming judgment (Mic 1:11). The verse speaks of mourning in Beth-ezel, and Micah, as he often does in this passage, appears to play on the town's name, which means "house of nearness" or "adjoining house." Its people would offer no support or standing to others in the disaster. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it, from the context, in the plain of Philistia, alongside the other towns Micah lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified, and that some have linked it with Azel in Zech 14:5. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the coastal lowland southwest of Jerusalem, in keeping with the towns named around it.

Beth-gamul was a city of Moab, named once in Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab alongside Kiriathaim and Beth-meon (Jer 48:23). It belongs to the list of towns of the "plain country" (the Moabite tableland) on which judgment is announced (Jer 48:21). The name probably means "house of the camel." Nothing more is recorded about it. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Umm el-Jemal, a deserted city in the Hauran near Bozrah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Conder placed it at Umm el-Jamal on the plateau south of Medeba. Others, the encyclopedia reports, prefer Jemeil, about 6 miles east of Dhiban, the biblical Dibon. The location shown here follows the Jemeil identification, east of Dhiban in present-day Jordan.

Beth-gilgal, meaning "house of Gilgal," was a place where some of the Levite singers lived after the return from exile. The KJV translates the name as "the house of Gilgal." Neh 12:29 lists it with the fields of Geba and Azmaveth as places where the singers had built villages around Jerusalem. From these villages they gathered for the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Gilgal. The location shown here follows that view and places it at the well-known Gilgal near Jericho in the Jordan valley. The verse itself gives no position beyond its link to villages around Jerusalem, so the exact site is uncertain.

Beth-haggan, meaning "house of the garden," was a place on the road Ahaziah king of Judah took as he fled from Jehu after Joram king of Israel was killed near Jezreel. The King James Version translates the name as "the garden house," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some read it as a proper place name. Jehu's men struck Ahaziah in his chariot at the ascent of Gur near Ibleam, and he escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). The route suggests Beth-haggan lay south of Jezreel, toward Ibleam. Its exact location is uncertain. Many identify it with En-gannim, the modern town of Jenin, which lies on a route south from Jezreel. The location shown here is only approximate and is placed near Megiddo, where Ahaziah's flight ended.

Beth-haram (spelled Betharam in the King James Version) was a town in the Jordan Valley east of the river. Joshua 13:27 lists it with Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon among the towns of the territory given to the tribe of Gad, land that had been the rest of the kingdom of Sihon, king of Heshbon. Numbers 32:36 probably refers to the same place as Beth-haran, one of the fortified towns the Gadites built. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Bethramphtha, mentioned by Josephus. In the first century Herod Antipas fortified it and renamed it Julias, and Eusebius says it was also called Livias. The same work places it at Tell er-Rameh in Wadi Hesban, about 6 miles (10 km) east of the Jordan, in present-day Jordan. The location shown here is in the Jordan Valley north-east of the Dead Sea.

Beth-haran was a fortified town east of the Jordan River, named in Num 32:36 among the fenced cities and sheepfolds the tribe of Gad built or rebuilt after Moses granted them land there. The surrounding chapter shows Gad and Reuben asking for this pasture country for their large flocks. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same place as Beth-haram, which Josh 13:27 lists among Gad's towns in the Jordan valley. Its exact site is uncertain. It is often placed at one of the mounds on the plain east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, such as Tell er-Rameh or Tell Iktanu. The location shown here places it in that area, northeast of the Dead Sea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house of grace."

Beth-horon was the name of a pair of towns, Upper and Lower Beth-horon, in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem. In 1 Chr 7:24, Sherah, a daughter in the line of Ephraim, is said to have built both towns along with Uzzen-sherah. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "house of the hollow" or "of the cavern," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of wrath." Easton's places the towns in Ephraim's territory on the road from Jerusalem to Joppa, about 2 miles apart, with the upper town about 10 miles northwest of Jerusalem. The steep pass between them was the route down which Joshua drove the Amorite kings (Josh 10:10–11). Easton's identifies them with the modern villages of Beit Ur el-Foqa (upper) and Beit Ur et-Tahta (lower), and the location shown here lies in that area. Because the name covers two neighboring sites, references to Beth-horon can mean either one.

Beth-le-aphrah was a town named only in Mic 1:10, in Micah's lament over the coming judgment on Judah. The King James Version renders it "the house of Aphrah." The name means "house of dust," and the prophet plays on it by telling its people to roll themselves in the dust as a sign of mourning. The verse sits among other wordplays on town names, beginning with Gath, so the place was probably one of several nearby towns threatened by the invasion. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the Shephelah, the low country between Joppa and Gaza, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it in the Philistine plain. Others link it with Ophrah in Benjamin. The location shown here follows that identification, probably the modern village of et-Taiyibeh northeast of Jerusalem.

Beth-lebaoth was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Simeon, named near the end of Simeon's list of thirteen cities and their villages in Josh 19:6. The name means "house of lionesses" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Because Simeon's towns lay within Judah's allotment, it was in the far south of the land, in the Negev region. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Lebaoth in Judah's list of southern towns (Josh 15:32). Both Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Beth-birei in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:31) as another name for the same place. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, north of Beersheba.

Beth-meon was a town of Moab named in Jeremiah's prophecy of judgment against Moab, listed alongside Kiriathaim and Beth-gamul (Jer 48:23). The verse gives no further detail about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as a shortened form of the same town elsewhere called Baal-meon (Num 32:38) and Beth-baal-meon (Josh 13:17). Those passages place it on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, a town the tribe of Reuben rebuilt after the conquest that later came back under Moabite control. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of the dwelling-place." The location shown here is probably the modern village of Ma'in, southwest of Madaba in Jordan, the site usually linked with Baal-meon.

Beth-pazzez was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, where it is named alongside Remeth, En-gannim and En-haddah (Josh 19:21). Nothing else is recorded about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "house of the dispersion," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "house of dividing asunder." The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it probably lay near modern Jenin, since it is listed with En-gannim, which is commonly linked to that area. The location shown here is a rough placement in that general region of the Jezreel Valley and the hills to its south, not a known site.

Beth-shemesh was a city on the border of the tribe of Issachar, listed in Joshua 19:22 between Shahazimah and the Jordan, where Issachar's boundary ended. The name means "house of the sun." Several places in the Bible share this name, including the better-known Beth-shemesh in Judah and another in Naphtali, so this one should be kept distinct. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Dothan and the Jordan, near Issachar's southern border, about 7.5 miles south of Beth-shean, and identifies it with Ain esh-Shemsiyeh. The location shown here follows that identification, in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean.

Beth-shittah, meaning "house of the acacia", was a place named in the flight of the Midianite army after Gideon's three hundred men blew their trumpets and the enemy camp turned on itself. The fleeing host ran toward Beth-shittah "in Zererath" and on toward the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath (Judg 7:22). This is its only mention in the Bible. The route suggests it lay east or southeast of the Midianite camp in the Valley of Jezreel, toward the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the modern village of Shatta (Shuṭṭa) in the Jezreel Valley, about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Beisan (Beth-shean). The location shown here follows that identification, although the exact site remains uncertain.

Beth-tappuah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in a group of towns near Hebron (Josh 15:53). Its name means "house of apples" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with Tappuah, named as a son of Hebron in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:43, which probably reflects the founding or settlement of the town by a clan from Hebron. The ISBE also mentions a possible link with Tephon in 1 Maccabees 9:50. The town is usually identified with the modern village of Taffuh, a few miles west of Hebron, on a high ridge with fertile gardens, old cisterns and an ancient road. The location shown here follows that identification.

Bethany beyond the Jordan was the place east of the Jordan River where John the Baptist was baptizing and where the events of John 1:19–28 took place. The King James Version reads Bethabara here, but the oldest manuscripts, followed by the Revised Version, read Bethany (Easton's Bible Dictionary). It is a different place from the Bethany near Jerusalem that was home to Mary, Martha and Lazarus. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Origen preferred the reading Bethabara on geographical grounds, that Grove suggested Beth-nimrah (modern Tell Nimrin), and that tradition places it at the ford east of Jericho. The location shown here follows that traditional site, probably the area now called Al-Maghtas in Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "house of song" or "house of affliction."

Bethesda was a pool in Jerusalem near the sheep market (or sheep gate) with five porches, or covered colonnades (John 5:2). The name is usually explained as "house of mercy". Some manuscripts call it Bethzatha or Bethsaida. The surrounding passage (John 5:3–9) describes many sick people lying in the porches, and Jesus healing a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, about AD 28 by inference from context. The site has been identified in several ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the large Birket Israel north of the Temple area. Robinson and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favour the intermittent spring called the Virgin's Fountain (Gihon) in the Kidron Valley. A third view, which Easton's Bible Dictionary notes was argued by Schick, places it at a rock-cut twin pool near St. Anne's Church, just inside St. Stephen's Gate. The location shown here follows the St. Anne's identification.

Bethlehem was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. It appears only once, in Josh 19:15, as the last of twelve cities with their villages in Zebulun's allotment. It is a different place from the better-known Bethlehem in Judah, and several places in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "house of bread." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it with Beit-Lahm, a village Easton places about 6 miles (10 km) west-northwest of Nazareth in Galilee. The location shown here matches that identification. Some scholars have suggested that the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem (Judg 12:8–10) came from this northern town rather than from Bethlehem in Judah, but the text does not say which one is meant.

Bethlehem Ephrathah is the name Micah uses for Bethlehem, the town in Judah. Micah 5:2 calls it small among the clans ("thousands") of Judah, yet foretells that a ruler in Israel will come from it, one "whose goings forth have been from of old." The added name Ephrathah sets it apart from another Bethlehem in Zebulun. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Ephrath or Ephrathah as the town's ancient name, linked with Rachel's burial on the road there (Gen 35:16–19; 48:7). It also notes that Ruth 1:2 calls the place Bethlehem-Judah but its people Ephrathites. Bethlehem was David's hometown, and Matt 2:6 quotes Micah's prophecy as pointing to Bethlehem in the land of Judah. The location shown here is the town of Bethlehem, about 9 kilometers (6 miles) south of Jerusalem.

Bethuel was a town in the far south of Judah's territory where the descendants of Simeon lived. It appears in 1 Chr 4:30 in the list of Simeonite towns, named alongside Hormah and Ziklag, which places it in the Negev region. Both Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Bethul in the parallel list of Simeon's towns at Josh 19:4. They also link it, the encyclopedia more cautiously as "probably," with the Bethel in southern Judah to which David sent spoil after recovering Ziklag (1 Sam 30:27). That Bethel is distinct from the better-known Bethel north of Jerusalem. The site has not been securely identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "filiation of God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "destroyed of God."

Bethul was a town given to the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Joshua's list of Simeon's towns, between Eltolad and Hormah (Josh 19:4). Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory, so Bethul was probably in the southern region near Beersheba. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same place as Chesil in Judah's town list (Josh 15:30) and Bethuel in the parallel list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:30). The name is usually explained as meaning "dweller in God." Its exact site has not been identified, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

Betonim was a town east of the Jordan that Joshua 13 lists among the places marking the territory given to the tribe of Gad. It appears only once, in Josh 13:26, in a line running from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and then from Mahanaim to the border of Debir. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to lie apparently on Gad's northern boundary, and it was in the region of Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Batneh (Khirbet Batneh), about 3 miles (5 km) southwest of es-Salt in modern Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification. The exact site remains uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "bellies."

Bezek was the place where Saul counted the men of Israel and Judah who had answered his call to arms. 1 Sam 11:8 records 300,000 from Israel and 30,000 from Judah. The surrounding chapter shows the muster was gathered to rescue Jabesh-gilead, across the Jordan, from Nahash the Ammonite. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both place it in the centre of the country near the Jordan valley, which suits a march to Jabesh-gilead. Easton's identifies it with the modern Ibzik, about 13 miles north-east of Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius mentions two villages of this name on the road from Shechem to Scythopolis, and links them with Khirbet Ibziq and the nearby height Ras Ibziq. The location shown here follows that identification. The name is shared with another Bezek, connected with Adoni-bezek in Judges 1, which may be a separate place.

Bileam was a town in the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan. It was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the remaining families of the Kohathite Levites (1 Chr 6:70). Bileam is named only in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be probably the same town as Ibleam (Josh 17:11) and identifies it with the modern site of Bel'ameh, about half a mile south of Jenin. The location shown here follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary also equates it with Gath-rimmon, which appears in the parallel list of Levitical towns in Josh 21:25. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the ancient of the people" or "the devourer."

Bilhah was a town in the far south of Judah where descendants of Simeon lived. It is named in the list of Simeonite towns in 1 Chr 4:29, alongside Ezem and Tolad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same place as Baalah in Josh 15:29 and Balah in Josh 19:3, which appear in parallel lists of towns in southern Judah allotted to Simeon. The site has not been identified. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Israel, based on its listing among other Simeonite towns. The town shares its name with Bilhah, Rachel's servant and the mother of Dan and Naphtali, but the verse gives no indication of any connection between them.

Biziothiah (spelled Bizjothjah in the King James Version) was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:28 next to Hazarshual and Beersheba among the towns in the Negev given to the tribe of Judah. It appears nowhere else. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "and her villages" (or "daughters") here, a difference of one Hebrew consonant. On that reading the word refers to the villages around Beersheba rather than a separate town, and the parallel list in Neh 11:27, which mentions "Beersheba, and in the villages thereof," fits that reading. This entry treats it as a place near Beersheba, following the Hebrew text. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Beersheba area.

Bor-ashan was a town in southern Judah, one of the places to which David sent a share of the spoil after defeating the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. The list names the towns where David and his men had moved about while living as fugitives. The King James Version spells the name Chorashan. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that another reading of the Hebrew gives Bor-ashan, which later English versions adopt. Both works suggest it is probably the same place as Ashan, a town assigned to Judah and later to Simeon (Josh 15:42; 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). Easton gives the meaning as "smoking furnace." The exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Bozez was one of two sharp rocks that stood on either side of the pass Jonathan crossed to attack the Philistine garrison; the other was called Seneh (1 Sam 14:4). The setting is the gorge of Michmash, known from the surrounding narrative. This is generally identified with the steep ravine now called Wadi Suweinit, northeast of Jerusalem, and the location shown here lies in that area. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Bozez on the northern side of the gorge. It notes that this cliff catches the sun for most of the day while the southern cliff stays in shade, and suggests the name may mean "shining." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives the meaning "mud" or "bog." The name appears only in this one verse.

Bozrah was a city listed among the cities of Moab in Jeremiah's message of judgment against that nation (Jer 48:24). It is distinct from the better-known Bozrah of Edom, because several places share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it in the "plain country" mentioned a few verses earlier, meaning the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually understood to mean "fortress" or "sheepfold." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Bezer, the city of refuge, possibly at Qusur Bashair southeast of Dibon. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with a modern Buzrah. The location shown here follows an identification with Bosra (Busra al-Sham) in the Hauran region of southern Syria, well north of Moab's usual heartland.

Buz was an Arabian region or tribe named in Jer 25:23, where it appears with Dedan and Tema among the peoples made to drink the cup of the Lord's wrath, alongside "all that are in the utmost corners." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a district in Arabia Petrea. The people probably took their name from Buz, son of Nahor and brother of Huz (Gen 22:21). Elihu, Job's young companion, is called "the Buzite" in Job 32:2, which suggests he came from this people. Its exact location is unknown. Because it is listed with Dedan and Tema, it was probably in northwestern Arabia, and the location shown here is a rough placement near Dedan, around modern al-Ula in Saudi Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "despised" or "plundered."

Cabbon was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named with Lahmam and Kithlish (Josh 15:40). The list places it in the same district as Lachish and Eglon, so it probably lay in the western foothills toward the coastal plain. Its site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Machbena, which appears in a genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:49). The location shown here is only an approximate point in the lowland district of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "as though understanding."

Cabul was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in the description of Asher's territory as a landmark the border reached after passing Bethemek and Neiel, toward Zebulun (Josh 19:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the line between Asher and Zebulun and links it with Chabolo, a place mentioned by the historian Josephus. It is generally identified with the modern village of Kabul, about 8 to 10 miles east-southeast of Acre (ancient Accho), near the edge of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. The same name is also given to the district of Galilean towns that Solomon gave to Hiram king of Tyre (1 Kgs 9:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests this town was probably one of them, though that connection is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "displeasing."

Cabul was the name Hiram, king of Tyre, gave to a district of cities in Galilee that Solomon handed over to him. By the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 9:11–12), these were twenty cities given in return for Hiram's cedar, timber and gold. When Hiram saw them, they did not please him, and he called them "the land of Cabul," a name still used when the account was written. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "good for nothing," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "displeasing; dirty." Easton's places the district in northwest Galilee near Tyre and suggests that Hiram later returned the cities, citing 2 Chr 8:2. The name is shared with a town of Asher (Josh 19:27). The location shown here is approximate and lies near that town, probably the modern village of Kabul east of Akko.

Caleb-Ephrathah was the place where Hezron, son of Perez and grandson of Judah, died, according to 1 Chr 2:24. After his death his wife Abiah bore him a son, Ashur, who became the father of Tekoa. The name appears nowhere else, and no ancient site bearing it has been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars follow the Greek Septuagint and read the verse not as a place name but as "after the death of Hezron, Caleb came to Ephrath," Hezron's wife. The name probably joins Caleb, Hezron's son, with Ephrathah, the name of Caleb's wife Ephrath (1 Chr 2:19) and an old name for Bethlehem (Gen 35:19; Mic 5:2). The location shown here follows that link and places it at or near Bethlehem, though this is an inference.

Calno was a city named in Isaiah's oracle against Assyria. In Isa 10:9 the Assyrian king boasts that Calno fared no better than Carchemish, just as Hamath fared no better than Arpad and Samaria no better than Damascus. The point is that each of these cities fell to Assyria in turn, so Jerusalem should expect the same. Calno is usually taken as another form of Calneh, a name found in Gen 10:10 and Amos 6:2. Its location is debated. Some place it in Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia, and connect it with the ancient city of Nippur in modern Iraq. Others identify it with Kullani, a town in northern Syria near Arpad, which suits the other Syrian cities in the list. The location shown here follows the southern Mesopotamian identification with Nippur. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "our consummation" or "altogether himself."

Canneh was a place named in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre as one of that city's trading partners, listed alongside Haran and Eden (Ezek 27:23). It appears only here, and its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia sets out several views. Gesenius and others take it as another form of Calneh (Gen 10:10; Amos 6:2) or Calno (Isa 10:9). The Targums, Eusebius and Jerome identify it with Ctesiphon on the Tigris. Some scholars read the Hebrew as "the sons of Eden" rather than as a place name. Smith's Bible Dictionary also treats it as Calneh. The location shown here follows the identification with the Calneh of Gen 10:10, which Jewish tradition places at the ancient city of Nippur in southern Iraq. Its listing with Haran and Eden suggests it was probably a Mesopotamian trading center.

Casiphia was the place where Iddo, a leading man, lived with his relatives the Nethinim (temple servants). Ezra sent messengers there to ask for ministers for the house of God (Ezra 8:17). The surrounding passage shows this happened while Ezra's returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava and had found no Levites among them. The name may be connected with the Hebrew word for 'silver' or 'money', and the Septuagint translates it as 'the place of the treasury' (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Its site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible names list place it in Babylonia, near the Ahava. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as lying somewhere between Babylon and Jerusalem. The location shown here is only a rough one in western Syria, which follows the 'between Babylon and Jerusalem' view.

Chephar-haammoni (ESV Chephar-ammoni; the KJV verse spells it Chepharhaammonai) was a town allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:24, where it is named alongside Ophni and Gaba. That verse closes a group of twelve cities with their villages.
