The name means "village of the Ammonites," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, which may point to a settlement of Ammonites at some point, though the text says nothing about its origin. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Kefr 'Ana, a ruined site about two miles northeast of Bethel. The location shown here follows a similar identification with Khirbat Kafr Ana, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.

Chesalon was a landmark on the northern border of Judah. Joshua 15:10 identifies it with "the side of mount Jearim," on the north side, where the boundary ran west from Baalah past Mount Seir before going down to Beth-shemesh and on to Timnah. The name probably means "hopes" or "confidence" (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the modern village of Kesla (Kesalon), on a mountain ridge in the western hills of Judah, about six miles northeast of Beth-shemesh. The ISBE notes that it was still a very large village in the 4th century AD and gives its elevation as about 2,087 feet. The location shown here follows the Kesla identification. The Bible mentions Chesalon only in this one verse.

Chesil was a town in the far south of Judah's territory, listed among the cities given to that tribe alongside Eltolad and Hormah (Josh 15:30). The name appears nowhere else in the Bible. In the parallel list of towns given to Simeon from within Judah's land, Bethul stands in the same position (Josh 19:4), and 1 Chr 4:30 has Bethuel. For this reason, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat Chesil and Bethul as the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the form "Chesil" may have come from a misreading of the text. Easton's identifies the site with Khelasa, and Smith's places it about 15 miles southwest of Beersheba. The exact site remains uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate. The name is often taken to mean "foolishness" or "ungodly."

Chesulloth was a town listed in Joshua 19:18 among the places on or near the border of the tribe of Issachar, named between Jezreel and Shunem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its place in the list suggests a position between those two towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with Chisloth-tabor, which Josh 19:12 names on the boundary of neighboring Zebulun. That would make it a border town shared by the two tribes. They place it at the modern village of Iksal, on the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley (Esdraelon), about 3 miles (5 km) west of Mount Tabor. The location shown here matches the Iksal identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fearfulness," while Easton's and Smith's render it "the loins" or "fertile places."

Chezib was a town in Canaan where Shelah, the third son of Judah by the daughter of Shua, was born (Gen 38:5). It is named only once. The surrounding chapter places Judah's household near Adullam, in the lowland hills west of Bethlehem, so Chezib was probably in the same area. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it as probably the same town as Achzib, a town of Judah's lowlands listed in Josh 15:44 and mentioned in Mic 1:14. Some also link it with Chozeba in 1 Chr 4:22. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "deceitful." The location shown here follows the Achzib identification and places the town in the Judean foothills near Adullam. The exact site is uncertain.

Chilmad was a place or region named once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, as one of the city's trading partners alongside Sheba and Asshur (Ezek 27:23). Nothing else is said about it, and its location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a place or country unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals: a link with Kalwadha near Baghdad; the Aramaic Targum's reading of the name as Media; and a different vocalization of the Hebrew that would make the word a phrase about Asshur rather than a place name. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Chilmad in northern Mesopotamia near ancient Nineveh, in the region of modern Mosul, Iraq, probably because the verse pairs it with Asshur (Assyria). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "teaching" or "learning."

Chinnereth is named in Deut 3:17 as the northern end of the territory Moses gave to the tribes of Reuben and Gad east of the Jordan. Their land ran along the Jordan valley from Chinnereth south to the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea), below the slopes of Pisgah. Here the name most likely stands for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Gennesaret or Tiberias, and the location shown here places it on that lake. The name is shared by several places. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the Hebrew word for 'lyre' and notes that it was also the name of a fortified city near the lake's shore, which gave its name to the surrounding district, and it treats Chinnereth as probably an old Canaanite name that the Israelites adopted. The city is often identified with Tel Kinrot on the northwest shore.

Chinnereth was a fortified city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, listed with Ziddim, Zer, Hammath and Rakkath among the tribe's fenced cities (Josh 19:35). The same name is also used for the lake later called the Sea of Galilee (the Sea of Chinnereth) and, in the plural form Chinneroth, for a surrounding district. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "lyre", places the city near the lake shore a little south of Tiberias, and suggests the town gave its name to the district. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the city is named only here and that no later writer mentions it. Many modern scholars identify it with Tel Kinrot (Tell el-Oreimeh) on the northwestern shore of the lake. The location shown here is only approximate and places it beside the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Chios is an island in the Aegean Sea, lying close to the coast of Asia Minor and separated from the mainland by a narrow strait of about 5 miles, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. It still bears the name Chios and belongs to modern Greece. It appears once in the Bible, on Paul's voyage toward Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Sailing south from Mitylene, his ship came "over against Chios" the next day, then reached Samos and finally Miletus (Acts 20:15). The phrase probably means they passed or anchored opposite the island overnight. Easton's Bible Dictionary says they sheltered in a roadstead there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests they anchored on the Asian coast facing it. No coordinates are given for the location shown here.

Chisloth-tabor was a place on the border of the tribe of Zebulun in Lower Galilee. In Josh 19:12 Zebulun's boundary runs eastward from Sarid "unto the border of Chislothtabor" and then on to Daberath and Japhia. The name links it to Mount Tabor, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "loins of Tabor," probably referring to the mountain's flanks. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Chesulloth, a town on the border of Issachar mentioned later in the same chapter. That would fit a site on the line between the two tribes. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the village of Iksal, about 2.5 miles west of Mount Tabor, and the location shown here matches that identification, near present-day Iksal, southeast of Nazareth.

Chitlish (spelled Kithlish in the King James Version) was a town in the lowland region of Judah, the Shephelah. It appears only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Cabbon and Lahmam (Josh 15:40). The next verse of that list goes on to name Gederoth and other towns of the same district, all within one group of settlements in the western foothills. Nothing else is recorded about the town. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with a place called Jelameh, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Shephelah among the neighboring towns of its list.

Clauda (Cauda in modern translations) was a small island south of Crete that the ship carrying Paul passed during a storm on his voyage to Rome. Driven by the wind, the ship ran under the island's shelter, and there the crew struggled to haul in the ship's boat (Acts 27:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 23 miles west of Cape Matala. It suggests that in the calmer water south of the island the crew also undergirded the ship and adjusted the sails. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as about 7 miles long and 3 miles wide. It is today identified as Gavdos, the Greek island off the southwest coast of Crete, formerly called Gozzo. No coordinates are given for it in this entry.

Cnidus was a city and harbor at the tip of a long peninsula on the southwest corner of Asia Minor, in the district of Caria within the Roman province of Asia. It is mentioned once, in the account of Paul's voyage to Rome, about AD 56 by inference from context. After leaving Myra, the ship sailed slowly for many days and only with difficulty came off Cnidus. The contrary wind then kept it from holding its course, so it turned south to shelter under Crete near Salmone (Acts 27:7). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ships coasting along southern Asia Minor turned north at this point, that the city had two harbors and the status of a free city, and that Jews lived there by the 2nd century BC. Its ruins lie at the promontory Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Cape Crio, in present-day Turkey, and the location shown here marks that site.

Colossae (spelled Colosse in the King James Version) was a city in Phrygia in western Asia Minor. Paul's letter to the Colossians is addressed to the believers there (Col 1:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the Lycus River, a tributary of the Maeander, about 12 miles from Laodicea and near the main road from Ephesus to the Euphrates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was also close to Hierapolis, that it was known for a distinctive wool, and that it declined as those neighboring cities grew. Both dictionaries infer from the letter that Paul had probably not visited the city himself, and that its church was founded through the work of Epaphras. The site was later called Chonae, and its ruins lie near the modern town of Honaz in southwestern Turkey, which matches the location shown here.

Coos (spelled Cos in modern translations) was a small island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Caria in southwest Asia Minor, northwest of Rhodes. It is now the Greek island of Kos, called Stanchio in older works. Paul's ship sailed straight there from Miletus on his return voyage to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. The next day it went on to Rhodes and then Patara (Acts 21:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the party spent the night there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Cos as a busy commercial center and a home of a Jewish community, known for its wine, fine cloth and medical school, and as the birthplace of Hippocrates. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note that Herod the Great was one of the island's benefactors.

Cozeba (spelled Chozeba in the King James Version) was a town of Judah, mentioned once in the genealogy of Judah's son Shelah. 1 Chr 4:22 lists "the men of Chozeba" alongside Jokim, Joash and Saraph, people linked with rule in Moab, and calls these records "ancient things." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Cozeba with Chezib, where Shelah was born (Gen 38:5), and with Achzib, a town in the lowlands of Judah (Josh 15:44). The Shelah connection makes this identification a natural inference. The location shown here places it in the Judean lowlands (the Shephelah) southwest of Jerusalem, in keeping with that view. Its exact site is uncertain.

Cun (spelled Chun in the King James Version) was a city belonging to Hadarezer, king of Zobah in Syria. After David defeated Hadarezer, he took a very large amount of bronze from Cun and from Tibhath, another of Hadarezer's cities. According to 1 Chr 18:8, Solomon later used this bronze to make the bronze sea, the pillars and the bronze vessels for the temple. In the parallel account in 2 Sam 8:8, the name Berothai appears in its place. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the two as the same city and connects it with Berothah in Ezek 47:16. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes the substitution. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the identification with Berothai at modern Bereitan in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, south of Baalbek.

Cushan is a place or people named once in the Bible, in the prayer-psalm of Habakkuk, where the prophet sees "the tents of Cushan in affliction" alongside the trembling "curtains of the land of Midian" (Hab 3:7). The parallel with Midian suggests a desert tent-dwelling people near Israel's southern lands. Its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a poetic or lengthened form of Cush, meaning an Arabian Cush. The Septuagint translates it as "Ethiopians," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia sees it as Cush used loosely. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a possible link with Cushan-rishathaim, the Mesopotamian king who oppressed Israel in Judg 3:8–10. The location shown here follows the identification with Cush and places it along the Nile in present-day northern Sudan, as a marker for the surrounding region rather than an exact site.

Cuth was a city of Mesopotamia whose people, after the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel, were among the foreigners the king of Assyria settled in the towns of Samaria. There they made an image of their own god, Nergal, alongside the gods of settlers from Babylon, Hamath and elsewhere (2 Kgs 17:30). The same place is called Cuthah in 2 Kgs 17:24, which lists it among the cities from which these settlers came. It is generally identified with ancient Kutha, a city known as a center of the worship of Nergal, at the site of Tell Ibrahim in central Iraq, northeast of Babylon. The location shown here follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "burning." In later Jewish tradition the Samaritans were sometimes called "Cutheans" after this group of settlers.

Cuthah was a city in Babylonia, one of the places from which the king of Assyria brought settlers to repopulate the cities of Samaria after the people of Israel were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). The same chapter later calls it Cuth and says its people brought the worship of their god Nergal with them (2 Kgs 17:30), which fits Cuthah's known role as a center of that god's cult. Easton's Bible Dictionary attributes the resettlement to Shalmaneser. It mentions a suggestion that the Cutheans were the same as the Cossaeans of the hill country north of the Choaspes River, and it identifies Cuthah with Tell Ibrahim, about 15 miles northeast of Babylon in present-day Iraq. The location shown here follows the Tell Ibrahim identification.

Dabbesheth was a town on the boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. The King James Version spells it Dabbasheth. It appears only once, in the description of Zebulun's border, which went up toward the sea past Maralah, reached Dabbesheth, and then reached "the river that is before Jokneam" (Josh 19:11). That river is probably the brook Kishon, which flows past Jokneam, so Dabbesheth likely lay on the western or southwestern edge of Zebulun's land. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Dabsheh, a ruined site east of Acre. Some scholars instead place it closer to Jokneam, near the edge of the Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows the Dabsheh identification. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Dalmanutha was a place on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in Mark 8:10. Jesus and his disciples came there by boat after he fed the four thousand. By inference from the following verses, this is where the Pharisees came to argue with him and ask for a sign from heaven. The parallel account in Matt 15:39 says he came instead to "the coasts of Magdala" (Magadan in some manuscripts), and Matthew adds that Sadducees were present too. For this reason Dalmanutha is usually placed near Magdala on the western shore. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest the small valley of 'Ain-el-Barideh ("the cold fountain"), about a mile from Magdala. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the western-shore identification near Magdala.

Dalmatia was a mountainous region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, in what is now coastal Croatia. Its name still survives there today. It is mentioned once in the Bible. In 2 Tim 4:10, Paul writes that Titus had gone to Dalmatia, while Demas had left for Thessalonica and Crescens for Galatia. The letter does not say why Titus went. The name first belonged to the land of the Dalmatae, an Illyrian tribe conquered by Rome. It was later used for the southern part of the Roman province of Illyricum and eventually for the whole province. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks Paul probably meant the whole province. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the region with Paul's own earlier preaching as far as Illyricum, mentioned in Rom 15:19. The location shown here is a point in the central Dalmatian coastal area.

Dannah was a city in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it appears just before Kirjath-sannah, also called Debir (Josh 15:49). Nothing else is said about it in the Bible. Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably south or southwest of Hebron, though no trace of the name had been found. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it about 8 miles southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Idhna, about 8 miles west of Hebron, and the location shown here follows the Idhna identification. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "murmuring," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "judging."

Debir was a place on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in Josh 15:7, where the boundary line ran up toward Debir from the valley of Achor and turned north toward Gilgal, opposite the ascent of Adummim. It is different from the better-known city of Debir (Kiriath-sepher) in the hill country south of Hebron, one of several places with this name. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with a Wadi Dabor near the northwest corner of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Thoghret ed-Debr, a pass near Tal'at ed-Damm and the so-called Inn of the Good Samaritan on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. It also notes that some scholars read the verse as having no place name here at all. The location shown here follows the Jericho-road identification.

Debir was a place on the border of the territory given to the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan. Josh 13:26 names "the border of Debir" alongside Mahanaim in describing Gad's boundary, so it probably lay not far from Mahanaim, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. This Debir is different from the better-known Debir in Judah's hill country, also called Kiriath-sepher. The Revised Version margin reads the name as Lidebir, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Lo-debar, the town where Mephibosheth lived (2 Sam 9:4). Its exact location is uncertain. The same encyclopedia mentions Ibdar, south of the Yarmuk River, as a possible site. The location shown here is in northern Jordan south of the Yarmuk, which fits that suggestion.

Destruction, or the City of Destruction, is a name in Isaiah's prophecy about Egypt turning to the LORD. Isa 19:18 says that five cities in Egypt would speak the language of Canaan and swear by the LORD of hosts, and that one of them would be called "the city of destruction." The Hebrew is Ir-ha-Heres, "city of overthrow." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as a wordplay on Ir-ha-Cheres, "city of the sun," a name for Heliopolis, which is called On elsewhere in the Bible. It also notes that some Hebrew manuscripts read "city of the sun" directly. Easton's Bible Dictionary likewise treats the name as an ideal title for On, or Heliopolis. Other readings of the name exist, and it is not certain that a literal city is meant. The location shown here follows the Heliopolis identification, an ancient site now within northeastern Cairo.

Dibon was a town in Judah where some of the people of Judah settled, along with its surrounding villages, after the return from the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:25). It appears in a list with Kirjath-arba (Hebron) and Jekabzeel, which suggests it lay in the south of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify it with Dimonah, a town in Judah's southern territory (Josh 15:22), and Easton's suggests it is probably the modern ed-Dheib. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate, in the Negev region of southern Judah. This Dibon is distinct from the better-known Dibon east of the Dead Sea in Moab, which shares the same name.

Dilean was a town in the lowlands (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38, where it is named alongside Mizpeh and Joktheel. It appears nowhere else in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gourd," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "cucumber"; Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "that is poor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the English Revised Version spells it "Dilan" and suggests it probably lay north of Lachish and Eglon, judging from the towns listed with it. Its site has not been identified with certainty, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Judean lowlands, west of Hebron.

Dimnah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, one of four Zebulunite towns assigned with their surrounding pasturelands to the Levite families of Merari (Josh 21:35). It is named only here, alongside Nahalal. Its name probably means "dung" or "dunghill" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:77 gives Rimmon in its place, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Dimnah is probably a copyist's variant of Rimmon, the Zebulunite border town also named Rimmon in Josh 19:13. The location shown here follows that identification, placing it in Lower Galilee near the modern village of Rummana, north of Nazareth. If Dimnah was instead a separate town, its site is unknown.

Dimonah was a town in the far south of Judah, listed among the cities of the tribe near the border with Edom (Josh 15:22). It appears only in this list, between Kinah and Adadah, so nothing more is recorded about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same place as Dibon, where people of Judah lived after the return from exile (Neh 11:25). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dunghill." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Negev, in the region east of Beersheba, consistent with the town's place in the list of Judah's southern cities.

Diviners' Oak was a landmark tree near Shechem, mentioned only in Judg 9:37. There Gaal, who had led Shechem in revolt against Abimelech, watched troops approaching the city. One company came down from the high ground, and another came "by the plain of Meonenim," as the King James Version renders it. The Revised Version translates the phrase "the oak of Meonenim." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that Meonenim means "soothsayers" or "diviners," so the name probably points to a tree linked with divination. Easton's also suggests it may be the same oak at Shechem where Abram camped and where Jacob later buried the household's foreign gods (Gen 35:4), though that identification is uncertain. Its exact spot is unknown. The location shown here places it in the area around Shechem, near modern Nablus.

Dizahab is a place named only in Deut 1:1, in a list of landmarks used to locate where Moses spoke his words to all Israel, east of the Jordan in the wilderness, alongside Paran, Tophel, Laban and Hazeroth. The name is usually understood to mean "region of gold." Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Dahab, a cape on the western shore of the Gulf of Aqaba in the Sinai Peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the list seems meant to fix the camp in the plains of Moab, that no place there bears a similar name, and that some names in the list resemble earlier stations of the wilderness journey. It also records Burckhardt's proposal of a harbor called Mina edh-Dhahab on the same gulf. The location shown here follows the Dahab identification on the Gulf of Aqaba.

Dragon Spring, called the "dragon well" in the King James Version and rendered "Jackal Well" in some modern translations, was a water source near Jerusalem. It is mentioned only once, in the account of Nehemiah's night inspection of the ruined city walls. Going out by the Valley Gate, he passed in front of this spring on his way to the Dung Gate, viewing the broken walls and burned gates (Neh 2:13). That route suggests the spring lay outside the walls, along the western or southern side of the city, probably in or near the valley below. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have identified it with the Pool of Gihon, and others have proposed different springs or pools around Jerusalem. This entry follows none of these specific identifications. The location shown here places it only generally within the Jerusalem area.

Dumah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah alongside Arab and Eshean (Josh 15:52). The name means "silence." Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near Hebron and identifies it with the ruins of a village called ed-Daumeh, about six miles southwest of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise places it between Hebron and Beersheba at ed-Daume. The location shown here, southwest of Hebron, matches that identification. The same name belongs to other places and to a son of Ishmael elsewhere in the Bible, and those should be kept distinct from this town in Judah.

Dumah is the name given to the subject of a short prophetic oracle in Isaiah, “the burden of Dumah” (Isa 21:11). In it a voice calls to the prophet out of Seir, the hill country of Edom, asking the watchman what remains of the night. The Hebrew name means “silence.” Interpreters differ on what it refers to. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a symbolic name for Edom, which would fit the mention of Seir. The STEPBible proper names index treats it as a city or region in Arabia. That view connects it with Dumah, a son of Ishmael whose descendants lived in northern Arabia (Gen 25:14), and it is often linked with the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal. The location shown here follows the Arabian identification and is only approximate. The same name belongs to other places in the Bible, including a town in Judah.

Dura was the plain in the province of Babylon where King Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image sixty cubits high and six cubits wide (Dan 3:1). It is mentioned only in this passage. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of the name as "circle." Its exact location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes an older identification with a tract below Tikrit on the Tigris, where the name Dur survives. The French scholar Jules Oppert placed it southeast of Babylon near mounds called Duair, where the base of a huge statue was found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the name refers to a wall or rampart (Babylonian duru) and so points to an area within Babylon itself. The location shown here is rough and places Dura at or very near the city of Babylon.

East Gate was a gate in Jerusalem mentioned once, in the account of the rebuilding of the city wall under Nehemiah. Shemaiah son of Shechaniah, called its keeper, repaired a section of the wall near the house of Zadok son of Immer (Neh 3:29). Because it had an appointed keeper and appears in the stretch of wall near the temple, it was probably a gate on the east side of the temple area rather than simply an outer city gate. Several gates in the Bible share this name, including the eastern gates of the temple in Ezekiel's vision, so the exact identity is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the eastern side of the Temple Mount, near the site of the later Golden Gate.

East Gate is the King James rendering of a gate of Jerusalem mentioned in Jer 19:2, where God sends Jeremiah to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, beside this gate's entrance, to proclaim judgment on Judah. The Hebrew name, Harsith, is understood in two ways. The King James Version takes it from a word for "sun," giving "east gate" (its margin has "sun gate"). Modern versions, following the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's view, read it as "Potsherd Gate." Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it the Potter's Gate, leading to the potter's field. The setting fits the potsherd reading, since Jeremiah breaks a potter's clay jar there. This entry follows the Potsherd Gate reading. The gate probably stood on Jerusalem's southern side, facing the Hinnom Valley, but its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here places it only generally within the city. It is distinct from other "east gates" in the Bible, such as those of the temple.

Ebez (spelled Abez in the King James Version) was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar, listed among its cities in Josh 19:20 alongside Rabbith and Kishion. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it at the north of the plain of Esdraelon and suggests the ruins of el-Beida, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name seems related to that of the judge Ibzan and regards everything else about it as conjecture. The location shown here follows an identification with Al-Bathan, a site in the hill country northeast of modern Nablus.

Ebron was a town on the northern border of the tribe of Asher, listed with Rehob, Hammon and Kanah in the description of Asher's territory reaching toward Sidon (Josh 19:28). The Hebrew name is Ebron, but the King James Version renders it "Hebron," which can be confused with the well-known Hebron in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a copyist's variant of Abdon, a Levitical city in Asher (Josh 21:30; 1 Chr 6:74), because the Hebrew letters for "r" and "d" are easily confused. The location shown here follows that Abdon identification. It places the town in western Galilee, probably at Tel Avdon (Khirbet Abdeh), inland from the Mediterranean coast near modern Nahariya. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Ecbatana, called Achmetha in the King James Version, was a city in the province of the Medes. According to Ezra 6:2, a scroll was found in its royal citadel or palace. The verses that follow show that it recorded King Cyrus's decree for rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, which was searched for under Darius. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Ecbatana as the old capital of the Median kings, where Cyrus held his court. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that Persian kings spent their summers there and kept royal archives in its citadel. Greek writers mention more than one Ecbatana, and Smith's Bible Dictionary links one of them with the ruins at Takht-i-Suleiman in northwestern Iran. The Ecbatana of Ezra is usually identified with the ancient city beneath modern Hamadan in western Iran, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Eder, called the "tower of Edar" in the King James Version, was a place where Israel (Jacob) set up his tent as he traveled south (Gen 35:21). The surrounding passage shows this was soon after Rachel died and was buried on the road to Bethlehem, and Gen 35:22 places Reuben's affair with Bilhah during the stay there. The name means "flock," so the phrase is usually understood as "tower of the flock," probably a watchtower used by shepherds. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Bethlehem and Hebron. It also links it with the "tower of the flock" in Mic 4:8, where the phrase points to Bethlehem and the royal line of David. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is in the Bethlehem area. The same name is used elsewhere in the Bible for a different place, a town in southern Judah (Josh 15:21).

Eder was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:21 among the "uttermost cities" of the tribe toward the border of Edom, alongside Kabzeel and Jagur. It belonged to the Negev district of Judah's territory. The name means "flock," and other places in the Bible share it, such as the Tower of Edar near Bethlehem (Gen 35:21). The site has not been securely identified. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no trace of it had been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Khirbet el-Adar, about 5 miles south of Gaza, as a possibility, but itself judges that site probably too far west for a town near Edom. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev southeast of Beersheba, consistent with the town's listing near the Edomite border rather than with any particular ruin.

Eglaim was a place in Moab mentioned only in Isaiah's oracle against Moab. There the cry of mourning over Moab's ruin is said to reach Eglaim and Beer-elim (Isa 15:8). Since the verse speaks of the cry going round the borders of Moab, the two places probably marked distant points of Moabite territory. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take the name to mean "two ponds" and suggest it is the same as En-eglaim of Ezek 47:10. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it possibly in southern Moab and notes that Eusebius's Onomasticon identified it with Agallim, a village eight Roman miles south of Areopolis. It adds that the site cannot now be identified with certainty. The location shown here is approximate, in southern Moab near the southeastern end of the Dead Sea, following the southern Moab view.

The Egyptian Sea is a body of water named in Isaiah's prophecy that the LORD would "utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea" and dry up "the river" into seven streams so that people could cross on foot (Isa 11:15). In the context of the chapter, this clears the way for scattered Israelites to return from Egypt and Assyria, and it probably echoes the crossing of the sea in the Exodus. The "river" is usually taken to be the Euphrates. Most interpreters identify the "tongue" of the Egyptian Sea as the Gulf of Suez, the northwestern arm of the Red Sea. Others suggest a branch of the Nile or the Mediterranean coast near Egypt. The location shown here follows the Red Sea identification and is placed only generally in the northern Red Sea.

El-bethel, meaning "God of Bethel," is the name Jacob gave to the place where he built an altar after returning from Paddan-aram. Genesis 35:7 explains the name: this was where God had appeared to him when he fled from his brother Esau. That earlier appearance is the vision of the ladder at Bethel described in Gen 28, so El-bethel is the altar site at Bethel, the town once called Luz. The surrounding verses of Gen 35 make the same link when God sends Jacob back to Bethel. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the scene of Jacob's vision. The location shown here lies at or near Bethel, which is commonly identified with the modern village of Beitin, north of Jerusalem.

El-elohe-Israel was the name Jacob gave to an altar he built after returning from Paddan-aram (Gen 33:20). The name means "God, the God of Israel." The preceding verse places the altar on a plot of ground Jacob bought outside the city of Shechem, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as facing the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name to the night at Peniel, when Jacob received the new name Israel (Gen 32:28). On that reading, Jacob dedicated his first altar in the land to God under the name now tied to his own. The same work notes other readings. The Greek Septuagint has "he called upon the God of Israel," and some scholars read "pillar" instead of "altar." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it at ancient Shechem, near modern Nablus.

El-paran was a place at the edge of the wilderness, named once in the Bible as the farthest point reached by Chedorlaomer and his allied kings when they struck the Horites of Mount Seir (Gen 14:6). The text describes it only as being "by the wilderness." By inference from the name and context, that wilderness is probably the Wilderness of Paran, the broad desert south of Canaan. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "the terebinth of Paran," suggesting a landmark tree or grove. According to the next verse, the kings then turned back toward En-mishpat, or Kadesh. Its exact site is unknown. Some identify it with Elath at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Sinai Peninsula, within the general region of the Wilderness of Paran.

Elishah was a coastal or island region of the Mediterranean, known in the Bible only as a source of fine dyed cloth. In Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, the city is pictured as a splendid merchant ship whose awning was made of blue and purple cloth from "the isles of Elishah" (Ezek 27:7). The name probably goes back to Elishah, a son of Javan in the table of nations (Gen 10:4), whose descendants were linked with the Greek-speaking peoples. Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Elis and the Peloponnesus in southern Greece. Many scholars instead identify it with Cyprus, often linked with Alashiya, a name for Cyprus in ancient texts outside the Bible. Others have suggested Sicily or southern Italy. The location shown here follows the Cyprus identification.

Elon was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan when the land was divided under Joshua. It is named only once, in the list of Danite towns, between Jethlah and Thimnathah (Timnah), near Ekron (Josh 19:43). The name means "oak" or "terebinth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Elon-beth-hanan, which belonged to one of Solomon's provision districts along with Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kgs 4:9). It also notes Conder's proposal of Beit 'Anan, northwest of Nebi Samwil. The site has not been firmly identified, and the location shown here is an approximate placement within the Danite region in the hills west of Jerusalem.

Elonbeth-hanan was a town listed in the second of King Solomon's twelve administrative districts. Each district was run by an officer who supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. This district was under the son of Dekar (Ben-deker) and also included Makaz, Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named alongside towns belonging to the tribe of Dan, which places it in the lowlands west of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the house of grace or mercy," and Smith's renders it "oak of the house of grace." Some connect it with Elon, a Danite town named in Josh 19:43. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here matches the area of the village of Beit Anan, northwest of Jerusalem, which has been proposed because the name is similar.

Elteke (spelled Eltekeh in the King James Version) was a city in the territory of the tribe of Dan. Joshua 21:23 lists it with Gibbethon among the Danite towns given, together with their surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it was assigned to the Kohathite clan. The town also appears in Dan's allotment in Josh 19:44. Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Beit Likia (Beit Liqya), northeast of Latrun in the hills west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification. Others place it farther west on the coastal plain near Ekron and connect it with Altaqu, a town named in Assyrian records of Sennacherib's campaign.

Eltekeh was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It is named only in the list of Dan's towns, alongside Gibbethon and Baalath (Josh 19:44). According to Smith's Bible Dictionary, a later passage (Josh 21:23) records that Eltekeh and its surrounding pasturelands were given to the Kohathite Levites as one of the Levitical cities. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "God is its fear" and identifies the site with Beit-Likia, northeast of Latrun, in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Other identifications of the site have been proposed, so its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Beit-Likia identification.

Eltekon was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in Josh 15:59 in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah. It appears in a group of six cities with their villages, alongside Maarath and Beth-anoth, and is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "founded by God." Because Eltekon is listed next to Beth-anoth, that encyclopedia places it a little north of Hebron, while noting that its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate placement in the Judean hills northwest of Hebron, consistent with that general area. No specific modern site is firmly identified.

Emek-keziz was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Josh 18:21 after Jericho and Beth-hoglah. The King James Version translates the name as "the valley of Keziz." Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "abrupt" or "cut off." It is mentioned only in this list of Benjamin's cities. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears between Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah. For that reason it probably lay in the Jordan plain, perhaps south of Jericho. Its exact site is unknown and the name has not survived in any modern place name. The location shown here is a rough placement in the lower Jordan Valley near Jericho, inferred from its neighbours in the list.

Emmaus was a village about sixty furlongs (roughly seven miles) from Jerusalem, to which two followers of Jesus were walking on the day of his resurrection (Luke 24:13). The following verses of the passage tell how Jesus joined them on the road unrecognized, and they name one of the travelers as Cleopas. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hot baths." Its site has long been disputed, and Smith's Bible Dictionary considered it still unidentified. Easton's notes proposals at el-Kubeibeh, northwest of Jerusalem, and at Khurbet Khamasa, southwest of the city. Another identification is Emmaus Nicopolis, modern Imwas near Latrun, about 18 miles west of Jerusalem. That distance fits better with the reading of 160 furlongs found in some ancient manuscripts. The location shown here follows the Emmaus Nicopolis (Imwas) identification.

En-gannim was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:34, where it appears between Zanoah and Tappuah. Its name means "spring of gardens." Nothing else is recorded about it in the Bible. The name is shared by another place, a Levitical town of the same name in the territory of Issachar, which should not be confused with this one. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify this Judean town with the modern site of Umm Jina, near Zanoah, south of the Wadi es-Sarar (the Sorek valley). The location shown here follows that identification, in the hill country west of Jerusalem.

En-haddah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar when the land was divided under Joshua. It is mentioned only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, where it appears next to En-gannim, Remeth and Beth-pazzez (Josh 19:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "swift fountain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "well of gladness." Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it is probably the village of Kefr Adan, about 3 miles (5 km) west of Jenin, near the En-gannim with which it is listed. Other scholars have proposed sites farther north, closer to Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows the Kefr Adan identification.

En-hakkore was a spring at Lehi in Judah that, according to Judg 15:19, God opened from a hollow place after Samson had killed a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Exhausted and thirsty, Samson drank and revived, and he named the spring En-hakkore. The narrator notes that it was still there at Lehi "unto this day." The preceding verse (Judg 15:18) records Samson calling out to God in his thirst, which explains the name. Easton's and Hitchcock's dictionaries render it "spring of him who called," as the Septuagint does. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew could also mean "spring of the partridge." The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the spring 'Ayun Kara near Zorah, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unknown. The rough location shown here follows the identification near Zorah.

En-hazor was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, listed with Kedesh and Edrei in Josh 19:37. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts it among Naphtali's fortified cities, based on the surrounding list, and treats it as a different place from the better-known Hazor. The name means "spring of Hazor" according to Smith's, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the grass of the well." Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary left it unidentified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name survives in Hazireh, on the slopes west of Kedesh in upper Galilee, though it notes that no spring has been found there to match the "En" (spring) in the name. The location shown here, in the hills west of Kedesh in northern Galilee, appears to follow that identification.

En-mishpat was an older name for Kadesh, a spring site in the wilderness south of Canaan. It appears only in Gen 14:7, where the four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer turned back to En-mishpat during their campaign and then struck the country of the Amalekites and the Amorites living in Hazazon-tamar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'fountain of judgment,' and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the place as Kadesh-barnea, the oasis where Israel later camped during the wilderness years. That link to Kadesh-barnea is an inference from the shared name Kadesh. The location shown here, in northeastern Sinai near the springs often associated with Kadesh-barnea, follows that identification. The exact site of Kadesh is still debated.

En-rimmon was one of the towns in southern Judah where people of Judah settled after returning from exile in Babylon, listed alongside Zareah and Jarmuth (Neh 11:29). The name probably means “spring of the pomegranate.” Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest it is the same place as the “Ain and Rimmon” given to Judah and later to Simeon (Josh 15:32; Josh 19:7; 1 Chr 4:32). That would make it a far southern town near the Negev. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius described it as a very large village south of Eleutheropolis. It identifies the site with Khirbet Umm er-Rumamin, about 9 miles (15 km) north of Beersheba. The location shown here follows that identification.

En-tappuah, meaning "spring of the apple" (or "apple spring"), was a spring on the border of the tribe of Manasseh. Joshua 17:7 traces Manasseh's boundary from Asher to Michmethah, near Shechem, and then along to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. By inference from the following verse, it was probably the spring of the town of Tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself, on the border, belonged to Ephraim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the boundary running south, east of Shechem. Both it and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify it with a spring at or near Yasuf, about 3 miles north of Lebonah. The location shown here, south of Shechem, follows that identification with the Yasuf area.

Enam was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It is listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah, alongside Zanoah, Engannim and Tappuah (Josh 15:34). This is its only mention in the Bible, and nothing is recorded about events there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "double spring," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fountain" or "open place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it together with Enaim, the place by the road to Timnah where Tamar sat (Gen 38:14), which suggests the two may be the same town. The exact site of Enam is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate.

Eneglaim was a place on the shore of the Dead Sea, named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's vision of the restored land. In that vision a river flows from the temple and turns the salt water fresh, so that fishermen spread their nets along the shore "from Engedi even unto Eneglaim" (Ezek 47:10). Its name probably means "spring of the two calves." The verse marks the two ends of a stretch of shoreline, so Eneglaim was evidently some distance from Engedi, but its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary says it cannot be determined which side of the sea it lay on. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it near the Jordan's mouth, noting Tristram's identification with 'Ain Hajlah and Robinson's with 'Ain Feshkah. The location shown here is rough and follows a different view, placing it near the southern end of the Dead Sea.

Ephah was a people and region of northern Arabia, named in Isa 60:6 alongside Midian and Sheba as sources of the camels and dromedaries that would come to Jerusalem bearing gold and incense. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Ephah as an Arabian tribe known for its camels. Its pairing with Midian fits Gen 25:4 and 1 Chr 1:33, which name Ephah as a son of Midian, so the tribe was probably understood as descended from him and closely linked to the Midianites. Its exact territory is unknown. The location shown here is approximate, placing it in northwestern Arabia near the Gulf of Aqaba, within the general area associated with Midian. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "weary" or "tired."

Ephes-dammim was the place in Judah where the Philistines camped before the battle in which David fought Goliath. It lay between Shochoh and Azekah, in the hill country west of Bethlehem overlooking the valley of Elah (1 Sam 17:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify it with Pas-dammim, where a later clash with the Philistines took place (1 Chr 11:13). The name is usually explained as "boundary of blood," which Easton's links to repeated fighting there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests instead that it may come from the deep red color of the local soil. Easton's connects the site with the modern Beit Fased near Shochoh, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the exact spot as undetermined. The location shown here is a point between Shochoh and Azekah, matching the description in 1 Sam 17:1.

Ephraim was a town near the wilderness where Jesus went with his disciples after he stopped moving openly among the Jews (John 11:54). The surrounding chapter shows that this withdrawal followed the raising of Lazarus and the council's decision to put Jesus to death, so it was probably a retreat to a quieter place before the final Passover, about AD 30 by inference from context. The text says only that Jesus stayed there with his disciples. The site is uncertain. It is commonly identified with the modern village of et-Taiyibeh (Taybeh), northeast of Jerusalem on the edge of the Judean wilderness, and some link it with the Old Testament towns of Ophrah or Ephron. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fruitful" or "increasing."

Ephron was a place on the boundary between the tribal territories of Benjamin and Judah, west of Jerusalem. Joshua 18:15 describes Benjamin's southern border running from the edge of Kirjath-jearim to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. The King James wording here does not use the name: where it reads "went out on the west," the place is identified only by inference from the parallel description of Judah's northern border in Josh 15:9, which mentions "the cities of mount Ephron" on the same stretch between Nephtoah and Kirjath-jearim. Several different places in the Bible share the name Ephron, and the exact site of this one is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dust."

Ephron was a town in the hill country north of Jerusalem, one of the places King Abijah of Judah took from Jeroboam of Israel after defeating him, along with its surrounding villages, Bethel and Jeshanah (2 Chr 13:19). The King James Version spells it "Ephrain", and the Hebrew text has both spellings. Its grouping with Bethel suggests it lay near the border between Judah and Israel. Many scholars identify it with the modern village of et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Bethel, and link it with Ophrah and with the Ephraim to which Jesus withdrew in John 11:54. The location shown here follows the et-Taiyibeh identification, though the identification is not certain. The name also belongs to Mount Ephron on Judah's border and to Ephron the Hittite, and should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "dust".

Esek was a well dug by Isaac's servants in the valley of Gerar, in the southern land where Isaac had settled. The herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen over it, claiming the water as theirs, so Isaac named the well Esek, meaning "contention" or "quarrel" (Gen 26:20). The surrounding narrative shows Isaac then moving on to dig another disputed well, Sitnah, and finally an undisputed one, Rehoboth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Esek near Gerar and Rehoboth but notes that the site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Gerar, in the western Negev of modern southern Israel, and does not mark a known site.

Eshan was a town in the hill country of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:52). The King James Version spells it "Eshean." It appears alongside Arab and Dumah in a group of towns in the uplands around Hebron. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the ruin of es-Simia near Dumah, south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia holds that no satisfactory identification has been found and notes a suggestion that the name may be a variant form of Beersheba. The location shown here lies close to Dumah, south-west of Hebron, and so follows the es-Simia identification.

Eshtemoh was a town in the hill country of Judah. It is named once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, between Anab and Anim (Josh 15:50). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Eshtemoa, a spelling found elsewhere. Under that name, connected passages describe it as a town assigned to the priests (Josh 21:14; 1 Chr 6:57) and as one of the places to which David sent spoil after defeating the Amalekites (1 Sam 30:28). The town is commonly identified with the modern village of es-Samu, about 9 miles (14 km) south of Hebron, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Etam was a town of the tribe of Simeon, named in 1 Chr 4:32 alongside Ain, Rimmon, Tochen and Ashan as one of the villages where the Simeonites lived. It appears only in this list. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:7 names Ain, Remmon, Ether and Ashan, so Smith's Bible Dictionary links the two passages, and Etam may correspond to the Ether of Joshua. The name is shared by other places in the Bible, including the rock where Samson stayed after fighting the Philistines (Judg 15:8) and a town near Bethlehem in Judah. This entry treats the Simeonite town as a separate place. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports Conder's identification with Khirbet Aitun in the hills northwest of Beersheba, and the rough location shown here follows that identification.

Etam was a city of Judah that King Rehoboam built up as a fortified town, listed with Bethlehem and Tekoa in 2 Chr 11:6. The surrounding passage presents it as one of the defensive cities he strengthened after the kingdom divided. Its place in that list suggests it lay near Bethlehem, in the hill country to the south. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus and the Talmud place there the springs that supplied Solomon's pools, Bethlehem and the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with 'Ain 'Atan, a strong spring at the head of the Wadi Urtas. The location shown here is Khirbet el-Khokh, a site in the same area near modern Artas. The name is shared by other places, including the rock of Etam where Samson took refuge (Judg 15:8) and a town of Simeon (1 Chr 4:32). These may be different places.

Eth-kazin was a town on the eastern border of the tribe of Zebulun. Josh 19:13 names it in the description of that boundary, between Gath-hepher (Gittah-hepher) and Rimmon, near Neah. The King James Version spells it Ittah-kazin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that this spelling comes from reading the Hebrew ending that means "toward" as part of the name itself, so the town's name is properly Eth-kazin. Its site has not been identified. The location shown here is approximate, in Lower Galilee near Gath-hepher, by inference from its place in the boundary list. Nothing else is recorded about the town.

Fair Havens was a harbor on the south coast of Crete where the ship carrying Paul to Rome stopped after a difficult passage along the island, near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary says the ship waited there a considerable time for a favorable wind. The ship's master and owner then chose to sail on against Paul's advice, because the harbor was not suitable for spending the winter (Acts 27:9–12). The ship was later wrecked on Malta. By inference from context, this happened about AD 56. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no other ancient writing mentions the harbor, but it is still known by its Greek name, Kaloi Limenes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 5 miles east of Cape Matala, in a bay open to the east and sheltered by two small islands. The location shown here matches that modern site.

Forest, more fully the House of the Forest, appears in Isa 22:8 as the place where Judah's armour was stored. Isaiah says that when Judah's defences were laid bare, the people looked to the weapons kept there. By inference from connected passages, this is the House of the Forest of Lebanon, a large hall Solomon built in Jerusalem. 1 Kgs 7:2 describes it as supported by rows of cedar pillars, which probably explains the name. 1 Kgs 10:17 says Solomon placed gold shields in it, which fits its use as an armoury. The building no longer survives, so its exact position is unknown. The location shown here places it within Jerusalem, near the royal and temple quarter. The Hebrew word for "forest" also has its ordinary meaning elsewhere, but this entry concerns only the building.

Gabbatha was the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat on the judgment seat to give his verdict at the trial of Jesus. John 19:13 calls it in Greek "the Pavement" and gives Gabbatha as its Hebrew (probably Aramaic) name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to mean "height" or "ridge." The Pavement was probably a stone-paved or mosaic platform outside the governor's residence, since Pilate brought Jesus out to it. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the temple mount by the fortress of Antonia, and a long tradition links it with a stretch of Roman paving near the "Ecce Homo" arch. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on the western hill, by Herod's palace. The location shown here is approximate and follows the temple-mount view.

Gamad is known only from Ezek 27:11, where the Gammadim (the people of Gamad) stood in the towers of Tyre and hung their shields on its walls. They appear next to the men of Arvad in Ezekiel's lament over the city. Whether Gamad was a place or a description of a group is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads the word as a term for a class of fighting men, such as "brave warriors," "valorous men," "short-swordsmen" or "daring ones," who defended Tyre's towers. Others take it as the name of a people or town that supplied soldiers to Tyre. The location shown here is rough. It places Gamad on the Syrian coast near Arvad, probably by inference from the two being named together in the verse.

Gareb was a hill near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer 31:39. In Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's rebuilding, a measuring line would run out over the hill Gareb and then around to Goath, marking a wider boundary for the restored city. By inference from the passage, the hill then lay outside or at the edge of the city. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a scab," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the hill of lepers, which would explain its place outside the city. The STEPBible proper names index describes it as a hill that was to be brought within Jerusalem's future boundaries. Its exact site is unknown. Some place it to the west or northwest of the ancient city, though this is uncertain. The location shown here is a general point within Jerusalem.

Gate Miphkad, called the Muster Gate in the ESV, was a gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. It is mentioned only once, in the list of workers who rebuilt the city wall after the return from exile. Malchiah, a goldsmith's son, repaired the stretch of wall as far as the house of the temple servants (the Nethinim) and of the merchants, opposite this gate, and up to the upper room at the corner (Neh 3:31). The Hebrew name probably means "appointment" or "mustering," which suggests a place where people were counted or assembled, though the text does not explain its use. Since the list runs around the wall in order, the gate was probably on the east side of the city, north of the temple area and near the wall's northeast corner. Its exact position is uncertain, and the location shown here is an approximate placement within Jerusalem.

n: Gate of the Children of the People
bio: The Gate of the Children of the People (called the People's Gate in some modern translations) was a gate of Jerusalem mentioned only in Jer 17:19. The LORD told Jeremiah to stand there, and then in all the gates of the city, to deliver a message about keeping the sabbath. The verse describes it as the gate through which the kings of Judah came in and went out, which suggests it was a main entrance used by the royal court and the general population. Its exact position is not known. Some have linked it with a gate near the palace or the temple, but the text gives no further detail. The location shown here is a general point within ancient Jerusalem rather than a precise site for the gate.

The Gate of the Foundation was a gate in Jerusalem, mentioned once, in the account of the priest Jehoiada's plan to crown the young Joash king in place of Queen Athaliah. Jehoiada divided the priests and Levites on duty into three groups: one at the king's house, one at the Gate of the Foundation, and the rest of the people in the temple courts (2 Chr 23:5). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 11:6 seems to call the same gate "the gate of Sur," so the two names probably refer to one entrance. Its exact position is unknown. Given the setting, it was probably connected with the temple or the royal palace beside it. The location shown here places it generally within Jerusalem near the temple area rather than at an identified site.

Gath-rimmon was a town in the territory of the half tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan. Along with Taanach, it was given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:25). The name, meaning "press of the pomegranate," is shared with a Levitical city of Dan listed just before it, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name here probably arose from a copying error. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:70 gives Bileam in its place, which Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to be Ibleam. Early Greek manuscripts give other names, such as "Baithsa" and "Jebatha." The location shown here follows the Ibleam identification, probably the modern site of Khirbet Belameh near Jenin.

Geba is the starting point of David's pursuit of the Philistines after his victory in the valley of Rephaim. He struck them down "from Geba until thou come to Gazer," driving them west toward the coastal plain (2 Sam 5:25). Several places in the Bible share this name. The best-known Geba is a town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, usually placed at the modern village of Jaba. The parallel account in 1 Chr 14:16, however, reads "from Gibeon" instead of "from Geba," and many readers take the two names to refer to the same starting point. The location shown here follows that Gibeon reading, at the site of el-Jib northwest of Jerusalem. Either way, the route ran from the hill country of Benjamin to Gezer at the edge of the lowlands. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a hill" or "cup."

Gebim was a small town north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible. In Isaiah's poem of an army advancing on Jerusalem (Isa 10:28–32), usually understood as the Assyrian army, its people gather to flee as the invader approaches (Isa 10:31). The name is usually explained as meaning "cisterns" or "trenches," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "grasshoppers." Its exact site is uncertain. The surrounding list of towns runs toward Jerusalem, and Gebim comes after Anathoth and Madmenah and just before Nob. On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between Anathoth and the ridge of Nob. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as probably the modern village of el-Isawiyeh, northeast of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another proposal, Jebia, farther north toward Shechem. The location shown here follows the el-Isawiyeh identification.

Geder was a Canaanite city whose king appears among the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan defeated by Joshua and the Israelites. Its only mention is in that list, where it comes next to Debir (Josh 12:13). The name probably means "wall," which may suggest a walled town (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same as Gedor in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:58). Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with the Geder of 1 Chr 4:39. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with Beth-gader (1 Chr 2:51) and with the home of Baal-hanan the Gederite (1 Chr 27:28). The location shown here follows the Gedor identification, a site in the hills north of Hebron, probably modern Khirbet Jedur.

Gederothaim was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:36, directly after Gederah. The name probably means "two sheepfolds" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "place of enclosures" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The verse closes its group with "fourteen cities," yet fifteen names appear. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have arisen when a scribe accidentally repeated the preceding Gederah. The Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "and its cattle shelters" rather than as a separate town. Others treat it as a distinct town. Its site is not known. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Judean lowland near Gederah.

Gedor was a place where clans of the tribe of Simeon went looking for pasture for their flocks, reaching its entrance as far as the east side of the valley (1 Chr 4:39). The surrounding passage says they found good, quiet pasture there, drove out the earlier inhabitants, including the Meunim, and settled in their place, in the days of King Hezekiah (1 Chr 4:40–41). The name is shared by other places in the Bible, and this Gedor's location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Gederah of Josh 15:36, in the lowland of Judah, or with Gerar, where the patriarchs grazed their flocks. The Greek Septuagint reads "Gerar" here, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers that reading probably correct. The location shown here follows the Gederah identification, near modern Gedera in Israel's coastal plain.

Geliloth was a landmark on the southern boundary of the tribe of Benjamin, where it met the territory of Judah. Josh 18:17 traces the border from En-shemesh toward Geliloth, "over against the going up of Adummim," and then down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. The name means "circles" or "regions." The parallel description of Judah's northern border in Josh 15:7 names Gilgal at the same point, and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries take Geliloth to be that place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead places it on the road climbing from Jericho toward the Ascent of Adummim, about 6 miles (10 km) from Jerusalem, and says no exact site can be fixed. The location shown here, in the Jordan Valley near Jericho, follows the Gilgal identification.

Geruth Chimham was a stopping place near Bethlehem where Johanan and the Judean survivors stayed on their way to Egypt (Jer 41:17). From the surrounding chapter, this was after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, the governor Babylon had appointed, when the group feared Babylonian reprisal. The Hebrew geruth is usually taken to mean a lodging place, and the King James Version renders it "habitation." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be an inn or khan on land at Bethlehem that David gave to Chimham, probably the son of Barzillai the Gileadite, who went with David to Jerusalem after Absalom's defeat (2 Sam 19:37–40). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a lodging place on the highway to Egypt, though it also notes that Josephus reads the word as "sheep pens." The location shown here is an approximate spot near Bethlehem.

Giah was a place near Gibeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Sam 2:24. After the battle at the pool of Gibeon, Joab and Abishai chased Abner. At sunset they reached the hill of Ammah, which lay "before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon." Giah is named only to fix where that hill stood. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a waterfall." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads it as Gai, matching the Hebrew word for "valley," and suggests the Hebrew form may have come from a copying error. The location shown here is a rough placement east of Gibeon, toward the wilderness, based on the verse's description of the route.

Gibeath-elohim, meaning "hill of God," was a place in the territory of Benjamin. It is named only in 1 Sam 10:5, where Samuel tells the newly anointed Saul that he will come there. He says a Philistine garrison is stationed at the site and that Saul will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, playing a lyre, tambourine, flute and harp as they prophesy. The verse also calls it a city. Its identification is uncertain. STEPBible Proper Names places it near Gibeah. Some readers take it to be Gibeah itself, since 1 Sam 10:10 says Saul met the prophets at "the hill." Others link it with Geba, where a Philistine garrison is mentioned in 1 Sam 13:3. The location shown here is only approximate, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.

Gibeath-haaraloth, meaning "hill of the foreskins," was the place where Joshua circumcised the Israelites with flint knives soon after they crossed the Jordan River into Canaan (Josh 5:3). The King James Version translates the name as "the hill of the foreskins" instead of giving it as a proper name. The surrounding chapter places the Israelite camp at Gilgal, and the circumcision is linked there to the naming of Gilgal, so the hill was probably at or near Gilgal in the Jordan Valley east of Jericho. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here, in the plain near Jericho, follows that inference.

Gidom was a place named only in Judg 20:45, in the account of the war between the other Israelite tribes and Benjamin after the outrage at Gibeah. As the defeated Benjamites fled toward the wilderness and the rock of Rimmon, Israel pursued them hard as far as Gidom and killed two thousand of them there. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it between Gibeah and the cliff of Rimmon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as the eastward limit of the pursuit from Gibeah toward the wilderness and notes that no modern place name preserving it has been found. Its exact site is therefore unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the hill country northeast of Gibeah, between Gibeah and Rimmon, by inference from the passage. The name has been taken to mean "desolation" or "cutting down."

Gilo, also spelled Giloh, was a town in the hill country of Judah. It appears here only indirectly, in the word "Gilonite" (someone from Gilo), used of Ahithophel, the father of Eliam, one of David's mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:34). Other passages give more about the town. Josh 15:51 lists Giloh among the towns of Judah's hill country. 2 Sam 15:12 says that Absalom sent for Ahithophel, David's counsellor, from his city Giloh when he began his revolt. The exact site is uncertain. It is often identified with Khirbet Jala, a few miles north-west of Hebron, and the location shown here lies in that part of the Judean hills.

Gimzo was a town of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible, near the edge of the Philistine plain. It was one of several towns in the low country and the south of Judah, along with their surrounding villages, that the Philistines captured and settled. The surrounding chapter places this in the reign of King Ahaz (2 Chr 28:18). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "fertile in sycamores," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "that bulrush." The site is generally identified with the modern village of Jimzu, about 3 to 3.5 miles (5 to 6 km) southeast of Lod (ancient Lydda), on an old route toward Jerusalem, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe. The location shown here follows that identification.

Goah was a place near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer 31:39, where the King James Version spells it Goath. In Jeremiah's prophecy of the city's future rebuilding, a measuring line goes out over the hill Gareb and then turns around to Goah, marking part of the boundary of the restored city. The surrounding verses describe the city's edges, so Goah was probably a point on the west or south side of Jerusalem, but its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a lowing" (the sound of cattle). Because no precise site has been identified, the location shown here simply places it at Jerusalem.

Gog is a name that appears with Magog in Rev 20:8, where Satan, released at the end of the thousand years, goes out to deceive the nations in the four quarters of the earth, called "Gog and Magog," and gathers them for battle in numbers like the sand of the sea. The pairing draws on Ezek 38–39, where Gog is a ruler "of the land of Magog" who invades Israel from the far north and is destroyed. In Revelation the two names seem to stand for the hostile nations as a whole rather than for one territory. Treated as a region, its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a view placing it in the steppes of Central Asia north of the Hindu Kush. The location shown here is a general area north of the Caucasus near the northern Caspian Sea, matching the "north country" of Ezekiel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "roof; covering."

Gudgodah was a stopping place of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. Deut 10:7 says they traveled there after leaving Mosera, where Aaron died according to the preceding verse, and went on from Gudgodah to Jotbath, described as a land of streams of water. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hor-hagidgad, the stop between Bene-jaakan and Jotbathah in the itinerary of Num 33:32, and notes that the Greek Septuagint calls both places Gadgad. The site has not been identified with certainty. The same encyclopedia suggests the old name may survive in Wadi Gudaghid, a tributary of Wadi Jerafeh that runs down into the Arabah valley roughly due west of Petra, though the consonants do not match exactly. The rough location shown here is in that area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "happiness."

Gur was a place near Ibleam, in the hill country at the southern edge of the plain of Jezreel. It is mentioned only once, as "the going up to Gur." There Jehu's men struck King Ahaziah of Judah in his chariot as he fled after Jehu killed Joram of Israel. Ahaziah escaped to Megiddo and died there (2 Kgs 9:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as an ascent rising from the plain of Jezreel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it a rise in the ground. Easton's and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "whelp," while Smith's gives "abode." The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Ibleam, which is probably the modern Khirbet Belameh near Jenin.

Gurbaal was a place or district where certain Arabians lived, mentioned only in 2 Chr 26:7. That verse says God helped King Uzziah of Judah against the Philistines, against these Arabians, and against the Mehunims.
