The name is usually taken to mean "dwelling of Baal," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests a temple of Baal probably stood there. The exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it, from the context, somewhere between Palestine and the Arabian peninsula. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) reads Gerar, perhaps because the Philistines are named just before. It also notes that the link with the Mehunims points eastward, possibly to a sanctuary on a mountain near Petra. The location shown here is approximate and follows the eastern view, placing Gurbaal in the highlands of Edom in southern Jordan.

Hadad-rimmon is a place named once, in Zech 12:11, where the prophet compares a coming great mourning in Jerusalem to "the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon." Its name combines two names of Syrian gods. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it as a place in the valley of Megiddo and connect the mourning with the lament for King Josiah, who was mortally wounded in battle near Megiddo (2 Kgs 23:29; 2 Chr 35:22–25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view: the name may join two divine names, and the weeping may be ritual mourning for a god such as Tammuz (compare Ezek 8:14). Jerome identified it with Maximianopolis, near Jezreel. Easton's identifies it with the modern village of Rummaneh at the foot of the Megiddo hills, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Hadashah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns of the Shephelah, the lowland hills of western Judah, where it is named between Zenan and Migdalgad (Josh 15:37). The name means "new." The Mishnah, as reported by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, calls it the smallest town in Judah. Its site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the Adasa mentioned in the history of the Maccabees, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unidentified. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Ibdis, in the southern coastal plain of Israel, which fits the town's place in the Shephelah list.

Hadrach was a region in Syria, named only once in the Bible, in Zechariah's oracle that opens "the burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach," with Damascus as its resting place (Zech 9:1). The following verses group it with Hamath, Tyre and Sidon as targets of the same judgment (Zech 9:2). Its exact location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Hatarikka, a land in Assyrian inscriptions that Assyrian kings campaigned against in the 8th century BC, placed north of Lebanon, probably near Hamath. Easton's Bible Dictionary records Rawlinson's suggestion of Edessa. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as lost. The location shown here is a rough point in the Hatarikka area of northern Syria, between Hamath and Aleppo, following that identification.

Haeleph was a town given to the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:28. The King James Version spells it Eleph. The Hebrew form includes the definite article, "the Eleph," which gives the spelling Haeleph. It appears in the last group of fourteen cities, alongside Zelah and Jebusi (Jerusalem), so it probably lay in the hill country near Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the view that identifies it with Lifta, an abandoned village on the northwestern edge of modern Jerusalem. Other scholars connect Lifta instead with Nephtoah, a spring on the border between Judah and Benjamin.

Hahiroth is a shortened form of Pi-hahiroth, the place where the Israelites camped just before passing through the sea after leaving Egypt. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Pi-hahiroth. In Num 33:8 the Hebrew text has the short form, though the King James Version renders it "Pihahiroth." That verse records that Israel set out from before it, crossed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness, traveled three days in the wilderness of Etham, and camped at Marah. The earlier accounts place Pi-hahiroth between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon (Exod 14:2; Num 33:7). Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near the northern end of the Gulf of Suez, close to modern Suez, which matches one common view of where the crossing took place.

Hakkephirim is a place named in Neh 6:2, where Sanballat and Geshem invited Nehemiah to meet them in the plain of Ono. Nehemiah understood the invitation as a plot to harm him. The Hebrew word means "the villages," and the King James Version translates it that way ("in some one of the villages"). Some modern translations instead treat it as the proper name of a particular village. Either reading places it in the plain of Ono, a lowland area near the coastal plain, well away from Jerusalem. That distance probably explains why Nehemiah suspected a trap. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it near ancient Ono, generally identified with Kafr Ana, near present-day Or Yehuda east of Tel Aviv.

Halhul was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah alongside Bethzur and Gedor (Josh 15:58). The Bible mentions it only in this list. Its name survives in the modern village of Halhul, a few miles north of Hebron near the road to Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it about 5 miles north-east of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives about 4 miles north. The location shown here matches this identification. Easton's records a Jewish tradition that Gad, David's seer, was buried there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the village's mosque is linked to the prophet Jonah by a tradition dating to at least the 14th century. Easton's takes the name to mean "full of hollows", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "trembling".

Hali was a town on the border of the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It is named only once, in the list of Asher's boundary towns, between Helkath and Beten and alongside Achshaph (Josh 19:25). The Bible says nothing more about it. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says no firm identification is possible, though it suggests the ruin of Khirbet 'Alia, about 13 miles northeast of Acre. The location shown here is only approximate, placing it in western Galilee inland from Acre, the general area of Asher's border towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "necklace," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "a precious stone" among other meanings.

Ham was a region east of the Jordan where Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him defeated the Zuzim during their campaign, as described in Gen 14:5. It is named between Ashteroth Karnaim and Shaveh Kiriathaim, which suggests a place in the highlands of Transjordan along the invaders' route south. This name is shared by several places and people in the Bible, including Noah's son. The site of this Ham is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "with them" instead of "in Ham." It also records suggestions that the name comes from "Ammon" or was an old name for Rabbath-ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it probably in Ammonite territory. The location shown here follows the identification with Rabbath-ammon, at modern Amman in Jordan. The name probably means "hot" or "heat."

Hamath-zobah was a place in Syria that Solomon attacked and overcame, mentioned only in 2 Chr 8:3. The surrounding passage describes his building of cities, and the next verse speaks of store cities he built in Hamath. The name joins Hamath, the major city on the Orontes River, with Zobah, an Aramean kingdom of David's time. Its exact identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may have been a second Hamath, distinguished from "Great Hamath" by the added name Zobah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no site of that name is known apart from Great Hamath. It suggests the double name may describe the reach of Solomon's conquests over parts of Zobah, which Hamath had perhaps absorbed. It also notes that one Greek manuscript reads "Beth-zobah." The location shown here follows the identification with Hamath itself, the modern city of Hama in Syria.

Hammoth-dor was a city in the territory of Naphtali that was assigned, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. It was one of three such cities from Naphtali, listed with Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge, and Kartan (Josh 21:32). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dwelling of the warm springs." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be the same place as Hammath, a fortified city of Naphtali (Josh 19:35). The ISBE also links it with Hammon in the parallel Levitical list (1 Chr 6:76) and places it at the hot springs of el-Hammam, just south of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here does not follow that identification. It places the city in far western Upper Galilee, near the present Lebanese border. The exact site remains uncertain.

Hamonah, meaning "multitude" or "horde," is the name of a city in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog, mentioned only in Ezek 39:16. The surrounding passage describes the burial of Gog's defeated army in a valley that would be called Hamon-gog, and says the land would be cleansed in this way. Hamonah is apparently a city near that burial valley, and its name recalls the multitude buried there. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as a figurative name for the place of slaughter and burial, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as a city, the latter placing it near Hamon-gog. No actual site is known. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Dead Sea, probably based on Ezek 39:11, which puts the burial valley "on the east of the sea."

Hanes was a city in Egypt, mentioned only in Isa 30:4. In a passage warning Judah against relying on Egypt for protection, Isaiah describes envoys at Zoan (Tanis) and ambassadors arriving at Hanes, probably Judah's delegation seeking an alliance with Pharaoh. Its location is uncertain. Some identify it with Heracleopolis Magna, a major city of Middle Egypt whose name survives in the modern village of Ihnasya el-Medina near Beni Suef. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention this view. Others, following the ancient Aramaic translation, take Hanes to be Tahpanhes, a fortified town on Egypt's eastern frontier in the Nile Delta, closer to Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this view. The location shown here follows the Heracleopolis identification.

Hannathon was a town on the northern boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Zebulun. The boundary description in Josh 19:14 says the border turned around on the north side to Hannathon and ended in the valley of Jiphthahel. This is its only mention in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts it among the cities of Zebulun, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the gift of grace." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Kefar Hananyah, which the Mishnah names as the northern limit of Lower Galilee, and places it at the modern village of Kefr 'Anan, about 3 miles southeast of er-Rameh. Others place it at Tell el-Bedeiwiyeh, at the edge of the Beth Netofa valley farther south and west. The location shown here follows the Kefr 'Anan identification.

Hapharaim was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Issachar. It is named only once, in the list of Issachar's towns, alongside Shion and Anaharath (Josh 19:19). By inference from the surrounding list, which also includes Jezreel and Shunem, it lay in or near the Jezreel Valley in lower Galilee. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "searching" or "digging," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "place of a moat." The exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia follows Eusebius, who placed it about 6 miles north of Megiddo, and links it with the ruins of el-Ferriyeh northwest of el-Lejjun. The location shown here places it somewhat farther east, near modern Afula in the Jezreel Valley.

Hara was a region in the Assyrian empire to which Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria deported the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh, along with Halah, Habor and the river Gozan (1 Chr 5:26). It is named only in this verse, and its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between the Tigris and the Euphrates along the banks of the Khabur, and both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary note the suggestion that it is a variant of Haran. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that the parallel accounts in 2 Kgs 17:6 and 18:11 omit Hara and add "the cities of the Medes," and that the Greek translation reads "mountains of the Medes." It suggests that the name may preserve a Hebrew word for "mountains" of Media. The location shown here follows the Khabur valley placement, in present-day northeastern Syria.

Harmon is a name that appears in Amos 4:3 in the original Hebrew and refers to the place where the wealthy women of Samaria would be thrown when their city fell. The King James Version does not treat it as a name and translates the word as "the palace." Other translations keep it as the proper name Harmon. The preceding verse in Amos 4 addresses these women as "cows of Bashan" on the mountain of Samaria and warns that they would be dragged out through breaches in the city wall. STEPBible's proper-names index suggests Harmon may be the destination of the exiled Israelites. The meaning of the word and the site it names are uncertain, and some translators connect it with Mount Hermon or a region beyond it. The location shown here is a rough placement near Samaria, the city the prophecy addresses, not an identified site.

Hazar-addar was a town on the southern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:4 it appears in the list of boundary points: the border ran south of the ascent of Akrabbim, passed on to Zin, went south to Kadesh-barnea, and continued to Hazar-addar and then Azmon. The name means "village of Addar," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, which identifies it with Addar (or Adar) in the parallel boundary description of Josh 15:3. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "an imprisoned generation." Easton's places it in the desert west of Kadesh-barnea. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Israel.

Hazar-gaddah was a town in the far south of Judah's territory, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:27. It appears among the towns of the Negev near the border with Edom, between Moladah and Heshmon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Judah's southern border, midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. Its name has been explained differently: Easton's gives "village of fortune," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "imprisoned band." The first part, Hazar, commonly means a settlement or enclosure. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the eastern Negev, southeast of Beersheba, based on its position in the town list.

Hazar-susah was a town in the Negev, in the far south of Canaan, assigned to the tribe of Simeon when the land was divided (Josh 19:5). It is listed alongside Ziklag and Beth-marcaboth among the Simeonite towns that lay inside Judah's territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "village of the horse." The parallel list of Simeon's towns in 1 Chr 4:31 gives a similar name, Hazar-susim. Easton's also treats it as the same place as Sansannah in Judah's town list (Josh 15:31) and links it with the horse and chariot depots of Solomon's day (2 Chr 1:14). The neighboring name Beth-marcaboth, "house of chariots," fits that connection. The town's exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev.

Hazar-susim was a town of the tribe of Simeon in the far south of Judah, the Negev region. It appears in 1 Chr 4:31 in a list of Simeonite towns, alongside Beth-marcaboth, Beth-birei and Shaaraim, which the text says were Simeon's cities until the reign of David. The name probably means "village of horses," and it sits next to Beth-marcaboth, "house of chariots," in the list. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:5 gives the name as Hazar-susah, which is generally taken to be the same place. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev near Beersheba, based on the town's place among the other Simeonite towns.

Hazer-hatticon, a name meaning "the middle village," is a place named in Ezekiel's vision of the ideal boundaries of the restored land of Israel. It appears in the description of the northern border, listed after Hamath, Berothah and Sibraim, and is said to lie "by the coast of Hauran," meaning at the edge of the Hauran region east of the Jordan (Ezek 47:16). It is mentioned nowhere else, and its exact site is unknown. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) suggests it is probably the same place as Hazar-enan, which the following verse gives as the border's endpoint. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Hamath in present-day central Syria.

Hazor was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:23 among the cities of the Negev allotted to the tribe of Judah, between Kedesh and Ithnan. It is one of several places in the Bible with this name and should not be confused with the better-known Canaanite city of Hazor in the north. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the name should probably be read together with the following word as a single place, Hazor-Ithnan, rather than "Hazor and Ithnan." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the town as unidentified, and its exact site remains uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, in keeping with the town's position in the southern list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "court" or "hay." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "castle."

Hazor was a town in the far south of Judah, the Negev, named in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:25. The verse is hard to divide. The King James Version reads "Hazor, Hadattah, and Kerioth, and Hezron, which is Hazor," but many readers join the names differently. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads "Hazor-Hadattah" ("new Hazor") as one town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this Hazor with Kerioth-Hezron, the town the verse says "is Hazor." So it is unclear whether one or two places called Hazor are meant here. Several other places in the Bible share the name, including another Hazor in the same southern list (Josh 15:23) and the well-known Canaanite city in the north. The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev of Judah.

Hazor was a town in the territory of Benjamin where Benjamites lived after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in Nehemiah's list of resettled places, alongside Ramah and Gittaim (Neh 11:33). The name was shared by several places in the Bible, including the better-known Canaanite city of Hazor in the north, so this town should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with Khirbet Hazzur, a ruin a little east of Nebi Samwil, northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here, which is only approximate, matches that general area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "court," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "castle."

Hazor-hadattah, meaning "New Hazor," was a town in the far south of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only in Josh 15:25, among the southernmost cities of Judah "toward the coast of Edom" in the Negev. The King James Version prints "Hazor, Hadattah" as two names, but many readers take them as a single compound name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "hadattah" looks like an Aramaic word, which is unusual in this region. Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the ruins of el-Hazzarah near Beit Jebrin. Eusebius and Jerome describe a "New Hazor" east of Ashkelon. The location shown here follows a placement in the eastern Negev, matching the verse's setting near the Edomite border, and is only approximate.

Helbah was a Canaanite town in the territory given to the tribe of Asher. It appears only in Judg 1:31, in a list of towns whose inhabitants Asher did not drive out, alongside Accho, Zidon (Sidon), Ahlab, Achzib, Aphik and Rehob. The name means "fatness" or "fertile." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it on the plain of Phoenicia, with Smith suggesting it lay not far from Sidon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it may be the same place as Mahalliba, named in Sennacherib's prism inscription, but says the site has not been found. Its exact location therefore remains unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the coastal region of Lebanon, north of Sidon.

Helbon was a place known for its wine, mentioned only in Ezek 27:18. In Ezekiel's lament over Tyre, Damascus is said to have traded with Tyre in "the wine of Helbon, and white wool." The name probably means "fat" or "fertile." Older geographers linked Helbon with Aleppo (Arabic Haleb). Smith's Bible Dictionary, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it at the modern village of Halbun, at the head of a fruitful valley on the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon, about 13 miles north-northwest of Damascus, an area still famous for its grapes. The location shown here follows the Halbun identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that ancient inscriptions mention Helbonian wine, including wine received by Nebuchadnezzar, and that the Greek geographer Strabo says the Persian kings prized it.

Helech is a name that appears in Ezekiel’s lament over the trading city of Tyre, in a verse describing the foreign soldiers who guarded its walls (Ezek 27:11). The Hebrew word sits alongside “the men of Arvad,” and the King James Version translates it as “thine army,” so the name does not appear in that translation. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) explains that it may be either a place, possibly in Cilicia in what is now southern Turkey, or a term for Tyre’s own army. If it is a place, it was probably another source of the hired defenders who hung their shields on Tyre’s walls. The location shown here is only approximate and sets it beside Arvad, the island city off the Syrian coast (modern Arwad), because the two names appear together in the verse. Its actual identity remains uncertain.

Heleph was a town named as the starting point of the boundary of the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali (Josh 19:33). From Heleph the border ran past Allon, Zaanannim, Adami, Nekeb, Jabneel and Lakum, ending at the Jordan. The name has been taken to mean "exchange" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries) or "changing; passing over" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The town is mentioned only here, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Naphtali's northern border, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the southern border and leaves it unidentified. The location shown here is in present-day southern Lebanon. It probably follows an identification with the village of Beit Lif, whose name may preserve the ancient one, which would put Heleph toward Naphtali's northwestern edge.

Heliopolis, Greek for "city of the sun," was an ancient Egyptian city that was a major center for worship of the sun god. In Jer 43:13, Jeremiah warns that the king of Babylon would break the sacred images of "Bethshemesh" ("house of the sun") in Egypt and burn the Egyptians' temples. This Bethshemesh is generally taken to be Heliopolis, which explains the entry's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Heliopolis as the same city called On elsewhere in the Bible. On was the home of Potipherah, priest of On, whose daughter Asenath married Joseph (Gen 41:45). It is probably also the Aven mentioned in Ezek 30:17. The location shown here is in the northeastern suburbs of modern Cairo, near Matariya and Ain Shams, where the city's remains, including a standing obelisk, are found.

Helkath-hazzurim was a field at Gibeon, north of Jerusalem, where twelve of Abner's men, fighting for Saul's son Ish-bosheth, met twelve of Joab's men, fighting for David, in a contest of champions. Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, so they all fell together, and the place took its name from that combat (2 Sam 2:16). The name is usually understood as "field of sword edges" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "field of rock", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "field of strong men, or of rocks." The duel settled nothing and led to a wider battle that Abner lost. By inference from the surrounding passage, the field lay near the pool of Gibeon, and the location shown here places it at Gibeon, generally identified with the modern village of el-Jib.

Heres is a place named in Judg 8:13 as the point from which Gideon son of Joash turned back after defeating the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna. The King James Version reads the Hebrew phrase as "before the sun was up," since heres can mean "sun." The Revised Version and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read it as a place name, "the ascent of Heres," probably a pass or slope Gideon climbed on his way back. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that both the text and the geography are uncertain. The following verses show Gideon going on to Succoth, so Heres was probably east of the Jordan, between the battlefield near Karkor and Succoth. The location shown here is a rough one in that area. A separate "Mount Heres" near Aijalon in Dan, mentioned in Judg 1:35 and discussed by Smith's Bible Dictionary, is a different place.

Hereth (spelled Hareth in the King James Version) was a forest or wooded area in the land of Judah where David went while fleeing from King Saul. The prophet Gad told David to leave "the hold", by inference from the surrounding passage his refuge near Mizpeh in Moab, and go into Judah, so David came to the forest of Hereth (1 Sam 22:5). The Hebrew name probably means "thicket." The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads "city" instead of "forest," and some scholars have suggested "Horesh" as an alternative reading. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that David's men may have fetched him water from Bethlehem's well while he was here (2 Sam 23:14–17). The site is uncertain. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both propose the village of Kharas, about 3 miles east of Keilah, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Heshmon was a town in the far south of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah in the Negev region toward the border of Edom (Josh 15:27). It appears between Hazar-gaddah and Beth-pelet, and nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "fatness," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "rich soil." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified and suggests it may have been the original home of the Hasmoneans. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, based on its position in the list of southern towns.

Hezron was a landmark on the southern border of Judah, named in the boundary description between Kadesh-barnea and Adar (Josh 15:3). The border ran past the Ascent of Akrabbim and the wilderness of Zin, up to Kadesh-barnea, on to Hezron, then up to Adar and around to Karkaa. The name probably means "enclosure." In the parallel boundary list in Num 34:4 the place appears as Hazar-addar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Hezron and Adar may have been close together. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a plain west of Kadesh-barnea, and the surveyor Conder proposed that the name survives in Jebel Hadhireh, a mountain northwest of Petra. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here corresponds to the site of Hazor in northern Galilee, a different identification from the southern setting the verse describes.

Hierapolis, meaning "holy city" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was a city of Phrygia in the Lycus valley of western Asia Minor. Its only biblical mention is in Col 4:13. There Paul says that Epaphras worked hard for the believers in Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis, which implies that a Christian community existed there. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the church was probably founded by Epaphras. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the city about 6 miles from Laodicea and about 12 from Colossae. It describes the city's hot calcium-rich springs, whose white deposits gave the site its later name, Pambuk Kalessi ("cotton castle"). It also notes a tradition that the evangelist Philip preached and was buried there. The location shown here is the ruined city beside the white terraces of Pamukkale, near modern Denizli in Turkey.

Hilen was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in 1 Chr 6:58 among the cities and their surrounding pasture lands given to the descendants of Aaron the priest. In the parallel list of priestly cities in Josh 21:15, and in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:51, the name appears as Holon, and the two are generally taken to be the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it probably west or southwest of Hebron. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is a point in that general area. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of caves."

Hill Mizar, called Mount Mizar in modern translations, is a hill named only once in the Bible, in Ps 42:6. There the psalmist, feeling downcast, says he will remember God "from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar." The setting suggests a spot in the far north, near the sources of the Jordan and the slopes of Mount Hermon. Its exact location is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "smallness" and places it on the eastern ridge of Lebanon. It connects the hill with David's flight from Absalom and suggests it may be the Jebel Ajlun, named "the little" in contrast to the greater heights of Lebanon and Hermon. Some readers take the name as a contrast between a small hill and mighty Hermon. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Hermon region.

Hobah was a place near Damascus, the farthest point to which Abram and his servants chased the defeated forces of the eastern kings after a night attack (Gen 14:15). From the surrounding chapter, this was the campaign in which Abram rescued his nephew Lot, who had been taken captive when Sodom was plundered. The verse places Hobah "on the left hand of Damascus." Because ancient Hebrew directions assume a person facing east, the left hand means north, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both read it as north of Damascus. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "hiding-place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with a site called Choba, about 60 miles northwest of Damascus. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it a short distance from Damascus itself.

Holon was a town of Moab on the "plain country," the high tableland east of the Dead Sea. It appears only in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab, where it is named with Jahazah and Mephaath as places on which judgment has come (Jer 48:21). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it was probably once an important town of that plateau. Its site is unknown, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no identification had been made. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the Moabite plateau, near the other towns listed with it. The name is shared with a different Holon, a town in the hill country of Judah given to the Levites (Josh 15:51; 21:15), which should not be confused with this Moabite town.

Horem was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, named in Josh 19:38 alongside Iron, Migdalel, Bethanath and Bethshemesh. It is one of the nineteen cities with their villages that close the list of Naphtali's towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe it as one of Naphtali's fortified or 'fenced' cities, and both give the name's meaning as 'consecrated.' The Bible records nothing else about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary, citing the explorer Van de Velde, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the modern Hurah, a mound at the south end of Wadi el-Ain, west of Kedesh in upper Galilee. The location shown here, in upper Galilee west of Kedesh, corresponds to that suggestion.

Hosah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in the description of Asher's territory in Josh 19:29. The border is traced past Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre, then turns to Hosah before running out to the sea near Achzib. This places Hosah near Tyre on the Phoenician coast. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it a little south of Sidon. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the name as Iaseiph, which some link with Kefr Yasif northeast of Acre. It also cites the suggestion that Hosah is the Assyrian Usu, possibly the mainland settlement facing island Tyre, near Ras el-'Ain south of the city. The location shown here is a tentative placement. The same name belongs to a Levite gatekeeper in Chronicles, a different figure.

Hukkok was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali in Galilee. It appears only once, in Josh 19:34, where Naphtali's border runs west from Aznoth-tabor to Hukkok and then meets Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Yakuk (Yaquq), in the hills west of Wadi el-Amud and northwest of the plain of Gennesaret, about 4 miles (6 km) from the Sea of Galilee. The ISBE notes that this identification seems rather far from Tabor, but it would place the town near where Zebulun and Naphtali met. The location shown here follows the Yakuk identification. A town called Hukok in Asher (1 Chr 6:75) is probably a different place. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "engraver" or "scribe."

Hukok was a city named in 1 Chr 6:75 alongside Rehob, each given "with her suburbs" (its surrounding pasturelands). From the surrounding list, it was one of the towns in the territory of Asher assigned to the Levite family of Gershon. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:31 names Helkath in the matching position, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Hukok as another name for Helkath. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead connects it with Hukkok, a town on the border of Naphtali mentioned in Josh 19:34. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in western Galilee, within the territory generally assigned to Asher, which fits its listing among Asher's towns.

Humtah was a town in the hill country of Judah, named only once in the Bible, in the list of cities allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:54). It appears in a group of nine towns with their villages that includes Hebron (also called Kirjath-arba) and Zior. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "place of lizards" and notes that Humtah is listed next to Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it comes between Aphekah and Hebron in the list. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hills near Hebron, inferred from its position in the town list.

Idalah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It appears only once, in the list of Zebulun's towns in Josh 19:15, where it is named between Shimron and Bethlehem (the Bethlehem of Galilee, not the Bethlehem of Judah). Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Zebulun's western border and identifies it with the modern Jeida in the Kishon valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Jerusalem Talmud equates it with a place called Churyeh, which the surveyor Conder linked to Khirbet el-Huwwara, south of Beit Lahm (Galilean Bethlehem). Both proposals lie in the same general area of the lower Galilee hills, and the location shown here is a point in that region. The meaning of the name is unclear and has been explained in different ways.

Idumea is the Greek form of the name Edom, the land of the descendants of Esau. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the King James Version also uses "Idumea" in Isa 34:5–6 and Ezek 35:15; 36:5, where newer translations have "Edom." In the New Testament it appears once. Mark 3:8 lists it among the regions, along with Jerusalem, the land beyond the Jordan, and the area around Tyre and Sidon, from which great crowds came to Jesus after hearing about what he was doing. By New Testament times the Edomites had settled mainly in the region south of Judea, so Idumea then meant largely that southern area, as the STEPBible names index describes it. The location shown here points to the older Edomite homeland southeast of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red" or "earthy."

Iim was a town in the far south of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, between Baalah and Azem (Josh 15:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the south of Judah, and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list places it in the Negev region, in line with the surrounding names in the list. Nothing else is recorded about it, and its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only an approximate placement in the Negev. A different place called Iim appears in Num 33:45 as a short form of Ije-abarim, a wilderness stopping place near Moab, and should not be confused with this town. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "heaps."

Illyricum was a Roman region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, northwest of Macedonia, covering much of present-day Croatia, Bosnia and Albania. It appears in the Bible only in Rom 15:19, where Paul says that he had fully preached the gospel of Christ from Jerusalem "round about unto Illyricum," marking it as the farthest point of his work so far. Easton's Bible Dictionary links this to his third missionary journey and to his travel through Macedonia in Acts 20:2, which would have brought him to Illyricum's borders. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "unto" may mean either up to the frontier or into the region itself. It favors the first reading, since Acts records no travel beyond Macedonia. The province was later known as Dalmatia, the name used in 2 Tim 4:10. The location shown here lies on the Dalmatian coast of modern Croatia.

Iphtah, spelled Jiphtah in the King James Version, was a town in the lowland hill country (the Shephelah) of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Ashnah and Nezib (Josh 15:43). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) places it in the same district group as Libnah, Ether and Ashan, which are listed in the neighboring verse. Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its site has not been identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement within the Shephelah, based on its position in that list, and does not mark a known ruin.

Ir-shemesh, meaning "city of the sun" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Dan. It is named in Josh 19:41, alongside Zorah and Eshtaol, at the start of the list of Dan's towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect it with Beth-shemesh ("house of the sun"), and this entry follows that identification. Elsewhere Beth-shemesh appears on the border of Judah (Josh 15:10) and as the town the ark reached when the Philistines returned it (1 Sam 6). The location shown here matches Tel Beth-shemesh, west of Jerusalem in the Sorek Valley. The ISBE also points to the related name Heres.

Irpeel was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:27, between Rekem and Taralah. By inference from that list, it belonged to the group of Benjamite towns in the hill country north and west of Jerusalem. The name is usually taken to mean "God heals." The site is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary says no trace of it had been found. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Rafat, a ruin north of el-Jib, the ancient Gibeon. The location shown here follows the Rafat identification, a few miles northwest of Jerusalem.

Ithlah (spelled Jethlah in the King James Version) was a town assigned to the tribe of Dan. It appears only once, in the list of Danite towns in Josh 19:42, next to Shaalabbin and Aijalon (Ajalon). That places it in the western foothills toward the coastal plain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "suspended" or "high" and describes it as a city on the borders of Dan. Nothing else is recorded about it. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Bayt Thul, west of Jerusalem, near the other towns named with it.

Ithnan was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev. It appears only once, in the list of towns given to the tribe of Judah, where it is named alongside Kedesh and Hazor (Josh 15:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the "Ethnan" mentioned by Jerome, but it notes that the site has not been identified, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise reports that no trace of it had been found. Its exact location is therefore unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Judah, based on its place in the town list.

Ituraea was a region in the far north-east of the Holy Land, mentioned in the Bible only at Luke 3:1. There Luke names it, with Trachonitis, as the territory ruled by Philip, brother of Herod, as tetrarch in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. It was the land of the Itureans. Smith's Bible Dictionary and others trace that people to Jetur, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:15). Its exact boundaries are uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south-east of Mount Hermon, in the district later called Jedur, between Trachonitis, Gaulanitis, Hermon and the plain of Damascus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Itureans lived mainly in the Lebanon mountains and the valley of Coele-Syria, perhaps extending south-east of Hermon. It also notes that Luke's two names may overlap. The location shown here follows the identification with the area around the base of Mount Hermon.

Iyim (spelled Iim in the King James Version) was a camping place of the Israelites near the end of their wilderness journey. From there they moved on to Dibon-gad (Num 33:45). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the name means "heaps" and treats it as a short form of Iye-abarim, the stop named in the previous verse (Num 33:44), which places the site "in the border of Moab." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it simply as one of the wilderness stations. The exact site is unknown. Since the next stop was Dibon-gad, Iyim was probably not far from Dibon, east of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan. The location shown here is only approximate and lies close to Dibon.

Jabez was a place where several families of scribes lived, according to the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles. The verse names three of these families, the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Suchathites, and identifies them as Kenites descended from Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab. The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it probably within Judah's territory. The location shown here is rough, near Bethlehem, probably by inference from the preceding verse (1 Chr 2:54), which lists Bethlehem among the descendants of Salma. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrow" or "trouble." The place should not be confused with the man named Jabez in 1 Chr 4:9–10, though Smith's and other dictionaries note that the shared name may suggest some connection.

Jabneel was a city near the Mediterranean coast that marked the western end of Judah's northern border. That boundary ran north past Ekron, through Shicron and Mount Baalah, then on to Jabneel before reaching the sea (Josh 15:11). The name probably means "God builds." It is very likely the same town as Jabneh, which Uzziah of Judah took from the Philistines and whose walls he broke down (2 Chr 26:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus assigns it to the tribe of Dan. Easton's Bible Dictionary says the Greeks later called it Jamnia, and that after Jerusalem fell in AD 70 it became a large city and the seat of a famous school. The location shown here is modern Yavneh, about 11 miles south of Jaffa and a short distance inland. Another Jabneel, a border town of Naphtali in Galilee, is a separate place.

Jabneel was a town named as a landmark on the boundary of the tribe of Naphtali in Josh 19:33. It is listed with Adami and Nekeb along the border line, which ran on to Lakum and ended at the Jordan. The name is usually taken to mean "building of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The same name was also used for a different town on the northern border of Judah, so the two should not be confused. Views on its site differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Kefr Yemmah, which it places on the south shore of Lake Merom in the far north. Others place it at modern Yavne'el, in the valley southwest of the Sea of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it in upper Galilee. The location shown here follows the Yavne'el identification.

Jabneh was a Philistine city whose wall was broken down by King Uzziah of Judah. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the surrounding chapter shows it is Uzziah. 2 Chr 26:6 records this campaign alongside his destruction of the walls of Gath and Ashdod and his building of towns in Philistine territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "building," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "building of God." Both dictionaries identify Jabneh with Jabneel, a town on the northern boundary of Judah near the Mediterranean coast (Josh 15:11). The city was probably the later Jamnia of the Greek period and is generally located at modern Yavne, south of Tel Aviv and inland from the coast. The location shown here follows that identification.

Jagur was a town in the far south of Judah's tribal territory, toward the border of Edom. It appears only once, in the list of the southernmost cities of Judah in Josh 15:21, where it is named alongside Kabzeel and Eder. These towns lay in the Negev, the dry region in the south of the land. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "place of sojourn," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "lodging." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "husbandman" or "stranger." The site has not been identified, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, east of modern Beersheba, based on its position in the list of southern towns.

Jair, in the phrase "the towns of Jair," is a region of small settlements east of the Jordan, listed in Josh 13:30 as part of the land given to the half-tribe of Manasseh. There they are described as sixty cities in Bashan, in a territory that ran from Mahanaim and took in the former kingdom of Og. The name comes from Jair, a descendant of Manasseh. The connected passages in Num 32:41 and Deut 3:14 say he captured these villages and named them after himself, Havoth-jair ("villages of Jair"). Those passages differ in where they place the towns, Deuteronomy in the Argob district of Bashan and Numbers in Gilead. STEPBible's proper-names index places them in Gilead. The exact extent of the region is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough point in northern Gilead.

Janim was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:53, where the King James Version spells it Janum. It appears in a group of towns with Beth-tappuah and Aphekah, in the uplands around Hebron. Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "slumber." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified. The location shown here follows an identification with the modern village of Bani Naim, east of Hebron, which fits the town's place in the Hebron hill-country list.

Janoah was a city taken by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria during the reign of Pekah king of Israel. Its people were deported to Assyria along with those of Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee (2 Kgs 15:29). The name means "resting place," and it is shared by more than one biblical town, so its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it in the north, in the territory of Naphtali, because it is listed with northern towns. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the village of Yanuch, about 6 miles east of Tyre. Another view links it with Yanun, southeast of modern Nablus, the site usually identified with the Janohah on Ephraim's border (Josh 16:6–7). The location shown here follows the Yanun identification.

Japhia was a town on the boundary of Zebulun's territory. In Josh 19:12 the border runs from Sarid east to Chisloth-tabor, out to Daberath and then up to Japhia. The following verse, not shown here, continues the line on toward Gath-hepher. The verb "goeth up" suggests the town stood on higher ground than Daberath. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Yafa, about 1.5–2 miles (2.5–3 km) southwest of Nazareth near the foot of the hills, and the location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the Jewish historian Josephus fortified the place during the war with Rome in the first century AD. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "enlightening" or "appearing." This is a different place from Japhia, the king of Lachish, and from Japhia, the son of David.

Jarmuth was a city in the territory of Issachar that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites. In Josh 21:29 it is one of four Issachar cities in the list, alongside Engannim. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Gershonite clan of Levites, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it that way. The parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6 gives Ramoth in this position, and Josh 19:21 names a Remeth among Issachar's towns, so these are probably the same place under different spellings. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have connected it with the Ramah of Samuel. Several places in the Bible share the name Jarmuth. This one is distinct from the Canaanite royal city of Jarmuth in the lowlands of Judah. Its exact site is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough position near the Jezreel Valley in Issachar's territory.

Jebusite, as a place name, refers in Josh 15:8 to the city of the Jebusites, which the verse identifies as Jerusalem. The passage describes the northern border of Judah's territory running up the valley of the son of Hinnom along the south side of the Jebusite city, then to the top of the mountain west of the Hinnom valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the Jebusites were the original inhabitants of Jebus, the older name of Jerusalem. It notes that they were not fully driven out until David captured the city and made it his capital in place of Hebron. The location shown here follows the identification with ancient Jerusalem, near the southeastern hill of the present Old City area, just above the Hinnom valley.

Jegar-sahadutha was the Aramaic name Laban gave to the heap of stones he and Jacob set up as a witness to the covenant they made when they parted. Jacob called the same heap Galeed, its Hebrew counterpart (Gen 31:47). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning as "heap of witness" or "pile of testimony." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Galeed does not match the Aramaic name exactly. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the second part of the name to the word for "witness" in Job 16:19. The surrounding chapter places the meeting in the hill country of Gilead, east of the Jordan, which Jacob's party reached after fleeing Haran. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a point in northern Gilead, in present-day northern Jordan.

Jehud was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, listed in Josh 19:45 alongside Bene-berak and Gath-rimmon. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named between Baalath and Bene-berak in the list of Danite towns, and gives the meaning of the name as "praised." It is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with el-Yehudiyeh, about 8 miles east of Jaffa on the coastal plain. That site corresponds to the modern Israeli town of Yehud, east of Tel Aviv, and the location shown here follows this identification.

Jekabzeel was a town in the south of Judah. After the return from exile in Babylon, some of the people of Judah lived there and in its surrounding villages (Neh 11:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as a fuller form of the name Kabzeel, which earlier passages place among the southernmost cities of Judah toward the border with Edom. By that identification it is the same town as Kabzeel, the home of David's warrior Benaiah. The name is usually explained as meaning "God gathers" or, in Hitchcock's Bible Names, "the congregation of God." Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev region of southern Judah.

Jeruel was a stretch of wilderness in Judah, named only in 2 Chr 20:16. When Moabites, Ammonites and their allies invaded during the reign of Jehoshaphat, the Levite Jahaziel told the king that the army of Judah would meet them as they came up by the cliff of Ziz, at the end of the valley, before the wilderness of Jeruel. The name is usually explained as meaning “founded by God.” The exact area is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the ascent from the Dead Sea toward Jerusalem, beyond the wilderness of Tekoa (compare 2 Chr 20:20) in the direction of En-gedi, and links it with the district then called el-Hasasah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a suggestion that the name may be a variant of Jezreel in Judah (Josh 15:56). The location shown here follows Easton's identification, in the Judean wilderness between Tekoa and En-gedi, and is approximate.

Jeshanah was a town of the northern kingdom of Israel. Together with its surrounding villages, it was one of three towns that King Abijah of Judah took from Jeroboam after defeating him. The other two were Bethel and Ephrain (2 Chr 13:19). The name probably means "old." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that most scholars read the same name in place of "Shen" in 1 Sam 7:12, where Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer between Mizpeh and Shen. It also links the town with Isanas, a place mentioned by the historian Josephus. The same work identifies Jeshanah with the modern Ain Sinia (Ein Sinya), about 3¼ miles north of Bethel, a site with a spring and ancient remains. The location shown here follows that identification.

Jeshua was a town in Judah where people of Judah settled after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in Neh 11:26, in a list of settlements that also includes Moladah and Beth-phelet. Those neighbouring towns lay in the Negev, so Jeshua was probably in the far south of Judah, in the region around Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Shema in Josh 15:26, and possibly Sheba in Josh 19:2. It also proposes Khirbet Sa'weh, a walled ruin on a prominent hill about 12 miles (19 km) east-northeast of Beersheba, as the site. The exact location is uncertain, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in that southern area. The name is the same as Joshua.

Jetur is named in 1 Chr 5:19 as one of the peoples, along with the Hagarites, Nephish and Nodab, against whom the tribes east of the Jordan made war. The surrounding passage identifies those tribes as Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The name belongs to a people as much as a place. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it to Jetur, one of the twelve sons of Ishmael (Gen 25:15), so this was probably an Ishmaelite tribe living in the lands east of the Jordan. Many scholars connect Jetur with the later region of Ituraea, mentioned in Luke 3:1. The location shown here follows that view, placing it in the hill country around Mount Hermon, in present-day southern Lebanon and southwestern Syria. Its exact territory at the time of this war is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "order," "succession," or "mountainous."

Jezreel is the place from which news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan reached Saul's household, according to 2 Sam 4:4. When the report arrived, the nurse of Jonathan's five-year-old son Mephibosheth fled with him, and in her haste he fell and became lame. The verse refers to the area where Saul's army had camped before the battle on Mount Gilboa. By inference from 1 Sam 29:1, which places the Israelite camp by a spring in Jezreel, this was the town and valley of Jezreel in the north, between Mount Gilboa and the hills of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification, probably at modern Tel Jezreel (Zer'in), overlooking the Jezreel Valley. Several places in the Bible share this name, including a town in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:56), so which Jezreel a passage means depends on its context.

Jokdeam was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah, alongside Jezreel and Zanoah (Josh 15:56). It belongs to a group of towns that includes Maon, Carmel and Ziph (Josh 15:55–57), which places it in the hills south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unidentified and suggests it probably lay south of Hebron. Its exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only an approximate position in that area. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "crookedness, or burning, of the people."

Jokmeam was a city marking the far edge of the district assigned to Baana son of Ahilud, one of Solomon's officers who supplied provisions for the royal household (1 Kgs 4:12; the surrounding passage describes these officers). The district included Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean, reaching to Abel-meholah and "beyond" this city. The King James Version reads "Jokneam" in this verse, while the Revised Version reads "Jokmeam." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Jokmeam as the Levitical city of Ephraim named in 1 Chr 6:68 and places it somewhere in the Jordan valley, which would suit a boundary running toward Abel-meholah. The location shown here instead follows the Jokneam identification, probably modern Tel Yokneam at the northwestern edge of the Jezreel Valley, not far from Megiddo. Several places share similar names, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "confirmation, or revenge, of the people."

Jokmeam was a city of Ephraim that was given, together with its surrounding pasture lands, to the Levites. In 1 Chr 6:68 it is named alongside Bethhoron. By inference from the surrounding verses, it went to the Kohathite families. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Joshua 21:22 has Kibzaim in this position, so the two names probably refer to the same town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it somewhere in the Jordan valley, reading the Jokmeam of 1 Kings 4:12 in the Revised Version, which the King James Version spells Jokneam, as the same town. The name is shared by more than one place, and the exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Jordan valley view, placing it north-east of Jerusalem toward the valley. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "confirmation, or revenge, of the people."

Joktheel was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38. It appears between Mizpeh and Lachish in that list, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is named just before Lachish. The name has been explained as meaning "subdued by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the site as unidentified. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Lachish area, by inference from its position in the town list. The same name was later given to a different place. According to 2 Kgs 14:7, King Amaziah captured Sela in Edom and renamed it Joktheel. That Edomite site should not be confused with this town in Judah.

Joktheel was the new name given to the Edomite stronghold of Selah after it was captured by a king of Judah. 2 Kgs 14:7 says he struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, took Selah in battle, and renamed it Joktheel, a name still in use when the account was written. The surrounding chapter shows that the king was Amaziah. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 25 describes the same campaign. Selah, meaning "rock," has traditionally been identified with the rock city of Petra in southern Jordan. Others place it at es-Sela, a site farther north near Bozrah. The location shown here follows the Petra identification. A different Joktheel, a town in the lowland of Judah, appears in Josh 15:38 and should not be confused with this one.

Jorkeam (spelled Jorkoam in the King James Version) is named once, in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants in the tribe of Judah, where Raham is called "the father of Jorkoam" (1 Chr 2:44). Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the name could belong to a person descended from Caleb or to a place in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a town, with Raham as its founder, since "father of" in these lists often marks the founder of a settlement. It also suggests that Jorkeam may be the same as Jokdeam, a town in the hill country of Judah listed in Josh 15:56. This entry treats Jorkeam as a city. The location shown here lies in the hills south of Hebron, near the other towns of that district, which fits the Jokdeam identification. The exact site is uncertain.

Jotbah was the hometown of Haruz, whose daughter Meshullemeth was the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of King Amon, who reigned two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 21:19). This is its only mention in the Bible, and the verse says nothing more about the place. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "goodness", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "pleasantness". Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Jotbathah, a stopping place of Israel in the wilderness, in the far south near the Gulf of Aqaba. Other scholars identify it with a site in Galilee. The location shown here follows the Jotbathah identification and is only approximate.

Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel, centered on Jerusalem, and in the time of Jesus it was the southernmost of the three divisions of Palestine, alongside Samaria and Galilee. In John 3:22, after his conversation with Nicodemus in Jerusalem, Jesus and his disciples went out into the Judean countryside, where he stayed with them for a time and baptized. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that after the Babylonian exile the name could refer to the whole country west of the Jordan. Under Roman rule it covered the former territories of Judah, Benjamin, Dan, Simeon and part of Ephraim, and was governed by a procurator as part of the province of Syria. The location shown here is a representative point at Jerusalem, standing for the surrounding region rather than a single site.

Judgment, called the Hall of Judgment in modern translations, was a porch or hall in King Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem. According to 1 Kgs 7:7, Solomon built it to hold his throne, where he sat to hear cases and give judgment, and it was paneled with cedar from one side of the floor to the other. The same structure is also called the porch of the throne. It was one of several connected buildings Solomon put up alongside the temple, and by inference from the surrounding passage it stood near the House of the Forest of Lebanon and his own residence. No remains have been identified. The location shown here is a general placement within the area of Solomon's palace on the hill south of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. This hall should not be confused with the New Testament "judgment hall" (the Roman praetorium).

Tahtimhodshi was a region that Joab and the army commanders passed through while carrying out David's census of Israel. It is named after Gilead and before Dan-jaan and the area around Sidon, which places it somewhere in the northeast of the territory being counted (2 Sam 24:6). The name is obscure and has been read in several ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as "the land of the newly inhabited," a region east of the Jordan and north of Gilead. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes Kitto's suggestion of the upper Jordan valley at the foot of Mount Hermon. Many scholars instead read the text as "the land of the Hittites toward Kadesh," meaning Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, and modern translations such as the ESV render it "Kadesh." The location shown here follows the Kadesh-on-the-Orontes identification, probably the modern site of Tell Nebi Mend in western Syria.

Kamon (spelled Camon in the King James Version) was the town where Jair, one of the judges of Israel, was buried (Judg 10:5). The surrounding verses describe Jair as a Gileadite who led Israel for twenty-two years and whose sons held thirty towns in Gilead, so Kamon is usually taken to have been a town of Gilead, east of the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the ruins of Kamm or Kumeim in northern Jordan. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead proposes Tell Qaimun (Jokneam) on the southern slopes of Mount Carmel, reasoning that Jair may have lived west of the Jordan while serving as judge. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Gilead identification and marks only the general area, not a specific site.

Kanah was a city named in Joshua's description of the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher. It appears in a list of towns running northward toward "great Zidon" (Josh 19:28), so it was probably near the northern edge of Asher's land. The name means "of reeds." It should not be confused with other places of the same name, such as the brook Kanah on the border of Ephraim and Manasseh. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the village of Qana, about 7 miles (11 km) southeast of Tyre in modern Lebanon, where Easton's notes nearby ruins and rock carvings thought to be Phoenician. The location shown here follows a different identification, placing it farther south in Lower Galilee, near the modern village of Kafr Kanna.

Karka (spelled Karkaa in the King James Version) was a place on the southern border of the territory given to the tribe of Judah. Josh 15:3 traces that border from Maaleh-acrabbim past Zin and Kadesh-barnea, then on to Hezron and Adar, after which it turns toward Karka. Azmon and the Brook of Egypt follow in the next verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it between Adar and Azmon, roughly midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea, and explains the name as meaning "floor" or "bottom." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning as "the pavement" or "ground" and notes that Eusebius mentioned a village in Judah toward the wilderness called Akarka. The same work states that the site cannot now be identified. The location shown here is only a rough estimate in the region west of Kadesh-barnea.

Karkor was the place east of the Jordan where the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna camped with about fifteen thousand men. These were all that remained of the eastern armies after a hundred and twenty thousand had fallen (Judg 8:10). The verses that follow (Judg 8:11–12) describe Gideon going up by the route of the tent-dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah, surprising this camp, routing the army and capturing both kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "foundation" and places Karkor in the open desert not far beyond Succoth and Penuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the site as unidentified and suggests it may correspond to a Qarqar mentioned in Assyrian records. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement east of the Jordan, in the region of Succoth and Penuel.

Karnaim is a place named in Gen 14:5 as part of the compound name Ashteroth Karnaim, where Chedorlaomer and his allied kings defeated the Rephaim during their campaign east of the Jordan. The name means "horns," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Some scholars treat Ashteroth Karnaim as one town. Others see two neighboring sites, Ashtaroth and Karnaim, possibly joined in the name. Some modern translations also read Amos 6:13, which in Hebrew has the word "horns," as a reference to a town called Karnaim. By inference from the surrounding names, it lay in Bashan, in what is now southern Syria. The site is often identified with Sheikh Sa'd, near Tell Ashtarah, and the location shown here falls in that area.

Kartah was a city in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. It was given, together with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Merarite families of the Levites, and is listed next to Jokneam (Josh 21:34). This is its only mention in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "city," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "calling" or "meeting." The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as the same place as Kattath in Zebulun's boundary list (Josh 19:15), and perhaps also as Kitron (Judg 1:30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says it may be a variant of Kattath or of Kartan. The location shown here is an approximate point in lower Galilee, within Zebulun's territory.

Kartan was a city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, given with its surrounding pasturelands to the Levites. Joshua 21:32 lists it as one of three Naphtalite cities, alongside Kedesh in Galilee, the city of refuge, and Hammothdor. From the surrounding passage, these cities were among those allotted to the Gershonite branch of the Levites. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:76 appears to give the name as Kiriathaim, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Kartan may be a shortened form of that name. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably near the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee, at the ruined village of el-Katanah. The location shown here is only a rough placement farther west, in the hill country of western Galilee.

Kattath was a city named among the towns in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun, listed with Nahallal, Shimron, Idalah and Bethlehem in Josh 19:15. Nothing else is recorded about it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Kitron, where Zebulun did not drive out the Canaanites (Judg 1:30), and Kartah, a town given to the Merarite Levites (Josh 21:34). Its site is uncertain. The Babylonian Talmud identifies it with Sepphoris (modern Tzippori), and the Jerusalem Talmud with Kuteineh, west of the Jezreel Valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia looks for it near Shimron, and Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with Kana el-Jelil. The location shown here follows the Sepphoris identification.

Kedesh was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:23 among the cities of Judah's southern district. By the context of the surrounding list, it lay toward the border of Edom in the Negev. Several places in the Bible share this name, and this Kedesh is distinct from the better-known northern towns called Kedesh. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the same as Kadesh or Kadesh-barnea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes this possibility, pointing out that Kadesh-barnea would otherwise be surprisingly missing from the list. It also mentions another proposal, a site called Kadus south of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Kadesh-barnea identification and places it in the northeastern Sinai, near the springs of the Ein el-Qudeirat area.

Kedesh was a city in the territory of the tribe of Issachar. It was one of the towns, with its surrounding pasturelands, given to the Levites (1 Chr 6:72). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it went to the Gershonite Levites and that the parallel list in Joshua 21:28 names Kishion in its place, so the two names may refer to the same town. Several places in the Bible are called Kedesh. This one should not be confused with Kedesh in Naphtali, the city of refuge in Galilee. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both mention Tell Abu Qades (Abu Kadeis), near Megiddo and Lejjun in the Jezreel Valley, as a possible identification, following the surveyor Conder. The location shown here follows that identification.

Kedesh-naphtali was the hometown of Barak son of Abinoam. Deborah summoned him from there and told him to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor to fight the Canaanite forces (Judg 4:6). The name means "Kedesh of Naphtali" and sets it apart from other towns called Kedesh. It was probably the same Kedesh in Naphtali that later passages name as a city of refuge (Josh 20:7) and a Levitical town (Josh 21:32), and that Tiglath-pileser of Assyria captured (2 Kgs 15:29). Its exact site is debated. Many place it at Tel Kedesh in Upper Galilee, northwest of the Huleh Valley. Others suggest a site near the southwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, closer to Tabor, because of the Kedesh mentioned in Judg 4:11. The location shown here follows the Upper Galilee identification.

Kerioth-hezron was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the tribe of Judah, listed among Judah's southern cities in Josh 15:25. The verse gives it a second name, Hazor. The King James Version reads the phrase as two places, "Kerioth, and Hezron, which is Hazor," while other readings, followed in this entry, treat it as one compound name, "Kerioth-hezron, which is Hazor." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Judas Iscariot may have come from this town, with "Iscariot" taken to mean "man of Kerioth." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's places it at the ruins of el-Kureitein, about 10 miles south of Hebron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the explorer Robinson, places it at Kuryatain, about 4.5 miles north of Tel Arad. The location shown here is only approximate and sits in the Negev of southern Judah.

Kibzaim was a city in the territory of Ephraim. Along with its surrounding pasture lands, it was given to the Levites. By inference from the surrounding passage, it went to the Kohathite family, together with Shechem, Gezer and Beth-horon, making the "four cities" of Josh 21:22. In the parallel list of Levitical cities, 1 Chr 6:68 gives the name Jokmeam in its place. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries therefore treat the two names as referring to the same town. Easton's and Smith's explain the name as "two heaps", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "congregation". Kibzaim is not mentioned anywhere else, and its site is uncertain. The location shown here follows an identification with a place called Kabus.

Kinah was a town in the far south of Judah, named in Josh 15:22 among the cities of the tribe's southernmost district, toward the border of Edom. It appears only in this list, alongside Dimonah and Adadah, and nothing else is recorded about it. The name resembles the Hebrew word for a lament or dirge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may instead come from the Kenites, who had settlements in the south. The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably near the Dead Sea in the Wady Fikreh. The location shown here is only approximate and follows a placement in the Negev, west of Arad, consistent with the town's listing among Judah's southern cities.

Kiriath-arim was a town whose people are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon, counted together with those of Chephirah and Beeroth as 743 people (Ezra 2:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a shortened form of Kiriath-jearim, and the parallel list in Neh 7:29 gives that fuller name. Kiriath-jearim was one of the Gibeonite cities and stood on the border of Judah and Benjamin. It is known as the place where the ark of the covenant stayed for twenty years. Its exact site is uncertain. One common view places it at Kiriath el-Enab (Abu Ghosh), about 9 miles (14 km) west of Jerusalem. Another, proposed by C. R. Conder, places it at Khirbet Erma, because the name Erma corresponds to Arim. The location shown here appears to follow the Khirbet Erma identification.

Kiriath-huzoth was a town in Moab where King Balak took the prophet Balaam after meeting him, when Balak had summoned Balaam to curse Israel (Num 22:39). The name probably means "city of streets." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "city of villages" and that the two first met at "the city of Moab" (Num 22:36), which it takes to be Kir of Moab. It concludes that Kiriath-huzoth was probably not far from there. According to the next verse, Balak sacrificed there and the following day took Balaam up to the high places of Baal (Num 22:40–41).
