Its exact site is unknown. Some identify it with Kiriathaim and others with Kerioth. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the Moabite highlands east of the northern Dead Sea, northwest of modern Madaba.

Kiriath-sannah was another name for Debir, a town in the hill country of Judah allotted to the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of Judah's towns, where it is named next to Dannah and identified with Debir (Josh 15:49). Elsewhere Debir is also called Kiriath-sepher (Josh 15:15; Judg 1:11), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats all three names as one place. That work notes that the Septuagint reads this name as "city of books." One explanation is that "sannah" arose as a copying slip for "sepher" ("book"). Another, from the scholar A. H. Sayce, holds that it is an old Canaanite name meaning "city of instruction." Debir's modern site is debated. Some place it at Tell Beit Mirsim and others at Khirbet Rabud, southwest of Hebron. The location shown here matches the Khirbet Rabud identification.

Kiriathaim was a town in the tribal territory of Naphtali, in Galilee, given with its surrounding pasture lands to the Levites. It is named in 1 Chr 6:76 alongside Kedesh in Galilee and Hammon, among the Naphtali towns allotted to the Levite family of Gershon. The name means "two cities." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates it with Kartan, which appears in the matching list of Levitical towns in Joshua 21:32. It should not be confused with the better-known Kiriathaim east of the Jordan, in the land of Reuben and later Moab, which shares the same name. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only an approximate placement in Upper Galilee.

Kitron was a Canaanite city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Judg 1:30 records that Zebulun did not drive out its inhabitants, or those of nearby Nahalol. The Canaanites stayed and lived among the Israelites, but were made to pay tribute. Kitron is not mentioned anywhere else under this name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it may be the same place as Kattath, listed among Zebulun's towns in Josh 19:15. Its location is uncertain. Easton's connects it with Cana of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Talmud identifies it with Sepphoris, near the modern village of Saffuriyeh (Zippori) in Lower Galilee. The location shown here follows the Sepphoris identification.

Koa was a people or region named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's allegory of Oholah and Oholibah, where it appears with Pekod, Shoa, the Babylonians, Chaldeans and Assyrians among the horsemen, captains and nobles who would come against Jerusalem (Ezek 23:23). The text gives no further detail, so its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a province or place in the Babylonian empire, while Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it might instead be a common noun meaning "prince" or "nobleman." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the people probably northeast of Babylonia. The location shown here follows an identification with the area of ancient Media, in the region of modern Hamadan in western Iran, and should be treated as approximate.

Laban was a place named in Deut 1:1 as one of several landmarks marking where Moses spoke to all Israel east of the Jordan, in the wilderness. It is listed with Paran, Tophel, Hazeroth and Dizahab. The verse is notoriously hard to interpret, and nothing more is said about Laban in the Bible. Its name probably means "white." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a city on the Israelites' desert route and probably the same as Libnah, a wilderness camp listed in Num 33:20. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this identification seems to rest on Laban being mentioned alongside Hazeroth, which also appears near Libnah in that list. Its actual location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough approximation in the lowlands west of Jerusalem.

Lahmam was a town in the lowland district (the Shephelah) of the tribe of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:40, where it is named between Cabbon and Kithlish. By inference from its surrounding entries, it belonged to the group of towns in the region around Lachish. Nothing else is recorded about it. Some manuscripts spell the name Lahmas, and the Revised Version margin notes this reading. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the modern site of el-Lahm, about 2.5 miles (4 km) south of Beit Jibrin, and the location shown here follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "provisions."

Laishah was a town north of Jerusalem, named in Isaiah's description of an invading army advancing on the city (Isa 10:30). The King James Version spells it "Laish", but it is a different place from Laish, the northern city later renamed Dan. The verse calls on Gallim to cry out so that Laishah and the "poor" town of Anathoth can hear. That grouping, and the march route described in the surrounding passage, places it near Anathoth and Gallim in the territory of Benjamin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Conder's suggestion that it is the village of el-Isawiyeh (modern Isawiya), on the eastern slope north-northeast of the Mount of Olives. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the same identification and places it about a mile northeast of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows the Isawiya identification, though the site is not certain.

Lakkum (spelled Lakum in the King James Version) was a town on the border of the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned only once in the Bible. In Josh 19:33 it is the last place named in a line of border points, after Heleph, Allon to Zaanannim, Adami, Nekeb and Jabneel, just before the boundary is said to reach the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as an unidentified town that apparently lay nearer the Jordan than the others listed. Its exact site is still uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Lower Galilee, in the area of Mount Tabor, which fits the general course of Naphtali's southern border running toward the Jordan.

Lasea was a city on the south coast of the island of Crete, mentioned once in the Bible as lying near Fair Havens, the anchorage where Paul's ship put in after struggling along the coast on its voyage toward Rome (Acts 27:8). That voyage is dated about AD 56, by inference from context. Crete is not named in this verse itself, but the surrounding account of the voyage places Fair Havens on Crete's southern shore. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary report that ruins identified as Lasea were found in 1856 a few miles east of Fair Havens, near Cape Leonda. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the ship's crew would have had to buy supplies from Lasea if they stayed long, which may help explain why the captain did not want to winter there. No coordinates are shown for this entry.

Lasha was a city named in Gen 10:19 as the furthest point of the Canaanites' territory, listed after Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim. It apparently marked the southeastern corner of the border, near the region of the Dead Sea. The Bible mentions it nowhere else. Its location is uncertain. Jerome, Eusebius's Onomasticon and the Jerusalem Targum identify it with Callirrhoe, a place known for its hot springs near the eastern shore of the Dead Sea, in the Wadi Zerqa Ma'in area. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both mention this view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the site may lie further south, possibly west of the Arabah, and considers a firm identification impossible. The location shown here follows the Callirrhoe identification, east of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan.

Lasharon was a Canaanite town whose king appears in the list of kings defeated by Joshua west of the Jordan (Josh 12:18). It is mentioned only here, and the verse says nothing more about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "the plain." Because the name can also be read as "of the Sharon," some interpreters take it as describing the preceding Aphek, meaning "Aphek in the Sharon plain," rather than as a separate town. Others treat it as its own city in Lower Galilee, near the modern village of Sharona, southwest of the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows the Sharona identification, which is probably the site of the ancient town, although this remains uncertain.

Leb-kamai is a name that appears in the Hebrew text of Jer 51:1, in an oracle where the Lord threatens to raise a destroying wind against Babylon and against those who dwell in Leb-kamai. The King James Version does not keep it as a name. It translates the Hebrew literally as "the midst of them that rise up against me." Many interpreters treat it as a coded name, formed by a letter-substitution cipher (atbash) that reverses the order of the Hebrew alphabet. Decoded this way, Leb-kamai spells Kasdim, the Hebrew word for the Chaldeans. On that reading it is a cryptic name for Chaldea, the region of southern Mesopotamia around Babylon, and it stands parallel to Babylon in the same verse. The location shown here follows that identification and marks the general area of Chaldea in what is now southern Iraq, not one specific site.

Lebaoth was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the territory assigned to the tribe of Judah. It appears near the end of the list of Judah's southern cities in Josh 15:32, alongside Shilhim, Ain and Rimmon. Its name probably means "lionesses," as Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Beth-lebaoth, a town later listed among the cities given to Simeon within Judah's land (Josh 19:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the parallel list in 1 Chr 4:31 gives the name as Beth-biri. The site has not been securely identified. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev, north of Beersheba.

Lebonah was a town in the hill country of Ephraim, mentioned only once in the Bible. In Judg 21:19 it serves as a landmark for locating Shiloh, where a yearly feast of the LORD was held: Shiloh lay north of Bethel, east of the highway from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah. Lebonah therefore stood a short distance north of Shiloh, near the main north–south road through the hills. The name probably means "frankincense," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. The town is generally identified with the modern village of al-Lubban, south of Nablus near the old road. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about two miles from Shiloh (Seilun), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes rock tombs nearby. The location shown here follows the al-Lubban identification.

Lehem is a place that may be named in 1 Chr 4:22, in the genealogy of Shelah son of Judah. The verse lists descendants who ruled in Moab and ends with a name the King James Version prints as one word, Jashubilehem, treating it as a personal name. Other translators divide it, reading it as 'and they returned to Lehem' or treat Lehem as a separate place. On that reading, these men of Judah had some connection with Moab and then came back home. Lehem is often taken as a shortened form of Bethlehem, the Judahite town whose name means 'house of bread.' Ruth's story also links Bethlehem with Moab. The location shown here follows the Bethlehem identification, south of Jerusalem. The verse itself calls these records 'ancient things,' and the exact meaning of the name remains uncertain.

Leshem was a town that the tribe of Dan captured when its allotted territory proved too small. According to Josh 19:47, the Danites attacked it, put it to the sword, settled there and renamed it Dan after their ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Leshem as another form of Laish, the name used for the same town in the fuller account of the Danite migration in Judges 18. As Dan, it later marked the northern limit of Israel in the phrase "from Dan to Beersheba." The site is generally identified with Tel Dan (Tell el-Qadi), near the springs of the Jordan at the foot of Mount Hermon in northern Israel, and the location shown here matches that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a name" or "a precious stone."

Luz was a city built in "the land of the Hittites" by a man from the older Luz, the Canaanite town that the tribes of Joseph captured and renamed Bethel. By inference from the surrounding passage (Judg 1:23–25), he was the man who showed the Israelite scouts the way into his city and was spared when it fell. He then moved away, founded a new town and gave it his home city's name, which was still in use when Judges was written. The name probably means "almond tree" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Luweiziyeh, about 4 miles northwest of Banias, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes no satisfactory identification. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the wider Hittite region of what is now southern Turkey and northern Syria.

Lycaonia was an inland region of central Asia Minor, in present-day south-central Turkey around the Konya plain. Acts 14:6 describes Paul and Barnabas fleeing there from Iconium to Lystra and Derbe, "cities of Lycaonia," and the surrounding countryside. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it west of Cappadocia and south of Galatia, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a mostly treeless, dry plain with salt lakes. Both note that Acts 14:11 mentions a local "speech of Lycaonia," a language different from ordinary Greek whose exact nature is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that in Paul's day Lycaonia was divided: a western part belonging to the Roman province of Galatia, which held Lystra and Derbe, and an eastern part under a client king. It takes the Lystra and Derbe district to be the part meant in Acts. Paul probably passed through the region again on later journeys (Acts 16:1; 18:23).

Lycia was a mountainous coastal region in the southwest of Asia Minor, opposite the island of Rhodes, in what is now southwestern Turkey. Luke mentions it when describing Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. After sailing past Cilicia and Pamphylia, the ship reached Myra, "a city of Lycia" (Acts 27:5), where Paul was moved onto a grain ship from Alexandria (Acts 27:6). This entry dates the voyage to about AD 56, by inference from context. Lycia's port of Patara also appears on an earlier journey of Paul (Acts 21:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Lycia came under Persian, Greek and then Roman control, becoming part of the Roman provincial system under the emperor Claudius. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a stopping place on Paul's travels rather than a scene of his work. The location shown here marks the general region.

Maacath was the homeland of the Maachathites, a people Israel did not drive out when it settled east of the Jordan. Joshua 13:13 says they and the neighboring Geshurites went on living among the Israelites "until this day." Maacath is the same territory called Maachah or Maacah elsewhere. Connected passages place it at the northern edge of Bashan near Mount Hermon, next to Geshur (Deut 3:14; Josh 12:5; 13:11). They also describe it as a small Aramean kingdom whose king later sent troops to help the Ammonites against David (2 Sam 10:6). Its exact borders are unknown. It probably lay in what is now southern Syria, east and southeast of Mount Hermon, toward the Golan and the Hauran. The location shown here is a rough placement in that general region.

Maarath was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:59. It appears in a group of six towns with their surrounding villages, named between Gedor and Beth-anoth. The Bible says nothing more about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolation." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it as probably the modern village of Beit Ummar, about 6 miles (10 km) north of Hebron. The village lies on the watershed just west of the road to Hebron, about a mile from Khirbet Jedur, which is thought to be ancient Gedor. The location shown here follows the Beit Ummar identification.

Maareh-geba was the place near Gibeah from which Israel's hidden ambush broke out against the Benjamites, while the main army drew up at Baal-tamar (Judg 20:33). This was during the war the other tribes waged on Benjamin over the crime committed at Gibeah, as the surrounding chapters relate. The King James Version does not treat the Hebrew as a name and translates it "the meadows of Gibeah." The Revised Version margin gives "the meadow of Geba (or Gibeah)." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to a Greek manuscript reading and proposes "to the west of Geba." The Syriac version reads it as "the cave of Geba." This entry treats it as a place name, following the STEPBible proper-names list. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough one near Gibeah, which is commonly identified with Tell el-Ful just north of Jerusalem.

Machbenah was a town in the territory of Judah, mentioned only once, in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants. 1 Chr 2:49 calls Sheva the "father of Machbenah." In these lists "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Machbenah is probably a place name rather than a person. The preceding verse (1 Chr 2:48) names Sheva's mother as Maachah, Caleb's concubine. The same verse links nearby towns such as Madmannah and Gibea to Caleb's family, which points to southern Judah. The exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it in the Judean lowlands (the Shephelah), east of Lachish. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "bond," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "poverty" or "the smiting of his son."

Madmen was a town in Moab, mentioned only in Jeremiah's prophecy against Moab, where it is told it will be cut down and pursued by the sword (Jer 48:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "dunghill." From the wider context of Jeremiah's oracles, Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the threatened sword to be that of the Babylonians. The Hebrew line contains a wordplay between "Madmen" and the verb for being silenced or cut down. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the initial "M" may have come from repeating the last letter of the word before it, so the name may originally have been "Dimon," another form of Dibon. Otherwise the town is unidentified. The location shown here lies close to Dibon (modern Dhiban, in Jordan), which fits that identification.

Madmenah was a town north of Jerusalem, named only in Isaiah's poetic description of an Assyrian army advancing on the city (Isa 10:31). In that passage, Madmenah "is removed" and the people of nearby Gebim gather to flee, picturing villages emptied in panic as the invader draws near. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it among the Benjamite villages along the northern approach and links the advance to Sennacherib. Easton's Bible Dictionary also puts it in Benjamin, not far north of Jerusalem. It notes that the same Hebrew word appears in Isa 25:10, where it is translated "dunghill." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the site has not been identified, so its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement just north of Jerusalem, inferred from the route described in the passage.

Magadan was a place on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus sailed there after sending away the crowd he had fed (Matt 15:39). The King James Version reads "Magdala," but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the better manuscripts read Magadan. In the parallel account, Mark 8:10 names the destination Dalmanutha instead, so the two were probably neighbouring districts on the western shore. Many link Magadan with Magdala, the home of Mary Magdalene. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the names as the same place, or as villages close together, and the name probably comes from the Hebrew word for "tower." The location shown here follows the identification with el-Mejdel (modern Migdal), at the southwest corner of the Plain of Gennesaret, about 3 miles northwest of Tiberias.

Mahalab was a place on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, in the description of that border near Tyre and Achzib in Josh 19:29. The King James Version does not show it as a name. It translates the Hebrew phrase as "from the coast to Achzib," but many modern translations read the same words as "from Mahalab to Achzib." Some scholars identify Mahalab with the town called Mahalliba in Assyrian records, and possibly with Ahlab, a town of Asher named in Judges. These links are inferences and remain uncertain. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here places it inland, southeast of Tyre, in the hills near the modern border between Lebanon and Israel.

Makaz was a town named only once in the Bible, in the list of Solomon's twelve district officers who each supplied food for the king's household for one month of the year. It belonged to the district of the son of Dekar, together with Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan (1 Kgs 4:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that those three towns probably match places on the border of Dan (Josh 19:41–42). This suggests Makaz lay in the same area, the low hill country west of Jerusalem. Its site has never been identified, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also reports a suggestion that it may be the same as Me-jarkon in the Danite list. The location shown here is only a rough placement near its companion towns, west of Jerusalem, and does not follow that identification.

Manahath was a place to which some Benjamite families from Geba were moved. It appears only once, in the genealogy of Benjamin, where the heads of the fathers' houses among the sons of Ehud are said to have been removed from Geba to Manahath (1 Chr 8:6). The verse does not say when or why this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rest." The Manahathites named among the descendants of Judah in 1 Chr 2:52–54 may be connected with the same place, but that link is uncertain. The location is not described in the text. The location shown here follows the identification with modern Malha (al-Maliha), southwest of Jerusalem, which fits a site within reach of Benjamin and Judah. A different Manahath, an Edomite person, appears in Gen 36:23 and is unrelated.

Mareal, spelled Maralah in the King James Version, was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun. Josh 19:11 traces Zebulun's border as it went up westward toward the sea, passing Maralah, reaching Dabbasheth and then the stream that lies before Jokneam. The verse indicates its position on the line of the border but says nothing else about the town. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on Zebulun's southern boundary, gives the meaning of the name as "trembling," and identifies it with the modern village of Ma'lul, about 4 miles (6 km) southwest of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification, with Ma'lul at the edge of the hills overlooking the Jezreel Valley. The identification rests on the similar name and a fitting position along the border, so it remains probable rather than certain.

Maroth was a town of Judah mentioned only once, in Micah's lament over the towns facing invasion (Mic 1:12). Micah says its people waited anxiously for good, but disaster came from the LORD as far as the gate of Jerusalem. The name means "bitterness" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and it probably forms part of the wordplay on town names that runs through Mic 1:10–15, contrasting "bitterness" with the good its people hoped for. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the passage to the Assyrian invasion and places Maroth not far from Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it in the western lowland of Judah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it an unknown town, probably in the Philistine plain. Its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is a rough point in the western lowland, following the lowland identification. Some have suggested it is the same place as Maarath (Josh 15:59).

Mashal was a city in the territory of the tribe of Asher that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levites (1 Chr 6:74). The surrounding passage assigns Asher's Levitical towns to the Gershonite branch of the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Mishal in the parallel list at Josh 21:30, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also equates it with Misheal in Asher's boundary list at Josh 19:26. Its site is uncertain. The fourth-century writer Eusebius placed it near Mount Carmel by the sea, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards it as unidentified. The location shown here is a rough placement in western Galilee, within Asher's territory. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "entreaty," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "a parable" or "governing."

Me-jarkon was a place in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan, named in Josh 19:46 together with Rakkon and the border near Japho (Joppa). The name probably means "waters of Jarkon" or "yellow waters." Views differ on what it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a river and identifies it with the Nahr el-'Auja, the modern Yarkon River, which rises near Antipatris and flows into the Mediterranean north of Jaffa. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as a town near Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text of the verse is difficult and that the Greek translation reads it as "from the river Jarkon." This entry follows the river identification, and the location shown here is a rough point on the Yarkon River north of Jaffa.

Mearah was a place near Sidon, mentioned only in Joshua 13:4 in the list of land the Israelites had not yet conquered when Joshua was old. The verse places it "beside the Sidonians" and traces a line from there to Aphek and the border of the Amorites. The Hebrew name means "cave," so it probably referred to a notable cavern or a settlement named after one. The Greek Septuagint omits the name or reads "from Gaza," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes is too far south. Some scholars suggest the word may be a garbled form of a Sidonian town name. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions two proposed sites: the cave of Jezzin in Lebanon, east of Sidon, or Mogheiriyeh ("little cave"), northeast of Sidon. The location shown here follows the Mogheiriyeh identification.

Meconah (spelled Mekonah in the King James Version) was a town in the south of Judah. It is named only once, in Neh 11:28, in a list of places where people of Judah lived after the return from exile in Babylon. It appears there next to Ziklag along with its surrounding villages, so it was probably near Ziklag. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a base or foundation." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been identified, and its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is a rough placement in the northern Negev, in the general area associated with Ziklag.

Melita is the island in the Mediterranean where the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome was wrecked. After the crew and passengers reached shore, they learned the island's name (Acts 28:1). It is the modern Malta, south of Sicily. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Paul and his companions stayed there three months before sailing on to Rome in another Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island. By inference from context, this was probably about AD 57. Tradition places the wreck at St. Paul's Bay on the island's northeast coast, and both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note how well that site fits the description in Acts. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the island at that time as a dependency of the Roman province of Sicily. Some older interpreters placed Melita at Mljet (Meleda) in the Adriatic Sea, but this entry follows the Malta identification.

Merathaim is a name used for Babylon or the land of Babylonia in Jer 50:21, part of Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon. In that verse the LORD commands an attacker to go up against 'the land of Merathaim' and the inhabitants of Pekod, and to destroy them completely. The Hebrew name means 'double rebellion.' Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as a symbolic name for Babylon, marking a rebellion greater than that of other nations. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the 'double' with the two captivities Babylon brought on Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Delitzsch's suggestion that it may also echo the Babylonian name Marratu, the 'bitter river' or Persian Gulf, and so refer to southern Babylonia. The location shown here places it at the site of Babylon itself, south of modern Baghdad in Iraq.

Meroz was a place in northern Israel that is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the Song of Deborah. After the victory of Deborah and Barak over Sisera, the angel of the LORD calls for a bitter curse on Meroz and its inhabitants because they did not come to help in the battle (Judg 5:23). The passage gives no further detail. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the harsh words may mean Meroz lay near the battlefield, so its people could easily have joined the fight or stopped Sisera as he fled. Its site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it near the Kishon River, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mention a possible identification with el-Murussus, north of the Jezreel Valley near Beth-shean. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the general area of Mount Tabor.

Mesha is a place named in Gen 10:30 as one end of the territory where the descendants of Joktan lived, which stretched from Mesha toward Sephar, "a mount of the east." The "their" of the verse refers, by context, to Joktan's thirteen sons listed just before it, many of whose names are linked with tribes of Arabia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Mesha as one of the boundaries of the Joktanites when they first settled in Arabia, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a plain on the borders of Arabia. Its exact site is unknown. Proposals range from northern or northwestern Arabia to the Red Sea coast further south. The location shown here is a rough placement in northwestern Arabia, east of the Gulf of Aqaba, marking the northern end of the Joktanite range. This is distinct from Mesha the king of Moab and from other people of that name.

Meshech-Tubal is the pairing of Meshech and Tubal, two peoples named together in Ezekiel's lament over Egypt. In Ezek 32:26 they appear among the fallen nations in the underworld, lying in their graves with the uncircumcised, killed by the sword, though they once spread terror in the land of the living. Elsewhere the two are listed as sons of Japheth (Gen 10:2), as traders in slaves and bronze with Tyre (Ezek 27:13), and as peoples ruled by Gog (Ezek 38:2). They are commonly identified with the Mushku and Tabal known from Assyrian records in eastern Anatolia, though some place them farther north toward the Black Sea and Caucasus. Their exact homeland is uncertain, and the location shown here is an approximate regional placement north of the Caucasus.

Metheg-ammah is named in the King James Version as a place David took from the Philistines after defeating and subduing them (2 Sam 8:1). The Hebrew phrase probably means "bridle of the mother city," and many readers take it as a figure of speech rather than a town name: David seized control of the Philistines' chief city. The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:1 says instead that David took "Gath and her towns," so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify that city as Gath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads differently, saying David took "the tribute," and that the Hebrew text may be damaged. If a separate place is meant, its site is unknown, though it would have been in the Philistine plain near Gath. The location shown here follows the Gath identification, probably modern Tell es-Safi.

Middin was a town of Judah listed among the six cities “in the wilderness” in the tribal allotment of Joshua 15, named between Betharabah and Secacah (Josh 15:61). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Hebrew word translated “wilderness” as a specific district, which Easton's Bible Dictionary places west of the Dead Sea near En-gedi. The name has been explained as “measures” (Easton) or “judgment; striving” (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may survive at Khirbet Mird, a fortified hilltop with ancient cisterns overlooking the el-Buqei'a plateau. It also notes that the Greek reading “Ainon” (springs) could point to the oasis of Ain Feshkha near Qumran. The location shown here lies in the el-Buqei'a basin west of the northern Dead Sea, closer to the Khirbet Mird view than to the coastal springs.

Migdal-el, whose name means "tower of God," was a fortified city given to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in the list of Naphtali's fortified cities, between Iron and Horem (Josh 19:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may come from an ancient tower dedicated to God. The site is uncertain. Eusebius's Onomasticon places it near Athlit on the coast south of Ptolemais (Acre). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have linked it with Magdala. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes either Khirbet Mejdel, about 3 miles north of Kedesh, or Mejdel Islim, about 5 miles farther northwest. The location shown here, in the hills of southern Lebanon northwest of Kedesh, follows a northern Galilean identification of this kind, closest to the Mejdel Islim proposal.

Migdal-gad was a town of the tribe of Judah, listed in Josh 15:37 among a group of cities in the lowland (Shephelah), the low hill country and coastal plain toward the west. Its name means "tower of Gad" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "tower of fortune" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The Bible mentions it only in this list, and its site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it was probably the town of el-Mejdel (al-Majdal), a short distance northeast of ancient Ashkelon, within the area of the modern city of Ashkelon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this would place it very close to the Philistine strongholds. The location shown here follows the el-Mejdel identification.

Minni was a kingdom named only in Jer 51:27, where it is summoned with Ararat and Ashchenaz to attack Babylon. The prophet pictures a banner raised and a trumpet blown to gather these northern nations against the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Minni as a province of Armenia, under Median rule at that time, and mentions a view that the name Armenia may come from Har-minni, "the mountainous country of Minni." Smith's Bible Dictionary also treats it as part of Armenia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the Minnai (Mannaeans) of Assyrian inscriptions, a people closely linked with Armenia or part of it. The exact boundaries are uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and follows the Armenian identification, placing it in the highlands of present-day Armenia.

Misgab was a place in Moab named in Jeremiah's prophecy against that nation, alongside Nebo and Kiriathaim. All three are described as overthrown, with Misgab "confounded and dismayed" (Jer 48:1). The name means "height" or "fortress." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the same Hebrew word appears in Isa 25:12, where the King James Version renders it "high fort." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that no site with a similar name has been found, and suggests the word may not be a town name at all but a title for a strong Moabite fortress, perhaps Kir-moab itself. The location shown here follows that identification, placing Misgab at Kir-moab, the modern town of Kerak in Jordan. Its actual site remains uncertain.

Mitylene was the chief city of the island of Lesbos, on its east coast in the Aegean Sea. Paul's ship stopped there near the end of his third missionary journey, as he and his companions travelled toward Jerusalem. The party picked Paul up at Assos, where he had come overland, and sailed on to Mitylene (Acts 20:14). By inference from the next stage of the voyage, which reached a point opposite Chios the following day, they probably spent one night there. This entry dates the voyage to about AD 54, an estimate inferred from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Mitylene was a free city in Paul's day and was known for its fine buildings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as having two harbours. The site is the modern town of Mytilene, still the main city of Lesbos, which matches the location shown here.

Mizpah, called "the land of Mizpeh" in the King James Version, was a district below Mount Hermon where Hivites lived. It is named in Josh 11:3 among the peoples summoned to join the northern alliance against Joshua. The surrounding chapter shows that this alliance was led by Jabin king of Hazor. Josh 11:8 mentions a "valley of Mizpeh" to the east, to which the defeated forces were chased, and this is probably the same area. The name means "watch-tower," and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew has the article, "the Mizpeh." Several other places in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with this one. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's suggests the modern village of Metulla, whose name also means "the look-out," at the northern tip of Israel, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Mizpeh was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in Josh 18:26 beside Chephirah and Mozah among the cities given to Benjamin when the land was divided. The name means "watchtower" or "lookout" and is shared by several places in the Bible, so it should not be confused with the Mizpeh of Gilead, Judah or Moab. This Benjaminite town is probably the same as the Mizpah mentioned elsewhere, where Israel gathered under Samuel (1 Sam 7:5–6) and where Gedaliah later governed after Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:23). Its site is disputed. Many scholars favor Tell en-Nasbeh, about 12 km north of Jerusalem, while others favor Nebi Samwil, a high hill just northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows the Nebi Samwil identification.

Mizpeh was a town in the lowlands, or Shephelah, of Judah, listed among the towns given to the tribe of Judah in Josh 15:38. It appears between Dilean and Joktheel in a group of towns that also includes Lachish and Eglon. The name means "watchtower" or "lookout point" and is shared by several places in the Bible, so this Mizpeh should not be confused with the better-known Mizpeh in Benjamin or the Mizpeh in Gilead. Apart from this one listing, nothing more is recorded about it. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the district around Lachish, inferred from the towns it is grouped with.

Mizpeh, called "Mizpeh of Moab," was a town in Moab where David went while fleeing from Saul. There he asked the king of Moab to let his father and mother stay under his protection until David knew what God would do for him (1 Sam 22:3). David's family ties to Moab through his great-grandmother Ruth, a Moabite, may explain why he turned there, though the text does not say so. The following verse (1 Sam 22:5) records that the prophet Gad told David not to stay in the stronghold but to go to the land of Judah, and he moved to the forest of Hareth. The name, meaning "watchtower," is shared by several biblical places, and this town's exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably the citadel of Kir-Moab, modern Kerak in Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification.

Moreh (little Hermon) was a hill in the Valley of Jezreel. It is mentioned only in Judg 7:1, where it marks the position of the Midianite camp. Gideon and his men camped beside the well of Harod, and the Midianites lay north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "hill of the teacher." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "stretching." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ridge called Little Hermon, Jebel ed-Duhy (today Givat HaMoreh), on the northern edge of the Jezreel plain opposite Mount Gilboa, with Shunem at its western foot. One commentator, Moore, placed the scene near Shechem instead. The location shown here follows the Little Hermon identification. This hill is distinct from the place called Moreh near Shechem that is linked with Abraham.

Moresheth-gath was a town in the lowland foothills of Judah, named only in Mic 1:14 among the places facing judgment in Micah's lament. There the prophet says Judah will have to give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath, probably meaning it would be lost to an enemy. The name likely means "possession of Gath." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be Micah's home town, since he is called "the Morasthite" (Mic 1:1; Jer 26:18), and it probably lay near Gath and Mareshah (Mic 1:15). Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Jerome placed it a little east of Eleutheropolis, modern Beit Jibrin. The location shown here, a rough one just east of Beit Jibrin, follows that identification.

Moriah is the land to which God sent Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering on one of its mountains (Gen 22:2). This is the only place where the land of Moriah is named, and the passage gives no precise location. Abraham saw the place from a distance on the third day of his journey. A later passage, 2 Chr 3:1, gives the name Mount Moriah to the hill in Jerusalem where Solomon built the temple, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this temple hill to be the mountain of Isaac's sacrifice, and this entry follows that view. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Samaritan tradition places the event on Mount Gerizim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions Moreh near Shechem as another proposed site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia leaves the question open.

Mortar was a district in or near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Zeph 1:11. The King James Version keeps the Hebrew name, Maktesh, which means "mortar" or "hollow." The name probably describes a basin-shaped hollow in the terrain. Zephaniah tells its inhabitants to wail because its merchants and those who handle silver will be cut off, which suggests it was a trading or money-dealing quarter. The neighboring verse mentions the Fish Gate and the "second" quarter of the city, so Maktesh was probably also a part of Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain. Many identify it with the central valley running through the old city, often called the Tyropoeon Valley, and the location shown here places it within Jerusalem in that area. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that it was the quarter where Phoenician traders lived.

Moserah was a campsite of the Israelites during their wilderness journey. They reached it from Beeroth of the children of Jaakan, and Deut 10:6 says Aaron died and was buried there, with his son Eleazar taking over as priest. Other passages (Num 20:28; Num 33:38) place Aaron's death on Mount Hor, so Moserah is usually taken to be the area at or near that mountain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat it as probably the same place as Moseroth (Num 33:30–31), which that list places before Bene-jaakan rather than after it. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "bond" and links it with el-Tayibeh, a small spring at the foot of the pass up Mount Hor. The location shown here follows the traditional identification of Mount Hor with Jebel Harun near Petra in southern Jordan, and it is only approximate.

Mount Baalah was a hill on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only in Josh 15:11. The border line ran from the side of Ekron northward to Shicron, passed along Mount Baalah, and then went out to Jabneel before ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the north-western boundary between Judah and Dan. It should not be confused with the town of Baalah (Kiriath-jearim) further east along the same northern border. Its exact site is unknown. By inference from its place in the sequence between Ekron and Jabneel, it was probably a low ridge in the coastal plain, and the location shown here is a rough position in that area, west of Ekron and near Jabneel (modern Yavne).

Mount Baalhermon (ESV Mount Baal-hermon) is a mountain named in Judg 3:3 as one boundary of the territory held by the Hivites of Mount Lebanon. These were among the peoples left in the land after the conquest, and the verse gives their range as running "from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath." The name links Baal with Hermon. It is probably Mount Hermon itself or part of it, a view supported by 1 Chr 5:23, which mentions Baal-hermon alongside Senir and Mount Hermon. A closely parallel boundary description in Josh 13:5 reads "from Baal-gad under mount Hermon unto the entering into Hamath," so some take Baal-hermon to be a place at the foot of Hermon, possibly Baal-gad. The location shown here follows the identification with the summit of Mount Hermon, on the modern border of Lebanon and Syria.

Mount Ephraim was the name for the hill country of central Israel, the highland region settled by the tribe of Ephraim, rather than a single peak. In Jer 4:15 a voice announcing disaster is heard first from Dan, at the far northern edge of the land, and then from Mount Ephraim, which lies much closer to Jerusalem. By inference from the passage, the two places mark the stages of an invader advancing from the north toward Judah. Other passages use the same phrase for the setting of events in Joshua, Judges and Samuel. Examples include the territory given to the descendants of Joseph in Josh 17:15 and the home of Micah in Judg 17:1. The location shown here places the region in the central highlands around modern Nablus, near ancient Shechem.

Mount Ephron was a hill or mountain range named as a landmark on the northern border of the tribe of Judah, where Judah's territory met Benjamin's. Joshua 15:9 traces the boundary from the spring of the waters of Nephtoah out to "the cities of mount Ephron," and then on to Baalah, also called Kiriath-jearim. The verse suggests the area held several towns. It probably lay between Nephtoah and Kiriath-jearim, west of Jerusalem, by inference from the order of the boundary description. Its exact identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the range on the west side of the Wadi Beit Hanina, northwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem and should not be taken as a firm identification.

Mount Gilead is the place named in Gideon's proclamation before his battle with the Midianites. God told him to announce that anyone who was fearful should 'return and depart early from mount Gilead', and 22,000 men left, leaving 10,000 (Judg 7:3). Since Gideon's army was camped by the well of Harod, west of the Jordan, this mountain probably lay in that area rather than in the better-known region of Gilead east of the Jordan. Views differ. Some take the name as an early copying slip for Mount Gilboa, which overlooks Harod. Others take it as a local name for a height near the spring, perhaps echoed in the modern name Ain Jalud. The location shown here follows an identification on the Gilboa ridge near the Harod spring. It is probably separate from the 'mount Gilead' where Jacob and Laban made their covenant, which was east of the Jordan.

Mount Heres was a hill in the territory of Dan, near Aijalon and Shaalbim, where the Amorites held on and refused to leave after Israel's settlement. According to Judg 1:35, the Amorites kept living there, but the tribes descended from Joseph later gained the upper hand and forced them to pay tribute. The Hebrew name, Har-heres, means "sun-mountain." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the same place as Ir-shemesh ("city of the sun"), which Josh 19:41 lists among Dan's towns. Because of the shared sun meaning, it is often linked with Beth-shemesh. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the low hill country west of Jerusalem, in the area of Beth-shemesh and the Aijalon and Sorek valleys.

Mount Horeb is the mountain where the Israelites, after the golden calf incident, stripped off their ornaments as a sign of mourning at God's command (Exod 33:6). Elsewhere in the Bible, Horeb is called "the mountain of God," where Moses saw the burning bush (Exod 3:1). Deuteronomy regularly uses the name Horeb for the place where the law was given, which Exodus calls Mount Sinai, so the two names are generally taken to refer to the same mountain or the same range. The prophet Elijah later traveled forty days to reach Horeb (1 Kgs 19:8). Its location is debated. Proposed sites include several peaks in the southern Sinai Peninsula and some in northwest Arabia. The location shown here follows the traditional identification with Jebel Musa in southern Sinai, near St Catherine's Monastery.

Mount Jearim was a mountain on the northern border of the tribe of Judah. In the description of that boundary, the line ran west from Baalah (Kiriath-jearim) to Mount Seir, then along the north side of Mount Jearim, and down to Beth-shemesh and Timnah (Josh 15:10). The verse equates Mount Jearim with Chesalon, so the name may refer to the ridge on which the town of Chesalon stood. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "forests," probably pointing to a wooded height. Chesalon is commonly identified with the modern village of Kesla, west of Jerusalem, and the location shown here matches that identification. This is the only verse in the Bible that mentions Mount Jearim.

Mount Lebanon is the mountain range of Lebanon, named in Judg 3:3 as the home of the Hivites. They were one of the peoples the Lord left in the land after Joshua's conquest to test the Israelites. The verse places the Hivite territory there, stretching from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath. That suggests the northern hill country beyond Israel's settled tribes. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes it as a range marking the northern border of the Promised Land. It is probably the Lebanon range that runs parallel to the Mediterranean coast in the modern country of Lebanon, west of the Beqaa Valley, with the Anti-Lebanon and Mount Hermon to the east. The location shown here is a point in the central part of the range, northeast of Beirut, standing for the range as a whole rather than a single peak.

Mount Moriah is the hill in Jerusalem where Solomon began building the temple of the LORD. 2 Chr 3:1 identifies it as the place where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite that David had set aside. The accounts in 2 Sam 24 and 1 Chr 21 describe David buying this threshing floor from Ornan, who is called Araunah in Samuel, and building an altar there after a plague was stopped. Gen 22:2 sends Abraham to offer Isaac on a mountain in "the land of Moriah." Jewish tradition identifies that mountain with the temple hill, though Genesis does not explicitly connect the two, and Samaritan tradition places Abraham's offering on Mount Gerizim instead. The location shown here is the Temple Mount in Jerusalem's Old City, the usual identification of the temple site.

Mount Perazim, meaning "mountain of breaches," is named only in Isa 28:21. There Isaiah says the LORD will rise up as he did at Mount Perazim and be angry as in the valley of Gibeon, to carry out his "strange work." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Baal-perazim, where David defeated the Philistines. In 2 Sam 5:20 David names that place for the way the LORD broke through his enemies like breaking waters. Isaiah therefore probably recalls that victory as an example of God acting in judgment, though this time against his own people. The exact site is uncertain. It is usually placed near the Valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem, where the Philistines had gathered. The location shown here is a rough one in that area, just outside Jerusalem.

Mount Seir was a hill or ridge on the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah, west of Baalah (Kiriath-jearim). Joshua 15:10 traces the border from Baalah westward to Mount Seir, then along the north side of Mount Jearim (Chesalon), down to Beth-shemesh and on to Timnah. It is a different place from the better-known Mount Seir, the mountain range of Edom south and east of the Dead Sea where Esau settled. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this Judean Seir as a mountain range lying between the Wady Aly and the Wady Ghurab, in the hill country west of Jerusalem. Its exact identification is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the hills between Kiriath-jearim and Beth-shemesh, which fits the order of landmarks in the boundary description.

Mount Sion is a name for Mount Hermon, used once in the King James Version. Deut 4:48 explains it directly: "mount Sion, which is Hermon." It marks the northern limit of the land east of the Jordan that Israel took from the Amorite kings Sihon and Og, which stretched from Aroer on the Arnon River in the south up to this mountain. It should not be confused with Mount Zion (sometimes spelled Sion) in Jerusalem, which is a different name in Hebrew. The ESV spells it Sirion, matching Deut 3:9, which, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, says the Sidonians called Hermon Sirion and the Amorites called it Shenir. The location shown here is the Hermon massif, probably the modern Jebel esh-Sheikh on the border of Lebanon and Syria.

Mount Zalmon was a wooded hill near Shechem in central Israel. During the conflict between Abimelech and the people of Shechem, Abimelech led his men up the mountain, cut down a tree branch, carried it on his shoulder, and told his followers to do the same (Judg 9:48). The next verse says they piled the branches against the stronghold where the people of Shechem had taken refuge and set it on fire. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Zalmon as a dark-forested hill south of Shechem, the modern Jebel Suleiman, and connects it with the 'Salmon' of Ps 68:14, where snow on the mountain is used as an image. Other identifications place it on one of the peaks beside Shechem, Mount Gerizim or Mount Ebal. The location shown here follows an identification on or near Mount Ebal, just north of Shechem. The exact site is uncertain.

Mount Zemaraim was a hill in the hill country of Ephraim where King Abijah of Judah stood to address Jeroboam and the army of Israel before a battle between the two kingdoms (2 Chr 13:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the Ephraim highlands north of Jerusalem and notes that the battle that followed ended in a heavy defeat for Jeroboam, who never recovered his strength and died soon after. The hill probably took its name from, or lay near, the town of Zemaraim listed among the cities of Benjamin in Josh 18:22. Its exact site is uncertain. Some place it northeast of Bethel, while others place it closer to the Jordan Valley. The location shown here lies north of Jericho, on the eastern edge of the hill country, and follows the second view.

Mozah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It is named only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities, alongside Mizpeh and Chephirah (Josh 18:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it comes between Chephirah and Rekem in that list. The Hebrew form carries the definite article, "ha-Motsah." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's take the name to mean "an issuing of water" or "fountain," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "place of hard stone." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the town may be the village of Beit Mizzeh, about 4 miles (6 km) northwest of Jerusalem near Qaloniyeh. The location shown here matches that area, near the modern Motza just west of Jerusalem. The Bible records nothing else about the town.

Myra was a city of Lycia, on the southwest coast of Asia Minor, where the ship carrying Paul as a prisoner to Rome put in after crossing the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia (Acts 27:5). The next verse, Acts 27:6, says that at Myra the centurion found a ship from Alexandria bound for Italy and moved the prisoners onto it. That ship was later wrecked at Melita (Malta). The voyage is dated to about AD 56, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the city about 2½ miles from the coast. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it later became a prominent port for ships from Egypt and Cyprus, and that it is linked by tradition with Nicholas, a bishop said to have been buried nearby. The location shown here matches the ruins at the modern town of Demre in southern Turkey.

Naamah was a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah in the division of the land under Joshua. It appears in Josh 15:41 in a group of sixteen cities with their villages, alongside Gederoth, Beth-dagon and Makkedah. This is its only mention in the Bible, and nothing else is recorded about it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "beautiful" or "agreeable." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some identify it with Na'aneh, and the location shown here follows that identification, near the modern village and kibbutz of Na'an southeast of Ramla. The town is distinct from the two women named Naamah in the Bible, Tubal-cain's sister and the mother of King Rehoboam.

Naarah, spelled Naarath in the King James Version, was a town on the southern border of Ephraim's territory. Joshua 16:7 traces this boundary down from Janohah to Ataroth, then to Naarath, and on to Jericho and the Jordan River, which places the town in the Jordan Valley not far from Jericho. It is probably the same place as Naaran, named in 1 Chr 7:28 among the towns of Ephraim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it north of Jericho on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "young person," and Easton's gives "girl." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius put it 5 Roman miles from Jericho. It also says no identification is certain, though el-Aujeh, about 5 miles northeast of Jericho, would fit. The location shown here, a few miles north of Jericho, follows that general area.

Naaran was a city named as the eastern limit of the lands held by the descendants of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. 1 Chr 7:28 lists it among their possessions and settlements, with Bethel and its towns, Gezer to the west, and Shechem and its towns. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "boyish" or "youthful" and places the town in Ephraim between Bethel and Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers it very probably the same place as Naarah, which Josh 16:7 names on Ephraim's border near Jericho. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here places it in the Jordan Valley north of Jericho, which fits its role as an eastern boundary point.

Nahaliel was a valley where the Israelites stopped during the last stage of their journey toward Canaan. Numbers lists it between Mattanah and Bamoth (Num 21:19), in the stretch of the route north of the Arnon River, on the borders of Moab east of the Dead Sea. The name is usually taken to mean "torrent valley of God" or "valley of God." Its exact location is uncertain. Eusebius placed it near the Arnon, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests one of the Arnon's tributaries, perhaps Wadi Waleh, or Wadi Zerqa Ma'in farther north. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ravine of the Zerqa Ma'in, known for the ancient hot springs of Callirhoe near the Dead Sea. The location shown here, on the eastern side of the Dead Sea, appears to follow the Zerqa Ma'in identification.

Nahalol was a Canaanite town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun. Judg 1:30 says Zebulun did not drive out its inhabitants or those of Kitron. Instead the Canaanites went on living among the Israelites and were made to pay tribute. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Nahalol as the same place as Nahalal, which Josh 19:15 lists among Zebulun's towns and Josh 21:35 names as a town given to the Levites. Its exact site is uncertain. Proposed identifications include the area of the ruined village of Ma'lul and other sites near the western Jezreel Valley. The location shown here follows an identification with the area of modern Ein Mahil, northeast of Nazareth in Lower Galilee.

Nain was a town in Galilee, mentioned in the Bible only once. Luke records that Jesus went there the day after healing a centurion's servant at Capernaum, with many of his disciples and a large crowd (Luke 7:11). Near the town gate he met a funeral procession and raised a widow's only son to life (Luke 7:12–17). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "green pastures" or "lovely," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "beauty" or "pleasantness." The town is usually identified with the modern village of Nein, on the northwestern slope of the Hill of Moreh (Jebel ed-Duhy, also called Little Hermon), overlooking the plain of Esdraelon (the Jezreel Valley), about 4 miles from Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes ancient tombs cut into the rock nearby.

Naphath is a place or region named in Hebrew in Josh 17:11, the list of towns that Manasseh held within the territories of Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. The King James Version does not show it as a name and translates the phrase as "even three countries." Other translations read it as "the three heights" or as a name, "Naphath" or "the third is Naphath." The word probably means "height" or "hilly region." It may be linked with Naphoth-dor, the heights of Dor, mentioned elsewhere in Joshua and Kings, but its exact meaning and location are uncertain. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Naphath as a region in Issachar containing towns that belonged to Manasseh. The location shown here is only approximate and places it near Megiddo, at the edge of the Jezreel Valley.

Naphath-dor was the district surrounding the coastal town of Dor, south of Mount Carmel. The name is usually understood as "the heights of Dor" or "the region of Dor," and the King James Version translates it as "the region of Dor" in 1 Kgs 4:11. There it appears as one of Solomon's administrative districts. The son of Abinadab governed it, and he was married to Solomon's daughter Taphath. The same Hebrew phrase occurs in Joshua's lists of Canaanite territories (Josh 11:2; 12:23), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the form in the margin of the Revised Version at Josh 12:23 and refers readers to Dor. Whether "heights" means the slopes of Carmel behind the town or the coastal strip itself is uncertain. The location shown here places it at Dor itself, probably the site of Tel Dor near modern Tantura on Israel's Mediterranean coast.

Naphish, spelled Nephish in the King James text, was a people or territory east of the Jordan. It is named alongside the Hagarites, Jetur and Nodab as one of the groups that the tribes of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh fought (1 Chr 5:19). The name matches Naphish, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31), and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the father of an Arab tribe. The place is therefore probably the land of that tribe, named after its ancestor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "refreshment" or "one who rests." The exact location is unknown. The location shown here is an approximate point in the region east of the Sea of Galilee, within the area the eastern Israelite tribes settled.

Naphoth-dor was the district around the Canaanite town of Dor on the Mediterranean coast. Its kings were among those summoned by Jabin king of Hazor to join a northern alliance against Joshua. The King James Version translates the phrase as "the borders of Dor on the west" (Josh 11:2), while the Revised Version margin keeps it as a place name, Naphoth-dor. The Hebrew word is usually understood as "heights" or "hilly district," probably referring to the coastal ridge and lower slopes of Mount Carmel inland from the town, though some take it simply as the region belonging to Dor. The same expression appears elsewhere for the territory of Dor (Josh 12:23; 1 Kgs 4:11). The location shown here marks Dor itself, usually identified with Tel Dor (Khirbet el-Burj) near modern Tantura on the coast south of Carmel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name under Dor.

Neah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Zebulun. It is mentioned only once, in Josh 19:13. That verse traces Zebulun's eastern border past Gath-hepher and Ittah-kazin to Rimmon, and from there toward Neah. The Hebrew reads "the Neah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "moved" or "moving," and Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the east side of Zebulun, not far from Rimmon. Its site has not been firmly identified, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it probably lay north of Rimmon (modern Rummaneh) and may be the same place as Neiel in Josh 19:27, on the border of Asher. The location shown here, in lower Galilee north of Rimmon, appears to follow that northern placement and the possible link with Neiel.

Neapolis, meaning "new city," was a port on the northern shore of the Aegean Sea where Paul and his companions first landed in Europe. They sailed from Troas to Samothrace and reached Neapolis the next day (Acts 16:11), after Paul's vision calling him to Macedonia. It served as the seaport for the inland city of Philippi, about 10 miles away by a road over the coastal ridge. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary add that Paul probably sailed from here again on his last journey toward Troas and Jerusalem (Acts 20:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the town originally belonged to Thrace and later fell within the Roman province of Macedonia. Most scholars identify it with modern Kavala in Greece, though some have placed it at Eski Kavala, about 10 miles to the west. The location shown here follows the Kavala identification.

Nebaioth was a pastoral people and their territory in the Arabian desert, mentioned as a place in Isa 60:7. There the rams of Nebaioth, along with the flocks of Kedar, are brought as acceptable offerings on God's altar when the nations come to glorify his house. The name is shared with Ishmael's firstborn son, and Kedar was another of his sons (Gen 25:13). So the tribe is probably understood as descended from him and known for its sheep. Many have identified Nebaioth with the Nabateans, the Arab people whose later capital was Petra in southern Jordan. Others question the link because the two names differ slightly in form. The location shown here follows the Nabatean identification and marks the area around Petra. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "words," "prophecies," or "buds."

Neballat was a town where people of the tribe of Benjamin settled after returning from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah's list of Benjamite towns, alongside Hadid and Zeboim and near Lod and Ono (Neh 11:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hidden folly," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "prophecy; budding." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the village of Beit Nebala (Bayt Nabala), about 4 miles from Lydda (modern Lod). Easton's places it north of Lydda and the encyclopedia northeast. The location shown here follows the Bayt Nabala identification. Its closeness to Lod and Ono fits a setting on the western edge of the hill country, toward the coastal plain.

Neiel was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the description of Asher's border in Josh 19:27. There it appears after the valley of Jiphthahel and Beth-emek and just before Cabul, so it probably lay near Asher's southeastern edge, close to the territory of Zebulun. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "dwelling-place of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "commotion of God." Its exact site is also uncertain. Easton's identifies it with the ruin of Y'anin (Yanin), less than 2 miles north of Cabul (modern Kabul). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the hilltop village of Mi'ar, halfway between Jiphthahel and Cabul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same place as Neah (Josh 19:13). The location shown here follows the Y'anin identification.

Netaim was a place in Judah where a group of potters lived and worked for the king, mentioned only in 1 Chr 4:23. The King James Version translates the Hebrew word as a common noun, "plants", giving "those that dwelt among plants and hedges." The Revised Version instead reads it as a place name, "the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors that reading. Because Gederah lay in the Judean Shephelah, the lowland foothills west of the Judean hills, Netaim is probably to be sought in the same area. The same encyclopedia notes that no likely site has been identified. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Shephelah and does not mark a known site.

Nezib was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:43). It appears in the same group of towns as Keilah and Mareshah. The name probably means "garrison" or "pillar" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "standing-place" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Eusebius and Jerome knew the place and put it on the road from Eleutheropolis (Beit Jibrin) to Hebron, about seven to nine miles from Eleutheropolis. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all identify it with the village of Beit Nasib (Beit Nuzib), which has ancient remains. The village lies about 2 miles southwest of Khirbet Kila (Keilah) and roughly 14 miles southwest of Jerusalem. The location shown here matches that identification.

Nibshan was a town in the wilderness of Judah, named only once, in the list of towns allotted to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:62). It belongs to a group of six wilderness towns, listed between Secacah (Josh 15:61) and the City of Salt, followed by Engedi. This places it in the dry country west of the Dead Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "soft" or "light soil." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the early church historian Eusebius knew of the place but gave no clue to where it was, and that the site has not been found. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is approximate and follows Easton's suggestion that it was probably near Engedi, on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

Nicopolis, meaning "city of victory," was the city where Paul planned to spend a winter. In Titus 3:12 he asks Titus to join him there once Artemas or Tychicus arrives to take his place. Several ancient cities had this name, and the letter itself does not say which one is meant. A later note added to the end of the letter calls it Nicopolis of Macedonia, which would be the city in Thrace. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, following Jerome, favour Nicopolis in Epirus in western Greece. That city was founded by Augustus Caesar to celebrate his victory over Antony at the battle of Actium in 31 BC, and it became the leading city of the region. Its ruins lie a few miles north of modern Preveza. The location shown here follows the Epirus identification. Whether Paul actually reached Nicopolis is not recorded.

Nimrah was a town east of the Jordan River, named in Num 32:3 among the places in the conquered land of Jazer and Gilead that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them for their livestock. It appears under this name only here. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take it to be probably the same place as Beth-nimrah, which Num 32:36 and Josh 13:27 list among the towns built or held by Gad. Easton's links it with the Nahr Nimrin, near one of the Jordan fords not far from Jericho. Smith's places it about ten miles north of the Dead Sea and three miles east of the Jordan. The location shown here follows that identification with the Nimrin area in the Jordan Valley. Easton's and Smith's give the name's meaning as "pure" or "limpid."

Nimrod, in the phrase "the land of Nimrod," is a figurative name for Mesopotamia used in Mic 5:6. There it stands in parallel with "the land of Assyria," in a prophecy that Israel's deliverer would turn back the Assyrian invader and lay waste his land. The name comes from Nimrod, the descendant of Cush whom Gen 10:8–12 describes as a mighty hunter. His kingdom began at Babel and other cities in Shinar, and from there he went into Assyria and built Nineveh. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the land of Nimrod as a name for Assyria, or for Shinar as part of it. Because Micah sets it beside Assyria, the phrase probably covers the wider Mesopotamian realm linked to Nimrod. The location shown here is in the Assyrian heartland near Nineveh, in northern Iraq, matching the parallel with "the land of Assyria" in the same verse. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "rebellion," but suggests it is probably an unknown Assyrian word.

Nodab was a people or clan east of the Jordan, named once in the Bible. It appears alongside the Hagarites, Jetur and Nephish as an enemy of the tribes of Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, who made war against them (1 Chr 5:19). Jetur and Nephish are listed elsewhere among the sons of Ishmael, so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Nodab to be probably an Ishmaelite or Arab tribe as well. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that the name is a copyist's variant of Kedemah or Nebaioth, two other sons of Ishmael. It also points to a possible echo of the name in Nudebe, a village in the Hauran region of southern Syria. The exact territory is unknown. The location shown here is only an approximate point in the region east of the Sea of Galilee, where the war took place.

Nohah is a place connected with the tribe of Benjamin. It is not named in the King James text. Some later translations find the name in Judg 20:43, where the KJV says the Israelites trod down the Benjamites "with ease." Nohah is also the name of Benjamin's fourth son (1 Chr 8:2), which suggests a clan settlement named after him. This entry links the place with Manahath, where the heads of the Benjamite families of Geba, descendants of Ehud, were moved (1 Chr 8:6). Both names probably come from a Hebrew root meaning "rest," which supports this connection. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at the traditional site of Manahath, probably modern Malha, southwest of Jerusalem. Its exact identity and location remain uncertain.

Nophah was a place named only once, in an old victory song about Israel's defeat of Sihon king of the Amorites (Num 21:30). The song says the land was laid waste from Heshbon to Dibon and "even unto Nophah, which reacheth unto Medeba," so Nophah was probably in the region north of the Arnon, near Medeba. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a city of Moab that the Amorites had taken, and gives the name's meaning as "blast." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text of this verse is hard to read. The Greek Septuagint renders the line differently, as women kindling a fire against Moab. That encyclopedia also links the name to Nobah, the town later called Kenath (Num 32:42). The location shown here follows that link and places it at Qanawat in southern Syria. Its actual site is uncertain.

The Old Gate was one of the gates of Jerusalem rebuilt under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:6 records that Jehoiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired it, laying its beams and setting up its doors, locks and bars. It appears again in Neh 12:39, in the route of the procession at the dedication of the wall. Its name is understood in different ways. The King James Version reads it as the "old gate," while the ESV renders it "Gate of Yeshanah," which may refer to a town called Jeshanah or to an older part of the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the north wall and says it was so called because the Jebusites built it. Its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here is a general point within Jerusalem's north side.

Ophni was a town in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:24, where it is named with Chepharhaammonai and Gaba among a group of twelve cities with their villages. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "mouldy". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "wearisomeness" or "folding together." Smith's Bible Dictionary links Ophni with Gophna, a town Josephus describes as important in the Roman period, and with the modern village of Jifna northwest of Bethel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says Jifna suits the position, about 2½ miles northwest of Bethel. It also notes that the change in the name's first letter makes the link less straightforward. The location shown here follows the Jifna identification.

Paddan is a shortened name for Paddan-aram, the region in upper Mesopotamia where Jacob's relatives lived. It appears in this form only once, in Gen 48:7, where the aged Jacob, blessing Joseph's sons in Egypt, recalls coming back from Padan (the King James spelling) when Rachel died on the road near Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem, and he buried her there. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a plain and takes it to mean Padan-aram. Other passages in Genesis place Paddan-aram around Haran, where Jacob lived with his uncle Laban and married Rachel and Leah. So this verse probably refers to his journey home from that stay.
