The exact limits of the region are uncertain. The location shown here marks the general area of Haran, near the modern town of Harran in southeastern Turkey.

Pai was the royal city of Hadad, a king of Edom who reigned after Baalhanan, according to 1 Chr 1:50. The same verse names Hadad's wife as Mehetabel, daughter of Matred. The parallel king list in Genesis 36:39 gives the city's name as Pau and the king's name as Hadar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two forms as the same place. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Pau as "howling" or "sighing." The text gives no clue to where the city stood, and its site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it remains unidentified. The location shown here is only an approximate placement within the territory of Edom, south of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan.

Parah was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities, where it is named between Avim and Ophrah (Josh 18:23). The name probably means "heifer," and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls it "heifer-town." Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with the ruins of Far'ah in the Wadi Far'ah, about 6 miles (10 km) northeast of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places the site about 3 miles northeast of Anata, ancient Anathoth, on a valley that runs into the Wadi Suweinit. Easton's describes the valley as a branch of the Wadi Kelt. The location shown here follows this Far'ah identification.

Parbar was a structure or area on the west side of the temple precinct in Jerusalem, named only in the list of gatekeepers' posts at 1 Chr 26:18: four guards at the causeway and two at Parbar. The word is rare and its meaning uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as an open area or suburb west of the temple. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposed Persian origin meaning something open to the light, which would suggest a colonnade or portico. It also connects the term to a related plural form at 2 Kgs 23:11, translated "suburbs" in the King James Version. STEPBible's proper-names list describes it as a colonnade or structure on the west side of the temple complex. The location shown here places it at the western side of the Temple Mount, an inference from the word "westward" in the verse.

Pas-dammim was a place where the Philistines gathered for battle against Israel. A barley field there became the scene of a stand by David and one of his mighty men. By inference from the preceding verse (1 Chr 11:12), that man was Eleazar son of Dodo. The people fled, but the two held their ground (1 Chr 11:13). The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:9–12 describes similar deeds without naming the place. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all treat Pas-dammim as the same place as Ephes-dammim, where the Philistines camped between Socoh and Azekah before David fought Goliath (1 Sam 17:1). Easton gives the name's meaning as "border of blood." The location shown here follows that identification, placing it in the Elah Valley area of the Judean lowlands, southwest of Jerusalem.

Patara was a port city on the southwest coast of Lycia, in what is now southwestern Turkey. It is mentioned once in the Bible, as a stop on Paul's voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey, about AD 54 by inference from context. Sailing by way of Cos and Rhodes, Paul's party reached Patara (Acts 21:1). The next verse says they found a ship there crossing to Phoenicia and boarded it, so Patara was where they changed vessels for the open-sea crossing. Easton's Bible Dictionary says this ship brought Paul to Tyre. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Patara as a wealthy harbor known for an oracle of Apollo and as the birthplace of Saint Nicholas. It places the ruins near the modern village of Gelemiş, and the location shown here matches that site.

Patmos is a small, rocky island in the Aegean Sea, off the southwest coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), where John says he was staying when he received the visions recorded in the Book of Revelation. It is named only once in the Bible, in Rev 1:9, where John describes himself as a companion of his readers in tribulation and says he was on the island "for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ." The verse does not say he was exiled, but early Christian tradition preserved by Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome holds that he was banished there under the emperor Domitian, about AD 95, and later returned to Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Rome used such islands as places of exile. The island still bears the name Patmos today and belongs to the Dodecanese group of Greece, and a cave there is traditionally shown as the place of John's visions.

Pau was the city of Hadar, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. Genesis lists Hadar as the successor of Baal-hanan son of Achbor and names his wife as Mehetabel, daughter of Matred (Gen 36:39). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:50 spells the name Pai. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "bleating." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its position is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Pau in the highlands of ancient Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea in what is now southern Jordan, as the general region where an Edomite royal city would have stood.

The Pavement was the place in Jerusalem where Pilate sat on the judgment seat to pass sentence on Jesus. John 19:13 gives its Hebrew (Aramaic) name as Gabbatha. The Greek word behind "Pavement" means a surface paved with stone, and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests a floor of coloured mosaic stones. Easton's also notes that Roman governors often set up their tribunals in open public places, and places this one probably in front of the governor's judgment hall. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as lying outside the Praetorium. Its exact site is uncertain. One traditional view links it to the area of the Antonia Fortress north of the temple. Another places it at Herod's palace in the western part of the city. The location shown here marks only a general point within Jerusalem and does not follow either view.

Peniel, meaning "face of God," is the name Jacob gave to the place where he wrestled through the night before meeting Esau. He named it because, he said, he had seen God face to face and his life had been spared (Gen 32:30). The next verse and later passages use the form Penuel. Judg 8:8–17 says Gideon later tore down the tower of Penuel, and 1 Kgs 12:25 says Jeroboam fortified it. The narrative places it near the Jabbok River (the modern Zarqa) east of the Jordan, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes it was not far from Succoth. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions Merrill's identification with Tulul edh-Dhahab, twin ruin-covered hills by the Jabbok, and Conder's suggestion of Jebel Osha. The location shown here follows the Tulul edh-Dhahab identification.

Perez-uzza, meaning "breach of Uzza," was the name David gave to the place where the LORD struck down Uzza during the first attempt to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 13:11). The surrounding passage and the parallel account in 2 Sam 6:6–8, which spells it Perez-uzzah, explain that Uzza died after taking hold of the ark when the oxen pulling its cart stumbled. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the threshing floor named Chidon in Chronicles and Nachon in Samuel. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Kirjath-jearim, where the journey began. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the route toward Jerusalem, close to the city.

Perez-uzzah, meaning "breach of Uzzah," was the name David gave to the place where the LORD struck down Uzzah (2 Sam 6:8). By inference from the surrounding passage (2 Sam 6:6–7), Uzzah had taken hold of the ark of God when the oxen stumbled while it was being carried toward Jerusalem, and he died there. The narrative calls the spot Nachon's threshing floor, and the parallel account in 1 Chr 13:9–11 calls it the threshing floor of Chidon. The name was still in use when the account was written. Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Kirjath-jearim, where the journey of the ark began. The location shown here is only a rough placement near Jerusalem, the destination of the journey.

Pharpar was one of the two rivers of Damascus that Naaman, the Syrian army commander, named alongside the Abana when Elisha told him to wash in the Jordan to be healed of his leprosy. Naaman asked whether these rivers were not better than all the waters of Israel, and he went away angry (2 Kgs 5:12). This is the only place the river is mentioned. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "swift," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that produces fruit." Both Easton's and Smith's identify Pharpar with the modern Awaj River, which rises on the southeast slopes of Mount Hermon and flows east, south of Damascus, into a marshy lake. Easton's notes that one of its branches is called Wady Barbar, a name it takes to preserve "Pharpar." The location shown here follows the Awaj identification.

Phenice (Phoenix in modern translations) was a harbor town on the south coast of Crete, west of Fair Havens. During Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, about AD 56 by inference from context, most of those aboard advised leaving Fair Havens, which was not suitable for wintering, to try to reach Phenice and winter there. Acts 27:12 describes it as a haven facing toward the southwest and northwest. The following verses (Acts 27:13–14) tell how a storm struck soon after they set sail, so the ship probably never reached it. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with modern Loutro, and the location shown here follows that identification. Some instead place it at the nearby bay of Phineka, just to the west. The name likely comes from the Greek word for palm tree. It is distinct from Phenice meaning Phoenicia, as in Acts 11:19.

Pi-beseth was a city of Lower Egypt named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's prophecy against Egypt. There its young men, along with those of Aven (On, or Heliopolis), are said to fall by the sword, and the cities are to go into captivity (Ezek 30:17). The name is generally taken to mean "house of Bast," after the Egyptian cat-headed goddess. The Greeks called the city Bubastis. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it on the easternmost (Pelusiac) branch of the Nile Delta and identifies its ruins as Tell Basta, near modern Zagazig. The location shown here matches that site. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it about 40 miles north of Memphis. It notes that excavations in 1887–90 found remains from many periods of Egyptian history, along with a large cemetery of sacred cats. It was also home to a major annual festival of the goddess.

Pillars, called the Hall of Pillars in modern translations such as the ESV and the "porch of pillars" in the King James Version, was one of the buildings in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem. According to 1 Kgs 7:6 it measured fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide, roughly 75 by 45 feet. In front of it stood a further porch with pillars and a "thick beam," which modern versions and the STEPBible Proper Names index render as a canopy. The surrounding verses place it among Solomon's other royal buildings, between the House of the Forest of Lebanon and the Hall of Judgment, though its exact purpose is not stated. It was perhaps an entrance colonnade or waiting hall, but that is an inference. No remains have been identified, so the location shown here is only an approximate position within the area of Solomon's palace and temple in Jerusalem.

Pithom was an Egyptian city that the enslaved Israelites built for Pharaoh, together with Raamses, as a "treasure" or store city while taskmasters forced them into hard labor (Exod 1:11). It is named only in this verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as Egyptian Pa-Tum, "house of Tum" (the sun-god Atum), links the city to Rameses II, and suggests it is probably the Patumos mentioned by the Greek historian Herodotus. Smith's Bible Dictionary also connects it with Herodotus's town on Egypt's eastern border. Easton's identifies Pithom with Tell el-Maskhuta in the Wadi Tumilat, west of modern Ismailia near the Suez Canal, where excavations in 1883 found brick ruins taken to be storage buildings. Some scholars instead place it at nearby Tell er-Retaba. The location shown here follows the Tell el-Maskhuta area identification.

Place, in this entry, is "the place of a skull," the site outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, called Golgotha in Hebrew (Aramaic). John 19:17 says Jesus went out to it carrying his own cross. The parallel accounts in Matt 27:33 and Mark 15:22 also give the name Golgotha, and Luke 23:33 in the King James Version calls it Calvary, from the Latin word for skull. John 19:20 adds that it was near the city. The reason for the name is not explained. Explanations include a skull-shaped rock formation or its use as a place of execution. Two main sites are proposed. One is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the site of long Christian tradition. The other is Gordon's Calvary, north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough point in Jerusalem and does not choose between them.

The Plain of Aven (ESV "Valley of Aven") is a place named once in the Bible, in Amos's oracle against Damascus and the Arameans (Syria). The Lord declares that he will break the bar of Damascus, cut off the inhabitant of the Plain of Aven and the ruler of Beth-eden, and send the people of Syria into captivity to Kir (Amos 1:5). Its exact identity is uncertain. The Hebrew word aven means "wickedness" or "idolatry", and the name may be a deliberate play on a place known for its worship. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Syrian Heliopolis, modern Baalbek in Lebanon. Others take it more broadly as the Beqaa Valley between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, where Baalbek stands. The location shown here follows the Baalbek identification.

Pool, called the King's Pool in modern translations, was a pool in Jerusalem that Nehemiah passed during his night inspection of the ruined city walls. After the Fountain Gate he reached the King's Pool, but the rubble was so thick there that the animal he was riding could not get through (Neh 2:14). The text does not describe the pool or give its exact position. Its route places it near the southern or southeastern end of the old city, close to the Fountain Gate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the Pool of Siloam, perhaps named for its nearness to the "king's garden" mentioned in other passages. The location shown here is in that general area of ancient Jerusalem, within the city rather than at a precisely fixed spot. Several places in the Bible are called simply "pool".

Pool (the ESV spells it Pool of Shelah; the King James Version calls it the pool of Siloah) was a reservoir in Jerusalem next to the king's garden. It sat near the Fountain Gate and the stairs that went down from the City of David. Neh 3:15 says that during Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls, Shallun son of Colhozeh, ruler of part of the Mizpah district, repaired the Fountain Gate along with the wall of this pool. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the Hebrew name shelah as "the dart" and links it with Shiloah, "sending," in Isa 8:6, and so with the Pool of Siloam. On that basis it probably lay at the southern end of the City of David, the ridge running south of the Temple Mount. The location shown here places it in that area. The word "pool" also names several other places in the Bible.

The Prison Gate (ESV "Gate of the Guard") was a gate in Jerusalem mentioned only in Neh 12:39. At the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, one of the two thanksgiving choirs marched along the wall past the Ephraim Gate, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the towers of Hananeel and Meah, and the Sheep Gate, then "stood still in the prison gate." Because the procession ended near the temple, the gate was probably close to the temple area in the northeast of the city. The text gives no reason for its name, though it may have been linked to a guardhouse. Its exact identity is uncertain. Some connect it with the "court of the prison" near the king's house (Neh 3:25), and others with the Miphkad or Muster Gate (Neh 3:31). The location shown here places it within Jerusalem near the temple mount.

Ptolemais was a coastal city south of Tyre where Paul and his companions landed on their voyage from Miletus to Jerusalem. After sailing from Tyre they reached Ptolemais, greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day before continuing their journey (Acts 21:7). The trip took place about AD 54, a date inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the city was originally called Accho (Acco in Judg 1:31) and was renamed Ptolemais after Ptolemy Soter when he controlled Coele-Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was the most prominent town on the Phoenician coast in Maccabean times. The site is generally identified with modern Acre (Akko) in northern Israel, on the bay north of Mount Carmel, and the location shown here matches that identification.

Pul is a distant nation named only in Isa 66:19. There God says he will send survivors to faraway peoples who have not heard of his fame, listing Pul with Tarshish, Lud, Tubal, Javan and the distant coastlands. The text gives no further detail, so its location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably the same as Phut or Put (Gen 10:6; Jer 46:9), an African people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats it as an African country. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes two views: the island of Philae in Egypt, or Libya. The location shown here follows the Libyan identification and places it in eastern Libya, in the region around Cyrene. This place is separate from Pul, the Assyrian king of the same name.

Puteoli was a port city on the coast of Campania in Italy, on the northern shore of what is now the Bay of Naples. It was the last stop on Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. After sailing from Rhegium with a south wind, his ship reached Puteoli the next day (Acts 28:13). The following verse, Acts 28:14, says believers were found there and Paul stayed with them seven days before going on to Rome by land. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Puteoli as the main harbor for the grain ships from Alexandria and the usual landing place for travelers to Italy from the eastern Mediterranean. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, its name refers to sulphur springs, which are common in the volcanic area. It is the modern town of Pozzuoli, near Naples, where remains of the ancient harbor and a large amphitheater survive.

Raamses was one of the two store cities, along with Pithom, that the Israelites were forced to build for Pharaoh while they were enslaved in Egypt (Exod 1:11). It is very probably the same place as Rameses, the spelling Smith's Bible Dictionary links it to. That city appears as the district where Jacob's family settled (Gen 47:11) and as the starting point of the exodus (Exod 12:37). Its exact site is uncertain. Many scholars identify it with the Egyptian royal city Pi-Ramesse at modern Qantir in the eastern Nile Delta, and others with Tanis. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the eastern Delta, near the Wadi Tumilat and modern Ismailia, and does not settle on any one excavated site.

Rabbith was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar, named only once, in the list of Issachar's towns alongside Kishion and Abez (Josh 19:20). The Hebrew form carries the definite article, "ha-Rabbith," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "multitude." Smith's also suggests the town may have stood on Issachar's boundary. Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it with the village of Raba, in the southern part of the Gilboa range, north of Ibzaq. The location shown here, in the hills southeast of the Jezreel Valley, follows that identification.

Racal (spelled Rachal in the King James Version) was a town in Judah. It appears only in 1 Sam 30:29, in the list of places to whose elders David sent a share of the plunder after he defeated the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag. The surrounding passage describes these as places where David and his men had moved about during his years as a fugitive. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "traffic," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "trader." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "Carmel" here. The two names look alike in Hebrew, and Carmel near Hebron features prominently in David's earlier story with Nabal and Abigail, so many scholars adopt that reading. The location shown here follows the Carmel identification, placing Racal at Carmel, probably the modern Khirbet el-Kirmil south of Hebron. Otherwise the town's location is unknown.

Rakkath was a fortified city in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in Josh 19:35, where it is listed between Hammath and Chinnereth among Naphtali's "fenced cities." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "shore," and Smith's places the town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Hammath is generally identified with the hot springs just south of Tiberias, so Rakkath was probably nearby. Rabbinic tradition, noted by Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, holds that Herod Antipas built Tiberias on the site of Rakkath. The encyclopedia adds that Tiberias stood on an older settlement, since builders disturbed ancient graves while digging its foundations. Smith's places Rakkath close to Tiberias rather than on its exact site. The location shown here follows the identification with Tiberias.

Rakkon was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It is named only once, in Josh 19:46, where it is listed after Me-jarkon and just before the border "before Japho," the coastal city later known as Joppa (modern Jaffa). That placement suggests it lay near the coast at the northwestern edge of Dan's allotment. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tell er-Rakkeit, on the seashore about 6 miles (10 km) north of Joppa, near the mouth of the river 'Aujeh, probably the modern Yarkon River. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a well-watered place not far from Joppa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew wording of this verse is difficult and that the Greek Septuagint reads it differently. The location shown here follows the Tell er-Rakkeit identification, north of present-day Tel Aviv.

Ramah was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Asher, named in Josh 19:29 as a landmark where the border turned toward the fortified city of Tyre before running on to Hosah and the sea at Achzib. Its name means "height" and is shared by several other places in the Bible, so this town should not be confused with the better-known Ramah in Benjamin. Its exact position is uncertain because the line of Asher's border cannot be traced with confidence. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals placing it about 3 miles east of Tyre or about 10 miles east-southeast of it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Rameh or Ramiyeh, a hilltop village in a basin of fields about 13 miles southeast of Tyre, in present-day southern Lebanon, where ancient cisterns and sarcophagi have been found. The location shown here follows that identification.

Ramah was a fortified city in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali. It appears only once, in the list of Naphtali's "fenced cities" in Josh 19:36, named between Adamah and Hazor. Several other places in the Bible share the name. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the name means "height," and towns called Ramah generally stood on high ground. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of er-Rameh (Rameh). The village lies on a mountain slope about 8 miles (13 km) west-southwest of Safed, in Upper Galilee, and about 15 miles (24 km) west of the north end of the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no ancient remains are visible above ground at the site, though it was probably occupied in ancient times.

Ramath-lehi, meaning "hill of the jawbone" or "height of Lehi," was the name Samson gave to the place where he threw away the donkey's jawbone he had used to kill a thousand Philistines (Judg 15:17). The surrounding passage places this at Lehi in Judah, where the Philistines had camped to capture him after the men of Judah handed him over bound. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek translation took the name to mean the "throwing up" of the jawbone, but that the Hebrew follows the pattern of names like Ramath-mizpeh. It also suggests the name Lehi may reflect a jaw-like shape in the landscape. The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Sorek Valley (Wadi es-Sarar), near Zorah and Timnah, and the rough location shown here follows that view.

Ramath-mizpeh, meaning "height of the watchtower," was a town east of the Jordan named in Josh 13:26 as a point on the boundary of the land given to the tribe of Gad, listed between Heshbon and Betonim. Nothing else is said about it in the text, and its identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Mizpah of Gilead. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the Mizpeh where Jacob and Laban made their covenant and places it at modern es-Salt. Smith's Bible Dictionary equates it with Ramoth-gilead. The location shown here follows the Ramoth-gilead identification and sits near the modern town of Ramtha in northern Jordan.

Ramathaim-zophim was a city in the hill country of Ephraim, named in 1 Sam 1:1 as the home of Elkanah, a descendant of Zuph and the father of Samuel. The name means "the two heights" or "two watchtowers" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and the "-zophim" part probably recalls Zuph, Elkanah's ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Ramathaim as a fuller name for Ramah, the town that later passages in 1 Samuel present as Samuel's home, the center of his work, and his burial place. It also links the name to "the land of Zuph" (1 Sam 9:5). Some have connected it with Arimathea of the New Testament. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's notes an identification with Nebi Samwil ("the prophet Samuel"), about 4 or 5 miles northwest of Jerusalem, and the location shown here follows that identification.

Ramoth, called "south Ramoth" in 1 Sam 30:27, was a city to which David sent part of the plunder he recovered from the Amalekites, along with Bethel, Jattir and other towns where he and his men had moved about. Its name means "heights" or "high places" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several places in the Bible share this name, so its identity is uncertain. Because the gifts went to the elders of Judah, this Ramoth is probably the "Ramath of the south" listed among the towns of Simeon in Josh 19:8, somewhere in the Negev. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead links it with a Levitical city of Issachar, also called Jarmuth and Remeth. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, following the link with "Ramath of the south."

Recah (spelled Rechah in the King James Version) is a name that appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Judah, where Eshton's descendants Bethrapha, Paseah and Tehinnah are summed up as "the men of Rechah" (1 Chr 4:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) takes Recah as a place but notes that nothing is known about it or where it was. It also notes that early Greek manuscripts read the name differently, as Rhechab or Rhepha. STEPBible's proper-name index reads Recah instead as a person or clan descended from Judah through Caleb. This entry treats it as a place. Its site is unknown, and the location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country of Judah near Bethlehem, inferred from its place in Judah's genealogy.

Rehob was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Asher, listed in Josh 19:28 with Hebron (probably Abdon), Hammon and Kanah, along the boundary that ran north toward Great Sidon. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it east of Sidon. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough position in the hills of the far north of Asher's territory, near the modern Israel–Lebanon border, matching Kanah and Hammon in the same verse. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "breadth" or "open space," belongs to several places in the Bible. Another Rehob of Asher appears elsewhere in Joshua, and there is a Rehob in the far north near Lebo-hamath. Whether any of these is the same town as this one is uncertain.

Rehoboth was a well dug by Isaac after he left the valley of Gerar, the third in a series of wells he opened there. The herdsmen of Gerar had disputed the two earlier wells, Esek and Sitnah (Gen 26:20–21), but no one quarreled over this one. So Isaac named it Rehoboth, meaning "broad places" or "room," saying that the LORD had made room for them and they would be fruitful in the land (Gen 26:22). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it at er-Ruheibeh, roughly 16 to 20 miles south or southwest of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links it with Rubuta in the Tell el-Amarna Letters. The location shown here follows the er-Ruheibeh identification. The name is shared by other biblical places, including Rehoboth "by the river" in Edom and the Assyrian city Rehoboth-Ir, which are separate from this well.

Rehoboth, called Rehoboth-Ir ("Rehoboth City") in some modern translations, was a city in Assyria named in Gen 10:11 alongside Nineveh, Calah and Resen. The verse can be read two ways. Either Asshur went out from Shinar and built these cities, or Nimrod went into Assyria and built them. It belongs to the account of the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom, dated by inference from context to about 1822 BC. The name means "broad places" or "streets." Smith's Bible Dictionary says nothing certain is known of its position. Easton's Bible Dictionary, following the Vulgate, takes the phrase to mean "the public squares of the city," that is, of Nineveh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the Assyrian Rebit Ninua, "streets of Nineveh," a district near that city, and also mentions the old capital Assur as a possibility. The location shown here follows the identification with the Nineveh area, near modern Mosul in Iraq.

Rekem was a city in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's towns in Josh 18:27, where it is named alongside Irpeel and Taralah. These belong to the second group of Benjamite towns, which also includes Jerusalem and Gibeah, so Rekem probably lay somewhere in the hill country north or northwest of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia states that the site is unknown, and no modern identification is firmly established. The location shown here is only a rough placement in that general area. The same name is also borne by a king of Midian and by a descendant of Caleb, but this entry concerns only the Benjamite town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "friendship," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "vain pictures."

Remeth was a town in the territory of the tribe of Issachar, listed alongside En-gannim, En-haddah and Beth-pazzez in the account of Issachar's inheritance (Josh 19:21). The name probably means "height." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as another form of the Ramoth of 1 Chr 6:73 and the Jarmuth of Josh 21:29, a Levitical town of Issachar. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats it as probably a separate place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it at the village of er-Rameh, about 11 miles southwest of Jenin (En-gannim). The location shown here is a rough placement farther north, in the eastern Jezreel plain between Jenin and the hills of Lower Galilee, within Issachar's allotment. The exact site remains uncertain.

Rephaim, in the phrase "land of Rephaim," is a name for Bashan, the kingdom of Og east of the Jordan. The King James Version translates it as "the land of giants." Moses gave this region, including the district of Argob, to the half tribe of Manasseh (Deut 3:13). The name comes from the Rephaim, an early people that Easton's Bible Dictionary describes as tall original inhabitants of the land who were later displaced. The Revised Version keeps the Hebrew name here. The nearby verse Deut 3:11 says that Og himself was among the last of the Rephaim, which probably explains why his kingdom carried the name. It is a regional name, not a single town. Bashan covered the high plateau east and northeast of the Sea of Galilee, roughly today's Golan Heights and northern Jordan. The location shown here is an approximate point within that region.

Resen was an ancient city in Assyria, named in Gen 10:12 as lying "between Nineveh and Calah" and called "a great city." It is one of four cities whose founding follows the account of Nimrod's kingdom. The King James Version credits the building to Asshur, while other readings, noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, credit Nimrod. The name probably reflects an Assyrian word meaning "fountainhead," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "bridle." Its exact site is unknown. Easton's Bible Dictionary favours the ruin mound of Karamless, east of the Tigris. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefer the ruins at Selamiyeh, about 3 miles north of Calah (modern Nimrud). The location shown here is only approximate, placed in the Nineveh area near modern Mosul in northern Iraq. The founding is dated to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Rhegium was a city at the toe of Italy, on the Italian side of the Strait of Messina, where Paul's ship stopped on his journey to Rome (Acts 28:13). After the shipwreck on Malta, the ship sailed by way of Syracuse and then "fetched a compass" to reach Rhegium, probably meaning it tacked or took a roundabout course against unfavorable winds, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains. It waited there one day until a south wind rose, then reached Puteoli the following day. The voyage took place about AD 57, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Rhegium as originally a Greek colony that later prospered under Roman rule, and notes that its coins showed the "twin brothers" who gave Paul's ship its name. It is the modern Reggio di Calabria, which matches the location shown here.

Rhodes is a large island in the southeastern Aegean Sea, off the southwestern tip of Asia Minor (modern Turkey). It still bears the name today and belongs to Greece. It is mentioned once in the Bible, as a stop on Paul's voyage from Miletus toward Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey. Sailing on a straight course, the ship reached Cos, the next day Rhodes, and from there went on to Patara on the Lycian coast (Acts 21:1). The voyage is dated about AD 54 by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Paul probably landed there. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Rhodes as a prosperous maritime and commercial center. Its capital city stood at the island's northeastern end and was famous for the Colossus, a huge bronze statue near the harbor. The name is usually taken to mean "rose."

Riblah was a town named as a landmark on the eastern border of the land promised to Israel. In Num 34:11 the boundary runs down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain, and then descends to the eastern shore of the Sea of Chinnereth (the Sea of Galilee). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the ancient Riblah on the east bank of the Orontes River in modern Syria, a town on the main caravan road north. Pharaoh Necho camped there after the battle of Megiddo, and Nebuchadnezzar later made it his headquarters during his campaign against Jerusalem. Easton's also links Ain with a nearby spring still called el Ain. The name belongs to more than one place, and some take the border Riblah to be a separate site farther south, since the boundary descends from it toward the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows the Orontes identification.

Rimmon was a town in the territory of Zebulun in Lower Galilee, given to the Merarite Levites as one of their four cities with surrounding pasturelands. In the list at Josh 21:35 the town appears as Dimnah, and many scholars take that name as a copying variant of Rimmon. The parallel list of Levitical cities in 1 Chr 6:77 gives the name as Rimmono, and Josh 19:13 places Remmon-methoar on Zebulun's border, probably the same town. The location shown here follows the identification with the village of Rummana, north of Nazareth. Several other places in the Bible share the name Rimmon, which according to Hitchcock's Bible Names means "pomegranate" or "exalted."

Rimmono was a town in the territory of Zebulun that was assigned, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite clan of Merari, according to 1 Chr 6:77. The King James Version renders the name as Rimmon, while the Hebrew form is Rimmono. It is probably the same place as the Rimmon (KJV "Remmon-methoar") on Zebulun's boundary in Josh 19:13. The parallel list of Levitical cities in Josh 21:35 gives Dimnah where Chronicles has Rimmono, and many scholars think one name arose from a copying variation of the other. The town is commonly identified with the modern village of Rummanah, at the northern edge of the Beit Netofa Valley in Lower Galilee, north of Nazareth. The location shown here follows that identification.

Rocks, called "the rocks of the wild goats" in the King James Version (Wildgoats' Rocks in the ESV), was a rugged area where Saul searched for David with three thousand chosen men from all Israel (1 Sam 24:2). The surrounding passage places this search in the wilderness of En-gedi, on the western shore of the Dead Sea, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes it as a rugged area near En Gedi. The name probably refers to the steep cliffs there, where wild goats such as the Nubian ibex still live. In the same episode David found Saul in a nearby cave and spared his life. The exact spot is not known. The location shown here is a rough placement in the En-gedi area.

Rumah was the hometown of Pedaiah, whose daughter Zebudah was the mother of Jehoiakim, king of Judah (2 Kgs 23:36). By inference, she was a wife of King Josiah, Jehoiakim's father. This is the only mention of the place in the Bible, and its location is uncertain. The name probably means "high place" or "elevation." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it may be the same as Arumah near Shechem (Judg 9:41), and note that Josephus appears to call it Arouma. Another view places it in Galilee at Khirbet Rumeh, a few miles north of Sepphoris. Smith's Bible Dictionary prefers identifying it with Dumah in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:52), a reading the Greek Septuagint supports. The location shown here follows the Arumah identification, in the hills southeast of Shechem (modern Nablus).

Sahar is a place named in some modern translations of Ezekiel 27:18, in a list of goods that Damascus traded with Tyre: "the wine of Helbon and the wool of Sahar." The King James Version reads the same Hebrew word as an adjective, "white wool," so the place name does not appear there. If it is a place, it was probably a wool-producing district within Damascus's trading area. The STEPBible Proper Names (TIPNR, Tyndale House) states that its exact location is unknown. Some suggest it was the steppe country northwest of Damascus, possibly the region later called es-Sahra. The location shown here is only approximate. It places Sahar in the hills northwest of Damascus, near Helbon, the wine-producing town named in the same verse. This is an inference from the pairing of the two names in Ezek 27:18.

Salamis was a city on the east coast of the island of Cyprus. It was the first place Barnabas and Saul (Paul) visited on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. There they preached in the Jewish synagogues, with John Mark as their assistant (Acts 13:5). The plural "synagogues" suggests a sizable Jewish community, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Because it was the harbor nearest the Syrian coast, it was a natural landing point after sailing from Seleucia, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. That work also describes Salamis as the most populous town of Cyprus in the Greek and Roman periods. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with modern Famagusta. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it a few miles north of that town. The location shown here matches the ancient ruins north of Famagusta.

Salim was a place near Aenon, where John the Baptist was baptizing because there was plenty of water there (John 3:23). Salim is named only to show where Aenon was, which suggests it was the better-known town. Its location is uncertain. One view, given in Easton's Bible Dictionary, links it with the Shalem of Gen 33:18, in the hills east of Shechem (modern Nablus), with Aenon in the Wadi Far'ah. Another view follows the fourth-century writer Eusebius, who placed Aenon about eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (Beth-shean, modern Beisan), near Salim and the Jordan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this with Tell Ridhghah and a nearby shrine called Sheikh Selim, close to several large springs. The location shown here follows this Jordan valley identification south of Beth-shean, west of the river.

Salmone was a landmark on the island of Crete that Paul's ship passed on its voyage to Rome. After slow progress against contrary winds, reaching only the area off Cnidus, the ship sailed under the shelter of Crete "over against Salmone" (Acts 27:7). The voyage is dated about AD 56, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Salmone as the promontory at the eastern tip of Crete, the modern Cape Sidero. Smith's calls it a bold headland visible from a long distance. The location shown here follows that identification, at Cape Sidero on the eastern tip of Crete.

Salt, called the City of Salt in modern translations, was one of six towns in the wilderness of Judah. It is named only once, in the list of Judah's territory, between Nibshan and Engedi (Josh 15:62). Its Hebrew name, Ir ha-Melach, means "city of salt" and probably reflects nearness to the salt deposits of the Dead Sea. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place it probably near the Valley of Salt at the southern end of the Dead Sea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Tell el-Milh ("the salt hill") on the route from Hebron toward Akaba as a possibility. Some modern scholars identify it with Khirbet Qumran on the northwestern shore. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the wilderness of Judah beside the Dead Sea, near Engedi, the town named next to it in the list.

Samos is a mountainous Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea, lying just off the coast of Asia Minor between Ephesus and Miletus. It is still called Samos today, and it belongs to Greece. Acts 20:15 names it as a stop on Paul's voyage south along the coast at the end of his third missionary journey. The ship passed Chios, reached Samos the next day, and arrived at Miletus the day after. The King James text adds that they stayed at Trogyllium, a point on the mainland opposite the island. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this phrase is missing from the oldest manuscripts. The same work says the island was famous in earlier times for its wealth and became part of the Roman province of Asia in 84 BC. Paul's passage probably took place around AD 54, an estimate based on context.

Samothrace (spelled Samothracia in the King James Version) is a mountainous island in the northern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Thrace and northwest of Troas. Its modern name is Samothraki. Paul and his companions stopped there on his second missionary journey, after a vision called him to Macedonia (Acts 16:11). Sailing from Troas, they made a straight run to Samothrace and reached Neapolis, the port of Philippi, the next day. The verse does not say they went ashore, but ancient ships usually anchored overnight rather than sail in the dark, so they probably stopped there for the night. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the island was famous in the ancient world as a sacred site, the center of the mystery cult of the Cabeiri, and that the statue known as the Victory of Samothrace was found there in 1863.

Sansannah was a town in the far south (the Negev) of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah, listed with Ziklag and Madmannah among Judah's southernmost cities (Josh 15:31). It is named only in this verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "palm branch", and Easton's Bible Dictionary adds "thorn bush." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat it as the same place as Hazar-susah, a city of Simeon (Josh 19:5), and probably Hazar-susim (1 Chr 4:31). This fits the way Simeon's towns lay within Judah's southern lands. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions the village of Simsim as one suggestion. The location shown here is only a rough position in the northern Negev, north-east of Beersheba, near the ruin of Khirbet esh-Shamsaniyat, which some scholars have proposed.

The Sea of Chinneroth is the name Joshua 12:3 uses for a lake marking part of the eastern boundary of the territory ruled by Sihon, king of the Amorites, which Israel took. The verse traces the border from the plain to this sea and then down to the 'sea of the plain,' the Salt Sea. Its position at the northern end of the Jordan valley, together with related names elsewhere in the Old Testament such as 'the sea of Chinnereth' (Num 34:11; Josh 13:27), identifies it with the freshwater lake later called the Sea of Galilee, Lake of Gennesaret or Sea of Tiberias, the modern Lake Kinneret in northern Israel. The name probably comes from the nearby town of Chinnereth or the surrounding district. The location shown here places it on that lake.

The Sea of Jazer is a body of water named only in Jeremiah's lament over Moab, where the spreading vines of Sibmah are said to reach "even to the sea of Jazer" (Jer 48:32). Jazer was a town east of the Jordan in the region taken from the Amorites. Interpretations differ. Some take the phrase to mean a pool, spring or small lake near Jazer. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards "sea" here as a copying slip carried over from the preceding clause. It notes that the parallel passage in Isa 16:8 reads simply "unto Jazer." No lake is known at Jazer, and the town's own site is uncertain. This entry treats the Sea of Jazer as a water feature and places it roughly in the area of Jazer, west of modern Amman. The location shown here is approximate.

The Sea of the Philistines is a name used once in the Bible, in Exod 23:31, where God sets the borders of Israel's promised land from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river. By inference from context, it refers to the Mediterranean Sea, specifically the part lying off the southern coast of Canaan, where the Philistines lived. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies it as that portion of the Mediterranean directly west of Palestine. Elsewhere the Hebrew Bible usually calls the Mediterranean simply "the sea," "the great sea," or "the western sea." In this verse it serves as the western limit of the land, with the Red Sea as the southern limit and the river, probably the Euphrates, as the eastern. The location shown here is a point in the Mediterranean off the southern coast, near Ashkelon and Ashdod.

Sebam, spelled Shebam in the King James Version, was a town east of the Jordan River. It appears in Num 32:3 in a list of places in the former kingdom of the Amorites that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses to give them because the land suited their livestock. The STEPBible proper-names index places it in the territory of Reuben. It is probably the same town as Sibmah, which appears later in the same chapter (Num 32:38) among the towns the Reubenites rebuilt. Later prophets mention Sibmah as a Moabite town known for its vineyards (Isa 16:8–9; Jer 48:32). The exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate, in the hill country near Heshbon and Mount Nebo in present-day Jordan.

Secacah was a town in the wilderness of Judah, the dry, thinly settled land west of the Dead Sea. It is named only once, in Josh 15:61, as one of six towns in this district assigned to the tribe of Judah, listed alongside Betharabah and Middin. The Bible gives no other details about it. Smith's Bible Dictionary says its exact position is unknown, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the ancient name has not survived. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with a ruin called Sikkeh east of Bethany, following a proposal by the surveyor Conder, who placed it at Khirbet es-Siqqeh, about 2 miles from Bethany. Other scholars place it closer to the Dead Sea, for example at Khirbet Qumran or in the Buqei'a valley. The location shown here follows the Sikkeh identification near Bethany.

Secu (spelled Sechu in the King James Version) was a place on Saul's route to Ramah, known for its "great well." It appears only once in the Bible. Saul stopped there while searching for David, who had fled to Samuel, and asked where the two were. He was told they were at Naioth in Ramah (1 Sam 19:22). By inference from the story, it lay between Saul's home at Gibeah and Ramah. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it is probably the modern Suweikeh, south of Beeroth, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Conder's identification with Khirbet Suweikeh, south of el-Bireh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a Greek reading that takes the phrase as "the cistern of the threshing-floor on the bare hill," possibly a spot within Ramah itself. The location shown here follows the Suweikeh identification.

Seirah (Seirath in the King James Version) was the place Ehud escaped to after he killed Eglon, king of Moab. He got away while Eglon's servants were still waiting outside the locked room, passed beyond "the quarries" (or carved images) near Gilgal, and reached Seirah (Judg 3:26). The name probably means "wooded" or "shaggy," pointing to a forested area. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the hill country of Ephraim, bordering Benjamin. This fits the next verse in Judges, where Ehud blows a trumpet in the mountains of Ephraim to rally Israel against Moab. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing in the text allows a firm identification, and Eusebius names the place without locating it. The location shown here is a rough placement in southeastern Ephraim, inferred from this context.

Seleucia was the seaport of Antioch in Syria, near the mouth of the Orontes River and about 16 miles from Antioch. Barnabas and Saul (Paul), sent out by the Holy Spirit at the start of the First Missionary Journey, went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus (Acts 13:4), about AD 45 by inference from context. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries say the city was founded by Seleucus Nicator, the first Seleucid king of Syria, and named after him, and that Pompey made it a free city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as a strongly fortified port and notes that the return voyage in Acts 14:26 probably also passed through it. Its site lies near the coast of modern southern Turkey, close to the village of Çevlik, where extensive ruins, including the old harbor, survive.

Seneh was one of two sharp rocky crags flanking the pass that Jonathan used to approach the Philistine garrison, the other being Bozez (1 Sam 14:4). The name probably means "thorn" or "acacia," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it came from thorn bushes growing on the rock. From the surrounding narrative, the pass lay at Michmash. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Seneh as the southern cliff of the gorge now called Wadi es-Suweinit, south of Michmash. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia hears an echo of the old name in that valley's modern name, "valley of the little thorn tree." Smith's Bible Dictionary places the pass about 6½ miles north of Jerusalem. The location shown here follows this gorge identification.

Sepharad is a place named only in Obad 1:20, where it is described as the home of exiles from Jerusalem who would one day possess the cities of the south (the Negev). The verse gives no clue to where it was, and its location has long been uncertain. Jewish tradition, going back to the Targum of Jonathan, identified it with Spain, which is why Spanish Jews are called Sephardim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with Saparda in Assyrian inscriptions, a place set either east of Assyria or in Asia Minor. Others, noted by Easton's Bible Dictionary, identify it with Sardis, the capital of Lydia in western Asia Minor. Jerome took the word to mean "boundary," meaning the exiles scattered to the ends of the earth. The location shown here follows the Sardis identification, near modern Sart in western Turkey.

Serpent's Stone is the meaning usually given to the "stone of Zoheleth," a landmark beside the spring of En-rogel just outside Jerusalem. There Adonijah, David's son, sacrificed sheep, oxen and fattened cattle and held a feast for his brothers the king's sons and the royal officials of Judah, as part of his bid to take the throne (1 Kgs 1:9). The wider chapter tells how, while they were gathered, Solomon was proclaimed king and Adonijah fled to the altar for safety. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the place as a rocky ledge near the village of Siloam that overhangs the Kidron Valley and is still known by the Arabic name ez-Zehwell or Zahweileh. The location shown here follows that identification, southeast of the old city near the meeting of the Kidron and Hinnom valleys.

Shaalabbin was a city in the territory allotted to the tribe of Dan. It appears in Josh 19:42 in the list of Danite towns, next to Ajalon (Aijalon) and Jethlah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as the same place as Shaalbim. If so, it is the town where, according to Judg 1:35, the Amorites held out against Dan. It also lay in one of the districts that supplied provisions to Solomon's court (1 Kgs 4:9). Easton's gives the name's meaning as "place of foxes" and identifies the site with the modern village of Selbit, about 3 miles north of Aijalon. The location shown here follows the Selbit identification.

Shaalim (spelled Shalim in the King James Version) was a district Saul passed through while searching for his father's lost donkeys. He went through the hill country of Ephraim and the land of Shalisha, then through Shaalim, and then through the land of the Benjamites, without finding the animals (1 Sam 9:4). Nothing else is said about it, and the Hebrew name is often understood to mean "land of foxes." Its location is uncertain because the route of the search is unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it apparently northwest of Jerusalem, perhaps near Shaalabbin in Dan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it lay on the western slopes, possibly east of Lydda, and notes that the name might originally have been "Shaalbim." The location shown here is only approximate and follows the general placement northwest of Jerusalem.

Shaaraim was a town listed among the cities of the tribe of Simeon in the far south of Israel. 1 Chr 4:31 says these towns belonged to the Simeonites until the reign of David. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gates." The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6 has Sharuhen in the same position, so the two names probably refer to the same place. The location shown here follows that identification and places it at Tell el-Far'ah (South), near the Besor stream in the western Negev. The name is shared by a different town in the lowlands of Judah (Josh 15:36; 1 Sam 17:52), which should not be confused with this Simeonite town.

Shahazumah (spelled Shahazimah in the King James Version) was a town on the boundary of the tribe of Issachar. It is named only once, in the description of Issachar's border, which reached Tabor, Shahazumah and Beth-shemesh before ending at the Jordan (Josh 19:22). Its listing between Mount Tabor and the Jordan suggests it lay somewhere along the line between them. The site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it should probably be sought southeast of Mount Tabor. The location shown here is only a rough placement, near the Jordan Valley south of the Sea of Galilee, and should not be taken as a known site.

Shalishah was a district that Saul and his servant passed through while searching for his father Kish's lost donkeys. Their route ran through the hill country of Ephraim, then the land of Shalishah, then the land of Shalim, and finally the territory of Benjamin, without finding the animals (1 Sam 9:4). Its exact location is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with the town of Baal-shalishah (2 Kgs 4:42), which may have given the district its name. Both place it northeast of Lydda on the western slopes of the central hill country. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes Conder's identification of Baal-shalishah with Khirbet Kefr Thilth. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the hill country north of Jerusalem, near Benjamin, following the general line of Saul's journey.

Shallecheth was one of the gates of the temple in Jerusalem, on its western side. In the Levites' rotation of gatekeeping duties, the lot for the west, together with this gate "by the causeway of the going up," fell to Shuppim and Hosah (1 Chr 26:16). The name probably means "casting out," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be a refuse gate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint renders it with a word for a building with chambers. The causeway is generally understood as an ascent rising from the Tyropoeon Valley to the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the gate with the Bab al-Silsila, the Chain Gate, in the west wall of the Temple Mount enclosure. The location shown here lies on the western side of the Temple Mount, which matches that identification. The exact site is uncertain.

Shamir was a town in the hill country of Judah. It appears only in the list of Judah's towns in Josh 15:48, where it is named first in a group alongside Jattir and Socoh. Because the name is shared by several places in the Bible, this Shamir should be kept distinct from others of the same name. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest Khirbet Somerah, a hilltop site with ancient walls, caves, cisterns and tombs, a few miles northwest of Debir and north of Anab. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it more generally, about eight to ten miles south of Hebron. The location shown here lies in the southern Judean hills, in the region of these proposals. The name may mean "thorn" or "point."

Shaphir (spelled Saphir in the King James Version) was a town of Judah named only once, in Micah's lament over the towns of the southwestern lowlands. In Mic 1:11 its inhabitants are told to pass away "having thy shame naked," which probably pictures them being led off as captives. The name probably means "beautiful" or "glittering," and like several other names in the passage it seems chosen for wordplay. Its exact location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers from the nearby mentions of Gath, Achzib and Mareshah that the town lay in southwestern Palestine. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the same encyclopedia connect the name with the villages of es-Suafir, a few miles southeast of Ashdod. Another suggestion links it with the white hill Tell es-Safi. The location shown here follows the es-Suafir identification.

Sharon was a district east of the Jordan, distinct from the better-known coastal plain of the same name. 1 Chr 5:16 says the people of Gad lived in Gilead, in Bashan and its towns, and in "all the suburbs of Sharon," meaning its pasture lands, as far as their borders. The Gadites are identified by inference from the surrounding passage. Unlike the coastal Sharon, the Hebrew name here has no definite article. Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two views. Kittel suggested the name is a scribal variant of "Sirion," another name for Mount Hermon, which would place Sharon in the pasture lands of Hermon. Others take it to mean the tableland of Gilead. The location shown here follows the Hermon identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "his plain."

Sharuhen was a town in the far south of Canaan, listed among the thirteen cities and their villages given to the tribe of Simeon within the territory of Judah (Josh 19:6). It appears by this name only in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it to be the same town called Shilhim in the parallel list of Judah's southern towns (Josh 15:32) and Shaaraim in the list of Simeon's towns (1 Chr 4:31). Its site is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Sheriah, a large ruin northwest of Beersheba. The location shown here follows a different identification, Tel Sharuhen (Tell el-Far'ah South), a mound beside the Besor stream in the western Negev, south of Gaza.

Shaveh-kiriathaim was the place where Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him defeated the Emim during their campaign in the time of Abraham (Gen 14:5). The name probably means "plain of Kiriathaim." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "plain of the double city" and takes it to be the valley in or beside which the town of Kiriathaim stood. Kiriathaim appears later as a town east of the Jordan, assigned to Reuben in Num 32:37 and later counted among the cities of Moab in Jer 48:1. Deut 2:10–11 says the Emim were the earlier inhabitants of the land of Moab, which fits that setting. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify the site with el-Qureiyat, about 7 miles north of Dibon in modern Jordan. The location shown here follows that Moabite identification and is approximate. The exact site is not certain.

Shebarim was a place near Ai, mentioned only in Josh 7:5. When Israel's first attack on Ai failed, the men of Ai chased the Israelites from the city gate as far as Shebarim and struck them down on the descent, killing about thirty-six men. The name probably means "breaks" or "ruins." The Revised Version margin renders it "the quarries," and the Greek Septuagint reads it not as a place name but as "until they were broken," meaning until the rout was complete. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the flight would naturally have run from Ai eastward toward the Israelite camp at Gilgal in the Jordan valley, and that no trace of the name has been found. Its exact site is therefore unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement just east of Ai, along the likely line of retreat.

Shema was a town in the far south of Judah, listed in Josh 15:26 among the cities of the tribe's southern district, the Negev, between Amam and Moladah. It appears only in this verse. Its name is often taken to mean "hearing" or "obeying" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat it as the same place as Sheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some link it with Sheba in the list of Simeon's towns (Josh 19:2). It suggests Shema is probably the same as Jeshua, a town resettled after the exile (Neh 11:26). That encyclopedia tentatively identifies the site with Khirbet Sa'wah, a walled ruin on a hilltop between Khirbet Attir and Khirbet el-Milh. The exact location is uncertain, and the location shown here is only approximate, placing it in the Negev east of Beersheba.

Shen was a place named only in 1 Sam 7:12, where Samuel set up a memorial stone "between Mizpeh and Shen" and called it Ebenezer after Israel's victory over the Philistines described in the surrounding chapter. The Hebrew reads "the Shen," meaning "the tooth," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably a prominent tooth-shaped rock or crag. Its site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek translation (the Septuagint) appears to read a different word, and suggests the name may be Jeshanah (as in 2 Chr 13:19), possibly the modern Ain Sinia north of Beitin. The location shown here is only rough. It places Shen northwest of Jerusalem, near Nabi Samwil, one proposed site of Mizpah, rather than following the Jeshanah identification.

Shibah is the name Isaac gave to a well his servants dug at the place that came to be called Beersheba. The King James Version spells it "Shebah." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the Hebrew word means "seven," and the Greek translation renders it "oath" (one edition reads "well of oath"). That encyclopedia treats Shibah as the name of the original well of Beersheba. The narrative explains that the city's name, Beersheba ("well of the oath" or "well of seven"), comes from this naming (Gen 26:33). In the surrounding passage, the servants report finding water on the same day Isaac made a sworn agreement with Abimelech, which probably accounts for the name. An earlier account (Gen 21:31) links the name Beersheba to an oath between Abraham and Abimelech. The location shown here is at ancient Beersheba, probably Tel Beer Sheva in southern Israel.

Shihor-libnath was a landmark named on the boundary of the territory of the tribe of Asher, apparently marking with Carmel its western limit (Josh 19:26). It is mentioned only once, and its exact identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as a river, probably the Nahr ez-Zerqa, the modern Nahal Tanninim ("crocodile river"), which flows from the Carmel range into the Mediterranean just north of Caesarea. The ISBE suggests the name "Shihor" echoes the name of the Nile, perhaps because both streams held crocodiles. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead suggests a small stream south of Athlit, while the Syriac Peshitta and Eusebius treated the name as two separate towns. The location shown here follows the Nahal Tanninim identification.

Shikkeron (spelled Shicron in the King James Version) was a place on the northern border of the territory of Judah. It is mentioned only once, in the boundary description of Josh 15:11. That line ran from the side of Ekron northward to Shikkeron, then passed along to Mount Baalah and on to Jabneel before ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Shikkeron therefore lay in the low country west of the hills, between Ekron and Mount Baalah. The exact site is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes C. Hauser's suggestion of Tell es-Sellakeh, northwest of the village of Aqir. On that view the boundary would follow a natural course over the ridge to Jabneel. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the general area of Ekron.

Shilhim was a city in the far south of the territory given to the tribe of Judah. It appears once, in the list of southern towns in Josh 15:32, near Lebaoth, Ain and Rimmon. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "aqueducts," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fountains." Easton's identifies it with Sharuhen, which appears in the parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:6, and with Shaaraim in 1 Chr 4:31. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Azubah, mother of King Jehoshaphat and called "the daughter of Shilhi" (1 Kgs 22:42), may have come from this town. The location shown here follows the Sharuhen identification and corresponds to Tell el-Far'ah (South), on the Wadi Ghazzeh southeast of Gaza. That site is the one most often linked with Sharuhen, though the identification remains uncertain.

Shiloah was a gently flowing water supply at Jerusalem, mentioned once in the Bible. In Isa 8:6 the prophet uses "the waters of Shiloah that go softly" as an image of the quiet security God offered Judah. He contrasts it with the people's delight in Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Shiloah with the stream later called Siloam, fed by Jerusalem's only perennial spring, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats the two names as the same place. On that view the waters were probably those running from the Gihon Spring along the southeastern hill of ancient Jerusalem toward the Pool of Siloam. The location shown here is in that area, in the old City of David south of the Temple Mount. The exact channel Isaiah had in mind is uncertain.

Shimron-meron was a Canaanite royal city whose king appears among the thirty-one kings Joshua defeated west of the Jordan (Josh 12:20). The verse names it right beside Achshaph, the same pairing found with Shimron in Josh 11:1. Because of this, Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all suggest it is probably the full name of Shimron, a town later assigned to Zebulun (Josh 19:15). Smith's renders the name "watch-height of Meron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Canaanite city, Samsimuruna, in Assyrian inscriptions, which some have linked with this place, and mentions a proposed site at es-Semeiriyeh near Acre. The location shown here follows the identification with Tel Shimron, on the northern edge of the Jezreel Valley west of Nazareth.

Shion was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Issachar. It appears only once, in the list of Issachar's towns in Josh 19:19, where it is named between Hapharaim and Anaharath. The surrounding list also includes Shunem, so the town probably lay in the same area, in the Jezreel Valley region of lower Galilee. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "overturning." Nothing else is recorded about the town, and its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Khirbet Sha'in, near the spring of 'Ain esh-Sha'in, about 4 miles (6 km) northwest of Mount Tabor. The location shown here matches that identification.

Shoa was a people or region named only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's allegory of Oholibah (Jerusalem). There it appears with the Babylonians, Chaldeans, Pekod, Koa and Assyrians among the nations whose horsemen, captains and lords would come against the city (Ezek 23:23). Since the text gives no further detail, its identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the name to Suti or Su, a district in the mountains north-east of Babylonia, in what is now Kurdistan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Schrader's identification with the Sutu of ancient inscriptions, a people living east of the Tigris. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Shoa, Pekod and Koa as districts of the Assyrian realm, and some have suggested a place within Babylonia itself. The location shown here follows the view that places Shoa east of the Tigris, roughly in the Zagros highlands of western Iran.

Shual, called "the land of Shual," was a district in the hill country of Benjamin. Its name means "fox," and it appears only in 1 Sam 13:17. During Saul's war with the Philistines, raiders went out from the Philistine camp at Michmash in three companies. One of them turned toward Ophrah, into the land of Shual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the other bands went west and east and that Israel held the pass to the south, so this band probably headed north. That would place Shual near Ophrah, which is commonly identified with et-Taiyibeh, northeast of Bethel. The district itself has not been identified. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both suggest it may be the same as the "land of Shalim" through which Saul searched for his father's donkeys. The location shown here is a rough placement north of Michmash.

Sibraim was a place named in Ezekiel's vision of the future boundaries of the land of Israel. It appears in Ezek 47:16 as a landmark on the northern border, listed after Hamath and Berothah and described as lying "between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath." The verse mentions it only once and gives no further detail. Smith's Bible Dictionary says the name means "twofold hope" and that the site has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be Khirbet Sanbariyeh, on the west bank of the Hasbani River about 3 miles southeast of Abil, near the modern Lebanon–Israel border. Its exact location remains uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the region of Hamath in central Syria, reflecting the verse's description of the area between the territories of Damascus and Hamath.

Sidon (Zidon), called "great Zidon" in Josh 11:8, was the leading Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel. In this passage, after Joshua defeated the northern Canaanite coalition at the waters of Merom, Israel chased the fleeing kings as far as great Zidon, Misrephoth-maim and the valley of Mizpeh, which marked the northwestern limit of the pursuit. The word "great" probably reflects the city's size and standing, or may refer to Sidon together with its surrounding territory. Other passages show Sidon as an ancient and important Canaanite city. The location shown here is the modern city of Saida (Sidon) on the coast of Lebanon, the standard identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing."

Sidon the Great was the name used for the Phoenician city of Sidon when describing the northern boundary of the territory of the tribe of Asher. Josh 19:28 lists towns such as Hebron, Rehob, Hammon and Kanah reaching "even unto great Zidon," so the city probably marked the limit of Asher's allotment rather than lying within it. The same phrase, "great Zidon," appears in Josh 11:8, where Joshua pursues the defeated northern kings as far as the city. The title "great" probably reflects Sidon's standing as the leading city of the Phoenician coast. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing." The location shown here is the coastal city of Sidon, the modern Saida in southern Lebanon.

Silla is a place named only once, in the account of the murder of King Joash of Judah. His servants conspired against him and killed him "in the house of Millo, which goeth down to Silla" (2 Kgs 12:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the phrase as "on the way that goeth down to Silla" and infers that Silla lay in a valley below Beth-millo, though nothing more is known of what or where it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word may mean "highway" and might not be a proper name at all, while the Septuagint and other ancient versions treat it as one. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that it refers to the area of the Pool of Siloam. The location is uncertain. The point shown here is a rough placement in Jerusalem, near the Millo.

Siphmoth was a town in the south of Judah, named once in the Bible (1 Sam 30:28). It was one of the places to which David sent a share of the spoil from Ziklag after he defeated the Amalekites. The surrounding passage presents these gifts as going to towns where David and his men had moved about while living as fugitives from Saul. It is listed between Aroer and Eshtemoa, which places it in the southern hill country of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name the meaning "fruitful places." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site has not been found and suggests that Zabdi the Shiphmite (1 Chr 27:27) probably came from here. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Judah, near Eshtemoa.

Sirah was a well or cistern from which Joab's messengers brought Abner back, without David's knowledge, after Abner had left David at Hebron (2 Sam 2:26 is not involved; see 2 Sam 3:26). The following verse, 2 Sam 3:27, says Joab then took Abner aside in the gate of Hebron and killed him in revenge for his brother Asahel. The name is often explained as meaning "turning" or "retiring", and Josephus also refers to it as a well. Since Abner was heading away from Hebron, the well was probably on the road north of the city. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with 'Ain Sarah, a spring and small reservoir about a mile north of Hebron on the road toward Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also mentions a stepped cistern called Hammam Sarah near Ramet el-Khalil as another possibility. The rough location shown here follows the 'Ain Sarah identification just north of Hebron.

Sitnah was the second of the wells that Isaac's servants dug in the valley of Gerar. The local herdsmen quarreled with them over it, as they had over the first well, so Isaac named it Sitnah, meaning "enmity" or "hostility" (Gen 26:21). The surrounding passage in Gen 26 gives the setting: the first well was called Esek ("contention"), and Isaac then moved on and dug a third well, which went undisputed and which he named Rehoboth. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with a place called Shutneh near Rehoboth, about 20 miles (32 km) south of Beersheba. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the site unknown but notes a similar name, Shutnet er Rucheibeh, for a small valley near Rucheibeh. The location shown here is rough and places Sitnah in the general area of Gerar, northwest of Beersheba.

The Skull was the place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified between two criminals (Luke 23:33).
