The KJV calls it "Calvary," from the Latin calvaria, which translates the Greek kranion, "skull." The parallel accounts in Matthew, Mark and John give its Aramaic name, Golgotha, "the place of a skull." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably named for its shape, a low, rounded, bare rise resembling a skull, and notes that Scripture never calls it a hill. Hebrews 13:12 places the crucifixion outside the city gate, and John describes the place as near the city. Its exact site is uncertain. The main traditional candidate is the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and another proposal is "Gordon's Calvary" near the Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate. The location shown here is only a rough placement in Jerusalem and does not settle between these views.

Soco (spelled Shoco in the King James text) was a town in Judah that King Rehoboam rebuilt and fortified, listed with Bethzur and Adullam among his defensive cities (2 Chr 11:7). The surrounding passage presents these towns as strongholds built after the kingdom divided. Two towns of this name appear in Judah's territory: one in the lowland hills (Josh 15:35), and one in the southern hill country (Josh 15:48). The Rehoboam fortress is usually taken to be the lowland town in the Valley of Elah. That is probably the Shochoh where the Philistines gathered before David fought Goliath (1 Sam 17:1). The location shown here follows that identification. It places Soco at a site commonly linked with Khirbet Abbad (Khirbet Shuweikeh), near Azekah and west of Bethlehem. Its nearness to Adullam in the same list fits this view.

Socoh was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland foothills of Judah. It appears in Judah's tribal allotment beside Jarmuth, Adullam and Azekah (Josh 15:35). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "tents" or "tabernacles." According to STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House), this is the Socoh near which the Philistines gathered before David fought Goliath, described in 1 Sam 17:1 as lying near Azekah, and the town Rehoboam later fortified (2 Chr 11:7). The name is shared by several places, including a second Socoh in Judah's hill country, so not every mention necessarily refers to this town. The location shown here is in the Elah Valley, which fits the usual identification with the ruins called Khirbet Shuweikeh (also Khirbet Abbad).

Socoh was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed in Josh 15:48 alongside Shamir and Jattir among the towns allotted to the tribe of Judah. Several places in the Bible share this name. This one is distinct from the Socoh in the Judean lowland, which was the scene of the Philistine gathering before David fought Goliath. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the hill-country town with a site about 10 miles southwest of Hebron that bears the name esh-Shuweikeh, the same Arabic name as the lowland Socoh. The location shown here, given only roughly, follows that general area south of Hebron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "tents" or "tabernacles." Beyond its place in the list of Judah's towns, the Bible records nothing further about this Socoh.

Straight Gate is the name used in this entry for the street called Straight in Damascus, where the Lord told Ananias to go to the house of Judas and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying there after his encounter on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:11). The verse names the street but does not describe it. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a long, broad street running east to west, about a mile long, and serving as the city's main thoroughfare. It notes that several major cities of Syria and Palestine had colonnaded 'straight streets' through their centers. It is probably the east–west street through the old city of Damascus known in Roman times as the Via Recta, and the location shown here lies in the old city. The events linked to it, Saul's conversion and stay in Damascus, are dated to about AD 32, by inference from context.

Suph is a place named in Deut 1:1 as a landmark for where Moses addressed Israel: beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness, in the Arabah ("the plain") opposite Suph, among Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth and Dizahab. The King James Version, following the Septuagint and other ancient versions, translates the word as "the Red sea." Easton's Bible Dictionary judges this the most likely reading, taking Suph as a shortened form of Yam Suph, the Hebrew name of the Red Sea. Other suggestions mentioned there include Suphah (Num 21:14), es-Sufah near Maaleh-acrabbim (Josh 15:3), and Zuph (1 Sam 9:5). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia concludes that no site can be identified with confidence. The location shown here follows the Red Sea reading and marks the general area of the northern Red Sea rather than a specific town.

Suphah is a place named in an old poem quoted in Num 21:14 from "the book of the wars of the LORD," which recalls what God did there and in the brooks of Arnon. The King James Version translates the Hebrew word as "Red sea," while its margin and the Revised Version read it as a place name: "Vaheb in Suphah." Easton's Bible Dictionary places Suphah at the southeastern corner of the Dead Sea, at Ghor es-Safieh, an identification first proposed by the explorer Tristram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the same as Suph in Deut 1:1 and treats its exact location as still unsettled. Its context near the Arnon points to the region of Moab east of the Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the "Red sea" reading and marks the Red Sea region generally.

Sur was a gate in Jerusalem, connected with the temple or the royal palace, named only in 2 Kgs 11:6. The priest Jehoiada planned to make the boy Joash king and overthrow Queen Athaliah. He divided the guards into three companies, one stationed at the king's house, one at the gate of Sur, and one at the gate behind the guard, so that the house would be secured. The parallel account in 2 Chr 23:5 calls this the "gate of the foundation," and the STEPBible proper-names index likewise suggests it may be the Foundation Gate. Its exact position within the temple and palace complex is not known, and the location shown here marks only the general temple area in Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a different Sur in Judith 2:28, a coastal place near Tyre whose site has not been identified.

Sychar was a town in Samaria where Jesus stopped on his way to Galilee and spoke with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. John 4:5, its only mention, places it near the plot of land Jacob gave to his son Joseph, a district traditionally placed just east of Shechem. Its exact identity is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Sychar as another name for Shechem itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the village of 'Askar on the lower slope of Mount Ebal, about a mile north of Jacob's well. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it a separate place east of Shechem and suggests the nearby mound of Tell Balata, which was occupied in New Testament times, noting the name may later have moved to 'Askar. The location shown here follows the view that Sychar was a separate site east of Shechem, near Jacob's well.

Syracuse was a major city on the east coast of Sicily, today the Italian city of Siracusa. Paul's ship stopped there for three days on his voyage as a prisoner to Rome (Acts 28:12). By inference from the surrounding passage, the ship had sailed from Malta, and after Syracuse it went on to Rhegium and Puteoli. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that its excellent harbor and fresh water made it a convenient stop for grain ships coming from Africa and Alexandria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes it as founded by settlers from Corinth in 734 BC on the islet of Ortygia. It became the most powerful Greek city in the western Mediterranean, withstood an Athenian siege in 414 BC, and fell to Rome in 212 BC. It then served as the capital of the Roman province of Sicily.

Syrtis was the name of dangerous shallow waters and shifting sandbanks off the north coast of Africa, long feared by sailors. The King James Version renders it "the quicksands" in Acts 27:17, while the Revised Version uses the Greek name. During Paul's voyage to Rome, a violent storm drove his ship south from Crete, and the crew feared being driven onto the Syrtis. They undergirded the hull, lowered the sail and let the ship drift. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both note that the coast had two such areas, the Greater and the Lesser Syrtis. They take the Greater Syrtis, between Tripoli and Barca near Cyrene, to be the one meant here, since the Lesser lay too far west to threaten the ship. The location shown here follows that view and places it in the Gulf of Sidra (Sirte) off modern Libya.

Taanath-shiloh was a town marking the eastern border of the territory allotted to the tribe of Ephraim. In Josh 16:6 the boundary runs from Michmethah around eastward to Taanath-shiloh, passes it on the east, and continues to Janohah. It is named only in this verse. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "approach to Shiloh," and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Taanath may have been an older Canaanite name to which Shiloh was added. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius placed a town called Thena about ten Roman miles east of Neapolis (modern Nablus) on the road to the Jordan. It identifies the site with the village of Ta'na, about 7 miles southeast of Nablus and near Yanun, the ancient Janoah. A Jewish tradition in the Talmud instead takes it to be Shiloh itself. The location shown here follows the Ta'na identification, now Khirbat Tana.

Tabbath was a city in the Jordan valley, mentioned only once in the Bible. When Gideon's three hundred men blew their trumpets and the Midianite army turned on itself, the fleeing host ran toward Beth-shittah in Zererath and to the border of Abel-meholah, "unto Tabbath" (Judg 7:22). Its place in this list suggests it marked one of the farthest points of the retreat, probably near the Jordan crossings. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south of Beth-shean near the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the ridge called Tabaqat Fahil on the eastern side of the river, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that no trace of the name has been found. The location shown here is a rough placement on the west side of the Jordan, south of Beth-shean, matching Easton's description. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "good" or "goodness."

Tabor (town) was a town in the territory of Zebulun that was given, with its surrounding pasturelands, to the Levite families descended from Merari (1 Chr 6:77). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it simply as a town of Zebulun. The parallel list of Levitical towns in Joshua 21 names different towns for Zebulun and does not mention Tabor, so its exact identity is uncertain. It is often linked with Chisloth-tabor, a place on Zebulun's border that Josh 19:12 places near Mount Tabor. The location shown here follows that identification, probably the modern village of Iksal, west of Mount Tabor in lower Galilee. Others connect the name more generally with the area around the mountain itself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "choice," "purity" or "bruising."

Tabor (Plain) was a landmark Samuel named when giving Saul directions after anointing him king. There Saul would meet three men going up to worship God at Bethel, carrying three young goats, three loaves of bread and a skin of wine (1 Sam 10:3). The King James word 'plain' translates a Hebrew term that the Revised Version, Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary render 'oak', so the place was probably a notable tree, 'the oak of Tabor'. It was on Saul's route home to Gibeah. Because the men were heading to Bethel, it was probably not far from that town. It is distinct from Mount Tabor in Galilee. Easton's suggests it may be the oak below Bethel where Rebekah's nurse Deborah was buried (Gen 35:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the site is now unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement near Bethel, north of Jerusalem.

Tadmor was a city that Solomon built "in the wilderness," listed alongside the store cities he built in Hamath (2 Chr 8:4). Its name probably means "palm tree." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify it with Palmyra, the later Greek and Roman name for a great oasis city in the Syrian desert. It sat on caravan routes between the Mediterranean and the Euphrates and is famous for its extensive Roman-era ruins. The location shown here follows that identification, in central Syria about 210 km (130 miles) northeast of Damascus. In the parallel passage, 1 Kgs 9:18, the written Hebrew text reads "Tamar," and the Bible's traditional marginal reading gives "Tadmor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this, and Easton's takes Tamar there as a separate town on Israel's southern border. This entry follows the Chronicles reading and the Palmyra identification.

Tamar is a place named among the cities Solomon built, described as "in the wilderness, in the land" (1 Kgs 9:18). The King James Version reads "Tadmor" here, but the written Hebrew text has "Tamar," a name meaning "palm" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several places in the Bible share this name, so its identity is debated. The parallel account in 2 Chr 8:4 has Solomon building Tadmor in the wilderness, which is generally taken as the oasis city later known as Palmyra in the Syrian desert. Others read the name as Tamar in the far south of Judah, near the Dead Sea, because the neighboring towns in the list (Gezer, Beth-horon, Baalath) lie in Solomon's southern territory. The location shown here follows the Tadmor identification, the site of Palmyra in central Syria.

Tappuah was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah between Engannim and Enam (Josh 15:34). The name means "apple." Several places in the Bible share this name, so the town must be told apart from others called Tappuah. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the Canaanite royal city of Josh 12:17, though that verse does not make clear which Tappuah is meant. Its site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Tristram's proposal of Artuf, near Zorah, and G. A. Smith's suggestion of Tuffuh west of Hebron. It also raises the possibility that this is the same place as Beth-tappuah (Josh 15:53), and concludes that no fully satisfactory identification has been found. The location shown here is only approximate.

Taralah was a town in the territory given to the tribe of Benjamin. It appears only once, in the list of Benjamin's cities in Josh 18:27, where it is named between Irpeel and Zelah in a group of towns that ends with Jebus, or Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "reeling." Nothing else is said about the town. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius's Onomasticon says only that it lay in Benjamin, which suggests the site was already unknown by his time, and it has not been identified since. The location shown here is a rough placement in the hill country west of Jerusalem. It is inferred from the town's place among its listed neighbours and should not be taken as a known site.

Tehaphnehes is a city in Egypt named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Egypt. There the day would be darkened when God broke 'the yokes of Egypt,' its proud strength would end, a cloud would cover it, and its 'daughters' (probably its dependent towns or its people) would go into captivity (Ezek 30:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as another spelling of Tahpanhes, the city in the eastern Nile Delta that appears in Jeremiah. There it is where Jewish refugees, Jeremiah among them, fled after the fall of Jerusalem (Jer 43:7–9). Tahpanhes is usually identified with the Greek Daphnae, the modern Tell Defenneh, a frontier site near the route between Egypt and Palestine. The location shown here follows that identification.

Tel-abib was a settlement of Jewish exiles beside the river Chebar in Babylonia. Ezekiel went there to the captives, sat among them, and stayed seven days overwhelmed before beginning his work as a prophet (Ezek 3:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as Ezekiel's place of residence. The Hebrew name is usually explained as "hill of barley-ears" or "heap of new grain." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal that it renders a Babylonian name meaning "mound of the flood," but treats this as uncertain. Its exact site is unknown. One older view placed the Chebar in upper Mesopotamia at the Khabur River. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead place it in southern Babylonia, the latter linking the Chebar to a canal near Nippur. The location shown here follows the Nippur identification and is only approximate.

Telaim was the place where Saul gathered and counted his army before attacking the Amalekites. According to 1 Sam 15:4, the muster numbered two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah. The name means "young lambs," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest it is probably the same as Telem, a town in the far south of Judah listed in Josh 15:24. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and Josephus read Gilgal instead of Telaim, and that some scholars also find the name in 1 Sam 15:7 and 1 Sam 27:8. The exact site is uncertain. The location shown here follows the Telem identification and places it roughly in the Negev south of Hebron, near Tell el-Milh. That fits a staging point for a campaign against the Amalekites, who lived in the southern desert.

Telem was a town in the far south of Judah. It appears only once, in the list of cities in the Negeb allotted to the tribe of Judah "toward the coast of Edom" (Josh 15:24), where it is named between Ziph and Bealoth. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both suggest it is probably the same place as Telaim, where Saul gathered his army before fighting the Amalekites (1 Sam 15:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the Greek Septuagint names a place Thelam in 2 Sam 3:12, possibly the same town. Its exact site is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a district called Dhullam south of Tel Malhata (el-Milh) and Aroer (Ar'arah) as a suitable match. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the northern Negev.

There, rendered in modern translations as "The Lord Is There" (Hebrew Yahweh-shammah), is the name given to the city at the very end of Ezekiel's vision of a restored land. In Ezek 48:35 the prophet gives the city's circumference as eighteen thousand measures, which the surrounding chapter describes as reeds or cubits, and declares that from that day its name will be "The LORD is there." The name marks the city as the place of God's presence, set within the redistributed tribal territories of Ezekiel's closing chapters. Ezekiel does not call this city Jerusalem in the verse, and readers have understood it either as a restored Jerusalem or as an idealized visionary city. The location shown here follows the Jerusalem identification, placing it on the site of the historic city.

Three Taverns was a stopping place on the Appian Way, the main Roman road from the south into Rome. When Paul was being taken to Rome as a prisoner, believers from the city heard he was coming and went out to meet him, some as far as Appii Forum and others at Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage (Acts 28:15). The Latin name, Tres Tabernae, means "three shops," and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as a halting place for travelers where several roads joined the Appian Way. Accounts of its distance from Rome differ. Easton's gives about 11 miles, while Smith's Bible Dictionary, working from the distances in the ancient Antonine Itinerary, places it near modern Cisterna, about 33 miles from the city. The location shown here follows the Cisterna identification. By inference from context, Paul's arrival there falls around AD 57.

Throne, called the Hall of the Throne in modern translations such as the ESV, was a hall in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem where the king sat to give judgment. 1 Kgs 7:7 says Solomon built this "porch for the throne," also called the porch of judgment, and panelled it in cedar from floor to floor. The STEPBible proper-names index treats the Hall of the Throne and the Hall of Judgment as two names for the same room. It was one of several buildings Solomon put up alongside the temple. The throne that stood there was probably the ivory-and-gold throne with six steps described in 1 Kgs 10:18–20, though the text does not say so directly. No trace of the building survives. The location shown here places it within Solomon's palace area on the hill just south of the Temple Mount.

Tiberias was a city on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, which John's Gospel also calls the Sea of Tiberias after it (John 6:1; 21:1). Its only direct mention in the Bible is John 6:23, where boats come from Tiberias to the area where Jesus had fed the crowd. Smith's Bible Dictionary, drawing on Josephus, says Herod Antipas built the city and named it after the Roman emperor Tiberius. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates its founding to about AD 16, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia to about AD 26. The city had a strong Greek and Roman character, and the Gospels never record Jesus visiting it. After the fall of Jerusalem it became a major center of Jewish learning, where the Mishnah and the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled. The modern city of Tiberias, in Israel, stands at or near the ancient site, which matches the location shown here.

Tibhath was a city belonging to Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of the Aramean kingdom of Zobah. After defeating Hadarezer, David took a great quantity of bronze from Tibhath and from Chun, another of his cities. Solomon later used this bronze to make the bronze sea, the pillars and the bronze vessels of the temple (1 Chr 18:8). The parallel account in 2 Sam 8:8 names the city Betah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary treats as the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be the Tubihi named in Egyptian records alongside Kadesh on the Orontes. It places the city on the eastern slopes of the Anti-Lebanon range, within Zobah's territory. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only approximate and places it in the region of the Beqaa Valley in modern Lebanon.

Timnah was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in Josh 15:57 alongside Cain and Gibeah as the last of a group of ten cities with their villages assigned to the tribe of Judah. Several places in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Timnah as distinct from the better-known Timnah on Judah's northern border, the town associated with Samson. Nothing else is recorded about it. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Tibna, near Jeba', and the location shown here, in the hills southwest of Bethlehem, follows that identification. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "portion", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "forbidding".

Timnath-heres was the town in the hill country of Ephraim where Joshua was buried, within the bounds of his own inheritance and on the north side of the hill Gaash (Judg 2:9). The name is usually explained as "portion of the sun." In Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 the same place is called Timnath-serah, with the letters of "heres" reversed. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that scholars differ over which form is original, that the change may have been made to avoid a name suggesting sun worship, and that Jewish and Samaritan tradition treats Heres as the original. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 10 miles southwest of Shechem. The site is uncertain. Some identify it with Khirbet Tibnah, others with the village of Kifl Haris, where Jewish and Samaritan tradition locates Joshua's tomb. The location shown here follows the Kifl Haris identification.

Tiphsah was a city on the Euphrates River that marked the northeastern limit of Solomon's dominion, with Azzah (Gaza) as the opposite limit in the southwest (1 Kgs 4:24). The name means "ford" or "crossing." Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Thapsacus, a wealthy town on the western bank of the Euphrates where the main caravan route between east and west crossed the river. The ISBE places it probably at the modern Qal'at Dibse in northern Syria, and the location shown here follows that Euphrates identification. The same name appears in 2 Kgs 15:16, where King Menahem attacks a Tiphsah. The name is shared by more than one place, and some scholars, such as Conder (noted in Easton's), connect that passage with Khurbet Tafsah near Shechem.

Tiphsah was a town attacked by Menahem king of Israel, who struck it, its people and its surrounding territory starting from Tirzah because its inhabitants would not open their gates to him. The text records that he also ripped open its pregnant women (2 Kgs 15:16). The name means "ford" or "crossing." Its location is uncertain, and the name is shared with another place. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects this Tiphsah with the Tiphsah of Solomon's northern boundary (1 Kgs 4:24), the town of Thapsacus on the Euphrates, which would make this a long campaign far from Israel. It also notes Conder's identification with Khirbet Tafsah, about 6 miles west of Shechem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts read a name close to Tirzah. The location shown here follows the Khirbet Tafsah identification near Nablus, which fits a town in the region of Tirzah.

Tishbe was the hometown of the prophet Elijah, who is called "the Tishbite" when he first appears to tell King Ahab that no dew or rain would fall except at his word (1 Kgs 17:1). The same verse says he was "of the inhabitants of Gilead." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word for "inhabitants" matches "Tishbite," so the Greek Septuagint reads "Elijah the Tishbite of Tishbi in Gilead." Its location is uncertain. Josephus places it in Gilead, east of the Jordan, and some identify it with el-Ishtib in the Gilead hills, about 22 miles south of the Sea of Galilee. Easton's prefers a Tishbi in Upper Galilee, the territory of Naphtali, mentioned in the apocryphal book of Tobit, from which Elijah would later have moved to Gilead. The location shown here follows the Upper Galilee identification.

Tochen was a town of the tribe of Simeon, listed in 1 Chr 4:32 with Etam, Ain, Rimmon and Ashan as one of a group of five cities with their villages. It is mentioned only here. The parallel list of Simeon's towns in Josh 19:7 does not include it, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint gives a name, Thokka, at that point, and infers that Tochen dropped out of the Hebrew text there. Its name is usually explained as meaning "measure" or "task" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "middle." The site has not been identified. Because Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory in the south, it probably stood in the Negev region, and the location shown here is only a rough placement.

Tolad was a town where the descendants of Simeon lived, named in a list of their settlements in 1 Chr 4:29 alongside Bilhah and Ezem. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies it with El-tolad, which appears in the parallel town lists of Joshua among the southern towns of Judah (Josh 15:30) and among the towns given to Simeon (Josh 19:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the south of Judah, since Simeon's towns lay within Judah's territory. The surrounding passage says the Simeonites held these towns until the reign of David. The exact site is unknown, and the location shown here is only approximate. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "productive," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a generation."

Tophel is a place named in Deut 1:1. It is one of several landmarks used to describe where Moses spoke to all Israel east of the Jordan, "between Paran, and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and Dizahab." The verse is the only mention of it, and none of the places listed with it has been located with certainty. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Tophel with Tafileh (et-Tafileh), a town southeast of the Dead Sea on the western side of the Edomite mountains. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it on the caravan road from Petra to Kerak, about 15 miles southeast of the Dead Sea, and notes that some linguistic difficulties make the identification uncertain. The location shown here follows the Tafileh identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ruin" or "folly."

Trachonitis was a rugged, rocky region east of the Jordan and south of Damascus. It is named only in Luke 3:1, which dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar. At that time Herod's brother Philip ruled Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis as tetrarch. The name means "stony," and both Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries link it with the Old Testament district of Argob. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient writers used the name for two volcanic lava fields. One is the inhabited el-Leja, a triangular area of broken basalt with cultivable soil inside its rough borders. The other is the barren, waterless es-Safa farther east. Easton's identifies Trachonitis with the Lejah, in present-day southern Syria. The location shown here is a general point in the surrounding area of that region.

Trogyllium was a town and promontory on the western coast of Asia Minor, where the ship carrying Paul stopped between Samos and Miletus on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 20:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as the rocky tip of the Mycale ridge, directly opposite the island of Samos, with a nearby anchorage still called St. Paul's port. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the strait between the promontory and Samos is barely a mile wide, and that several early manuscripts lack the words "tarried at Trogyllium." Even so, the ship would have passed the promontory and probably stopped there. The voyage took place about AD 54, a date inferred from context. The location shown here is on the mainland coast facing Samos, in present-day western Turkey.

Ummah was a city in the territory given to the tribe of Asher, listed near the end of Asher's boundary description along with Aphek and Rehob (Josh 19:30). It is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Its location is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably 'Alma, in the coastal highlands about five miles east-northeast of Ras en-Nakhura. This entry follows that identification, placing it at the modern village of Alma el Shaab in southern Lebanon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another view: a slight change to the Hebrew text would make the name read Acco, the coastal city later called Ptolemais, modern Akko. It treats this as a conjecture that many scholars nonetheless accept. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "vicinity", while Smith's gives "union".

Upper Beth-horon was a town on the southern boundary of the tribe of Ephraim. Joshua 16:5 traces Ephraim's border on the east side from Ataroth-addar to "Bethhoron the upper." Its name implies a companion town lower down the slope. Connected passages mention Lower Beth-horon on the same border (Josh 16:3) and record that Sheerah, a descendant of Ephraim, built both towns (1 Chr 7:24). Solomon later fortified both towns (2 Chr 8:5). The two towns stood along the ascent from the coastal lowlands into the hill country, on the route that runs northwest of Jerusalem. Upper Beth-horon is probably the modern village of Beit Ur al-Fauqa, and the location shown here lies in that area.

Uzzen-sheerah was a town built by Sheerah, a woman of the tribe of Ephraim, who also built Lower and Upper Beth-horon (1 Chr 7:24). The verse calls her "his daughter." By inference from the surrounding genealogy, Easton's Bible Dictionary takes her to be Ephraim's daughter. The town's name appears to include hers, and it probably stood near the two Beth-horons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads the phrase not as a place name but as "and the sons of Ozan, Sheera," and that no satisfactory identification had been proposed. Some identify the site with the village of Beit Sira, a few miles west of Beth-horon, partly because the names sound alike. The location shown here follows the Beit Sira identification.

The Vale of Hebron ("Valley of Hebron" in modern versions) was the valley around the town of Hebron, in the hill country of southern Judah. It is named only once, in Gen 37:14, where Jacob sends his son Joseph out from this valley to check on his brothers and the flocks. Joseph then travels north to Shechem, and from there to Dothan, where his brothers sell him. By inference from the passage and from earlier chapters of Genesis, which place Abraham and Isaac near Hebron and Mamre, this valley was where Jacob's family was living at the time. The location shown here marks the general area surrounding Hebron rather than a precise spot, since the text does not say which of the valleys near the town is meant. Hebron is identified with the present-day city of Hebron (al-Khalil) in the West Bank.

The Valley of Aijalon is the valley named in Joshua's command during the battle in which the LORD gave the Amorites over to Israel: "Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon" (Josh 10:12). It is the only verse that names the valley itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the town of Aijalon, which was assigned to Dan, later given to the Levites, and lay near the border between Judah and Israel. Easton's identifies the town with modern Yalo, at the foot of the Beth-horon pass. By inference, the valley is the broad lowland west of Gibeon through which the fleeing Amorites would have passed on their way down from the hill country. The location shown here places it in that lowland, near Yalo.

The Valley of Baca is a valley mentioned only in Ps 84:6, a psalm about longing for God's house. It describes travelers who pass through the valley and make it a place of springs, while rain fills the pools. The Hebrew name is usually connected either with weeping or with a kind of balsam tree that grows in dry ground, so the Revised Version renders it "valley of weeping" with "balsam trees" in the margin. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests three possibilities: an actual valley somewhere in Palestine, any one of the valleys pilgrims crossed on their way to the sanctuary on Zion, or a figurative "valley of weeping." Its exact location is uncertain. The location shown here places it just outside Jerusalem, following the view that it was a real valley on the pilgrims' approach to the city.

The Valley of Beracah was a valley in Judah where King Jehoshaphat and his people gathered on the fourth day after their enemies were destroyed, and there they blessed the LORD. The place was named for that act, since Beracah means "blessing," and the name was still in use when Chronicles was written. By inference from the surrounding chapter, the gathering followed the defeat of the Moabites, Ammonites and people of Mount Seir, who turned on one another, and three days spent collecting the spoil. Judah's army had set out into the wilderness of Tekoa (2 Chr 20:20), so the valley probably lay in that region. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it not far from Engedi and identifies it with the valley of Bereikut. The location shown here follows that identification, at a site between Bethlehem and Hebron near Tekoa.

The Valley of Gerar was the valley near the city of Gerar where Isaac camped and lived after leaving the city itself (Gen 26:17). In the surrounding passage, Abimelech, king of the Philistines at Gerar, had asked Isaac to move away because he had grown too powerful. In this valley Isaac then reopened wells his father Abraham had dug and dug new ones, which led to disputes with the local herdsmen. The valley was probably a seasonal stream bed (a wadi) with groundwater suitable for wells and pasture. Gerar lay in the western Negev, between Gaza and Beersheba, but its exact site is debated. Proposals include Tel Haror (Tell Abu Hureira) and Tell Jemmeh. The location shown here lies along the stream valley now usually called Nahal Gerar (Wadi esh-Sheria), probably the valley meant in the text.

The Valley of Gibeon was the low ground around the town of Gibeon, north of Jerusalem. It is named only in Isa 28:21, where the prophet warns that the LORD will rise up in anger as he did at Mount Perazim and in the valley of Gibeon, to do his "strange work" against his own people. The verse recalls a well-known past victory, and two connected passages are possible references. Mount Perazim points to David's defeat of the Philistines at Baal-perazim (2 Sam 5:20), and the parallel account of his second victory says he struck them from Gibeon to Gezer (1 Chr 14:16). Others connect it with Joshua's victory at Gibeon, when the sun stood still (Josh 10:10–14). The site is not described further. The location shown here is the area around Gibeon, generally identified with the modern village of al-Jib.

The Valley of Jericho was the lowland surrounding the city of Jericho, which Deut 34:3 calls "the city of palm trees." It appears once, in the account of Moses viewing the promised land from Mount Nebo just before his death. As he looked out, the Lord showed him the south and "the plain of the valley of Jericho" stretching as far as Zoar. By inference from the setting, this is the broad, low-lying part of the Jordan Valley on the west side of the river, just north of the Dead Sea. Mount Nebo stood opposite it across the Jordan. The location shown here is the area around ancient Jericho, near the modern town of Jericho in the lower Jordan Valley. The verse does not mark the valley's exact limits.

The Valley of Mizpeh was a valley in the far north of Canaan, named in Joshua 11:8 as one of the places to which Israel chased the northern kings after defeating them at the waters of Merom. The pursuit went in several directions: northwest to Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward to the valley of Mizpeh. The verse gives no further detail. Because Josh 11:3 places Hivites "under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh," the valley is probably the same region, lying below Mount Hermon. Its exact site is uncertain. Some place it in the Marj Ayun (the biblical Ijon area) in southern Lebanon, and others in the valleys running along the western foot of Hermon. The location shown here lies near the northern end of the Hula Valley, close to modern Metula, which fits a placement just south of Marj Ayun.

The Valley of Shaveh was the place where the king of Sodom went out to meet Abram as he returned from defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings allied with him (Gen 14:17). The text identifies it with the "king's dale," which is probably the same King's Dale where Absalom later set up a pillar for himself (2 Sam 18:18). The next verse says Melchizedek, king of Salem, also met Abram, which suggests the valley lay near Salem, usually taken to be Jerusalem. Its exact site is uncertain. A common view places it in or near the Kidron Valley just east of Jerusalem, and the rough location shown here follows that identification near the city. It is distinct from Shaveh-kiriathaim (Gen 14:5), a similar name for a different place east of the Jordan.

The Valley of Shittim is a valley named only once in the Bible, in Joel's prophecy of a future day when a fountain will flow from the house of the Lord and water it (Joel 3:18). The name means "valley of acacias." Acacias grow in dry ground, so the image is probably of water reaching a parched place. Its location is uncertain. Some link it with Shittim, the camp of Israel on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan, across from Jericho, where Israel stayed before entering Canaan (Num 25:1; Josh 2:1). Others take it as a dry valley running from the Jerusalem area down toward the Dead Sea, such as the Kidron, or as a symbolic name for any arid valley. The location shown here follows the association with Shittim on the plains of Moab, northeast of the Dead Sea.

The Valley of Sorek was the valley where Delilah lived, the woman Samson loved after his exploits at Gaza (Judg 16:4). The name probably means "choice vine," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, which suggests the valley was known for its vineyards. It is generally identified with the modern Wadi es-Sarar (Wadi Surar), a seasonal stream bed that drains the western Judean hills and runs northwest toward the Mediterranean. Easton's places its mouth about eight miles south of Joppa and traces its course past Makkedah and Jabneel. The location shown here lies in the lowlands west of the hill country, near the old border between Judah and Philistine territory. That setting fits the story, in which the Philistine rulers approach Delilah, though the text itself does not say whether she was a Philistine.

The Valley of the Passengers (ESV "Valley of the Travelers") is a valley named in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog as the place where Gog and all his multitude would be buried. It is described as lying "in Israel… on the east of the sea," and the passage says it would "stop the noses of the passengers," probably meaning that the dead would block or overwhelm those travelling through. It would then be renamed the Valley of Hamon-gog, meaning "the multitude of Gog" (Ezek 39:11). Its location is uncertain. "The sea" is usually taken to be the Dead Sea, and some interpreters connect the Hebrew word for "passengers" with the Abarim mountains east of it. Others place the valley on a route east of the Mediterranean or the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows the view that it lay east of the Dead Sea, in the region of Moab.

The Valley of Zeboim was a valley in the territory of Benjamin. It is mentioned only in 1 Sam 13:18. During Saul's war with the Philistines, raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp at Michmash. One went toward Bethhoron, and another took the road along the border that overlooked the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness. The wilderness there is probably the barren country sloping down to the Jordan Valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it near Gibeah and identifies it with a ravine north of Jericho called Wady Shakh-ed-Dub'a, meaning "ravine of the hyena." The location shown here follows the identification with Wadi ed Dubba, in the hills east of Michmash toward Jericho. This valley is a different place from Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain near Sodom, although the two names look alike in English.

The Valley of Zephathah was a valley at Mareshah in the lowland of Judah, where King Asa drew up his army against Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chr 14:10). By inference from the surrounding passage, Asa defeated Zerah's large force there and pursued it as far as Gerar. Mareshah is generally identified with Tel Maresha, near modern Beit Guvrin, so the valley was probably one of the broad wadis running through the low hills near that town. The exact valley is uncertain. The Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "the valley north of Mareshah" instead of giving a place name, and some have connected the name with the Wadi es-Safiyeh in the same district. The location shown here places the valley just north of Mareshah, which fits both readings.

The Valley of Zered was a valley or stream course east of the southern end of the Dead Sea where the Israelites camped during their wilderness journey, after leaving the border of Moab and before moving on to the Arnon (Num 21:12). The KJV spells it "Zared." Deut 2:13–14 calls it the brook Zered and marks its crossing as the end of thirty-eight years of wandering. Lying between Edom and Moab, it probably formed a boundary between the two, by inference from these passages. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the "brook of the willows" (Isa 15:7) and the "river of the wilderness" (Amos 6:14), and names Wady el-Aksy as one identification. It is more commonly identified with the Wadi al-Hasa in modern Jordan, which flows into the southeastern Dead Sea. The location shown here follows the Wadi al-Hasa identification.

Waheb is a place named in a short poem that Num 21:14 quotes from the Book of the Wars of the LORD, a lost collection of songs. The Hebrew text reads something like "Waheb in Suphah, and the brooks of Arnon." The King James Version does not show Waheb as a name. It renders the line as "What he did in the Red sea," reading the Hebrew as a verb and taking Suphah as the Red Sea. Many modern translations instead treat Waheb as a place name. Because the poem goes on to the Arnon valleys, Waheb was probably a site near the Arnon, on the border of Moab, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) places it possibly in Moab. Its exact location is unknown. The location shown here is rough and follows the reading that links the line with the Red Sea.

The Way of Holiness is the name Isaiah gives to a highway he foresees in the prophecy of Isa 35. In his description it is a road on which the unclean will not travel. It is meant for those who walk it, and even the simple will not lose their way on it (Isa 35:8). The surrounding chapter pictures the desert blooming and the redeemed returning to Zion with singing, so the highway is a road leading back to Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index describes it as a prophesied highway reserved for the redeemed and leading to Zion. It is a road in a prophetic vision, not a known physical route. The location shown here is only a rough placement at Jerusalem, its destination, and does not mark an actual road.

Willows, or the Brook of the Willows, was a stream named in Isaiah's lament over Moab. Isaiah pictures the Moabites, fleeing disaster, carrying the wealth they had stored up away across this brook (Isa 15:7). The name probably comes from the willows or poplars that grew along watercourses in the region. The text does not say where it was. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it on Moab's southern boundary and calls it Wady el-Aksa. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as a stream running from Moab to the Jordan or the Dead Sea and notes that it is generally identified with the brook Zered, probably the modern Wadi al-Hasa. STEPBible's proper-names list also treats it as a boundary of Moab, possibly near the Zered. The location shown here is only a rough placement on the east side of the Jordan Valley, so the brook's exact site remains uncertain.

Yiron was a fortified town in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, spelled "Iron" in the King James Version. It appears only once, in the list of cities given to Naphtali when the land was divided among the tribes (Josh 19:38). It is named alongside Migdalel, Horem, Beth-anath and Beth-shemesh, near the end of a list that totals nineteen cities with their villages. Nothing else is recorded about it. The site is generally identified with the modern village of Yaroun in southern Lebanon, close to the present border with Israel, and the location shown here follows that identification. STEPBible's proper-names index, from Tyndale House, likewise treats it as a Naphtali town known only from this allotment list.

Zaanan was a town of Judah named only once in the Bible, in Micah's lament over the towns of the Shephelah, the low hill country west of Jerusalem (Mic 1:11). Micah says that the inhabitant of Zaanan "came not forth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is wordplay: the town's name sounds like the Hebrew verb for "to go forth," so the people of a town whose name suggests going out stay shut in. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "place of flocks." Both Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest it is probably the same place as Zenan, a town in the lowland of Judah listed in Josh 15:37. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Judean Shephelah, consistent with that identification.

Zair was a place mentioned only in 2 Kgs 8:21, where King Joram of Judah went with all his chariots during a campaign against the Edomites, who had revolted from Judah's rule. Surrounded by the Edomites, he attacked by night and struck them and their chariot commanders, and the people fled to their tents. The name probably means "little." The parallel account in 2 Chr 21:9 has "with his princes" in place of "to Zair," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a copying variant of the same words. The site has not been firmly identified. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably east of the Dead Sea. Other suggestions link it with Mount Seir, with the town of Zoar (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or with ez-Zuweirah near the southern Dead Sea (Conder). The location shown here puts it just south of the Dead Sea, on a likely route into Edom.

Zalmon was a hill or mountain near Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim. It appears in Ps 68:14, where the King James Version spells it "Salmon": when the Almighty scattered kings, it was "white as snow in Salmon." The meaning of this verse is difficult. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the scattered kings are pictured like snowflakes blown across the mountain in winter. The same mountain appears in Judg 9:48, where Abimelech and his men cut branches on Mount Zalmon and used them to set fire to the stronghold of Shechem. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the southern peak of Mount Gerizim, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Mount Ebal, whose Arabic name may echo Zalmon. The location shown here follows the Mount Ebal identification.

Zanoah was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Jezreel and Jokdeam among the cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:56). The name was also used for another Zanoah in Judah's western lowland, so the two should be kept distinct. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this hill-country town with 1 Chr 4:18, where Jekuthiel is called the "father" (probably the founder) of Zanoah. It identifies the site with Zanuta (Zenuta), a ruin on a hill about 12 miles south of Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it about 10 miles southwest of Hebron. The location shown here follows the Zanuta identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "forgetfulness" or "desertion."

Zeboim was a town resettled by people of the tribe of Benjamin after the return from the Babylonian exile. It appears only once, in a list of settlements in Neh 11:34, between Hadid and Neballat. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as inhabited by Benjamites after the Captivity. Its location is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons that, because it is listed beside Hadid and Neballat, it lay in the coastal lowland near Lydda (modern Lod), and it notes that the site is lost. The location shown here is instead near the southern end of the Dead Sea, the region associated with the similarly named Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain mentioned with Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis. This entry follows that Dead Sea placement, though the two names may refer to different places.

Zelzah was a place named only once in the Bible, where Samuel told Saul he would meet two men by Rachel's tomb on the border of Benjamin. They would tell him that his father's lost donkeys had been found and that his father was now worried about him (1 Sam 10:2). Nothing else is said about it, and no similar name has been found in the region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the phrase as "leaping greatly" rather than as a place-name, and that the Hebrew text may be damaged. Its location depends on where Rachel's tomb stood. Gen 35:19 places the tomb near Bethlehem, while Saul's route here may suggest a site farther north. The location shown here follows Smith's Bible Dictionary, placing Zelzah near the traditional tomb south of Jerusalem. The name has been explained as meaning "shadow" (Smith's) or "noontide" (Hitchcock's).

Zemaraim was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Benjamin. It is listed in Josh 18:22 between Beth-arabah and Bethel, in the group of Benjamin's eastern towns near the Jordan valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the ruins of es-Samra, about 4 miles (6 km) north of Jericho, and the location shown here follows that identification. Others, noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, think it lay closer to Bethel, perhaps south of that town. Smith's Bible Dictionary and other works connect the town with Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim. According to 2 Chr 13:4, King Abijah of Judah stood on that mountain to speak to Jeroboam's army. The hill probably took its name from the town and lay nearby. The name is often explained as meaning "double fleece" or "wool."

Zenan was a town in the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It is named only once, in the list of towns of the Shephelah, the lowland hill country between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain. There it appears in a group of sixteen towns alongside Hadashah and Migdal-gad (Josh 15:37). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat it as probably the same place as Zaanan, mentioned in Mic 1:11 among towns of the same region. Its exact site is unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement within the western Judean lowlands, near the other towns of its group. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "coldness," "target" or "weapon."

Zephath was a Canaanite city in the south of the land. According to Judg 1:17, the tribes of Judah and Simeon fought together, killed its Canaanite inhabitants, destroyed the city completely, and renamed it Hormah. The new name probably plays on the Hebrew idea of something devoted to destruction, and Hormah also appears in earlier wilderness accounts such as Num 21:3. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of the name Zephath as "watchtower" or "beacon." Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions an identification with the pass of es-Sufah but prefers S'beita, the ancient town of Shivta in the Negev desert of southern Israel. The location shown here follows the S'beita identification.

Zer was a fortified city in the territory given to the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned only once, in the list of Naphtali's fenced cities in Josh 19:35, where it is named between Ziddim and Hammath, alongside Rakkath and Chinnereth. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "flint", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perplexity." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads this verse differently, as "the fortified cities of the Tyrians," which reflects a Hebrew wording that does not contain the name Zer. The site has not been identified. Because it is listed with Hammath and Chinnereth, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place it near the western or southwestern side of the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here is only a rough placement within Naphtali's hill country in Galilee, and it lies to the north and west of that lakeside area.

Zeredah (spelled Zereda in the King James Version) was the hometown of Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite and an official of Solomon who rebelled against the king (1 Kgs 11:26). Jeroboam later became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. The verse calls him an Ephrathite, which here means a man of the tribe of Ephraim, so the town probably lay in the hill country of Ephraim. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it in the north of Mount Ephraim and suggests it may be the same place as Zaretan, Zererath or Zartanah, which are mentioned elsewhere near the Jordan Valley. The name is similar to that of other biblical places, and its exact site is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the central hill country, near Shechem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "ambush," and Easton's renders it "the fortress."

Zeredah, spelled Zeredathah in the King James text of 2 Chr 4:17, was a place in the Jordan plain. King Solomon had the bronze furnishings of the temple cast in the clay ground between Succoth and this town. The parallel account in 1 Kgs 7:46 names the place Zarthan (Zarethan), and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two names as the same site. It adds that Solomon set up the foundries here where Hiram made the great bronze castings. The same name is also used for other places, most notably Zeredah in Ephraim, the home town of Jeroboam (1 Kgs 11:26). That town is a separate place from this one in the Jordan valley. The location shown here is in the Jordan valley near Succoth, probably at the modern Tell es-Sa'idiyeh east of the river. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ambush" or "change of dominion."

Zererah (spelled Zererath in the King James Version) was a place or district in the Jordan Valley. It is mentioned only in Judg 7:22, where the Midianite army, thrown into confusion by Gideon's three hundred men, fled toward Beth-shittah "in Zererath" and on toward the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath. Its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the same as Zereda or Zeredathah. Zeredathah in 2 Chr 4:17 corresponds to Zarethan in the parallel 1 Kgs 7:46, a site near the Jordan. Easton's also notes that some identify it with Zahrah, about 3 miles west of Beth-shean. The location shown here lies in the central Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean, near the river. That fits the link with Zeredathah and Zarethan, and it fits the Midianites' flight eastward toward the Jordan.

Zereth-shahar was a town given to the tribe of Reuben, east of the Dead Sea. It is mentioned only once, in the list of Reuben's cities, where it is named with Kiriathaim and Sibmah and placed "in the mount of the valley" (Josh 13:19). The STEPBible Proper Names take this to mean a mountain or height in the plain beside the Dead Sea. The name is usually understood to mean "splendor of the dawn." Its exact site is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the ancient name may survive at the hot springs near Machaerus, on the eastern shore, but holds that no firm identification is possible. The location shown here follows that general area, near the hot springs at ez-Zara (ancient Callirrhoe) on the east coast of the Dead Sea.

Ziddim was a fortified city in the tribal territory of Naphtali, listed first among that tribe's "fenced cities" alongside Zer, Hammath, Rakkath and Chinnereth (Josh 19:35). It is mentioned only in this allotment list, so nothing more is known of its history. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sides", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "the declivities". Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with Kefr Hattin (Hattin), about 5 miles west or northwest of Tiberias, near the slopes of the Horns of Hattin above the Sea of Galilee. The location shown here follows that identification. Its listing beside Chinnereth and Rakkath fits a site in the region west of the lake.

Zimri was a people or country whose kings appear in Jeremiah's list of nations made to drink the cup of God's wrath. It is named alongside Elam and the Medes (Jer 25:25), right after the kings of Arabia and the "mingled people" of the desert. Nothing else is known about it, and its location has not been identified. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest the name may be connected with Zimran, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:2), whose descendants probably lived in Arabia. That would link Zimri with the Arabian peoples in the preceding verse. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southwestern Iran, near ancient Elam, which reflects its pairing with Elam and the Medes in the same verse.

Zior was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once in the Bible in the list of cities given to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:54). It appears as the last of a group of nine cities with their villages that also includes Hebron, so it probably lay in the same district near Hebron. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "littleness," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "smallness." Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the modern village of Si'air, about 4.5 miles north-northeast of Hebron. The encyclopedia describes it as a sizable village with farmland, a nearby spring, and rock-cut tombs that point to an ancient settlement. The location shown here follows the Si'air identification.

Ziph was a town in the far south of Judah, in the Negev, listed among the cities given to the tribe of Judah near the border of Edom. It is named between Ithnan and Telem in Josh 15:24 and does not appear again in the biblical narrative. It is distinct from the better-known Ziph in the hill country of Judah, near Hebron, where David hid from Saul. The name is shared by several places, so care is needed in telling them apart. The site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably at the pass of Sufah, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regard its location as unknown. The location shown here is only a rough placement in the Negev, consistent with its listing among Judah's southern towns.

Ziphron was a place named on the northern border of the land promised to Israel, listed in Num 34:9 just before Hazar-enan, where that border ended. The verse gives no further detail, so its exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it south-east of Hamath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as the same place as Sibraim, which appears in Ezekiel's description of Israel's northern border. The location shown here is a rough placement in the Syrian interior east of Homs, matching the general idea that the border ran eastward from the Hamath region toward the desert. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "sweet odour." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "falsehood of a song" or "rejoicing."

Ziz was the ascent or cliff, called the "cliff of Ziz" in the King James Version, by which the invading armies of Moab, Ammon and their allies climbed toward Judah in the time of King Jehoshaphat. In 2 Chr 20:16 the people of Judah are told to go down against the enemy the next day and to find them at the end of the valley, before the wilderness of Jeruel. From the surrounding chapter, the invaders had gathered at Hazazon-tamar, identified with En-gedi, so Ziz was probably a pass leading up from the Dead Sea shore toward Tekoa. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as the En-gedi pass itself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name with the Wadi Hasasa (Easton's Bible Dictionary gives Tell Hasasah), north of En-gedi. The location shown here follows that Wadi Hasasa identification.

Zobah-Hamath is the area named in 1 Chr 18:3, where David defeated Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of Zobah, "unto Hamath" while he was going to establish his rule by the Euphrates. The phrase probably describes the stretch of Aramean territory reaching from the kingdom of Zobah north toward Hamath, the city usually identified with modern Hama on the Orontes River in Syria. Zobah itself is generally placed in the region north of Damascus, around the Beqaa Valley, though its exact extent is uncertain. The location shown here is an approximate point in central Syria, south-east of Homs, representing the surrounding region rather than a specific town. A similar name, Hamath-zobah, appears in 2 Chr 8:3 as a place Solomon captured. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls it a fortress of Zobah and notes that some take it to be distinct from Hamath, though this is uncertain.

Zophim, or "the field of Zophim," was a place at the top of Pisgah in Moab. Its name means "field of watchers" or "lookouts," which suggests a high vantage point. King Balak of Moab brought the prophet Balaam there and built seven altars, offering a bull and a ram on each, in the hope that Balaam would curse Israel from that spot (Num 23:14). From the surrounding passage, it was Balaam's second viewpoint over the Israelite camp, and in place of a curse he again spoke a blessing. The exact site is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Tal'at es-Safa, an ascent leading up to the ridge of Mount Nebo from the north. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be the place later called Mizpah of Moab. The location shown here is on the Pisgah–Nebo ridge, east of the northern end of the Dead Sea in present-day Jordan.

Zuph was the district Saul and his servant reached while searching for his father's lost donkeys. There Saul proposed turning back so his father would not start worrying about them instead (1 Sam 9:5). The next verse shows that a town in this district held the seer Samuel, and Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with Samuel's city, Ramah. Easton's suggests the region was named after Zuph, an ancestor of Samuel's father Elkanah (1 Chr 6:35; compare 1 Sam 1:1, where Elkanah is from Ramathaim-zophim). Its exact extent is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in Benjamin near its northern border, Tyndale House's proper-names index places it in Ephraim, and Smith's Bible Dictionary tentatively links it with Soba, west of Jerusalem. The location shown here is a rough one in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, near the area traditionally associated with Samuel's Ramah.

Aram-naharaim, meaning "Aram of the two rivers," is the Hebrew name for the region of upper Mesopotamia, the land between the Euphrates on the west and the Tigris on the east. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the King James Version translates it as "Mesopotamia," as in Gen 24:10, where Abraham's servant travels there to find a wife for Isaac. The name also appears in the title of Ps 60. Easton's Bible Dictionary links it with the "field of Aram" (Hos 12:12, Revised Version), meaning the open country of Aram, and treats Padan-aram, the home of Abraham's relatives, as one part of it. The location shown here is an approximate point in northern Mesopotamia, in what is now northeastern Syria and northern Iraq. It stands for a broad region, not a single site.

Aram-zobah was an Aramean region named in the heading of Psalm 60, which places the psalm at the time when David fought "Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah" and Joab struck down Edomites in the Valley of Salt. It is probably the same as the kingdom of Zobah. Other passages, such as 2 Sam 8:3 and 1 Sam 14:47, describe Zobah as an Aramean state whose king Hadadezer fought David. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it probably in the region between the Euphrates and the Orontes, in what is now Syria. Its exact extent is uncertain. The location shown here is only a rough placement in southern Syria near Damascus, and it does not mark a known site.

Ashdod's is a possessive form of Ashdod, a Philistine city near the Mediterranean coast, roughly midway between Gaza and Joppa. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as one of the chief centers of the worship of Dagon (1 Sam 5:5). It was assigned to the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:47), but Easton's notes that Judah never actually held it. Because it stood on the main road from Egypt into Palestine, it was strongly fortified. King Uzziah of Judah broke down its walls (2 Chr 26:6), and it was later taken by the Assyrians, with Sargon's capture of it mentioned in Isa 20:1. In the New Testament it appears under the Greek name Azotus, where Philip was found after leaving Gaza (Acts 8:40). Easton's identifies it with the village of Eshdud, and the location shown here follows that identification, at the ancient mound a few miles inland from the modern city of Ashdod.

Benjamin's Gate was a gate of ancient Jerusalem, probably on the northern or northeastern side of the city. Its name most likely comes from the road it opened onto, which led north into the tribal territory of Benjamin. The KJV uses the form "Benjamin's gate" in Zech 14:10, where it marks one boundary point of Jerusalem in a prophecy of the city's future. Under the name "gate of Benjamin" it appears in Jeremiah's time. There Jeremiah was arrested at it while trying to leave the city (Jer 37:13), and King Zedekiah was sitting in it when Ebed-melech appealed for the prophet (Jer 38:7). Jer 20:2 mentions a "high gate of Benjamin" by the temple. Some identify it with the Sheep Gate or another northern gate, but its exact position is uncertain. The location shown here places it on the northeastern side of the city, near the temple area.

Egypt's is the possessive form of Egypt, the land along the Nile River in northeastern Africa, used where something is described as belonging to Egypt, such as its rulers, people, or goods. No verses are supplied for this entry, so its exact contexts cannot be described here. By inference from the name, it refers to the same country that appears throughout the Bible as a major neighbour of Israel, a place of refuge and of bondage, and a regional power. The location shown here is a point near modern Cairo, in the area of ancient Heliopolis (biblical On). It stands for the country as a whole rather than a single town.

Ham, as a place name, here refers to Egypt, called "the land of Ham" in several psalms recalling the exodus (Ps 78:51; Ps 105:23, 27; Ps 106:22). The name comes from Noah's son Ham, whose descendants in Gen 10:6 include Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "hot" or "heat," and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes a link with an Egyptian word meaning "black." Several places share this name. Another Ham appears in Gen 14:5 as the home of the Zuzims, east of the Jordan, and is usually treated as a separate town. The location shown here is in the Nile Delta near modern Cairo, which places it in Egypt rather than at the town east of the Jordan. No verses are attached to this entry, so this identification rests on the coordinates and on those connected passages.

Jaar is a possible place name in Ps 132:6. The Hebrew word means "forest" or "wood," and the King James Version translates it that way: "we found it in the fields of the wood." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, this is the only verse where it may be a proper name, and the Revised Version margin reads "the field of Jaar." The psalm recalls the search for a dwelling place for the Lord, so "it" probably refers to the ark of the covenant. On that reading, the same encyclopedia suggests Jaar may be a shortened form of Kiriath-jearim ("town of forests"), where the ark stayed for about twenty years before David brought it to Jerusalem. The rough location shown here puts it in the hills west of Jerusalem, in the general area of Kiriath-jearim. Whether the word is a place name at all is uncertain.

Jerusalem's is the possessive form of Jerusalem, the hill city in the Judean highlands that became the capital of Israel and the site of the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that it was also called Salem, Jebus, Ariel and "the holy city." It is first mentioned as Salem in Gen 14:18, and later as Jerusalem under its king Adonizedek in Josh 10:1. David captured it from the Jebusites and made it his capital, Solomon built the temple there, and after the kingdom divided it served as the capital of Judah. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon destroyed it, it was rebuilt after the exile under Cyrus, as described in Ezra and Nehemiah, and the Romans destroyed it again in AD 70. The location shown here is the Old City of present-day Jerusalem. No verses are attached to this particular form of the name.

Samaria's refers to the city of Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, here under a possessive form of its name. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as built by King Omri on a solitary hill a few miles northwest of Shechem, which he bought from Shemer for two talents of silver and made his capital in place of Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:24). The same dictionary recounts sieges by Ben-hadad of Syria in the days of Ahab and Jehoram, and a three-year Assyrian siege that ended with the city's capture and the deportation of Israel's tribes (2 Kgs 17:3; 18:9–12). Herod the Great later rebuilt it as Sebaste, and Philip preached there (Acts 8:5). The location shown here is the hill at the modern village of Sebastia, the site Easton's identifies as ancient Samaria. No verses were supplied for this particular form of the name.

Zion's is the possessive form of Zion, used in phrases such as "for Zion's sake" (Isa 62:1). Zion was one of the hills on which Jerusalem was built. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes it as the south-eastern hill, which David captured from the Jebusites and where he built a citadel and palace, so that it became known as "the city of David" (2 Sam 5:7; 1 Chr 11:5). In later Old Testament books the name often stands for Jerusalem as a whole, and sometimes for the people of Israel (Ps 87:2; Ps 51:18). In the New Testament it can refer to the people of God or to the heavenly city (Heb 12:22; Rev 14:1). Later tradition gave the name "Mount Zion" to Jerusalem's south-western hill. The location shown here follows the eastern identification and lies on the ridge near the Temple Mount and the City of David.
